ignored: A stray letter or abbreviation, here the C in °C (Celsius).

etymology: Borrowed from English CD.

senses.note: Pronounced 'ci-di'. Invariable: i CD.

ignored: A stray letter or abbreviation, here part of the acronym P.D.O.
A stray letter or abbreviation (N for nord), not a flashcard word.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English OK.

senses.note: Very common in speech. Native alternatives: va bene, d'accordo.

ignored: A stray abbreviation (S = sud) pulled from a garbled context, not a real flashcard word.

senses.note: Abbreviation of sud.
Usually written l'SMS (said esse-emme-esse), plural gli SMS. Also called messaggio or messaggino.

ignored: A single-letter chess abbreviation (for torre), not a vocabulary word; the contexts are unrelated noise.

senses.note: Abbreviation of torre in chess notation.
Said 'tivù' and sometimes written that way. It is feminine because it's short for la televisione. It doesn't change in the plural.

etymology: From Latin ad. In a few phrases, a stems from Latin ā, ab.

fact.text: It comes from Latin ad, which shares an ancient root with English 'at'. That's why a covers both 'to' and 'at': a casa means 'at home' and also '(to) home'.

senses.note: Merges with the article: al, allo, alla, ai… Used with cities: a Milano. Often ad before a vowel.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French abandoner.

fact.text: Comes from Old French 'a bandon', 'under someone's control'. Ban, an order or jurisdiction, is Frankish. To abandon something was to hand it over to another's power.

senses.note: Reflexive abbandonarsi a = to give in to (e.g. abbandonarsi ai ricordi).

etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.
ignored: This is just abbandonare with the pronoun mi attached; study it on the abbandonare card.

senses.note: abbandonare + mi; 'Non abbandonarmi' = Don't leave me.

etymology: From a- + basso (“low”) + -are.

fact.text: Built from a- + basso ('low') + -are, so literally 'to make low'. English 'bass', the lowest singing voice, took its spelling from Italian basso.

senses.note: Abbassa la voce! = Keep your voice down! Also used for turning down volume.

etymology: Univerbation of a + bastanza (“sufficience”), from the verb bastare (“to suffice”). Cognate with Spanish bastante.

fact.text: Built from a + bastanza 'sufficiency', from the verb bastare 'to be enough'. It's the same root as the everyday exclamation Basta! meaning 'Enough!'

senses.note: Before an adjective it can also mean 'quite, fairly': abbastanza bravo.

etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from French habillement.

fact.text: Borrowed from French habillement, 'clothing', which is related to habiller, 'to dress'.

senses.note: Usually singular and collective. Negozio di abbigliamento = clothes shop. Single garments are 'vestiti'.

etymology: From abbonare + -mento.

senses.note: Also a season ticket or travel pass, e.g. abbonamento mensile = monthly pass.
Note the double b. un chilo abbondante = a good kilo (slightly over).

etymology: From a- + braccio (“arm”) + -are, possibly corresponding to a Vulgar Latin *adbracchiāre, from Latin ad- + bracchium + -o. Compare Spanish abrazar.

fact.text: Built from braccio, 'arm': it literally means to take someone into your arms. English 'embrace' works the same way, from French bras, 'arm'.

senses.note: Reciprocal: abbracciarsi = to hug each other. Noun: un abbraccio = a hug.

etymology: Deverbal from abbracciare (“to embrace, hug”) + -o.

fact.text: Contains braccio (arm), so a hug is literally taking someone into your arms. English embrace comes from the same Latin word for arm, bracchium.

senses.note: 'Un abbraccio' is a common warm sign-off in messages and letters.

etymology: From Latin habilis.

fact.text: Comes from Latin habilis ('easy to handle, fit'), from habere 'to have'. English able and ability come from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Also means 'fit', e.g. abile al servizio militare (fit for military service).

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin habilitātem.

senses.note: Invariable: l'abilità, le abilità.

etymology: From abit(are) + -ante.

senses.note: Same form for men and women: l'abitante, gli/le abitanti.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin habitāre (frequentative of habeō).

fact.text: From Latin habitare, 'to dwell', which comes from habere, 'to have'. English 'inhabit', 'habitat' and 'inhabitant' come from the same root.

senses.note: For where you live: abito a Roma, abito in via Verdi. For being alive, use vivere.

etymology: From Latin habitātiōnem.

senses.note: Formal or bureaucratic. In everyday speech, say casa.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin habitus (“habit, appearance”), a noun based on habeō (“have”).

fact.text: There's a well-known proverb, l'abito non fa il monaco: 'the habit doesn't make the monk'. Italians use it the way English speakers say 'don't judge a book by its cover'.

senses.note: Plural abiti = clothes. Abito da sera = evening dress. Abito da sposa = wedding dress.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin habituāre.

fact.text: From Latin habitus, 'condition, habit', so it is linked to English habit and habitual. To get accustomed is really to make something a habit.

features.construction: abituare qualcuno a qualcosa; reflexive abituarsi a (essere)

senses.note: Abituarsi a = to get used to; essere abituato a = to be used to.

etymology: From abituare + -si.

senses.note: Takes a + noun or infinitive: mi sono abituato al freddo / ad alzarmi presto.

etymology: From Late Latin habituātus, perfect passive participle of habituō (“to bring into a condition or habit”), derived from Latin habitus (“habit”). Doublet of habitué.

senses.note: Essere abituato a + noun or infinitive: sono abituato a vivere da solo.

etymology: Inherited from Latin habitūdinem. By surface analysis, abito + -itudine.

fact.text: Shares its Latin root with abito (suit, dress). In the same way, English habit can mean both a routine and a nun's robe.

senses.note: Avere l'abitudine di + infinitive = to be in the habit of doing.

etymology: From Latin acadēmicus, from Ancient Greek ἀκαδημικός (akadēmikós).

fact.text: Goes back to the Akademeia, the grove of the hero Akademos outside Athens where Plato taught his students.

senses.note: A member of an academy, or a university scholar. Feminine: accademica. Also an adjective: academic.

etymology: From a- + cadere.

fact.text: Literally 'to fall towards' (a- + cadere, to fall). English 'accident' comes from Latin accidere, built the same way: something that falls upon you.

senses.note: Used only with things as the subject: è accaduto ieri. Succedere is the everyday word for this.

From a- + campo (“field”) + -are.

senses.note: Usually reflexive: accamparsi (aux. essere). Mi accampo sul divano = I'll camp on the sofa.
senses.prompt: to camp, to set up camp

etymology: From a- + canto (“corner, side”).

senses.note: Accanto a + noun = next to. La porta accanto = next door.

etymology: From a- + carezza (“caress”, noun) + -are.

fact.text: English 'caress' came from French caresse, which borrowed Italian carezza. Carezza itself comes from caro, 'dear', so a caress is literally a 'dear' gesture.

senses.note: Accarezzare il gatto = to stroke the cat. Figuratively: accarezzare un'idea = to toy with an idea.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin accēdere.

senses.note: Takes 'a': accedere al sistema, alla cassaforte. Also 'to log in'. Uses essere in this sense.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin accelerāre (“to quicken, hasten, accelerate”), from ad (“to, towards, at”) + celerō (“to quicken”).

fact.text: Its gerund 'accelerando' is the musical term for gradually speeding up. The root is Latin celer 'swift'.

senses.note: Also transitive: accelerare il passo = to quicken one's pace.

etymology: Inherited from Latin accendō, from ad- + candeō.

fact.text: From Latin accendere, built on candere, 'to glow'. The same root gives English candle, candid and incandescent.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: acceso. It also means to light (a fire, a cigarette).
From accendere 'to light'. Accendisigari is also used.

etymology: From Latin accentus.

fact.text: Latin accentus literally means 'singing to', from ad + canere, 'to sing'. It is a translation of the Greek word prosōidía.

senses.note: Also word stress and the written accent mark (è, perché).

etymology: From Latin accessus.

senses.note: accesso a Internet = Internet access; effettuare l'accesso = to log in.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin acceptāre.

senses.note: Transitive: accettare un consiglio, un invito. 'Accettare di + infinitive' = to agree to do.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin aciārium, derived from Latin aciēs (“sharp point”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”). Cognates include French acier, Friulian açâr, Galician aceiro, Portuguese aço, Romansh atschal, and Spanish acero.

fact.text: Comes from Latin aciēs, 'sharp edge', from a root meaning 'sharp' that also gave English 'acute' and 'acid'. Steel was the metal that took a keen edge.

senses.note: D'acciaio = made of steel. Acciaio inossidabile = stainless steel.

fact.text: Literally 'accidents', in the old sense of a sudden fit or stroke. It comes from curses like 'ti venga un accidente!' ('may a stroke strike you!').

senses.note: A mild oath that can also show amazement ('wow!', 'good heavens!').

etymology: Borrowed from Ligurian anciôa, from Vulgar Latin *apiuva, from Latin aphyē, from Ancient Greek ἀφύη (aphúē).

senses.note: Plural acciughe. Also called alice, especially in the south.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *accolligere, derived from Classical Latin ad- + colligere (whence the Italian cogliere).

fact.text: Comes from Latin ad- + colligere 'to gather', the same verb behind cogliere and English collect. To welcome someone is to gather them in.

senses.note: Irregular: accolgo, accolgono; past participle accolto. Adjective: accogliente (welcoming).

etymology: From Latin accommodāre.

fact.text: You will hear the reflexive form all the time: 'Si accomodi!' is the polite way to invite someone to come in or sit down, used in shops, offices and homes.

senses.note: Si accomodi! = Please have a seat / come in. Aggiustare and riparare are more common for 'fix'.

fact.text: It looks like English 'accommodate', but it is spelled with one m and usually means to take a seat or come in. Hosts, doctors and shop staff say it constantly.

senses.note: Prego, si accomodi! = Please, have a seat / do come in. Very common polite invitation.

etymology: From a- + compagno + -are.

fact.text: Built on compagno, from Latin com- (with) + panis (bread): a companion was originally someone you shared bread with. English companion and company have the same root.

senses.note: Accompagnare qualcuno a casa = to take/walk someone home.

etymology: Univerbation of a + conto.

fact.text: Fused from a conto, 'on account'. In English you can also pay something 'on account', meaning a partial payment toward a total still owed.

senses.note: Versare un acconto = to pay a deposit. Also an advance on wages. The balance owed is il saldo.

etymology: Deverbal from accordare + -o.

fact.text: The verb accordare is usually traced to Latin ad + cor, cordis 'heart', so agreeing is being heart to heart. English accord and concord share the same root.

senses.note: Essere d'accordo = to agree; D'accordo! = OK! Also 'chord' in music.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *accorrigere, from Latin ad- + corrigō (“to correct”).

senses.note: Takes di: mi sono accorto dell'errore. Irregular: mi accorsi, accorto.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English account. Doublet of conto.

fact.text: Italian borrowed 'account' from English for online profiles, but for money you use 'conto', a word from the same Latin root. So: conto in banca, account email.

senses.note: Invariable. Used for online/user accounts; a bank account is un conto.

etymology: From a- + credito (“credit”) + -are.

features.construction: transitive: accreditare qualcosa su un conto

senses.note: Banking: accreditare lo stipendio sul conto = to pay the salary into the account.

etymology: Deverbal from accusare + -a.

senses.note: In court, l'accusa = the prosecution. Also a charge: accusa di furto = a theft charge.

etymology: From Latin accūsāre.

senses.note: Also: accusare un dolore = to feel a pain; accusare ricevuta = to acknowledge receipt.

etymology: From Latin acētum (“vinegar”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin acetum, linked to acere (to be sour). English acid belongs to the same sour-tasting family.

senses.note: Aceto balsamico = balsamic vinegar, a speciality of Modena.

etymology: From acido + -are.
ignored: Bad parse: the context fragment 'Acidi-c' belongs to the adjective acidico, not this rare technical verb.

senses.note: Rare technical verb.
Mostly technical or scientific. In everyday speech, acido (sour, acid) is more common.

etymology: From Latin acidus.

senses.note: Also means sour (latte acido = sour milk) and, figuratively, sharp or caustic in tone.

etymology: Inherited from Latin aqua.

fact.text: Comes straight from Latin aqua, which also gave English aquarium, aquatic and aqueduct. In Venice, 'acqua alta' (high water) is the seasonal tide that floods St Mark's Square.

senses.note: Acqua naturale = still water; acqua frizzante/gassata = sparkling water.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *acquīsītāre, from Latin acquīsītus, ultimately from Latin adquīrere.

senses.note: More formal than comprare. Also 'to gain' (acquistare peso). Gli acquisti = shopping or purchases.

etymology: From Latin ad.

fact.text: Latin ad comes from the same Proto-Indo-European root as English 'at', so the two words are distant cousins.

senses.note: Form of a used for smoother sound, mainly before a-: ad esempio, ad Anna.

etymology: From Latin adaptāre (“to fit, adjust, modify; to adapt, fit or adjust to”).

senses.note: Adattarsi (with essere) = to adapt oneself; also to fit or suit: non si adatta = it doesn't fit.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin adaptus, from ad- + aptus (“suitable”).

senses.note: Usually followed by a or per: adatto ai bambini, adatto per il lavoro.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin addictus and adapted to native detto.

fact.text: Comes from Latin addictus, 'assigned, handed over'. English 'addict' has the same origin: in Rome an addictus was a debtor handed over to his creditor.

senses.note: Often 'addetto a' + a task: addetto alle vendite = sales assistant. Feminine: l'addetta.

etymology: From a Dio (“to God”), from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Compare Aragonese, Asturian, Extremaduran, and Spanish adiós; Catalan adeu; Dutch ajuus; English, French, and Occitan adieu; German tschüss; Greek αντίο (antío); Galician and Portuguese adeus; Maltese addiju; Mirandese adius; Romanian adio; Serbo-Croatian ади̏о/adȉo; Slovene adȋjo.

fact.text: Comes from 'a Dio', meaning 'to God'. French adieu and Spanish adiós come from the same idea of leaving someone in God's care.

senses.note: A final, often dramatic goodbye. For everyday goodbyes use ciao or arrivederci.

etymology: From a Dio (“to God”), from Medieval Latin ad Deum (“to God”). Compare Aragonese, Asturian, Extremaduran, and Spanish adiós; Catalan adeu; Dutch ajuus; English, French, and Occitan adieu; German tschüss; Greek αντίο (antío); Galician and Portuguese adeus; Maltese addiju; Mirandese adius; Romanian adio; Serbo-Croatian ади̏о/adȉo; Slovene adȋjo.

fact.text: Comes from 'a Dio', meaning 'to God'. French adieu and Spanish adiós come from the same idea of leaving someone in God's care.

senses.note: A final goodbye, e.g. dire addio. For an everyday 'bye', use ciao or arrivederci.
Also of limbs: mi si è addormentata la gamba = my leg went to sleep.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *addessum. Documented since the late thirteenth century.

fact.text: Usually traced to Latin ad ipsum (tempus), 'at this very (time)'. The word has been recorded since the late 1200s.

senses.note: Same meaning as ora. Per adesso = for now.

etymology: From Latin adolēscentem.

fact.text: Latin adolescere meant 'to grow up'. Its present participle gave 'adolescent' and its past participle, adultus, gave 'adult'. So an adolescent is someone still growing and an adult is someone who has grown.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: un adolescente / un'adolescente.

etymology: From Latin adulēscentia.

senses.note: Nell'adolescenza = in one's teens.

etymology: From Late Latin adoperāre, from Latin ad + operāre.

senses.note: Means the same as usare. Reflexive adoperarsi per = to strive, to do one's best for.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin adōrāre. Cf. the older aorare.

fact.text: From Latin adorare, 'to pray to' (ad 'to' + orare 'to speak, pray'). English 'oration' and 'oracle' come from the same root.

senses.note: Also means 'to worship'. Common in casual speech: Adoro la pizza! (I love pizza!)

etymology: From Latin adoptāre.

senses.note: For children, and figuratively: adottare un metodo = to adopt a method.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin adultus.

fact.text: Latin adultus meant 'grown up' and is the participle of adolescere, 'to grow up'. So adult and adolescent are the same Latin verb: one means 'grown', the other 'growing'.

senses.note: Also a noun: un adulto, gli adulti = adults.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin adultus.

fact.text: Latin adultus meant 'grown up' and is the participle of adolescere, 'to grow up'. So adult and adolescent are the same Latin verb: one means 'grown', the other 'growing'.

senses.note: Feminine: l'adulta. It is also an adjective: una persona adulta.

etymology: From Latin āerius.

senses.note: Prendere l'aereo = to take the plane. Also an adjective: posta aerea = airmail.

etymology: From aero- + porto.
From a (“to”) + fare (“do”), probably based on the model of French affaire. Cognate with Sicilian affari.

fact.text: Literally a + fare, 'to do', modelled on French affaire. English 'affair' comes from the same French à faire: an affair was simply 'something to do'.

senses.note: un buon affare = a good deal. The plural affari means business: fatti gli affari tuoi = mind your own business.
Same form for masculine and feminine. Plural: affascinanti.

etymology: From a- + fascino + -are.

fact.text: Built on fascino 'charm', from Latin fascinum, a spell or bewitchment. To fascinate someone was originally to put them under a spell.

senses.note: mi affascina = it fascinates me; affascinante = charming, fascinating.

etymology: a- + fatto.

fact.text: Made from a- + fatto, it originally meant 'completely'. Because it is so often paired with non ('non... affatto' = not at all), many speakers now hear it alone as a negative.

senses.note: Mostly used with non: non è affatto vero. Said alone as a reply, it usually means 'not at all!'

etymology: From Latin affirmāre.

senses.note: Affermare che + indicative. Affermarsi = to become established or successful.

etymology: From Latin affirmātīvus. By surface analysis, affermare + -ivo.
Borrowed from Latin affirmātiōnem (“affirmation, declaration”), derived from affirmō (“to affirm, assert”).

senses.note: A spoken or written claim. A bank statement is an estratto conto.

etymology: From Latin affectus (noun).

fact.text: The same word is also an adjective with a very different meaning: affetto da means 'suffering from', as in affetto da diabete. Both come from Latin afficere, 'to act upon'.

senses.note: con affetto = with love (as a sign-off in letters).

etymology: From Late Latin affectuōsus.

senses.note: Saluti affettuosi = love/warm regards, a common way to sign off a letter.

etymology:
Univerbation of a + fin(o) + che.
Compare similar constructions with French afin que, Spanish a fin de que and Portuguese a fim de que.

fact.text: Made by fusing a + fine + che, literally 'to the end that'. Compare French afin que and Spanish a fin de que.

senses.note: Always followed by the subjunctive: affinché tu capisca.

etymology: From Medieval Latin affictāre, itself from fictus.

fact.text: Look out for 'Affittasi' signs on Italian buildings. The word means 'for rent', just as 'Vendesi' means 'for sale'.

senses.note: Can mean renting from someone or renting out (letting). Affitto = rent.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin affictum, deverbal from affictāre.

senses.note: Pagare l'affitto = to pay the rent. The sign 'affittasi' means 'for rent'.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *affrontāre, from Latin ad- + frons + -āre. By surface analysis, a- + fronte + -are.

fact.text: Comes from Latin ad- + frons 'forehead', so literally 'to put your forehead to' something. English 'affront' and 'confront' share the same 'front' root.

senses.note: Transitive: affrontare un problema, la vita, un nemico.

etymology: From Latin agentem.

senses.note: Also a police officer: agente di polizia. Used for women too: l'agente (f).

etymology: Derived from Medieval Latin agentia.

senses.note: Agenzia di viaggi = travel agency; agenzia immobiliare = estate agency.

etymology: From Late Latin adiectīvum [nōmen], translation of Ancient Greek ἐπίθετον [ὄνομα] (epítheton [ónoma]).

fact.text: Latin adiectivum means 'thrown on' or 'added', a translation of Greek epitheton, which also meant 'added'. An adjective is literally a word added to a noun.

etymology: From Latin adiungere (“add, join to”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin adiungere (ad- 'to' + iungere 'to join'). To add something is literally to join it on.

senses.note: Irregular: aggiunsi (passato remoto), aggiunto (past participle).

etymology: From a- (“to”) + giusto (“just”, “right”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).

senses.note: Aggiustare la bici. Reflexive aggiustarsi = to sort itself out.

etymology: From Latin aggredior, from ad- (“towards”) + gradior (“to walk”).

fact.text: From Latin aggredior, 'to step towards' (ad- + gradior, 'to walk'). English 'aggression' and 'aggressive' come from the same root.

senses.note: Used for physical attacks and muggings: è stato aggredito per strada.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan aize, from Vulgar Latin *adjace(m), from Latin adjacēns, present participle of adjaceō (compare Medieval Latin in aiace). Cognate with Old French aise, eise, French aise and aisance; compare also Catalan eina. Doublet of adiacente.

fact.text: This shares its origin with English 'ease' (via Old French aise). Both probably go back to Latin adjacens, 'lying nearby'.

senses.note: Mostly in 'a proprio agio' = at ease. Plural gli agi = comforts, luxuries.

etymology: Borrowed from French agir, itself borrowed from Latin agere.

senses.note: To take action or behave, not to act a role (that's recitare). -isc- verb: agisco.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ālium.

senses.note: A clove of garlic is uno spicchio d'aglio.

etymology: From earlier aco, from Latin acus (“needle”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”). Compare Romanian ac.

fact.text: From Latin acus, from an Indo-European root meaning 'sharp'. The same root is behind English 'acute', 'acid' and 'acumen'.

senses.note: Also pine needles and a compass needle. Plural aghi (agora is archaic).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus. Doublet of Augusto.

fact.text: Ferragosto, the 15 August holiday when much of Italy shuts down, comes from Latin Feriae Augusti, 'Augustus's holidays'. The month itself is named after Emperor Augustus.

senses.note: Months are lowercase and usually take no article: ad agosto = in August.

etymology: From Latin agricola (“farmer”).

fact.text: From Latin agricola 'farmer', from ager (field) + colere (to cultivate). The Roman general Agricola, Tacitus's father-in-law, had a name that literally meant 'farmer'.

senses.note: Uncommon; the everyday word is agricoltore. The adjective agricolo means 'agricultural'.

etymology: From Latin agricultūra.
From agri- + turismo.

fact.text: Italy regulated agriturismo by national law in 1985. To use the name, a place must be a real working farm where tourism is a side activity.

senses.note: A working farm that offers rooms and meals, often made with its own produce.
All-purpose cry of surprise, realization, pain or irony. Ah, ecco! = Oh, I see!

ignored: A contraction of a + i (preposition plus article), better learned on the card for the preposition 'a'.

senses.note: a + i = ai: ai pascoli (to the pastures).

etymology: Inherited from Latin adiūtāre. The archaic aggiutare represents the expected outcome in Italian. The modern form may reflect influence from central or southern Italo-Romance (cf. Sicilian ajutari), where in many places /-j-/ would be the regular outcome.

fact.text: From Latin adiutare 'to help', which came into English through Old French as 'aid'.

senses.note: Takes a direct object: aiutare qualcuno a fare qualcosa (to help someone do something). Aiuto! = Help!

etymology: From Late Latin adiūtus.

senses.note: The noun l'aiuto also means help or assistance.

etymology: From Late Latin adiūtus.

senses.note: Aiuto! = Help! Plural aiuti = aid (aiuti umanitari).
a + il. In dish names it means 'with': spaghetti al pomodoro.

etymology: From Latin āla.

fact.text: English aisle comes from Latin ala via Old French ele, meaning the side wing of a church. Its s was added later through confusion with isle.

senses.note: Irregular plural: le ali. In football, an ala is a winger.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *alba, from Latin albus (“white”). Compare French aube.

fact.text: Comes from Latin albus 'white', for the pale light of daybreak. English 'albino' and 'album' (originally a blank white tablet) share the root.

senses.note: all'alba = at dawn

etymology: From Medieval Latin alberga, from Proto-West Germanic *harjabergu.

fact.text: Comes from a Germanic word for 'army shelter'. The same compound gave English harbour and French auberge, 'inn'.

senses.note: The traditional Italian word; hotel is also common. Plural: alberghi.

etymology: From older alboro m (via dissimilation), from albore m (via masculinization of the ending), from Latin arborem f.

fact.text: From Latin arbor, which was feminine. Italian made it masculine and turned the first r into an l. English arboretum comes from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Also means a ship's mast. L'albero di Natale = Christmas tree.

etymology: From Medieval Latin alcohol, ultimately from Arabic اَلْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”).

fact.text: Comes from Arabic al-kuḥl, 'kohl', the fine powder used as eye makeup. It came to mean any refined essence, and the meaning later moved to distilled spirits.

senses.note: Usually invariable; alcoli is mostly a chemistry plural. The variant alcool also exists.

fact.text: Comes from Arabic al-kuhl, 'kohl', the fine powder used as eye makeup. Alchemists later used the word for any refined essence, and eventually for distilled spirits.

senses.note: Also spelled alcol. Invariable.

etymology:
From Vulgar Latin *alicūnus, from Classical Latin aliquem (“someone, something”) + ūnum (“one”).
Cognate with French aucun, Spanish alguno, Galician algún, Portuguese algum.

senses.note: Non c'è alcun problema = there isn't any problem. In the plural, alcuni/alcune means 'some, a few'.

ignored: Has the same meaning as the adjective card alcuno, which is studied separately.

senses.note: Mostly plural: alcuni/alcune = some, a few. Singular in negatives: senza alcun dubbio.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin alphabētum, from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from alpha and beta (the first two letters of the Greek alphabet), from Phoenician 𐤀 (ʾ /⁠aleph⁠/, “ox”) and 𐤁 (b /⁠beth⁠/, “house”), so called because they were pictograms of those objects.

fact.text: Named after alpha and beta, the first two Greek letters. These go back to Phoenician aleph ('ox') and beth ('house'), which began as pictures of those things.

senses.note: Short for negozio di alimentari; doesn't change in the plural: un alimentari, due alimentari.

etymology: From alimentare + -zione.

senses.note: un'alimentazione sana = a healthy diet. In technical use it also means power supply.

ignored: It is a contraction of a + la, so it is better learned with the preposition a.

senses.note: a + la: alla fine = in the end. Also 'in the style of': pasta alla romana.

etymology: Univerbation of all' (“to the”) + arme (“weapons”, archaic plural of arma), literally “to the weapons, to arms”.

fact.text: Literally all'arme, 'to arms!', a battle cry. It reached English through French alarme, so English 'alarm' is really an Italian call to arms.

senses.note: Dare l'allarme = to raise the alarm. Falso allarme = false alarm.

etymology: Borrowed from French allègre, from Latin alacer (“lively; happy, cheerful”). Compare the doublet alacre.

fact.text: English borrowed it as a musical term for a fast, lively tempo. In everyday Italian it simply means cheerful or merry.

etymology: From a- (“to, towards”) + lena (“energy, vigour”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).

fact.text: Built from a- + lena, an old word for energy or vigour, so training literally means giving someone stamina. Lena survives in the phrase di buona lena, 'with a will'.

features.construction: transitive; reflexive allenarsi = to train oneself

senses.note: Allenarsi = to train, work out: mi alleno ogni giorno. Allenare una squadra = to coach a team.

etymology: From allergia + -ico.

senses.note: Used with a: allergico al polline (allergic to pollen).

etymology: Inherited from Latin allevāre (“to lift up, alleviate”).

fact.text: From Latin allevare, meaning to lift up or to lighten, the same root as English alleviate. Raising animals or children was seen as lifting them up.

senses.note: Also to bring up children. Allevamento = farm (for animals) or breeding.

etymology: Deverbal from alloggiare + -o.

fact.text: Comes from alloggiare, which is related to loggia and, through French loge, to English lodge and lodging.

senses.note: Vitto e alloggio = board and lodging. It can also mean a flat.

etymology: From a- + lontano + -are.

fact.text: Built from lontano ('far'), so it literally means 'to make far'. Avvicinare, its opposite, is built the same way from vicino ('near').

senses.note: Transitive. For 'to go away / move away' yourself, use allontanarsi.
senses.prompt: to move away, to push away

fact.text: Built on lontano, 'far': allontanarsi literally means 'to make oneself far'.

senses.note: Allontanarsi da qualcosa/qualcuno. Non allontanarti! = Don't wander off!

etymology:
Inherited from Latin ad illam hōram (“at that hour”).
Compare French alors, Occitan alara, Spanish alora, and Catalan aleshores.
By surface analysis, all' + ora.

fact.text: Literally 'at that hour': it comes from Latin ad illam horam, so it is really all' + ora. French alors was formed the same way.

senses.note: Very common for starting a sentence: Allora, cosa facciamo? Also 'back then': allora vivevo a Roma.

etymology:
Univerbation of al + meno, literally, “at the least”.
Compare Spanish al menos, Portuguese ao menos, French au moins, Catalan almenys.

senses.note: Also used for wishes: Almeno fosse vero! = If only it were true!

fact.text: Built on Alpi (the Alps), yet it is used for climbers of any mountain. Don't confuse it with alpino, a soldier of Italy's famous mountain troops, the Alpini.

senses.note: il/la alpinista (l'alpinista); plural alpinisti (m), alpiniste (f).

etymology: From Latin Alpīnus.

senses.note: The adjective alpino/alpina also means 'alpine', as in rilievo alpino.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin altitia, from Latin altus (“high”). Compare Portuguese and Spanish alteza, Catalan altesa. By surface analysis, alto (“high”) + -ezza.

senses.note: Also altitude; Sua Altezza = His/Her Highness.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin altitūdinem.

fact.text: From Latin altus 'high', which also gives Italian alto. English borrowed alto from Italian for the voice part sung 'high', above the tenor.

senses.note: For a person's height use altezza or statura instead.

etymology: From Latin altus (“high”), from Proto-Italic *altos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eltós, derived from the root *h₂el- (“to grow, nourish”). Cognate with English old and Welsh allt.

fact.text: Comes from Latin altus 'high', from a root meaning 'to grow'. It is a distant cousin of English old (grown up), and gives us altitude.

senses.note: Tall for people, high for things. Can also mean loud (voce alta) or deep (alto mare).

fact.text: Said alone, 'Altrettanto!' is the standard reply to a good wish: 'Buon appetito!' 'Altrettanto!' (Same to you!).

senses.note: Agrees with its noun: altrettanta, altrettanti, altrettante. Also used as an adverb and a pronoun.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin alterā mente. Documented since the thirteenth century.

fact.text: Comes from Latin altera mente, literally 'with another mind'. Latin mente 'mind' is also where the Italian adverb ending -mente comes from.

senses.note: Also means 'or else': Sbrigati, altrimenti perdiamo il treno.

fact.text: From Latin alter 'the other (of two)', the root of English alter, alternate and alternative.

senses.note: Un altro / un'altra = another: un'altra volta. D'altra parte = on the other hand.

etymology: Inherited from Latin alterum, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂élteros.

fact.text: From Latin alter 'the other (of two)', the root of English alter, alternate and alternative.

senses.note: Agrees with what it replaces: altro, altra, altri, altre. In shops, 'Altro?' means 'Anything else?'

etymology: From Latin aliter ubī. By surface analysis, univerbation of altro + ove.

fact.text: Can be read as altro ('other') + ove ('where'), literally 'other-where', which is built just like English elsewhere.

senses.note: Andare altrove = to go somewhere else.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”).

fact.text: Built on Latin altus 'high', the same root as Italian alto and English altitude. To raise something is literally to make it high.

senses.note: Alzare la mano = raise your hand. Reflexive alzarsi = to get up.
Reflexive: mi alzo alle sette. Also means to stand up. Alzare without -si = to raise or lift.

etymology: Inherited from Latin amantem.

senses.note: il/la amante, depending on the person's gender. Often implies an affair.

etymology: Inherited from Latin amāre.

fact.text: English amateur comes via French from Latin amator, 'lover', from amare. An amateur is someone who does something for the love of it.

senses.note: Strong word: ti amo is romantic. For liking things, use piacere.

etymology: From Latin amārus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eh₃mós (“bitter, raw”).

fact.text: The name just means 'bitter'. Italians often sip one after a big meal to help digestion, and almost every region has its own brand, like Averna from Sicily or Montenegro from Bologna.

senses.note: Don't confuse with amare (to love). Forms: amaro/amara/amari/amare.

etymology: Old Italian, from Old Occitan ambaissada, from Gaulish ambaxtos.

fact.text: This goes back to Gaulish ambaxtos, 'servant' or 'envoy', and came into Italian through Old Occitan. English 'embassy' and 'ambassador' come from the same Celtic word.

senses.note: Informally it can also mean a message passed on through someone.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ambientem, present active participle of ambiō (“surround”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin ambire 'to go around', which also gives English ambient. Ambition shares the root too: Roman candidates went around asking for votes.

senses.note: Also 'setting, circle' (l'ambiente di lavoro) and, in house listings, 'room'.

fact.text: Comes from French ambulance, which first meant a mobile field hospital that moved with an army. The root is Latin ambulare, 'to walk', which also gives English 'amble'.

senses.note: Chiamare un'ambulanza = to call an ambulance.

etymology: From Latin ambulātōrius.

fact.text: From Latin ambulatorius, 'related to walking' (ambulare 'to walk'). Outpatients walk in and out, so they are 'ambulatory'. Ambulance and amble come from the same root.

senses.note: A doctor's or vet's consulting room; also a hospital's outpatient department.

etymology: From America + -ano.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian: la letteratura americana. Un americano = an American.

etymology: From Latin amiantus, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓μῐ́ᾰντος (ămĭ́ăntos).

fact.text: From Greek amiantos, 'undefiled', because fire cleans it without burning it. English took a different Greek word instead: asbestos, 'unquenchable'.

senses.note: Mass noun, usually singular.

etymology: From Latin amīca (“friend”).

senses.note: Plural amiche (with h). Masculine: amico/amici. 'La mia ragazza' is the usual word for girlfriend.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin amicitia.

senses.note: fare amicizia (con qualcuno) = to make friends (with someone).

etymology: From Latin amīcus. Compare Catalan amic, French ami, Portuguese amigo, Romanian amic, Sardinian amícu, Spanish amigo.

fact.text: Comes from Latin amicus, related to amare 'to love'. English amicable and amiable come from the same family.

senses.note: Plural amici (hard c becomes soft). Feminine: amica, amiche.
Ammalarsi di: mi sono ammalato d'influenza = I came down with the flu.
senses.prompt: to fall ill, to get sick

etymology: Probably from a- + mazza (“club, baton”) + -are, or alternatively possibly related to Latin mactāre, through a Vulgar Latin root *mactiāre, although this is less likely. Compare Sicilian ammazzari, Spanish mazar, Portuguese maçar, Occitan massar, Romansh mazzar, Venetan masar, Friulian maçâ, Istriot masà. See also archaic Italian mattare.

fact.text: Probably built on mazza, a club, so it first meant to club someone. In Rome the exclamation Ammazza! just means Wow!

senses.note: More everyday than uccidere. Ammazzarsi di lavoro = to work oneself to death.

etymology: Inherited from Latin admittere. By surface analysis, a- + mettere.

senses.note: Irregular like mettere: ammisi, ammesso.

etymology: From Latin administrātor.

senses.note: Amministratore delegato = CEO. Feminine form: amministratrice.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin admirāri.

fact.text: From Latin ad + mirari, to wonder at. The same mirari, from mirus 'wonderful', is behind English miracle and mirror.

senses.note: Appartamento ammobiliato = furnished flat. Synonym: arredato.
Past participle of ammuffire (to go moldy), from la muffa (mold).

etymology: Inherited from Latin amōrem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin amor, from amare, 'to love'. The same verb is behind English amorous and amateur, someone who does something for the love of it.

senses.note: Also used to address someone: amore (mio) = darling, my love.

etymology: Inherited from Latin amplus.

fact.text: From Latin amplus, the same word that gave English 'ample' and 'amplify'. Something ampio has plenty of room.

senses.note: Also 'spacious' (un ampio salone) and 'loose' for clothes. Plurals: ampi, ampie.

etymology: From Medieval Latin analysis, from Ancient Greek ἀνάλυσις (análusis).

senses.note: Invariable: le analisi. Also medical tests: fare le analisi del sangue = to have blood tests.

etymology: Assuming that anco represents the original form, likely a rebracketing of ancora as anc'ora. A borrowing from Old Occitan ancui (“on this day”) has also been suggested, but this would explain neither the stress position of anche, nor the lack of a final -ui (an acceptable ending in Italian; cf. lui).

senses.note: Goes before the word it refers to: anche io = me too. Can also mean 'even'.
Goes before the word it refers to: anch'io = me too.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *hancōra, probably from Late Latin in hanc hōram (“until this hour”). Compare French encore, Occitan and Catalan encara.

fact.text: Probably from Latin in hanc horam 'until this hour', like French encore, which English borrowed. Stress the first syllable instead (àncora) and it means 'anchor'.

senses.note: Non ancora = not yet. Stressed on the o: ancóra.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin andāre, of uncertain origin, with suppletion from vādō.

fact.text: Vado, vai, va and vanno come from a different Latin verb, vadere. The same verb gave Spanish vamos, which became the English slang word 'vamoose'.

senses.note: Irregular: vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno. Takes essere: sono andato/a.

etymology:
From andarsi + -ne.
Compare French s'en aller, Catalan anar-se'n and to a lesser extent Spanish irse and andarse.

fact.text: Its imperative 'Vattene!' is the everyday way to say 'Go away!' or 'Get out of here!', and 'Me ne vado' simply means 'I'm off'.

senses.note: me ne vado, te ne vai…; past: me ne sono andato/a.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ānellus, diminutive of ānus (“circle”). Compare Catalan anell, French anneau, Portuguese anel, Spanish anillo.

senses.note: Engagement ring = anello di fidanzamento; wedding ring is often la fede.

etymology: Inherited from Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos).

fact.text: Greek ángelos originally just meant 'messenger'. Christian writers used it for God's messengers, and that became the word's main meaning.

senses.note: Plural: gli angeli. angelo custode = guardian angel.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin angulus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂engulos (“joint?”), from *h₂eng-, *ang- (“corner, hirn”).

senses.note: Also 'angle'. All'angolo = on the corner.

etymology: From Latin anima, from animus, from Proto-Italic *anamos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂enh₁mos, a nominal derivative of *h₂enh₁- (“breathe”). Doublet of alma.

fact.text: Latin anima meant 'breath, soul', so a living thing was one that breathed. The same root gives English animal and animate.

senses.note: Plural anime. Riposi in pace l'anima sua = may his/her soul rest in peace.

etymology: From Latin animālem, possibly borrowed.

fact.text: Comes from Latin animalis, 'living', from anima, 'breath, soul'. An animal is literally a 'breathing thing', and English animate comes from the same root.

senses.note: Animale domestico = pet.

etymology: Inherited from Latin annus, from Proto-Italic *atnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-no-, probably from *h₂et- (“to go”).

fact.text: Latin annus gave English annual and anniversary. Say the double n clearly: with a single n, ano means 'anus'!

senses.note: Ages use avere: ho trent'anni = I am thirty.

fact.text: It comes from the same root as English 'annoy' (Latin in odio, 'in hatred'), but it mostly means boredom: mi annoio means I'm bored, not I'm annoyed.

senses.note: Mi annoio = I'm bored. Annoiare (non-reflexive) = to bore someone.

etymology: From annoiare.

fact.text: False friend: it means bored, not annoyed. English annoy and Italian noia (boredom) both come from Latin 'in odio', meaning 'hateful'.

senses.note: Not 'annoyed' (that is infastidito/seccato). Annoiarsi = to get bored.

etymology: From Latin adnuere, annuere.

fact.text: From Latin adnuere, ad + nuere 'to nod'. Latin numen, a god's 'nod' or will, comes from the same root.

senses.note: Intransitive -isc- verb: annuisco. Say 'annuì' alone, not 'annuì la testa'.

etymology: From Latin annullāre.

fact.text: Like English 'annul', it comes from Late Latin annullare, from ad- + nullus ('none'). To cancel something is literally to bring it to nothing.

senses.note: annullare un volo/un appuntamento. Also to annul (a contract, a marriage).

etymology: In the sense "act of announcing", deverbal from annunciare + -o. In the concrete senses, borrowed from Late Latin annūntium, from Latin ad- + nūntium (“notice, announcement”).

senses.note: Also means an ad: annunci di lavoro = job ads. Also spelled annunzio.

etymology: Alteration of annasare, probably influenced by muso (“muzzle, snout”).

fact.text: The older form was annasare, built on naso 'nose'. The vowel probably changed under the influence of muso 'snout, muzzle', so you sniff like an animal.

senses.note: Means smelling something on purpose. To give off a smell is profumare or puzzare.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin anxia, derived from Classical Latin anxius (“anxious”).

senses.note: essere in ansia per = to be worried about

etymology: From Latin anxiōsus.

senses.note: Also 'eager': ansioso di partire = eager to leave.

etymology: From Medieval Latin antenātus.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin antenatus, 'born before': ante (before) + natus (born). The same Latin roots appear in English antenatal and natal.

senses.note: Mostly used in the plural: i miei antenati = my ancestors.

etymology: Deverbal from anticipare + -o.

senses.note: Also a deposit. In anticipo = early, ahead of time.

etymology: Inherited from Latin antīquus (“ancient”).

senses.note: Also 'antique, old': mobili antichi. Plural: antichi / antiche.

fact.text: Nothing to do with being 'against pasta'! Anti- here comes from Latin ante 'before' and pasto means 'meal', so it is what you eat before the meal.

senses.note: Plural of l'antipasto (m.): gli antipasti.

etymology: From anti- (“prior to, before”) + pasto (“meal”).

fact.text: Has nothing to do with pasta and is not 'anti' anything. It is ante (before) plus pasto (meal), so it literally means 'before the meal'.

senses.note: The course served before il primo (usually pasta or risotto).

etymology: From antipatia + -ico.

fact.text: In Italian, an antipatico person is someone others dislike: the opposite of simpatico.

senses.note: The opposite of simpatico: mi è antipatico = I don't like him.

etymology: Ultimately from Vulgar Latin *anteānus. Documented from the thirteenth century.

fact.text: Comes from Vulgar Latin *anteanus, from ante (before), meaning someone born earlier. English ancient comes from the same word, through Old French ancien.

senses.note: Also a noun: un anziano = an elderly man; gli anziani = the elderly. Più anziano can mean senior.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin aperītīvus, from Late Latin apertīvus, from Latin aperiō, and partly from French apéritif.

fact.text: Ultimately from Latin aperire, 'to open': an aperitivo is meant to open up your appetite before dinner.

senses.note: Also the pre-dinner drinks-and-snacks hour: andare all'aperitivo.

etymology: Inherited from Latin apertus.

fact.text: All'aperto means 'outdoors, in the open air', as in cenare all'aperto, to dine outside.

senses.note: Also the past participle of aprire (to open): ho aperto la porta.

etymology: From Latin apertūra. The sense of "aperture" was a later learned development. Doublet of ouverture.

fact.text: It comes from Latin apertura, 'opening', which gave English both 'aperture' and, through Old French overture, 'overture', the piece that opens an opera. The Italian plural is spelled 'aperture'.

senses.note: E.g. the opening of a shop or exhibition. Also openness (of mind) and a camera's aperture.

etymology: Borrowed from Spanish apartamiento and adapted to appartare.

fact.text: English 'apartment' came via French appartement from this Italian word. It is based on the idea of 'setting apart': a private section set apart within a larger building.

etymology: From Late Latin appertinēre, from Latin pertinēre; influenced by pars (“part”). Compare English appertain.

fact.text: From Late Latin appertinere, from pertinere. It shares a root with English pertain, and its form was influenced by pars, meaning part.

senses.note: Appartenere a qualcuno/qualcosa. Conjugated like tenere: appartengo, appartieni. Takes essere or avere.

etymology: From appassionare.

fact.text: Beethoven's Piano Sonata No. 23 is known as the 'Appassionata'. The nickname came from a publisher after Beethoven's death.

senses.note: Also a noun for a fan or enthusiast: un appassionato di musica (a music lover).

etymology:
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *ad poenam.
By surface analysis, univerbation of a + pena (“pain, trouble”).
Compare French à peine, Spanish apenas, etc.

fact.text: Literally a + pena, 'with pain/trouble': something done only with difficulty is barely done. French à peine works the same way.

senses.note: È appena arrivato = he has just arrived. Also 'barely' and 'as soon as' (appena posso).

etymology: From Latin appendere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin appendere 'to hang on', the same word behind English append and appendix: something 'hung on' to the end of a book.

senses.note: To hang things, not people (that's impiccare). Past participle: appeso.

etymology: From Latin appetītus.

fact.text: Italians say 'Buon appetito!' before almost every shared meal. English has no exact native equivalent, so English speakers borrow the French bon appetit.

senses.note: Buon appetito! = Enjoy your meal!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin applicātiōnem.

fact.text: Careful: a job or visa application is not this word in Italian. It is una domanda or una candidatura. This word means an app or the act of applying something.

senses.note: Used for software apps and for applying something, such as a cream or a rule. A job application is una domanda.

etymology: Inherited from Latin appōnere (“to appoint; to place near”). By surface analysis, a- + porre.

fact.text: 'Tutto apposto' is a very common misspelling of 'tutto a posto' (everything's fine). 'Apposto' is really the past participle of this verb, meaning affixed or added.

senses.note: Conjugates like porre: appongo, apposi, apposto. Typical phrase: apporre la firma (to sign).

etymology: Univerbation of a + posta.

senses.note: Non l'ho fatto apposta = I didn't do it on purpose. Can also mean 'specially'.
Often describes a worrier, e.g. an overprotective parent.

etymology: From Late Latin appretiāre, from Latin pretium.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin appretiare, built on pretium 'price'. English appreciate has the same source, and so do price, precious and praise. To appreciate something was first to set a price on it.

senses.note: Transitive: apprezzo il tuo aiuto. Also 'to value, to esteem'.

etymology: From a- + profitto + -are. Compare Portuguese aproveitar, Spanish aprovechar.

senses.note: Used with di: approfittare dell'occasione = to take the opportunity. Also approfittarsi di qualcuno = to exploit someone.

etymology: From appropriare.

senses.note: 'In modo appropriato' = appropriately.
Also a romantic date: ho un appuntamento con Giulia.

etymology: Deverbal from appuntare + -o.

fact.text: The same word works as an adverb meaning 'exactly' or 'precisely'. A one-word reply of 'Appunto!' is a very common way to say 'Exactly!' or 'That's just my point!'

senses.note: Usually plural: prendere appunti = to take notes.

etymology: From Latin Aprīlis.

senses.note: Months are lowercase in Italian: ad aprile, in aprile.

etymology: From Latin aperīre. Compare Sicilian ràpiri.

fact.text: Comes from Latin aperire 'to open', which also gives English aperture and aperitif, the drink that 'opens' your appetite.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: aperto (ho aperto). Opposite: chiudere.

etymology: From Latin aquila.

fact.text: From Latin aquila, probably 'the dark bird', from aquilus 'blackish'.

senses.note: Always feminine, even for a male eagle: l'aquila maschio.

etymology: Feminine form of arancio (“orange (tree)”), from Arabic نَارَنْج (nāranj), from Persian نارنگ (nârang), from Sanskrit नारङ्ग (nāraṅga).

fact.text: It travelled from Sanskrit nāraṅga through Persian and Arabic nāranj. English orange has the same source.

senses.note: The fruit. The tree is l'arancio (masculine); the colour is arancione.

fact.text: The fruit's name comes from Persian narang. Italian 'una narancia' became 'un'arancia', losing the n to the article.

senses.note: Plural arancioni, though it is also often left unchanged: le maglie arancione/arancioni.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin ārea. Doublet of aia (“threshing floor”).

senses.note: Plural aree. Also 'field, sector': l'area economica.

etymology: From Latin argentum, from Proto-Italic *argentom. See also the obsolete variant form ariento, possibly from a Vulgar Latin *aregentum; cf. also Old Galician-Portuguese and Old Spanish arento, Spanish arienzo.

fact.text: Latin argentum gives silver its chemical symbol Ag. Argentina is named after it too, because explorers hoped to find silver around the Río de la Plata.

senses.note: Plural gli argenti = silverware.

etymology: Inherited from Latin argilla.

fact.text: Via Latin from Greek árgillos, 'white clay, potter's earth'. It may be linked to argós, 'shining white', from the same root as Latin argentum, 'silver'.

senses.note: In pottery and art, creta is a common synonym.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin argūmentum.

fact.text: This is a false friend: it usually means a topic, not a quarrel. An argument in the sense of a row is una lite or una discussione in Italian.

senses.note: Cambiare argomento = to change the subject. Can also mean a reason or line of reasoning.

etymology: Metathesis from Latin āera, Greek-type accusative of āēr, from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr, “air”). See also aere.

fact.text: English took 'aria' (an opera song) straight from Italian. 'Malaria' comes from mala aria, 'bad air', because the disease was once blamed on swamp air.

senses.note: Also 'look': hai l'aria stanca = you look tired. Darsi delle arie = to put on airs.

etymology: From Late Latin arma (“weapon”), from Latin arma (“defensive arms, weapons of war, war, defense, tools”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂(e)rmos (“fitting”), from the root *h₂er- (“to join”).

fact.text: Italians often call the Carabinieri, the military police, simply l'Arma, short for Arma dei Carabinieri.

senses.note: Irregular plural: l'arma → le armi (like l'ala → le ali). Arma da fuoco = firearm.

etymology: From the older armario, borrowed from Latin armārium.

fact.text: From Latin armārium, a chest for tools or weapons (arma). French armoire comes from the same word.

senses.note: Also a cupboard or cabinet. Plural: armadi.

etymology: From Latin armāre.

senses.note: Also to equip or fit out (a ship). Armarsi di pazienza = to arm oneself with patience.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin harmonia, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̔ρμονῐ́ᾱ (hărmonĭ́ā).

fact.text: From Greek harmonia, which first meant a joint or fastening, from a root meaning 'to fit together'. Musical harmony is literally sounds that fit together.

senses.note: In armonia con = in harmony with.

etymology: From a- + rabbia (“rabies; anger”) + -are.

fact.text: Built on rabbia, which means both 'anger' and 'rabies', so getting angry is literally 'becoming rabid'.

senses.note: Almost always reflexive: arrabbiarsi (mi arrabbio, mi sono arrabbiato). Con qualcuno = with someone.

etymology: From arrabbiare + -si.

fact.text: Built on rabbia, which means both 'anger' and 'rabies' (from Latin rabies). Getting angry is literally becoming rabid.

senses.note: Reflexive: mi arrabbio, mi sono arrabbiato. arrabbiarsi con qualcuno = to get angry with someone.

etymology: From arrabbiare, from rabbia.

fact.text: Built on rabbia, which means both 'rage' and 'rabies' (Latin rabies), so an angry person is literally 'rabid'. Penne all'arrabbiata are 'angry' pasta, named for their fiery chilli.

senses.note: Arrabbiato con qualcuno = angry with someone. Arrabbiarsi = to get angry.

etymology: From arrendere + -si.

senses.note: Irregular: mi sono arreso. Arrendersi a qualcuno = to surrender to someone.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *arrestāre, from Latin ad- (“to”) + restō, restāre (“stop, remain behind, stay back”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin ad- + restare, 'to stay back'. To arrest someone is literally to make them stop, and the verb still means 'to halt' too.

senses.note: Also 'to stop, halt': arrestare un'emorragia. Reflexive arrestarsi = to come to a stop.
arresti domiciliari = house arrest; arresto cardiaco = cardiac arrest. Can also mean a stop.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin adrīpāre, perhaps influenced from Gallo-Italic or Old French in comparison to arripare. By surface analysis, a- + riva (“shore”) + -are.

fact.text: Built from Latin ad 'to' + ripa 'shore', so it first meant 'to reach the shore'. English arrive has the same origin.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono arrivato/a. Arrivare a = to reach, to manage to.

etymology:
Univerbation of a (“to”) + rivederci (“seeing ourselves again”). Compare French au revoir, Romanian la revedere, Catalan a reveure and Spanish hasta la vista.
Compare also parallel and more distant cognates Bulgarian довиждане (doviždane) and Russian до свида́ния (do svidánija) (both related to Proto-Slavic *viděti (+ Proto-Slavic *do)), Ukrainian до побачення (do pobačennja), Polish do zobaczenia, and Arabic إلى اللقاء.

fact.text: Literally 'to seeing each other again' (a + rivederci), so it says the same thing as French au revoir and Spanish hasta la vista.

senses.note: The formal version, to one person addressed as Lei, is ArrivederLa.
Gli arrivi = arrivals (airport board). Also a race's finish line. Arrivo! (verb) = I'm coming!

etymology: From arrostire + -o, ultimately of Germanic origin. See there for more.

senses.note: Also used as an adjective: pollo arrosto = roast chicken.

etymology: From Latin artem (“art”, “skill”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂r̥tís, from the root *h₂er- (“to join, put together”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin articulus, derived from artus, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂r̥tús. Compare also the doublet artiglio.

fact.text: Latin articulus meant 'small joint', from artus, 'joint'. The same root gives English articulate.

senses.note: Covers newspaper articles, grammar articles, legal clauses and items for sale.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin artificiālis.
Borrowed from Latin artificium.

fact.text: Italian calls fireworks fuochi d'artificio, literally 'fires of artifice'. The word comes from Latin artificium, from artifex, 'craftsman', from ars (art) plus facere (to make).

senses.note: fuochi d'artificio = fireworks.
Craft work, the craft sector, or handmade goods: artigianato locale = local crafts.

etymology: From arte + -ista.

senses.note: Singular is the same for both genders: un artista / un'artista. Plurals: artisti (m), artiste (f).

etymology: From Late Latin ascella or Vulgar Latin *axella, from Latin axilla.
Borrowed from Latin ascēnsor, equivalent to ascendere + -tore.

senses.note: Prendere l'ascensore = to take the elevator.

etymology:
From Latin ascia (“axe”).
In spite of the similar pronunciation, unrelated to French hache, ultimately from Frankish *happjā (“axe, hatchet”).

senses.note: Irregular plural: asce.

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of asciuga (“to dry”) + mano (“hand”).

fact.text: A compound of asciuga 'dries' and mano 'hand', so it literally means a 'hand-dryer'.

senses.note: Used for any towel; asciugamano da bagno = bath towel.

etymology: From earlier *asciucare, from Latin exsūcāre, from ex- + sucus (“juice, moisture”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin exsucare, from ex- 'out' + sucus 'juice, moisture', so it meant 'to squeeze the juice out'. Sucus is also the root of English 'succulent'.

senses.note: Transitive with avere. asciugarsi = to dry oneself; asciugacapelli = hairdryer.

etymology: From Latin exsūctus, past participle of exsūgō, from ex + sūgō. Compare Sicilian asciuttu, Spanish enjuto, Portuguese enxuto, Catalan eixut.

fact.text: Pastasciutta, 'dry pasta', is the Italian name for drained pasta served with a sauce, as opposed to pasta in brodo, which is served in broth.

senses.note: Use for things that are not wet (towel, hair). Secco is used for dried-out things and for dry wine.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ascultāre, variant of auscultāre. Doublet of auscultare, a borrowing from Latin.

senses.note: Takes a direct object with no preposition: ascoltare la musica = to listen to music.
Dare ascolto a = to heed. Gli ascolti = TV/radio ratings.

etymology: From Latin asylum, from Ancient Greek ἄσυλον (ásulon).

fact.text: Same word as English 'asylum': from Greek asylon, 'a place that cannot be seized'. Italian uses it both for asylum and for the safe little world of kindergarten.

senses.note: Asilo nido = daycare (ages 0–3). Asilo politico = political asylum.

etymology: From Latin āsthma, from Ancient Greek ἆσθμα (âsthma, “laborous breathing”).

fact.text: Most Greek words ending in -ma are masculine in Italian (il problema, il sistema), but asthma is normally feminine: l'asma. The Greek original meant 'panting'.

senses.note: Feminine: l'asma bronchiale. Masculine use is old or popular. The plural is rare.
Medical term for a fungal infection. Invariable: le aspergillosi.

etymology: Inherited from Latin exspectāre, aspectāre. By surface analysis, a- + spettare.

fact.text: From Latin exspectare, which also gave English 'expect'. The reflexive form aspettarsi does mean 'to expect'.

senses.note: No word for 'for' needed: aspetto l'autobus = I'm waiting for the bus.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin aspectus, perfect passive participle of aspiciō (“to behold, see”).

fact.text: Also the io form of aspettare, so 'aspetto' can mean 'I wait'. It also means 'waiting' in sala d'aspetto, the waiting room.

senses.note: Also 'aspect'. Note: sala d'aspetto = waiting room.

etymology: From Latin asperum (“rough”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂esp- (“to cut”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese áspero (“rough”), French âpre, Romanian aspru.

fact.text: Latin asper, 'rough', is behind English 'exasperate', which literally meant to make something rough.

senses.note: Also means sour or tart (taste) and rugged (terrain). Example: un aspro inverno = a harsh winter.

etymology: From a- + saggio (“test, sample”) + -are. Compare Piedmontese assagé.

fact.text: Built on saggio, 'test, sample', which comes from Latin exagium, 'a weighing'. That same Latin word gave English 'assay' and 'essay', both originally meaning a trial or attempt.

senses.note: Used for trying food. 'To taste of' something is sapere di.

ignored: This is assaggiare with the clitic lo attached, not a separate word. Study it on the assaggiare card.

senses.note: assaggiare + lo; the pronoun attaches to the infinitive.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin exagium, 'a weighing, a test'. English essay comes from the same word: it originally meant 'a trial'.

senses.note: Comes from assaggiare, 'to taste'. Un assaggio can also mean a foretaste or preview of something.

etymology: From Arabic حَشَّاشِين (ḥaššāšīn, “hashish users”) or أَسَاسِيُّون (ʔasāsiyyūn, “fundamentalist”). Compare Piedmontese assassin, sassin.

fact.text: Same source as English 'assassin', which probably comes from the Arabic name of a medieval sect, the Hashshashin. But Italian uses it for any murderer, not only for killers of famous people.

senses.note: Means any murderer, not just a political assassin. Feminine: l'assassina. Also an adjective: uno sguardo assassino.

etymology: Deverbal from assegnare + -o.

senses.note: Pagare con un assegno = to pay by cheque. Can also mean an allowance or benefit (assegno familiare).

etymology: From Latin absentem.

senses.note: Same form for both genders (assente/assenti). Uno sguardo assente = a vacant, faraway look.

etymology: From Latin absentia.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *assēcūrāre. By surface analysis, a- + sicuro + -are.

fact.text: Built on sicuro 'safe', from Latin securus. English assure, ensure, insure and secure share that root. Insurance is l'assicurazione.

senses.note: Also to insure or assure. Assicurarsi che = to make sure that.
Assicurarsi di + inf. / che + subjunctive: assicurati che sia chiuso.
Short for lettera assicurata, mail with a declared value. Registered mail is una raccomandata.

etymology: From assicurare + -zione.

senses.note: assicurazione sulla vita = life insurance
l'assistente (m/f): il/la assistente by gender. assistente di volo = flight attendant.

etymology: From associare + -zione.
From assoluto + -mente.

fact.text: On its own it is really just an intensifier, so Italians often add sì or no (assolutamente sì, assolutamente no) to make the answer clear.

senses.note: Assolutamente sì = absolutely; assolutamente no = absolutely not.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *(as)similiāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). By surface analysis, a- + somigliare. Doublet of assimilare and assembrare.

senses.note: Takes a: assomiglia a sua madre. Also somigliare; assomigliarsi = to look alike.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin assūmere, from ad- + sūmō.

fact.text: False friend: this verb doesn't mean 'assume' as in 'suppose'. Italian uses supporre or presumere for that. Here it means to hire someone or to take on a role.

senses.note: Irregular: assunsi, assunto. 'Essere assunto' = to be hired.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin absurdus.

fact.text: From Latin absurdus 'out of tune, jarring', linked to surdus 'deaf'. Something absurd was originally something that sounded wrong to the ear.

etymology: From Latin abstractus.

senses.note: Adjective: astratto, astratta, astratti, astratte. The noun l'astratto (the abstract) is rare.

etymology: Replaced s- of staccare by a-.

fact.text: English attack comes from this verb via French attaquer. 'Attaccare battaglia' meant to join battle, so attach and attack are really one word.

senses.note: Also means 'to attack'. attaccare un poster al muro = to stick a poster on the wall.

etymology: From attaccare.

senses.note: Also a fit or bout: attacco di panico = panic attack, attacco di cuore = heart attack.

etymology: From atteggiare + -mento.

fact.text: False friend: Italian attitudine means aptitude or flair, not attitude. If you mean someone's attitude, say atteggiamento.

senses.note: Behaviour or stance: un atteggiamento positivo, avere un atteggiamento ostile.

etymology: From Latin attendere.

fact.text: Doesn't mean 'to attend' a class or event; that is frequentare or partecipare a. Attendere means to wait for something, as on phone lines: 'Attendere prego'.

senses.note: More formal than aspettare; takes a direct object, so no 'per'. Attenda, prego = please hold.

etymology: From attento + -mente.

senses.note: Also 'closely' or 'attentively': ascoltare attentamente.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin attentātus, perfect passive participle of attentō.

fact.text: From Latin attentare, 'to try, to attempt', the same root as English attempt. The idea is close to the English phrase 'an attempt on someone's life'.

senses.note: A deliberate violent attack, e.g. a bombing; attentato alla vita di = attempt on the life of.

etymology: From Latin attentus.

senses.note: Attento! = Watch out! Agrees: attento, attenta, attenti, attente.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin attentiōnem.

senses.note: Fare attenzione (a) = to pay attention, be careful. Attenzione! = Watch out!

fact.text: Italians say a pregnant woman is 'in dolce attesa', which literally means 'in sweet waiting'.

senses.note: sala d'attesa = waiting room; in attesa di = waiting for.

etymology: Variant of atomo, from Latin atomus (“moment, instant”).

fact.text: A variant of atomo, 'atom'. Greek atomos meant 'indivisible', so a moment was the smallest slice of time that could not be cut any further.

senses.note: Un attimo! = Just a moment! / Hang on!

etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin āctivitātem.

senses.note: Invariable: le attività. It can also mean a business.

etymology: From Latin actus.

senses.note: Also a legal document or record (gli atti), and an act of a play. mettere in atto = to put into practice.

etymology: From Latin āctōrem (“doer”, “actor”).

fact.text: In Italian law, l'attore is also the plaintiff, the party who brings a lawsuit. This keeps the Latin meaning of actor, 'doer'.

senses.note: Feminine: attrice (actress).

etymology: From attraverso + -are.

fact.text: Built on attraverso 'across', from traverso, which comes from Latin transversus 'turned across'. English 'traverse' and 'transverse' come from the same source.

senses.note: Attraversare la strada = to cross the road. Also used for going through a hard time.

etymology:
Univerbation of a + traverso (from Latin trānsversus).
Compare French à travers, Portuguese através and Spanish a través de.

senses.note: Takes the noun directly: attraverso il bosco. Also 'across'. Io attraverso = I cross (attraversare).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin augurāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin augur, a Roman priest who read omens from the flight of birds. Wishing someone well was once foretelling good luck for them. Same root as English 'inaugurate'.

features.construction: augurare qualcosa a qualcuno; augurarsi che + congiuntivo

senses.note: Ti auguro buon viaggio = I wish you a good trip. Auguri! = Best wishes! / Happy birthday!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin augurium. Related to Old Italian agurio, which was inherited.

fact.text: Comes from Latin augurium, from augur, a Roman priest who read omens in the flight of birds. English 'inaugurate' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Tanti auguri! = best wishes / happy birthday!

etymology: From Latin aula, from Ancient Greek αὐλή (aulḗ, “courtyard”).

fact.text: Via Latin aula from Greek aule 'courtyard'. The word went from an open courtyard to a hall, and then to the room where lessons are held.

senses.note: Also a lecture hall or courtroom. Aula magna = a university's main hall.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin augmentāre (“to increase”), from Latin augmentum (“growth, increase”), from augeō (“increase”).

fact.text: Goes back to Latin augere 'to increase', the same root behind English augment, auction (bidding the price up) and author.

senses.note: Transitive verbs take avere; intransitive ones take essere: i prezzi sono aumentati (prices have gone up).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin augmentum.

fact.text: Comes from Latin augmentum, from augere, 'to grow'. It is related to English 'augment' and, surprisingly, to 'auction': a sale where the price keeps growing.

senses.note: Aumento (di stipendio) = pay rise. In aumento = on the rise. Verb: aumentare.

etymology: From Latin authenticus, from Ancient Greek αὐθεντικός (authentikós).

senses.note: Plurals: autentici (m), autentiche (f).

etymology: From auto + -ista.

fact.text: Not 'autistic' (that is autistico). This word is auto, 'car', plus -ista: someone whose job is driving, like a chauffeur, bus driver or truck driver.

senses.note: A professional driver (bus, taxi, private). Any driver of a car = conducente or guidatore. Feminine plural: autiste.

etymology: Clipping of automobile.

senses.note: Feminine because it is short for l'automobile: la mia auto. It doesn't change in the plural: le auto.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French autobus.

fact.text: Borrowed from French autobus, a blend of auto and omnibus. Omnibus is Latin for 'for everyone', and English bus is just its last syllable.

senses.note: Invariable: l'autobus, gli autobus.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin auctōrem.

fact.text: From Latin auctor, which is linked to augere 'to increase, make grow'. English 'augment' and 'authority' come from the same family.

senses.note: Feminine: autrice. Also 'perpetrator': l'autore del furto.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin auctōritātem, derived from auctor.

fact.text: Comes from Latin auctoritas, built on auctor, which also gave English 'author'. Originally, an authority was someone whose word carried weight because they were the originator.

senses.note: Invariable: l'autorità, le autorità.

etymology: From auto- + strada.

fact.text: Italy opened one of the world's first motorways in 1924: the Autostrada dei Laghi, which linked Milan with the lakes near Varese.

senses.note: US English: highway or freeway. Most Italian autostrade charge tolls.

etymology: From auto- + sufficiente.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural is autosufficienti.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin autumnus (“autumn, fall”), of uncertain etymology. First attested in 1306, replacing several inherited forms (cf. proto-Italian octummio, attested in a Latin document from 762, via Late Latin autumnius). The Latin etymon is directly continued by Romanian toamnă, Aromanian toamnã (unless these reflect the variant in a-), Italian autono (Northern Italy, 15th c.), Romansh utuon (Engadine), Spanish otoño (→ Logudorese Sardinian atónzu, Campidanese atógniu), Portuguese outono, and via Vulgar Latin *atumnus by Friulian atum (“october”), Romansh atun (Sursilvan), aton (Surmiran). Provençal autoun (“autumn harvest”) could be Latin-influenced; French automne is likely, and Catalan autumne certain to be a borrowing from Latin.

fact.text: Comes from Latin autumnus, whose own origin is a mystery. One theory says it was borrowed from Etruscan, which had a similar word, atune.

senses.note: Seasons are lowercase: in autunno (in autumn).

etymology: From Late Latin ab ante.

fact.text: Italians call out "Avanti!" when someone knocks on the door. It means "Come in!" It can also mean "Go ahead!" or "Come on!"

senses.note: Andare avanti = to go on / carry on. Avanti! = Come in! / Go ahead!

etymology: From Latin avārus.

fact.text: From Latin avarus 'greedy', the same root as English avarice. Molière's comedy L'Avare (The Miser) is called L'avaro in Italian.

senses.note: Also a noun: un avaro, a miser. Forms: avaro/avara/avari/avare.

etymology: Inherited from Latin habēre.

fact.text: In ho, hai, ha and hanno the h is silent. It survives from Latin habere and is kept so that you can tell them apart in writing from o (or), ai (to the), a (to) and anno (year).

senses.note: Irregular: ho, hai, ha, abbiamo, avete, hanno. Also the main auxiliary for past tenses: ho mangiato.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin adverbium.

fact.text: From Latin adverbium, ad- 'towards' + verbum 'word, verb': a word added to the verb. It was probably a loan translation of Greek epirrhema.

etymology: From Latin adversārius.

senses.note: Feminine: l'avversaria. Also an adjective: la squadra avversaria.

etymology: From avvertire + -mento.

fact.text: Not an advertisement! The verb avvertire means 'to warn' or 'to notify'. An ad in Italian is una pubblicità.

senses.note: From avvertire, 'to warn'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin advertere, with change of conjugation.

fact.text: Not 'to advertise', although both come from Latin advertere 'to turn toward'. In Italian, to advertise is pubblicizzare or fare pubblicità.

senses.note: Also to notify and to sense: avvertire un dolore = to feel a pain.

etymology: From Latin ad- + via.

fact.text: Built from Latin ad- (to) + via (way), so it literally means 'to put on the way', which is how you get something going.

senses.note: Avviare il motore / il computer = to start the engine / the computer. Avviarsi = to set off.

etymology: From a- + vicino + -are.

fact.text: Built from a- + vicino ('near') + -are, so it literally means 'to make near'. Vicino goes back to Latin vicinus, the source of English vicinity.

senses.note: Reflexive avvicinarsi (a) = to approach, to come closer (auxiliary essere).
senses.prompt: to bring closer, to move near

fact.text: It is built on vicino (near), from Latin vicinus (neighbour), which is also the root of English vicinity.

senses.note: Use a before the place or person: mi sono avvicinato alla porta.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin advocātus.

fact.text: From Latin advocatus, 'one called to help' (ad + vocare), which is also where English 'advocate' comes from.

senses.note: Feminine: avvocata, or the older avvocatessa. Also used as a title: 'l'avvocato Rossi'.

etymology: From Latin vulturius, from vultur.
Borrowed from Old Spanish hazienda, from Latin facienda. Doublet of faccenda.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old Spanish hazienda, the same word as English 'hacienda'. Both come from Latin facienda, 'things to be done'. Italian faccenda ('chore, matter') comes from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Any business or firm: lavorare in un'azienda. Plural: le aziende.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin āctiōnem.

fact.text: In finance it means a company share: la Borsa trades azioni, and a shareholder is an azionista.

senses.note: Azione! = Action! (film set). In finance, le azioni = shares.

etymology: From Medieval Latin lazulum (through a variant lazurum and with rebracketing of the initial l- as the article l'), from Arabic لَازَوَرْد (lāzaward, “lapis lazuli”), from Persian لاجورد (lâjvard, “lapis lazuli”). Cognate with English azure, French azur, and Portuguese and Spanish azul.

fact.text: Same root as English azure: Persian lajvard, lapis lazuli, whose initial l- was mistaken for the article l'. Italy's national teams are nicknamed gli Azzurri.

senses.note: Different from blu (dark blue). Gli Azzurri = Italy's national sports teams.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *bábbọ, accusative-ablative form of *bábbọs, childish term of onomatopoeic origin.

fact.text: Even though the word is regional, every Italian knows Babbo Natale, 'Daddy Christmas', which is the Italian name for Santa Claus.

senses.note: Used mainly in Tuscany and central Italy. Elsewhere people say papà.

etymology: From older basciare, inherited from Latin bāsiāre (“to kiss”).

fact.text: From Latin basiare. The Latin word basium (kiss) was made famous by the poet Catullus: 'da mi basia mille', give me a thousand kisses.

senses.note: Baciarsi = to kiss each other.

etymology: Inherited from Latin bāsium (“kiss”). Cognate with Sicilian vasu.

senses.note: Baci e abbracci = hugs and kisses, a common way to sign off a message.

etymology: From Early Medieval Latin batāre.

senses.note: Takes a: badare ai bambini. Non badare a spese = spare no expense.

etymology: Uncertain.

fact.text: Italians say food is 'da leccarsi i baffi', good enough to lick your whiskers. 'Ridere sotto i baffi', laughing under your mustache, means to laugh up your sleeve.

senses.note: Usually plural for a mustache: i baffi. Also an animal's whiskers.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French bagage.

fact.text: Came through Old French bagage, which also gave English baggage. It goes back to Old Norse baggi, 'bundle', probably the source of English bag as well.

senses.note: Countable: un bagaglio = a piece of luggage, often plural i bagagli. Bagaglio a mano = hand luggage.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *baneāre, from Late Latin balneāre, from Latin balneum. Compare French baigner, Sicilian vagnari, Spanish bañar.

fact.text: Comes from Latin balneum, 'bath', which also gave Italian bagno (bath, bathroom). So to wet something is, in origin, to bathe it. Compare French baigner and Spanish bañar.

senses.note: Bagnare le piante = water the plants. Also used for rivers and seas: il Po bagna Torino.

fact.text: A common proverb is 'piove sempre sul bagnato', meaning it always rains on what's already wet. People say it when luck, good or bad, keeps landing on the same people.

senses.note: Past participle of bagnare (to wet, bathe). Bagnato fradicio = soaking wet.

etymology: Inherited from Latin baneum, variant of balneum.

senses.note: Also means bath. Fare il bagno = to have a bath, or to go for a swim.

etymology: From Late Latin balbitāre (cf. also balbūtīre), a derivative of balbāre, from Latin balbus (“stammering”). Compare French balbutier.

senses.note: Also transitive: balbettare una scusa = to stammer out an excuse.

etymology:

Medieval Latin balcōbor.
