Borrowed from Medieval Latin balcōnem. Compare Old Italian balco (“scaffold”).

fact.text: English borrowed 'balcony' from this word in the 1600s. It goes back to a Germanic word for 'beam', a relative of English 'balk'.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin ballāre.

fact.text: From Late Latin ballare 'to dance'. English 'ball' (a formal dance) and 'ballet' come from the same root, and so, through Old French and Provençal, does 'ballad', first a song for dancing.

senses.note: Regular -are verb with avere: ho ballato. Can also take an object: ballare il tango.

etymology: From ballare (“to dance”).

fact.text: English ball, meaning a dance party, comes from the same root: Late Latin ballare, 'to dance', via French bal. It has nothing to do with the round thing you throw.

senses.note: Also a formal ball. 'Essere in ballo' = to be at stake / involved.

etymology: Onomatopoeic bambo for the first stammerings of children, plus -ino (diminutive suffix).

fact.text: Built from bambo, an imitation of a small child's first babbling, plus the diminutive -ino. English borrowed bambino for a baby, especially in images of the infant Jesus.

senses.note: Means a young boy or a child of unspecified gender. A girl is bambina; the plural bambini means 'children'.

etymology: Onomatopoeic variant of bambino.

fact.text: The idiom 'andare in bambola' means to lose your concentration or go to pieces. Sports commentators often use it about a team that suddenly falls apart.

senses.note: Also slang for an attractive woman, as in 'Ciao, bambola!'

etymology: Borrowed from French banal, derived from ban (“declaration, announcement”).

fact.text: Comes from French banal, from feudal 'ban', a lord's decree. 'Banal' things, like the lord's mill or oven, were shared by every tenant, so the word came to mean 'common to all', then 'commonplace'.

senses.note: Also 'banal, trite'. Same form for both genders; plural banali.

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic bank (“bench”), from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeg- (“to bend”). Cognates include Spanish banco and Portuguese banco. Doublet of banco and panca.

fact.text: From Lombardic bank, 'bench': early money-changers worked at benches. Italian 'banca rotta' ('broken bench') gave English the word 'bankrupt'.

senses.note: Only the financial bank. A riverbank is la riva or la sponda.

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic bank, from Proto-West Germanic *banki, from Proto-Germanic *bankiz. Doublet of banca and panca. Cognate with Sicilian vancu.

fact.text: From Lombardic bank, 'bench', like its twins banca (bank) and panca (bench). Medieval money-changers worked at such benches, which is how English got bank via banca. English bench comes from the same Germanic root.

senses.note: Also a counter, a market stall, a bench, or a school of fish. An office desk is la scrivania.

fact.text: Originally a brand name: Bancomat is the trademark of Italy's interbank cash-machine network. It became so common that Italians now use it for any ATM, and for their debit card too.

senses.note: Invariable: i bancomat. Colloquially also means the debit card itself.
Combines banca + nota. Coins are monete.
English loanword, invariable: la band, le band. Gruppo is also common.

etymology: From Old Occitan, of Germanic origin, from Frankish *bindā (“tie, join, link”). Compare French bande.

senses.note: A town brass/marching band or a gang of crooks; a rock band is usually un gruppo or una band.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English bar. Doublet of barra.

fact.text: An Italian bar is mostly a coffee place: people drink a quick espresso standing at the counter, and often pay at the till first and then show the receipt.

senses.note: Plural doesn't change: i bar. Mainly serves coffee and snacks, though alcohol is sold too.

etymology: From Latin barba, from Proto-Italic *farðā, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰeh₂ (“beard”).

fact.text: English 'barber' comes from the same Latin barba, so a barber was originally the beard-trimmer. Italians also say 'che barba!' to mean 'what a bore!'

senses.note: Farsi la barba = to shave. Colloquially, che barba! = how boring!

From Late Latin barca, derived from Latin baris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris), itself probably from Egyptian bꜣjr (“transport ship”).

fact.text: Probably goes back to an ancient Egyptian word for a transport ship. It came through Greek baris into Latin, and English barge and bark (a sailing ship) are relatives.

senses.note: Usually a smaller vessel; a large ship is a nave. Andare in barca = to go boating.

etymology:
The origin of this word is uncertain. Both a pre-Celtic origin (ancient Ligurian) and a Celtic origin have been argued for.
Numerous toponyms of the Western Alps find their etymology in this term and its variations: e.g., the comune of Balme, the Colle della Barma and the village of Barmasc (which also contains the ancient ligurian suffix -asc/ascu).

fact.text: Possibly pre-Celtic (ancient Ligurian) or Celtic in origin. It survives in Western Alpine place names such as Balme and the Colle della Barma.

senses.note: Alpine dialect word (Piedmont, Aosta Valley) for a cave or rock overhang. Rare in standard Italian.

etymology: From Latin basis, from Ancient Greek βάσις (básis).

fact.text: Comes from Greek básis, originally 'a step', from bainein 'to go'. That verb also gives English 'acrobat', literally a tiptoe-walker.

senses.note: 'Di base' = basic; 'a base di' = based on/made with; 'in base a' = according to.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English baseball.

senses.note: Masculine: giocare a baseball.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bassus, possibly of Ancient Greek origin.

fact.text: The musical word 'bass' in English was originally spelled 'base'. It changed to its current spelling under the influence of Italian basso, 'low'.

senses.note: For height only. For length, use corto. Opposite: alto.

fact.text: Literally 'it suffices': it is the he/she/it form of the verb bastare (to be enough), frozen into an exclamation.

senses.note: Also 'Basta così' = that's enough like that; 'Basta!' = stop it!

etymology: From Medieval Latin bastardus, perhaps from Frankish.

fact.text: One popular theory links it to Old French 'fils de bast', meaning 'packsaddle son': a child conceived on a traveller's saddle blanket rather than in the marriage bed. The real origin is still debated.

ignored: Rare adjective use; the common insult is covered on the noun card bastardo.

senses.note: Literally born out of wedlock; for dogs, mixed-breed (cane bastardo). Often an insult.

etymology: From Medieval Latin bastardus, perhaps from Frankish.

fact.text: One popular theory links it to Old French 'fils de bast', meaning 'packsaddle son': a child conceived on a traveller's saddle blanket rather than in the marriage bed. The real origin is still debated.

senses.note: Insult, as in English. Can also mean an illegitimate child (dated) or a mongrel dog. Feminine: bastarda.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastāre (“to be enough; to suffice”), possibly derived from a modification of Late Latin bastum (“stick, staff, rod, pole”), from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō, “to lift, carry, bear, support (weight)”). Compare Sicilian bastari, Spanish and Portuguese bastar, French baster.

fact.text: The exclamation 'Basta!' (enough!) comes from this verb, which may go back to Greek bastazo, 'to carry or bear a weight'.

senses.note: Basta! = Enough! Basta + infinitive = all you need is to...
Bastoncini di pesce = fish fingers/sticks; i bastoncini also = chopsticks or ski poles.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin battālia, variant of battuālia, from Latin battuō.

fact.text: From Late Latin battalia, from battuere 'to beat'. The same root gives English battle, batter and combat, and Italian battere 'to beat'.

senses.note: Also figurative: una battaglia legale = a legal battle.

etymology: Inherited from Latin battere, from earlier battuere.

fact.text: From Latin battuere, 'to beat'. Through French the same root gave English battle, battery, batter and combat.

senses.note: Batti il cinque! = Give me five! / High five! Also 'to defeat' and 'to type'.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of battere.

fact.text: Comes from the past participle of battere (to beat or strike), so a quip is literally 'a hit'. Compare English 'a striking remark'.

senses.note: Fare una battuta = to crack a joke. It also means an actor's line or a musical bar.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin beātus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin beatus, meaning happy or blessed. The same root is behind English beatitude and beatify.

senses.note: Beato te! = Lucky you! Also a title for beatified people: il beato Angelico.

etymology: From becco (“beak, bill”) + -are.

fact.text: Built from becco, 'beak', so it literally means 'to beak' something. The slang sense 'to catch someone out' grew from the quick jab of a bird's peck.

senses.note: Colloquially also 'to catch, nab': ti ho beccato! = caught you!

etymology: Inherited from Latin beccus, from Gaulish *bekkos, from Proto-Celtic *bekkos.

fact.text: A rare Gaulish word in Italian. Suetonius wrote that a general born in Toulouse was nicknamed Beccus as a boy, Gaulish for a rooster's beak.

senses.note: Colloquial: chiudi il becco! = shut your trap! Also a gas burner (becco Bunsen).

etymology: From French bédouin, from Arabic بَدَوِيّ (badawiyy).

fact.text: Came into Italian through French bédouin, from Arabic badawiyy, meaning a desert dweller (badw = desert, open country).

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. Feminine: beduina.

etymology: Apocopic form of bene.

fact.text: Italian and English use the same word to open a sentence: beh works just like English 'well…'.

senses.note: Used to start a sentence or hesitate: 'Beh, vediamo.' Also written 'be''.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bellitia. By surface analysis, bello + -ezza.

senses.note: Che bellezza! = How lovely! / How wonderful!

etymology: Inherited from Latin bellus.

fact.text: Latin bellus came from Old Latin duenelos, a diminutive of duenos 'good' (later bonus), so 'beautiful' started out as 'little good'. English belle and embellish share the root.

senses.note: Before a noun it changes like the article: bel ragazzo, bello studente, bell'uomo, bei/begli.

etymology:
Univerbation of ben(e) + che.
Compare French bien que.

fact.text: A fusion of bene (well) + che (that), just like French bien que.

senses.note: Takes the subjunctive: benché sia stanco, esce.

etymology: Inherited from Latin bene.

fact.text: Comes from Latin bene, which also gave English benefit, benevolent and benefactor.

senses.note: Opposite: male. Sto bene = I'm fine. Va bene = OK.

etymology: From Latin benedīcere. By surface analysis, bene- + dire.

fact.text: Literally 'to speak well', from Latin bene 'well' + dicere 'to say', which also gives English benediction. Its opposite is maledire, 'to curse'.

senses.note: Conjugated like dire, but the tu imperative is benedici. Past participle: benedetto.

etymology: From Latin benna (“carriage”), from Gaulish benna (“carriage”).

fact.text: A rare survivor from Gaulish, the Celtic language of ancient France, where benna meant a wicker cart. English 'bin' is probably also of Celtic origin.

ignored: The only context is a garbled subtitle line, and the real meaning (excavator bucket) is too technical to be useful here.

senses.note: Technical: the scoop of an excavator or crane.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bene venūtus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, derived from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“a welcome guest or arrival”), from which many modern Germanic forms descend, such as English welcome. By surface analysis, ben (“well”, apocopic form of bene) + venuto (“come”, past participle of venire)

fact.text: Literally 'well come'. Vulgar Latin bene venutus may be a translation of a Germanic word for a welcome guest, from the same root that gave English 'welcome'.

senses.note: Agrees with the person or people welcomed: benvenuto, benvenuta, benvenuti, benvenute.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bene venūtus, presumably a calque of a Frankish term, derived from Proto-Germanic *wiljakwemô (“a welcome guest or arrival”), from which many modern Germanic forms descend, such as English welcome. By surface analysis, ben (“well”, apocopic form of bene) + venuto (“come”, past participle of venire)

fact.text: Literally 'well come'. Vulgar Latin bene venutus may be a translation of a Germanic word for a welcome guest, from the same root that gave English 'welcome'.

senses.note: Dare il benvenuto a qualcuno = to welcome someone. As an adjective it agrees: benvenuta, benvenuti.

etymology: Borrowed from German Benzin.

fact.text: Watch out at the pump: gasolio sounds like gasoline but means diesel. Gasoline is benzina, a word borrowed from German Benzin.

senses.note: Fare benzina = to fill up the tank. Diesel is gasolio.

etymology: From a contraction of earlier bevere, from Latin bibere, from Proto-Italic *pibō, from Proto-Indo-European *píph₃eti. Cognate with Albanian pi, literary Armenian ըմպել (əmpel), Hindi पीना (pīnā), and Irish ibh.

fact.text: Bere is a shortened form of the older bevere, from Latin bibere. That is why the stem bev- shows up in bevo and bevuto. English 'imbibe' and 'beverage' are related.

senses.note: Irregular: most forms use the stem bev- (bevo, bevuto), but the future is berrò.

etymology: From Old French bersail (“target for an arrow”), from berser (“to hunt with bow and arrow”), from Latin vervēx (“wether, kind of goat; blockhead, idiot”).

senses.note: Colpire il bersaglio = to hit the target; also used figuratively (bersaglio di critiche).

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin bēstia, but some sources consider it inherited. Cognate to biscia, which is definitely inherited.

senses.note: Also an insult (brute, idiot); andare in bestia = to fly into a rage.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *bibanda, from Latin bibenda, from bibendum.

fact.text: From Latin bibenda, 'things to be drunk'. It is related to Bibendum, the Michelin Man's name, which comes from Horace's 'nunc est bibendum' (now we must drink).

senses.note: Somewhat formal or written. In everyday speech, una bibita or qualcosa da bere.
Used in the plural: tiny young fish, fried or cooked in a frittata. A Ligurian specialty.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin blancus. Doublet of blanco, a borrowing from Spanish.

fact.text: Comes from Medieval Latin blancus, a Germanic loan related to English 'blank'. It replaced classical Latin albus, which survives in words like 'albino' and 'album'.

senses.note: Pasta in bianco = plain pasta (butter or oil, no tomato sauce). In bianco e nero = in black and white.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin bibita, from Latin bibere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin bibere, 'to drink', the same root behind English 'imbibe' and, via Old French, 'beverage'.

senses.note: Usually a cold, non-alcoholic drink; the general word for any drink is 'bevanda'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin bibliothēca, from Ancient Greek βιβλιοθήκη (bibliothḗkē, “library”). By surface analysis, biblio- + -teca.

fact.text: Watch out: Italian libreria looks like 'library' but means bookshop (or bookcase). For a library where you borrow books, use biblioteca, from Greek for 'book chest'.

senses.note: Can also mean a bookcase. A bookshop is 'libreria'.

etymology: From Late Latin bīcārium (cf. also Old French bichier, pichier, compare modern French pichet, English beaker, pitcher, German Becher, Dutch beker), itself possibly from bacarium, or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos).

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin bicarium, the same word behind English beaker (via Old Norse) and pitcher (via Old French pichier).

senses.note: Un bicchiere d'acqua = a glass of water. Glass the material is il vetro.

etymology: From bicicletta, by shortening.

senses.note: Short for bicicletta. Invariable: la bici, le bici. andare in bici = to cycle.

etymology: Borrowed from French bicyclette. By surface analysis, biciclo + -etta.

senses.note: Often shortened to la bici (invariable). Andare in bicicletta = to ride a bike.

etymology: Pseudo-anglicism, derived from big shot.

fact.text: This is a pseudo-anglicism: in Italian it's a noun meaning a star or top name, not an adjective. At the Sanremo song festival, the established artists compete in the 'Big' category.

senses.note: Invariable: i big della musica. Common in journalism.

etymology: From biglietto + -eria.

senses.note: From biglietto 'ticket'. Also a box office at a theatre or stadium.

etymology: From French billet, from Old French billette, derived from Latin bulla (“document”).

fact.text: Comes from French billet, ultimately from Latin bulla, a sealed document. English bill and bulletin come from the same source.

senses.note: Also a card or short note: biglietto d'auguri = greetings card.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bilancia, from Latin bilanx (“balance with two scalepans”), from bi- (see Latin bis) and lanx.

fact.text: From Latin bilanx, from bi- 'two' + lanx 'dish', meaning a scale with two pans. English balance comes from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Also the zodiac sign Libra (la Bilancia).

fact.text: Italian property listings don't count the kitchen and bathroom as rooms, so a bilocale is usually a one-bedroom flat: a living room plus a bedroom.

senses.note: Compare monolocale (studio) and trilocale (three rooms).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin binārius.

fact.text: This comes from Latin binarius, 'consisting of two', the same source as English 'binary'. A railway track is made of two rails side by side.

senses.note: At stations, binario 5 = platform 5 (track 5). The platform you stand on is la banchina.

etymology: Medieval Latin blondus, of Germanic origin: probably from Frankish *blund (“a mixed color between golden and light-brown”), from Proto-Germanic *blundaz (“mixed, blinding”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰlendʰ-. Compare French blond.

senses.note: Agrees in gender: biondo, bionda. 'Una birra bionda' is a lager.

etymology: Borrowed from German Bier.

fact.text: Borrowed from German Bier. Latin had its own beer word, cerevisia, which survives in Spanish cerveza, but Italian took its word from the north.

senses.note: Una birra can also mean a glass or bottle of beer: due birre, per favore.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin biscoctus. Synchronicallty bis- (“twice”) + cotto (“baked, cooked”). Doublet of biscuit.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin biscoctus, 'twice-cooked'. English biscuit comes from the same word via French. In English 'biscotti' means one kind of cookie, but in Italian it covers them all.

senses.note: Covers any sweet biscuit or cookie, not just the hard almond kind English calls biscotti.

etymology: From bisogno + -are.

senses.note: Impersonal: bisogna partire = we must leave; bisogna che tu venga = you need to come.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Frankish *bisunnijabor.
Vulgar Latin *bisonium
Italian bisogno
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *bisonium, borrowed from Frankish *bisunnija.

fact.text: This is a Germanic word in Italian. It comes from Frankish via Vulgar Latin and shares its root with French besoin. Watch out: 'fare i bisogni' is a polite way to say relieving oneself, often said of pets.

senses.note: avere bisogno di = to need (ho bisogno di te); non c'è bisogno = there's no need

etymology: Borrowed from English beefsteak.

fact.text: Borrowed from English 'beefsteak' and respelled the Italian way. Say bis-tecca aloud and you can still hear beef-steak.

senses.note: Famous dish: bistecca alla fiorentina, a thick T-bone steak from Florence.

etymology: Borrowed from French bloquer.

senses.note: Bloccarsi = to get stuck or jam: il computer si è bloccato.

etymology: Borrowed from French bleu (“blue”) from Middle French bleu, from Old French blou, bleve (“pallid, wan, discoloured/discolored, blue”), from Frankish *blāu, from Proto-Germanic *blēwaz (“blue, yellowish-gray”). Doublet of biavo.

fact.text: Italian treats two blues as separate colours: blu is dark blue and azzurro is sky blue. Italy's national sports teams are called gli Azzurri.

senses.note: Invariable: le macchine blu. Usually means dark blue; light/sky blue is azzurro.

etymology: From Latin bucca.

fact.text: Italians wish each other good luck by saying 'In bocca al lupo!' (into the wolf's mouth). The traditional reply is 'Crepi!' (may it die), not 'thank you'.

etymology: From boccia + -are.

fact.text: From boccia, the bocce ball. In the game, 'bocciare' means knocking an opponent's ball away. At school, being bocciato can mean repeating the whole year.

senses.note: Transitive: the teacher fails you. Essere bocciato = to fail (an exam or the school year).

fact.text: One of the most common sounds in spoken Italian. It usually comes with a shrug and pushed-out lips, and it can carry anything from honest doubt to total indifference.

senses.note: Informal interjection for doubt, often with a shrug. Also spelled bho.

etymology: From Latin bulla.

fact.text: Latin bulla meant 'bubble' and also the round seal attached to papal documents. That is why a papal decree is called a bull in English.

senses.note: Also 'blister' on the skin.
Acqua bollente = boiling water. Figuratively it can also mean hot or passionate.

etymology: From bolla + -etta.

fact.text: Being broke in Italian is 'essere in bolletta'. The word is a diminutive of bolla, a seal on official documents, from the same Latin bulla as the papal bull.

senses.note: For utilities: la bolletta della luce/del gas. A restaurant bill is il conto.

etymology: From bolletta + -ino.

senses.note: bollettino meteo = weather report; bollettino postale = postal payment slip.

etymology: From Latin bullīre (“to bubble, boil”), from bulla (“bubble”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin bulla, 'bubble'. The same word gave English 'ebullient' (bubbling over) and the papal 'bull', which was named after its round seal.

senses.note: Works both ways: l'acqua bolle (the water boils) and bollire le patate (boil the potatoes).

etymology: From Latin bombus (“a boom”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek bómbos, an imitation of a booming or buzzing sound. The same word gave the bumblebee genus its name, Bombus.

senses.note: Colloquially, è una bomba! = it's amazing / a smash.

etymology: From bombardare + -mento.
Deverbal from bonificare + -o.

fact.text: It comes from bonificare, 'to make good', which also means to drain marshland. So a bonifica is land reclamation, while a bonifico is a money transfer.

senses.note: Fare un bonifico = to make a bank transfer.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bordum (“plank, board”), from Frankish *bord, from Proto-Germanic *burdą (“board; table”).

fact.text: It comes from Frankish *bord, a relative of English 'board'. That is why a bordo means 'on board' a ship, just as in English.

senses.note: Also rim or border. A bordo = on board (a ship or plane).

etymology: From borgo + -etto.
ignored: In the context, Borghetti is a surname, not the noun borghetto.

senses.note: Diminutive of borgo (village). Can also mean a shanty town.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin bursa.

fact.text: Comes from Greek byrsa, 'hide, leather', through Late Latin bursa. English 'purse', 'bursar' and 'reimburse' come from the same leather bag.

senses.note: Also means 'stock exchange' (la Borsa) and 'scholarship' (borsa di studio).

etymology: borsa + -etta.

fact.text: A small borsa (bag). Borsa comes from Late Latin bursa 'leather bag', which also gave English purse, bursar and reimburse.

senses.note: Diminutive of borsa (bag). Called a purse in US English.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin boscus, borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.

fact.text: Probably a Germanic word that came into Latin as boscus, perhaps from Frankish *busk. English 'bush' likely comes from the same Germanic root.

senses.note: Usually smaller than a foresta; wood as a material is il legno.

etymology: Borrowed from French bouteille.

fact.text: Borrowed from French bouteille, from Old French boteille, the same source as English bottle. Both go back to Late Latin butticula, a little cask.

senses.note: Usually plural: i bovini. Singular il bovino = a bovine animal.

etymology:
From Vulgar Latin *bottia, a Germanic borrowing, from Frankish *boce (“knob”), from Old High German bozzan (“to beat”), from Proto-West Germanic *bautan (“to push, strike”). Compare French bosse, Occitan bossa; also Romanian bot.
Alternatively, a northern variant of Italian boccia, from a Latin root *buttia, from Latin buttis.

senses.note: Le bozze can also be printer's proofs. Correggere le bozze = to proofread.

etymology: Inherited from Latin brachium, bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn).

fact.text: From Latin bracchium 'arm', which through French bras also gave English 'bracelet' and 'embrace', literally putting something around the arm or in your arms.

senses.note: Irregular plural: le braccia (body); i bracci for arms of objects, rivers, buildings.

etymology: Uncertain, from Old French braon (“slice of meat”) or Old Spanish brahon, from Frankish *brādon, from Proto-Germanic *brēdô. Compare English brawn.

fact.text: Probably from a Germanic word for a slice of meat, which also gave English brawn. The original idea was a torn-off chunk, later a 'piece' of a text.

senses.note: Leggere un brano = to read a passage. Also used for a song or track: il nuovo brano della band.

etymology:
Uncertain. Probably from Vulgar Latin *bravus, from a fusion of Latin prāvus and barbarus. Less likely from Provençal brau (“show-off”), from Gaulish *bragos (compare Middle Irish breagha (modern breá) 'fine', Breton braga 'to strut'). Or perhaps borrowed from a descendant of Proto-Germanic *hrawaz (“raw, uncooked”). Or possibly from a root *bravus, from bravium. Borrowed into French and English as brave.
Pierre Carpentier, in an 18th-century edition of du Cange's 17th-century dictionary of medieval and modern Latin, argued Latin branus originated in a misreading of Italian and Spanish bravo. However, George Nicholson argues the opposite in a 1950 Festschrift article, namely bravo being a misreading of Latin branus, which would have the origin du Cange had originally argued for, from Old French brahaigne (“barren”) (see barren). Compare English gravy, possibly a misreading of French grané (“stew”).

fact.text: Today it rarely means 'brave' (that is coraggioso), even though English brave was borrowed from it. It usually means skilled or well-behaved.

senses.note: Used for people: è bravo a cucinare = he's good at cooking. Bravo! = well done!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin brevis (“short”).

fact.text: From Latin brevis, short, which also gave English brief, brevity and abbreviate.

senses.note: In breve = in short. For physical length use corto.
Same form for masculine and feminine. As a noun, un brillante = a cut diamond.

etymology: From Late Latin brodium, from Frankish *broþ, from Proto-Germanic *bruþą, the same root as English broth. Compare French brouet, Old French breu, Catalan brou, Piedmontese breu, Friulian brût, Sicilian brodu, Spanish bodrio, Portuguese brodo.

fact.text: This is a Germanic word in Italian. It comes from Proto-Germanic *bruþą, the same root that gave English 'broth'.

senses.note: Pasta in brodo = pasta served in broth. Idiom: tutto fa brodo = every little bit helps.

etymology:
From a Vulgar Latin *brusiāre, itself of uncertain origin; possibly from a form *prustiāre < *per-ust(u)lāre, from Latin per + ustulāre (compare perurere), or alternatively from a corruption of *combustulāre, from a change of prefix of ambustulāre, influenced by combustus; see ambūrēre. However, an Italian word brustolare (cf. abbrustolire), from a related root *brustulāre, from ustulāre, also exists. The initial br- may also be of Germanic origin.
Compare French brûler (Old French brusler), Dalmatian brusur, Occitan bruslar, buizar, Romansh brischar, Venetan bruxar.

senses.note: avere when transitive (ho bruciato la cena), essere when intransitive (la casa è bruciata).
Mi sono bruciato la mano = I burned my hand. Figuratively: to ruin one's chances.

etymology: Derived from Latin brūtus. Doublet of bruto.

fact.text: From Latin brutus, 'dull, stupid', the same source as English 'brute' and 'brutal'. Italian also has the doublet bruto, meaning 'brutish'.

senses.note: Also means 'bad' or 'nasty': brutto tempo means bad weather. 'Brutta copia' is a rough draft.

etymology: From the verb bucare, from buca, or from either Old Frankish *būk (“cavity, stomach”) or Gothic *𐌱𐌿𐌺𐍃 (*būks), both from Proto-Germanic *būkaz (“belly, torso”). Compare Occitan/Catalan buc ("torso; cow's chest"). More at bouk.

fact.text: Fare un buco nell'acqua, literally to make a hole in the water, means to try something and get nowhere.

senses.note: The plural buchi adds an h to keep the hard k sound.
Same form for men and women (il/la buddista). Also used as an adjective: un monaco buddista.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan bauzia, from Old Frankish *bausī (“deceit”) (possibly through a Vulgar Latin *bauscia (compare also Friulian bausie, Dalmatian bosca, Old French boisie), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bausuz (“puffed up, arrogant, bad”). Cognate with Dutch boos, German böse, English boast.

fact.text: In Piedmont and Liguria, bugie are also sugar-dusted fried pastries eaten at Carnival. The word came through Occitan from Frankish and is related to German böse, 'bad'.

senses.note: Dire una bugia = to tell a lie.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *burius (“red, dark”), either from Latin burrus (“reddish-brown”) or, less likely, from Latin furvus (“dark, dusky”).

senses.note: Avere paura del buio = to be afraid of the dark. Buio pesto = pitch dark.

etymology: Univerbation of buona (“good”) + notte (“night, nighttime”).

fact.text: In colloquial speech, '... e buonanotte!' means 'and that's that!' or 'end of story'. It is said when something is settled or hopeless.

senses.note: Said when going to bed or parting late at night. Buonasera is the general evening greeting.

etymology: Univerbation of buona (“good”) + notte (“night, nighttime”).

fact.text: In colloquial speech, '... e buonanotte!' means 'and that's that!' or 'end of story'. It is said when something is settled or hopeless.

ignored: This rare noun use is covered by the interjection buonanotte ('good night'), which has its own card.

senses.note: Mostly used as a greeting: Buonanotte!

etymology: Compare French bonsoir, Romanian bună seara.

fact.text: In much of Italy, people switch from buongiorno to buonasera early, often right after lunch. Many Italians say it in the mid-afternoon, not just in the evening.

senses.note: Also written 'buona sera'. A polite greeting for both arriving and leaving.

fact.text: In much of Italy, people switch from buongiorno to buonasera early, often right after lunch. Many Italians say it in the mid-afternoon, not just in the evening.

ignored: Rare noun use; the ordinary meaning is studied on the interjection card buonasera.

senses.note: As a noun: dare la buonasera = to say good evening.

etymology: Univerbation of buono (“good”) + giorno (“day”).

senses.note: Used from morning to early afternoon. Later in the day, switch to buonasera.

ignored: Noun use of the greeting; the interjection buongiorno is studied on its own card.

senses.note: Used until early afternoon; afterwards say buonasera.

etymology: Inherited from Latin bonus. Doublet of bonus, a later borrowing.

fact.text: Comes from Latin bonus 'good', the same word English borrowed as bonus, literally a 'good' extra.

senses.note: Shortens to buon before most masculine nouns (buon giorno). Also means tasty (è buono!). Very good: buonissimo.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French burre, from Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτυρον (boúturon). Doublet of butirro.

fact.text: Don't mix it up with Spanish 'burro', which means donkey! The Italian word comes through Old French from Greek boútyron, the same source as English 'butter'.

senses.note: Usually uncountable. al burro = with butter (e.g. pasta al burro).

etymology: Borrowed from Old French boiste, whence French boîte (“box”). Derived from Medieval Latin buxida, inflected form derived from Latin buxētum (“boxwood plantation”), from Latin buxus (“boxwood”).

fact.text: Like English box, it goes back to Latin words for boxwood, a wood once used to make small containers. It is related to French boîte, 'box'.

senses.note: Also a bag, especially a shopping bag (busta della spesa).

etymology: From Old French bouter (“to strike”), of Germanic origin. Compare Neapolitan vottare and Sicilian vottare.

fact.text: Comes from Old French bouter, 'to strike, push', which is of Germanic origin. English 'butt' (to ram with the head) comes from the same Old French verb.

senses.note: buttare via = to throw away; buttare fuori = to throw out (a person). buttare la pasta = to put the pasta in.

etymology: Borrowed from French cabine.

senses.note: Cabina telefonica = phone booth. A wooden mountain cabin is una baita or capanna.

etymology: Deverbal from cacciare + -a, from Late Latin captiāre. Related to English chase, catch.

fact.text: It comes from Late Latin captiare, 'to try to catch'. That verb came into English twice through French, giving both chase and catch.

senses.note: 'Andare a caccia' = to go hunting. Il caccia (m., invariable) = fighter jet.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *captiāre, from Latin captus. Doublet of cazzare.

fact.text: Comes from Vulgar Latin *captiare 'to try to catch'. The same word passed through French into English twice, giving us both chase and catch.

senses.note: Also very common as 'to throw out, drive away': cacciare qualcuno di casa.

etymology: From Latin cadāver.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cadaver, probably from cadere 'to fall', so a corpse is 'one who has fallen'. The popular claim that it stands for 'caro data vermibus' (flesh given to worms) is a myth.

senses.note: Stress on the second syllable: ca-DA-ve-re.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cadēre, from Latin cadĕre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cadere 'to fall', the same root behind English cadence (a falling of the voice), decay and accident (something that 'falls' upon you).

senses.note: Takes essere: sono caduto/a. Irregular future: cadrò. Past remote: caddi.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of cadere (“to fall”).

senses.note: Also figurative: la caduta dell'Impero; caduta dei capelli = hair loss.

etymology: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish قهوه (kahve), from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa).

fact.text: Order 'un caffè' in Italy and you get an espresso. Ask for a long milky coffee with a caffè latte. The word came via Ottoman Turkish kahve from Arabic qahwa.

senses.note: Invariable: due caffè. Also means a café.

etymology: From Latin calx (“heel”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin calx, 'heel', so the sport is basically called 'kicking'. Every June, Florence still plays calcio storico, a very rough Renaissance version of the game.

senses.note: Also means 'kick' (plural calci): prendere a calci = to kick. Giocare a calcio = to play soccer.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin calculāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin calculare, from calculus, 'small pebble'. Romans counted with pebbles on an abacus, so calculating originally meant moving little stones around.

senses.note: Also 'to reckon, to take into account': calcolare i tempi = to plan the timing.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cal(i)dus. Doublet of calido, which was borrowed.

senses.note: Ho caldo = I'm hot (I feel hot); fa caldo = it's hot (weather).

etymology:
Origin uncertain. Possibly from Late Latin cauma, from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma, “heat, heat of the sun”). Compare Late Latin caumāre (“to rest during the heat (of the day), to siesta”), Sursilvan Romansh cauma (“resting place for livestock, especially during the noon heat”). If the Italian (and Ibero-Romance) word calma originally referred to the heat of the sun, especially around noon (and later to quiet during this time of the day), it may have been influenced by words like Latin calor (“heat”) and cal(i)dus (“hot”), accounting for cal- instead of the expected cau-.
Compare also Proto-Germanic *kalmaz (“frozenness, cold”).

fact.text: Probably from Greek kauma, 'midday heat': the still hour when everyone rested out of the sun. English calm came from this same word by way of French.

senses.note: Calma! = Calm down! Con calma = take your time, no rush.
Reflexive: mi calmo, ti calmi… 'Calmati!' = Calm down! Takes essere: mi sono calmato.

etymology: From calmare (“to calm”) + -o.

fact.text: English 'calm' came from Italian calma. That word is usually traced to Greek kauma, 'burning heat': the stillness of the hot midday hours, when everyone rested.

senses.note: Also used for a still sea (mare calmo). Feminine calma.

etymology: From Latin calōrem.

fact.text: It comes from Latin calor, the root of English calorie, which was first a unit of heat. Be careful: a calorie in Italian is caloria, not calore.

senses.note: For hot weather Italians usually say il caldo. Calore also means warmth, as in warmth of feeling.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus (“shoe”).

fact.text: On 6 January Italian children get 'la calza della Befana', a stocking the kindly witch Befana fills with sweets, or with coal if they've been naughty.

senses.note: Can also mean sock, but short socks are usually calzini.

etymology: From cambiare + -mento.

senses.note: A change or shift, not money: small change is il resto or gli spiccioli.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin cambiāre, from change in conjugation of cambīre. Doublet of cangiare. Cognate with Neapolitan cagnà.

fact.text: English 'change' comes from the same Late Latin word, cambiare, through Old French changier. So this Italian verb and the English one are siblings.

senses.note: Avere when transitive (ho cambiato idea); essere when intransitive (tutto è cambiato).

etymology: Deverbal from cambiare + -o. From verb cambiare inherited from Vulgar Latin cambiāre (“to change, exchange”) from Late Latin cambiō, or from corresponding noun Latin cambium (“change”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂emp- (“to bend, curve”). Compare Spanish cambio and Portuguese câmbio.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin cambiare, 'to exchange'. The same Latin verb passed through Old French changier to give English 'change', so the two words are close relatives.

senses.note: Coins given back are 'il resto', not il cambio. Also means exchange rate and gearbox (cambio manuale).

etymology: From Latin camera, from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára). Doublet of zambra.

fact.text: False friend: this means room, and a photo camera is una macchina fotografica. English camera is short for camera obscura, Latin for 'dark room'.

senses.note: camera da letto = bedroom; camera singola/doppia in hotels

etymology: From camera (“room”) + -iere. Compare Spanish camarero, Late Latin camerārius (“chamberlain”).

fact.text: Built from camera ('room'), so it first meant a chamber servant. It is a cousin of English 'chamberlain'. Watch out: in Italian, camera means room, not camera.

senses.note: Feminine: cameriera (waitress, or maid).

etymology: From Late Latin camisia, from Transalpine Gaulish, of Germanic origin, from Proto-West Germanic *hamiþi.

fact.text: From Late Latin camisia, which also gave French chemise. English later borrowed that as 'chemise', a loose undergarment.

senses.note: A button-up shirt; a T-shirt is una maglietta. Camicia da notte = nightgown.

etymology: From Latin camīnus, from Ancient Greek κάμῑνος (kámīnos).

fact.text: It comes from Greek kaminos, 'furnace', through Latin caminus. English chimney has the same origin, via French cheminée.

senses.note: Can also mean chimney. Don't confuse it with cammino (path, journey), which has a double m.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French camion.

senses.note: Invariable: il camion, i camion.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *camellus, from Latin camēlus, from Ancient Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos), of Semitic origin.

fact.text: It reached Latin through Greek kámēlos from a Semitic word, compare Hebrew gāmāl and Arabic jamal.

senses.note: Plural: cammelli. Also short for a camel-hair coat.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, cammino + -are. Compare French cheminer, Spanish caminar and Portuguese caminhar.

fact.text: Built on cammino 'path, way', from Late Latin camminus, thought to come from Gaulish (Celtic). It is related to Spanish camino and French chemin.

ignored: Noun use of the infinitive; studied on the verb card camminare.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cammīnāre. By surface analysis, cammino + -are. Compare French cheminer, Spanish caminar and Portuguese caminhar.

fact.text: Built on cammino 'path, way', from Late Latin camminus, thought to come from Gaulish (Celtic). It is related to Spanish camino and French chemin.

senses.note: For 'to go for a walk', say fare una passeggiata.

etymology: From a Neapolitan word supposedly from Spanish camorra (“dispute, quarrel”).

fact.text: Comes from a Neapolitan word, possibly from Spanish camorra, 'quarrel, brawl'. The exact origin is still debated.

senses.note: The crime organisation of Naples and Campania. A member is a camorrista.

etymology: From Late Latin campānia (whence also Spanish campaña, Portuguese and Occitan campanha, French champagne), from campāneus, based on Latin campus (“level field”). Doublet of champagne, borrowed from French.

fact.text: From Late Latin campania, 'open country', from campus, 'field'. English 'campaign' (armies taking the field) and the French region Champagne come from the same source.

senses.note: Andare in campagna = to go to the countryside. Also means campaign (political or military).

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English camper.

fact.text: Borrowed from English but only means the vehicle (a motorhome), never a person who goes camping. Like most English loans, it does not change in the plural.

senses.note: Invariable: i camper. A person who camps is un campeggiatore.

etymology: From Medieval Latin or Late Latin campiōnem, campiōnem (“champion, fighter”), from Frankish *kampijō (or a Lombardic equivalent) from Proto-Germanic *kampijô, based on Latin campus (“level ground”).

fact.text: This word comes from Latin campus, meaning 'field'. A champion was originally a fighter who took the field, often on someone else's behalf.

senses.note: Also means 'sample': un campione gratuito = a free sample. A female champion is la campionessa.

etymology: From Latin campus (“wild field”). Compare English camp.

fact.text: In Venice almost every square is called a campo, because they were once grassy fields. Only St Mark's gets the name piazza. English camp and campus come from the same Latin campus.

senses.note: Also a sports pitch (campo da calcio) or a field of study. No signal = non c'è campo.

etymology: Inherited from Latin canālem.

fact.text: English canal and channel both come from Latin canalis, 'pipe, groove'. Channel came through Old French. Italian kept one word for both.

senses.note: Also a canal (i canali di Venezia) and a TV channel (cambiare canale).

etymology: From Latin cancellāre. Sense “to cancel” influenced by English cancel.

fact.text: From Latin cancellus, 'lattice', because crossed-out writing looks like a grid. The same root gives Italian cancello ('gate').

senses.note: Also means 'to cross out' and, under English influence, 'to cancel' (an event, for example).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cancrum. Compare the doublet granchio (“crab”), inherited through a Vulgar Latin diminutive form.

fact.text: Latin cancer meant 'crab'; its 'tumour' sense copied Greek karkinos, which meant both. Italian also inherited the ordinary word for a crab, granchio, from the same Latin root.

senses.note: Also used figuratively for a social evil. Cancro is also the star sign Cancer.

etymology: From the Latin canis, canem (“dog”). Cognate with Sicilian cani.

fact.text: It can also mean 'awful' after a noun: fa un freddo cane means it's bitterly cold. A bad actor or singer can also be called un cane.

senses.note: Cagna = female dog. Attenti al cane = beware of the dog.

etymology: From French kangourou, from Guugu Yimidhirr gangurru.

fact.text: Comes from gangurru in Guugu Yimidhirr, an Aboriginal Australian language. The popular story that 'kangaroo' means 'I don't understand' is a myth.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il cantante / la cantante.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cantāre, frequentative of canō. Cognate with French chanter, Occitan and Spanish cantar.

fact.text: From Latin cantare, a frequentative of canere (to sing). The same family gives English chant and cantata.

senses.note: In slang it can also mean to squeal, as in confessing to the police.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cantherius.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cantherius, which meant a gelding or pack horse and also a supporting beam. The word may go back to a Greek term for a pack donkey.

senses.note: Also a shipyard (cantiere navale). Lavori in corso signs often mark a cantiere.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *canthus (“corner”), from Gaulish *cantos, denoting the location for liquor storage, from Proto-Celtic *cantos (“corner”), from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂ndʰ-. Perhaps cognate with Ancient Greek κανθός (kanthós, “corner of the eye”), but this is unconvincing.

fact.text: Not a canteen, even though English 'canteen' comes from this word through French cantine. A canteen in Italian is a mensa. A cantina is a cellar or winery.

senses.note: Also a winery: cantina sociale = wine cooperative.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cantiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin chaos from Ancient Greek χάος (kháos).

fact.text: Greek kháos meant 'gap, void'. In the 1600s the Flemish chemist van Helmont based the new word 'gas' on it, so 'gas' is a cousin of chaos.

senses.note: Invariable and usually singular. Stress falls on the first syllable: CA-os.

etymology: From Latin capācem (“capacious; capable, able”).

fact.text: Shares its root with English capacity: Latin capax meant able to hold a lot. It can still mean roomy, as in una borsa capace, a roomy bag.

senses.note: Essere capace di + infinitive: sono capace di nuotare = I can swim.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin capācitātem.

senses.note: The plural doesn't change: le capacità. It can also mean volume or holding capacity.

etymology: From Latin capillus.

fact.text: From Latin capillus, 'hair', which also gave English capillary, a blood vessel as fine as a hair. Don't mix it up with cappello, 'hat', which has a double p.

senses.note: I capelli (plural) = a person's hair; un capello = one hair. Body or animal hair is pelo.

Inherited from Latin capiō (“to take in, understand”), from Proto-Italic *kapiō, from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂pyéti, from the root *kap- (“to seize, grab”). Compare Galician, Spanish, and Portuguese caber (“to fit”), Catalan capir (“to understand”), and German kapieren (“to understand”).

fact.text: American slang 'capeesh?' comes from capisce? 'do you understand?'. The root is Latin capere 'to seize', meaning to grasp an idea.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: capisco, capisci, capisce, capiamo, capite, capiscono. Capito? = Got it?

ignored: Infinitive with an attached pronoun (capire + li); the meaning is studied on the card for capire.

senses.note: capire + li (them).

ignored: Infinitive capire plus the pronoun ti, not a headword; study it on the capire card.

senses.note: capire + ti: the infinitive drops its final -e and the pronoun is attached.

etymology: Noun use of the above adjective.

senses.note: Feminine means the city. Masculine 'il capitale' means capital in the sense of money.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin capitaneus, from Latin caput.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *capitāre, from Latin caput. Compare Romanian căpăta.

fact.text: Comes via Vulgar Latin *capitare from caput 'head', the same Latin root as English capital, chapter and captain.

senses.note: Often impersonal: capita che… = it happens that…; mi capita = it happens to me.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin capus, from Latin caput, from Proto-Italic *kaput, from Proto-Indo-European *káput. Doublet of chef.

fact.text: From Latin caput 'head'. The same root gave French chef, which originally meant 'head, chief', and English 'captain' and 'cape' (a headland).

senses.note: Also 'head' (da capo = from the top) and 'item of clothing' (capo d'abbigliamento).

etymology: From capo d'anno (literally “head of [the] year”).

fact.text: A fusion of capo d'anno, literally 'head of the year', the same idea as Hebrew Rosh Hashanah, which also means 'head of the year'.

senses.note: Often capitalized. Also means the New Year's Eve celebrations: Cosa fai a Capodanno?

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin cappellus, diminutive from Late Latin cappa.

fact.text: Watch the double p. Capello with one p means a single hair, and capelli means hair. So 'mi piacciono i tuoi cappelli' (your hats) is easy to mix up with 'i tuoi capelli' (your hair).

senses.note: Cappellino = small hat or cap (diminutive).

etymology: From cappa.

senses.note: A heavy overcoat; a lighter jacket is 'la giacca'.

etymology: From cappuccio (“hood, cowl”) + -ino. The coffee gets its name from the color of the beverage, which is reminiscent of the color of monks' habits.

fact.text: Named after the Capuchin friars, whose brown hooded habits (cappuccio means 'hood') matched the drink's colour. Italians rarely order one after late morning.

senses.note: Plural cappuccini. Usually drunk at breakfast.

etymology: From carabina + -iere.

fact.text: The name comes from carabina, 'carbine'. The Carabinieri were set up in 1814 in the Kingdom of Sardinia (Piedmont) as soldiers armed with carbines. Today they are one of Italy's main police forces.

senses.note: A member of the Carabinieri, Italy's military police force. An ordinary policeman is a poliziotto.

etymology: From Latin charactērem (““characteristic”, “mark””), from Ancient Greek χαρακτήρ (kharaktḗr).

fact.text: A character in a story or film is not un carattere but un personaggio. Carattere means someone's personality or temper, or a written letter or symbol.

senses.note: Ha un brutto carattere = he/she is bad-tempered. Also means a written character or a font.

etymology: From Latin carcerem, from Proto-Italic *karkros, from Proto-Indo-European *kr-kr- (“circular”), reduplication of *(s)ker- (“to turn, bend”), in the sense of “enclosure”. Cognate to Old Catalan càrcer/carçre, Spanish cárcel and Portuguese cárcere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin carcer, the root of English incarcerate. In ancient Rome, the carceres were also the starting gates for chariot races.

senses.note: Masculine in the singular (il carcere) but feminine in the plural (le carceri). Andare in carcere = to go to prison.

etymology: From Late Latin carricāre (“to load, to charge”).

senses.note: Battery charge or a charge in battle. Also a public office: in carica = in office.

etymology: From Late Latin carricāre, from Latin carrus. Cognate with Sicilian carricari.

fact.text: From Late Latin carricare, 'to load a wagon', from carrus, 'wagon'. English charge (via French) and cargo (via Spanish) come from the same verb, and car comes from carrus.

senses.note: Also to upload (files), charge (a battery) and wind (a watch).

etymology: From the short past participle of caricare (“to load”) in Tuscan; compare the Standard Italian participle caricato.

fact.text: Comes from caricare (to load). English cargo, which came through Spanish cargar, goes back to the same Late Latin verb for loading a cart.

senses.note: Also an adjective: carico di = loaded with. A carico di = at the expense of.

etymology: From caro + -ino.

fact.text: Built from caro 'dear' plus the diminutive ending -ino, so it literally means 'little dear'.

senses.note: Also 'nice, kind': che carino da parte tua! = how sweet of you!

etymology: Inherited from Latin carnem (“flesh”, “meat”), from Proto-Italic *karō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin caro/carnem, 'flesh', the root of English carnivore. Carnival likely comes from carne levare, 'to remove meat', before Lent.

senses.note: Also 'flesh'. In carne e ossa = in the flesh.

etymology:
From Latin carnem levāre (“to take away/remove meat”), calque of Ancient Greek ἀπόκρεως (apókreōs). Compare Old Italian carnasciale (“carnival”) from carnem laxāre, Romanian cârneleagă from carnem ligat, Sicilian carnaluvari and carruali, Spanish carnestolendas (“three days preceding the beginning of Lent”) from carnis tollendus.
Other theories suggest it comes from Latin carneālis (“meaty”) or carnuālis (“feast”).

fact.text: Probably from Latin carnem levare, 'to take away meat', referring to the feast before the Lenten fast. English carnival was borrowed from this Italian word.

senses.note: The festival before Lent. Famous ones are held in Venice and Viareggio.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cārus.

fact.text: Just like English dear, which in British English can also mean pricey, this word means both 'beloved' and 'expensive'.

senses.note: Also means expensive: è troppo caro = it's too expensive.

etymology: From Latin carōta, from Ancient Greek κᾰρωτόν (kărōtón).

Borrowed from Old Occitan carreira or its variants (compare modern Occitan carrièra, also French carrière), from Late Latin carrāria, from Latin carrus. Compare the inherited doublet carraia, now archaic.

fact.text: Goes back to Late Latin carraria, a road for carts, from carrus (cart). So it shares a root with English 'car'. A career was first a road you raced along.

senses.note: fare carriera = to get ahead in one's career. Archaic: di gran carriera = at full speed.

etymology: Inherited from Latin charta, from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “papyrus, paper”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek khartēs, 'papyrus, paper', via Latin charta. English card, chart and charter all come from the same word.

senses.note: Carta igienica = toilet paper. Also 'map' or 'menu'.

fact.text: Named after an English inventor, J. Harrison Carter, who patented an enclosed chain case for bicycles in the 1880s. In Italian his surname became the general word for a protective casing.

senses.note: Invariable: il carter, i carter. Also means the oil sump or crankcase of an engine.

etymology: From cartola (“little paper”) + -lina.
From carta (“paper”) + -one (“augmentative suffix”).

fact.text: English cartoon comes from this word. Renaissance artists drew full-size preparatory sketches on heavy paper, cartoni, before painting frescoes.

senses.note: Also a cardboard box or carton. 'Cartoni animati' are cartoons.

etymology: Inherited from Latin casa (“house”).

fact.text: In Latin, casa meant a humble hut or cottage; the grand word for house was domus. The Italian diminutive casino, 'little house', gave English casino.

senses.note: a casa = at home / home (no article): vado a casa.

etymology: From casale + -ingo; compare Piedmontese casalengh.

fact.text: The plural 'i casalinghi' also means household goods. A shop sign reading 'casalinghi' sells pots and pans, not husbands.

senses.note: Often humorous. The feminine la casalinga (housewife) is far more common. As an adjective: homemade.

etymology: From casa + -ino; cognate with Piedmontese casin.

fact.text: This is a false friend. Casino (stress on -si-) means a mess, or originally a brothel. 'Little house' came to mean a pleasure house. A gambling casino is casinò, with the stress at the end.

senses.note: Very common: che casino! = what a mess! A gambling casino is casinò, stressed on the last syllable.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cāsus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin casus, from cadere, 'to fall': a case is what 'befalls' you. That is why it also means 'chance', as in per caso, 'by chance'.

senses.note: per caso = by chance; in caso contrario = otherwise; non è il caso = there's no need.

etymology: Inherited from Latin capsa. Doublet of capsa.

fact.text: English 'cash' comes from this word (or French casse), meaning 'money box'. Both go back to Latin capsa (box), which also gave English 'case'.

senses.note: Pagare alla cassa = pay at the checkout. The person is il cassiere / la cassiera. Also means crate, or speaker.

fact.text: Literally a 'strong box': cassa (box, chest) + forte (strong). Because both parts are treated as words, both change in the plural: casse + forti.

senses.note: Both parts change in the plural: le casseforti.

etymology: From cassa + -etta (diminutive suffix).

senses.note: Also a cassette tape. Cassetta delle lettere = letterbox. Cassetta degli attrezzi = toolbox.

fact.text: Built on cassetto, 'drawer', which is a diminutive of cassa, 'box' or 'crate'. Italian cassa is also where English 'cash' comes from, by way of French.
Literally means chestnut-coloured. It is related to castagna (chestnut), from Latin castanea, which is also where the chest- in English chestnut comes from.

senses.note: Mainly for hair and eyes (capelli castani). For other brown things use marrone.

etymology: Inherited from Latin castellum, diminutive of castrum.

fact.text: Latin castellum meant 'little fort', from castrum, 'fort'. Castrum also gave English place names ending in -chester, -caster and -cester, like Manchester and Lancaster.

senses.note: Castello di sabbia = sandcastle. Castelli in aria = castles in the air.

etymology: From an older castore, from Latin castōrem, from Ancient Greek Κάστωρ (Kástōr).

senses.note: Un no categorico = a flat no. Plural: categorici, categoriche.

etymology: Inherited from Latin captīvus (“captive” → “caught by the devil” → “bad”). Compare the semantic development of French chétif (“puny, scrawny”) and Galician cativo.

fact.text: From Latin captivus 'captive'. Christian writers spoke of the 'captivus diaboli', a captive of the devil, and the word drifted to mean 'bad'.

senses.note: Cattive notizie = bad news; cattivo tempo = bad weather.

etymology: Inherited from Latin captīvus (“captive” → “caught by the devil” → “bad”). Compare the semantic development of French chétif (“puny, scrawny”) and Galician cativo.

fact.text: From Latin captivus 'captive'. Christian writers spoke of the 'captivus diaboli', a captive of the devil, and the word drifted to mean 'bad'.

senses.note: Feminine: la cattiva. I buoni e i cattivi = the good guys and the bad guys.

etymology: From cattura + -are.
Borrowed from Latin causa. Doublet of the inherited cosa. Cognates include English and French cause, Portuguese and Spanish causa.

fact.text: A learned borrowing of Latin causa. The same Latin word also passed down naturally through spoken Latin and became cosa, 'thing', so causa and cosa are twins.

senses.note: a causa di = because of. It can also mean a lawsuit (fare causa = to sue).

etymology: From causa + -are.

From Late Latin caballus (“horse”), from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), of disputed origin. Compare Portuguese cavalo, Asturian caballu,
Galician cabalo, Dalmatian caval, Catalan cavall, French cheval, Spanish caballo, Romanian cal,
Corsican cavallu, Sardinian cabaddu, Sicilian cavaḍḍu.

fact.text: Comes from Latin caballus, a humble pack horse or nag, which replaced the classical equus. English cavalry and cavalier come from the same root.

senses.note: Also a knight in chess and horsepower: un motore da 100 cavalli.

fact.text: Cavare means 'to pull out or extract', as in cavare un dente (to pull a tooth). So cavarsela literally means pulling yourself out of a tricky situation.

features.construction: pronominal: cavarsela (me la cavo, te la cavi…)

senses.note: Me la cavo = I get by. Past: me la sono cavata. Cavarsela con l'inglese = to get by in English.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan cavilla (compare modern cavilha), from Vulgar Latin *cāvic(u)la, from Classical Latin clāvicula, diminutive of clāvis (“key”). Compare the doublets cavicchia (inherited from Latin), clavicola (borrowed from Latin).

fact.text: Goes back to Latin clavicula, 'little key', the same word that gave English 'clavicle' (collarbone). The ankle bone was thought to look like a small peg or key.

senses.note: Slogarsi la caviglia = to sprain one's ankle.

fact.text: It is also a polite stand-in for a much ruder word. 'Cavoli tuoi!' means 'That's your problem!' And cavolfiore (cabbage + flower) is the source of English 'cauliflower'.

senses.note: Che cavolo fai? = What the heck are you doing? Col cavolo! = No way! Literally 'cabbage'.

etymology: Derived from Late Latin caulus, from Latin caulis,, through a southern Italian language. Possibly borrowed from Neapolitan cavolo or Sicilian cavulu. Doublet of caule.

fact.text: It is also a polite stand-in for a much ruder word. 'Cavoli tuoi!' means 'That's your problem!' And cavolfiore (cabbage + flower) is the source of English 'cauliflower'.

senses.note: Also a mild euphemism: Cavolo! = Damn! Che cavolo fai? = What the heck are you doing?

etymology: From cazzo + -ata.

fact.text: It can also mean something ridiculously easy. 'È una cazzata!' is a crude way of saying 'It's a piece of cake!'

senses.note: Often plural: dire cazzate = to talk bullshit. Milder alternative: sciocchezze.

etymology:
Of uncertain origin.
The most plausible etymon is Latin captiāre, interjection of the Latin verb captiō (“catching, capture”) as "to chase out", in the sense of to insert, to forcefully put in. Thus, the noun captum as accusative singular of captus (“having been taken in, captured”).
Antonio Lupis concludes that the term cazzo does not derive from cazza ("ladle") because cazzo is an original term from the Umbrian-Tuscan area since 1300CE.
Another possible etymon is Old Italian cazza (“ladle”), from Late Latin cattiam, in turn from Ancient Greek κυάθιον (kuáthion), diminutive form of κύαθος (kúathos, “ladle for wine”); cf. also cazzuola. Another is Byzantine Greek ἀκάτιον (akátion, “mainmast”). See also caspita.

senses.note: Very vulgar. Common as an intensifier: che cazzo...? = what the f...?

etymology: cazzo (“dick”) + -one.

senses.note: Offensive insult. Among friends it can be used teasingly, like 'goofball'.
Form of ci before ne/lo/la: ce n'è = there's one/some; ce ne sono = there are some.

etymology: From the past participle of the verb cecare, from Latin caecāre (corresponding to caecātus).

senses.note: Southern/central regional word. The standard Italian word is cieco.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin caelebs (“unmarried”).

fact.text: This doesn't have to mean 'celibate'. On Italian forms it simply means 'single (man)', and the box for women says nubile. It comes from Latin caelebs, 'unmarried', whose origin is unknown.

senses.note: Used of men; an unmarried woman is nubile. Common on official forms. Plural: celibi.

etymology: From Latin cella, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelnā.

fact.text: Latin cella meant a small storeroom or chamber. It gave English both 'cell' and 'cellar'.

senses.note: A room-like cell, such as in a prison or monastery. A biological cell is usually la cellula.

etymology: From cellula (“cell”) + -are.

fact.text: Comes from cellula (cell). Long before mobile phones, il cellulare was the police van, which has small cells for holding prisoners.

senses.note: Often shortened to il cell in speech; telefonino is a common synonym.

etymology: From Latin caementum, uncertain if inherited or borrowed. Cognate to the doublet and variant cimento.

fact.text: From Latin caementum, from caedere 'to cut': it first meant rough-cut stone chips and rubble used in Roman building, not the binding powder.

senses.note: Often used loosely for concrete too: una casa di cemento.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cēna, from Proto-Italic *kertsnā, from Proto-Indo-European *kért-s-nh₂ (“portion”), from *ker-, *sker-. Compare Spanish cena, Portuguese ceia and Romanian cină.

fact.text: Leonardo da Vinci's famous Last Supper is called L'Ultima Cena in Italian.

senses.note: Cenare = to have dinner. Andare a cena = to go out for dinner.

etymology: From Latin cēnāre (“to dine”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin cenare, to dine. The related noun cena gives Leonardo's famous painting its Italian name: L'Ultima Cena, The Last Supper.

senses.note: Takes avere: ho cenato. The noun is la cena (dinner).

etymology: From centi- + metro, modelled on French centimètre.

senses.note: Followed by di: un centinaio di persone. Plural is feminine: centinaia (hundreds).

etymology: From Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.
From cento + cinquanta.
From cento + diciannove.
From cento + diciassette.
From cento + diciotto.

fact.text: Italian university degrees are graded out of 110. The top result is 110 e lode (110 with honours), and Italians often say 'centodieci e lode' to mean 'perfect'.

etymology: From cento + dodici.
From cento + due.
From cento (“hundred”) + mila (“thousand”).

fact.text: Mille (a thousand) has a special plural, mila, used for every higher thousand: duemila, centomila. It goes back to Latin mille, whose plural was milia.

etymology: From cento + novanta.
From cento + quaranta.
From cento + quattordici.
From cento + quindici.
From cento + sedici.
From cento + sessanta.
From cento + settanta.
From cento + tredici.
From cento + trenta.
From cento (“hundred”) + tre (“three”).
From cento + ottanta.
From cento + undici.
From cento (“hundred”) + uno (“one”).
From cento + venti.
Borrowed from Latin centrālis.

senses.note: Ufficio centrale = head office. As a noun, la centrale = power station or headquarters.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin centrum, from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “sharp point”). The nonstandard pronunciation with -é- might be due to influence of entrare.

fact.text: From Greek kentron, 'sharp point'. The idea is the fixed point of a pair of compasses, which you turn around to draw a circle.

senses.note: In centro = downtown, in the town centre.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin circāre, from Latin circa, circus.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin circare, 'to go around' (from circus, a circle). Through Old French cerchier, the same verb became English search.

senses.note: No word for 'for' is needed: cerco le chiavi. Cercare di + infinitive = to try to.

etymology: From Latin circulus, which is derived from circus. Cognate to the borrowed doublet circolo.

fact.text: Its learned twin circolo comes from the same Latin circulus but usually means a club or society, as in a circolo culturale.

etymology:
From Latin cērōtum (“wax plaster”), ultimately from Ancient Greek κηρός (kērós, “beeswax”).
Cognate with Piedmontese siròt.

fact.text: Early plasters were made with wax. The word goes back through Latin cērōtum, 'wax plaster', to Greek kērós, 'beeswax'. It is related to Italian cera, 'wax'.

etymology: From certo + -mente.

senses.note: Common reply: Certamente! = Of course!
certificato medico = doctor's note / medical certificate.

etymology: Inherited from Latin certus.

fact.text: Latin certus was originally a past participle of cernere 'to sift, decide', so being certain first meant something like 'decided' or 'settled'.

senses.note: Before a noun = 'a certain' (una certa età); sono certo = I'm sure. The adverb certo means 'of course'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin certus.

fact.text: Latin certus was originally a past participle of cernere 'to sift, decide', so being certain first meant something like 'decided' or 'settled'.

senses.note: Often on its own: Certo! = Sure! / Of course! As an adjective, un certo = a certain.

etymology: From Latin cerebellum, derived from cerebrum, from Proto-Italic *kerazrom, from a Proto-Indo-European form *ḱerh₂-s-rom, from the root *ḱerh₂- (“head”). The alternative plural cervella derives from the Latin plural form cerebella. Doublet of the borrowing cerebello; cf. the derived cerebellare.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cerebellum, meaning 'little brain'. In English, 'cerebellum' names only one part at the back of the brain, but in Italian it became the word for the whole brain.

senses.note: The feminine plural 'le cervella' is used for brains as food and in idioms (farsi saltare le cervella).

etymology: Borrowed from French champagne, from Champagne, from Late Latin campania. Doublet of campagna.

fact.text: A doublet of Italian campagna (countryside). Both come from Late Latin campania, 'open plain', which also named the French region where the wine is made.

senses.note: Invariable: il/lo champagne, gli champagne. Usually 'lo champagne' because of the initial 'sh' sound.

etymology: Borrowed from French chance. Doublet of cadenza.

fact.text: Came via French from Latin cadentia, 'a falling', as of dice. The same root gave Italian cadenza and English cadence, so chance and cadence are word twins.

senses.note: French loanword, pronounced the French way; invariable: le chance. Avere una chance = to have a chance.

etymology: From Latin quid (but also usurping some roles of Latin quod), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís.

senses.note: Never changes form: l'uomo che vedo, la casa che compro. After a preposition use cui instead: su cui.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English check-in.

senses.note: Invariable English loanword: il check-in, i check-in. Fare il check-in = to check in.

etymology: From Latin quis, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís, *kʷos.

senses.note: Does not change for gender or number. Also means 'whoever / those who': chi cerca trova.

etymology: Onomatopoeic. Some link it to Old French claquer (“clap, clack, clatter”), which is ultimately from Proto-Germanic *klakōną (“to clap, chirp”). Cognate with Spanish cháchara and French tchatche.

fact.text: The related noun chiacchiere ('chatter') is also the name of crunchy fried Carnival pastries dusted with sugar, eaten all over Italy before Lent.

senses.note: chiacchierare con qualcuno di qualcosa; can also mean to gossip.

etymology: From Latin clāmāre, from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₁- (“to shout”). Doublet of clamare, a borrowing.

fact.text: Comes from Latin clamare 'to shout', the root of English clamour, exclaim and proclaim. Latin cl- regularly became Italian chi-.

senses.note: Also 'to phone'. Reflexive chiamarsi: Mi chiamo Anna = My name is Anna (lit. I call myself Anna).
Fare una chiamata = to make a call. From the verb chiamare (to call).

etymology: From the Latin ablatival locution clārā mente (literally “with a clear mind”). By surface analysis, chiara (“clear”) + -mente (“-ly”).

fact.text: From Latin clara mente, 'with a clear mind'. That's why every Italian -mente adverb is built on the feminine adjective: mens (mind) was a feminine noun in Latin.

senses.note: Can also mean 'obviously': Chiaramente ha ragione.

ignored: This is a verb with an attached pronoun (chiarire + lo); the base verb chiarire should be its own card.

senses.note: Chiarire + lo (it). The pronoun attaches to the infinitive, which drops its final -e.

etymology: Inherited from Latin clārus. Compare Albanian qartë.

senses.note: Also 'light' for colours: blu chiaro = light blue. Chiaro! = Got it!

etymology: Inherited from Latin clārus. Compare Albanian qartë.
ignored: This is the adjective used as a noun. The list's meaning 'light (vs dark)' belongs on the adjective card chiaro.

senses.note: Mostly used as an adjective: blu chiaro = light blue. Also chiaro di luna = moonlight.

etymology: From Latin clāvem, from Proto-Italic *klāwis, of ultimately Proto-Indo-European origin.

fact.text: Comes from Latin clavis, 'key'. The collarbone is called the clavicle, meaning 'little key', and the musical clef comes from the same word.

senses.note: Chiudere a chiave = to lock. Chiave inglese = wrench/spanner.

etymology: Inherited from Latin quaerere, with dissimilation of /r–r/ to /d–r/.

fact.text: From Latin quaerere (to seek, ask), the source of English query, quest, question and inquire. The first r turned into d so the word didn't have two r's.

senses.note: chiedere qualcosa a qualcuno. chiedere a qn di fare qc = to ask someone to do something.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin ecclēsia, a borrowing from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, “assembly”).
The original geminated -cc-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in many regional Italian varieties.

fact.text: From Latin ecclesia, from Greek ekklēsía, 'assembly'. The same word gives English 'ecclesiastical'. The Latin e- dropped off over time, leaving the chi- of the Italian word.

senses.note: andare in chiesa = to go to church (no article). Plural chiese.

etymology: Clipping of chilogrammo.

fact.text: Chili means 'kilos', not chili peppers. A chili pepper is a peperoncino. Italian writes the k sound as ch, as in chilometro.

senses.note: Short for chilogrammo. Mezzo chilo = half a kilo.

etymology: From chilo- + grammo.

fact.text: Italian spells the 'k' sound as ch-, so the Greek prefix kilo- ('thousand') becomes chilo-. In shops, people simply ask for un chilo or mezzo chilo.

senses.note: Usually shortened to chilo in everyday speech: un chilo di pane.

etymology: From chilo- + metro.

fact.text: Italian has no native letter k, so Greek kilo- becomes chilo-, where 'ch' sounds like k. The same goes for chilo (kilo) and chilogrammo.

senses.note: Stress on the second syllable: chi-LO-metro.

etymology: From chimico (“chemical”).

fact.text: Like English chemistry, it is a shortened form of alchemy (Italian alchimia), which came from Arabic al-kimiya.

senses.note: Also the feminine of chimico: la chimica can mean a (female) chemist.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin quī sapit (“who knows”). Cognate with Spanish and Galician quizá, Portuguese quiçá. By surface analysis, univerbation of chi + sa, literally “who knows”.

fact.text: This is chi + sa ('who knows') fused into one word. Spanish quizá ('maybe') comes from the same Latin phrase, qui sapit.

senses.note: Also means 'perhaps'. Chissà se... = I wonder if...

etymology: Inherited from Latin clūdere, variant of claudere.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle chiuso, passato remoto chiusi.

etymology: From chi (“who”) + -unque (indefinite suffix). Formed similarly to, and possibly influenced by, Latin quicumque. Compare also French quiconque.

senses.note: Also means 'whoever'. Usually takes the subjunctive: chiunque sia = whoever it is.

etymology: Uncertain. Rohlfs and Von Wartburg favoured Late Latin ecce hīc. Maiden casts doubt on this etymology, pointing out that Italian ci is an unstressed 'weak' form, while Latin hic otherwise survives in Italian only in stressed forms (reinforced by Latin ecce or eccum) such as ciò, qua, and qui. (It should also be noted that all of the latter trigger syntactic doubling in a following word, thanks to their original final /k/, while ci does not.) Maiden proposes instead an origin in Latin hince, variant of hinc (“hence, from here, from this person”), pointing out that in parts of southern Italy there exists a 1PL pronoun 'nci (cf. also 'nce). Treccani, on the other hand, proposes an origin in Latin hīce, a variant of hīc (“here”). In any case, the Italian term is certainly cognate with Neapolitan ce, Sicilian cci and Sassarese zi, all three of which share similar adverbial senses, with the latter two also having pronominal senses.

fact.text: The same little word also means 'there', which is why 'there is' is c'è (ci + è) and 'there are' is ci sono.

senses.note: Ci vado = I'm going there. C'è / ci sono = there is / there are.

senses.note: Unstressed form of noi; also 'to us' and 'ourselves'. Goes before the verb: Ci vede = He sees us.

etymology: Borrowed from Venetan s-ciao, sciavo (“slave”) (in particular the expression s-ciao vostro (literally “(I am) your slave”), in essence meaning "I am at your service", or "your humble servant"), from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”) (whence also standard Italian schiavo); in the Venetan language originally pronounced /stʃaʊ/. Development and use is similar to the Southern German and Central European greeting of servus and Swedish tjena.

fact.text: Comes from Venetian s-ciao vostro, 'I am your slave', meaning 'at your service'. It comes from the same root as schiavo (slave) and is similar to the greeting servus.

senses.note: Use only with friends or with people you address as tu. Otherwise say buongiorno.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *cisque-unus, from Latin quisque ūnus, and influenced by cadauno. Cf. French chacun, Catalan cadascun.

fact.text: Comes from Vulgar Latin *cisque-unus, from Latin quisque unus, meaning 'each one'. French chacun comes from similar roots.

senses.note: Singular only; feminine ciascuna. Before a noun it becomes ciascun/ciascuna (ciascun libro).

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cibus. Contrast Portuguese cevo and Spanish cebo (“bait”).
From Latin caecus, from Proto-Italic *kaikos (“blind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ikos (“one-eyed”).

fact.text: A dead end is a vicolo cieco, a blind alley.

senses.note: Forms: cieco, cieca, ciechi, cieche. Also a noun: un cieco, a blind person.

etymology: From Latin caecus, from Proto-Italic *kaikos (“blind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kéh₂ikos (“one-eyed”).

fact.text: A dead end is a vicolo cieco, a blind alley.

ignored: This is the adjective used as a noun. The list's meaning 'blind' belongs on the adjective card cieco.

senses.note: Feminine: la cieca. The adjective cieco means 'blind'.

etymology: From Latin caelum, from Proto-Italic *kailom, from Proto-Indo-European *keh₂i-lom (“whole”), from *keh₂i-.

senses.note: Also means 'heaven': il regno dei cieli = the kingdom of heaven.

etymology: From Cilento + -ano.

senses.note: Also an adjective: fichi cilentani = figs from Cilento (south of Salerno).

etymology: From Latin cȳma, from Ancient Greek κῦμα (kûma).

fact.text: Comes via Latin cyma 'young cabbage sprout' from Greek kyma 'wave, swelling'. The plant sense survives in cime di rapa, the turnip tops loved in Puglia.

senses.note: in cima a = at the top of: in cima alla montagna.

etymology: From Late Latin coemeterium, Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek koimētḗrion, 'sleeping chamber', from koimáō, 'to put to sleep'. Early Christians thought of the dead as sleeping. English cemetery has the same origin.
Usually traced to a Chinese greeting, ts'ing ts'ing ('please, please'), which sailors brought back via English 'chin-chin'. It also happens to sound like clinking glasses.

senses.note: Said when clinking glasses. Also written cincin.

fact.text: Comes via the sailors' pidgin toast 'chin-chin', from Chinese qǐng qǐng, a polite 'please, please'. The clinking sound helped it stick.

senses.note: Said when clinking glasses. Also written cin cin; salute! is the alternative.

etymology: From cincia (“tit”) + allegra (“happy”, “joyous”).

fact.text: It literally means 'cheerful tit': cincia (tit) + allegra (happy), perhaps because of its lively song.

senses.note: A common garden bird. Any tit is una cincia.

etymology: Borrowed from French cinéma, from Ancient Greek κίνημα (kínēma, “movement”).

fact.text: It is masculine because it is short for cinematografo. It goes back to Greek kinema, 'movement', the same root as English 'kinetic'.

senses.note: Masculine and invariable: i cinema. Andare al cinema = to go to the movies.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cīnquāgintā.
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + cinque (“five”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + due (“two”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + nove (“nine”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + quattro (“four”).
