From cinquanta (“fifty”) + sei (“six”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + sette (“seven”).
From cinquanta (“fifty”) + tre (“three”).

fact.text: Tre on its own has no accent, but at the end of a compound number it takes one: ventitré, cinquantatré, centotré.

etymology: From cinquanta (“fifty”) + otto (“eight”).

fact.text: Tens drop their final vowel before otto and uno, so it is cinquantotto rather than cinquantaotto, and likewise cinquantuno.

etymology: From cinquanta (“fifty”) + uno (“one”).
Inherited from Latin cīnque.

fact.text: Shares an ancestor with English 'five': Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe. The name Pompeii is thought to come from an Oscan word for five, which makes it a distant relative.

ignored: Using the number as a noun is a secondary use; the numeral cinque is studied on its own card.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cīnque.

fact.text: Shares an ancestor with English 'five': Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe. The name Pompeii is thought to come from an Oscan word for five, which makes it a distant relative.

etymology: From cinque (“five”) + cento (“hundred”).

fact.text: Il Cinquecento is the 1500s, meaning the 16th century. Una Cinquecento is also the classic small Fiat 500 car.

etymology: From cinque + mila.

fact.text: One thousand is mille, but from two thousand on Italian uses the plural form -mila (duemila, cinquemila), inherited from Latin mille and its plural milia.

etymology: From Spanish chocolate, from Classical Nahuatl chocolātl.

fact.text: This came into Italian through Spanish, which took it from Nahuatl, the Aztec language.

senses.note: La cioccolata is also common, especially for hot chocolate.

fact.text: Literally 'ciò è' (that is), it is also a very common filler word in casual speech, much like English 'I mean' or 'like'.

senses.note: Correct spelling is cioè, with the accent. Introduces a clarification: Domani, cioè lunedì.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.

fact.text: Italians also used the word for an old-fashioned pocket watch, because those thick round watches looked like an onion. It comes from Latin cepulla, 'little onion'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin circā.

fact.text: English borrowed the same Latin word, but mostly uses it for dates (circa 1500). In Italian it is everyday speech for any rough amount: circa un'ora, about an hour.

senses.note: Usually goes before the number: circa venti persone = about twenty people.
Usually follows the noun: l'area circostante = the surrounding area.

etymology: Derived from Latin citāre (“to summon”), from cieō (“move, stir”), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey-.

fact.text: Latin citare meant 'to set in motion, to summon'. Its prefixed forms gave English excite, incite and recite.

senses.note: Citare in giudizio = to sue (legal).

etymology: From Latin citō.
ignored: In the context this is the verb form 'I quote' from citare (study it there); the adverb 'soon' is rare and Latin-style.

senses.note: A rare, Latin-style adverb. In everyday Italian, 'cito' is usually 'I quote' (from citare).

etymology: From cittadino + -anza.

senses.note: Can also mean a town's citizens as a whole: la cittadinanza è invitata = the townspeople are invited.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cīvitātem (“city”). Doublet of city.

fact.text: From Latin civitatem through the old form cittade. The final accent marks the lost last syllable. English city comes from the same Latin word, via French.

senses.note: Invariable: le città. In città = in town/downtown.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English city. Doublet of città.
ignored: Unadapted English loanword; the ordinary Italian word for city is città.

senses.note: Unadapted English loan, invariable; for an ordinary city use città.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin ecce hoc, from ecce (“behold, voilà”) + hoc (“this”). Compare Sicilian zoccu, Catalan açò, French ce.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin ecce hoc, 'behold this'. It shares its ecce with ecco ('here is') and is related to French ce.

senses.note: Refers to ideas or facts, not objects: ciò che = what, that which.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin classis.

fact.text: Latin classis first meant a division of Roman citizens called up for military service, and it is probably linked to a root meaning 'to call out'.

senses.note: Also means classroom, and style: avere classe = to have class.

etymology: From Latin classicus (“relating to the classes of Roman citizenry, especially the highest”), from classis.

fact.text: Latin classicus first described citizens of the highest class in Rome. Later it came to mean first-class writers, and from there 'classic'.

senses.note: Also 'typical': il classico errore. Liceo classico = a high school focused on Latin and Greek.
Usually cliccare su: clicca sul link. Spelling gains an h before e/i: clicchi.

etymology: From Latin clientem.

fact.text: In ancient Rome a cliens was a dependent who owed loyalty and support to a powerful patron, who in return gave protection.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il/la cliente, i/le clienti. Also a hotel guest.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin clīma, from Ancient Greek κλῐ́μᾰ (klĭ́mă, “region, zone”), from κλῐ́νω (klĭ́nō, “to slope, incline”).

fact.text: Greek klíma meant 'slope, incline' (from klínō, to lean, related to English incline). Ancient geographers tied a region's weather to how steeply the Earth slopes toward the sun.

senses.note: Masculine despite the -a ending: il clima, i climi.

etymology: Borrowed from French clinique, ultimately from Ancient Greek κλινική (klinikḗ).

fact.text: Comes from Greek klinē 'bed': clinical medicine was practised at the patient's bedside. It is related to klinein 'to lean', a cousin of English recline.

senses.note: In Italy it often means a private hospital (clinica privata). Plural: cliniche.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English clown.

fact.text: Italian took this word straight from English, but it also has its own word for a clown, pagliaccio, best known from Leoncavallo's opera Pagliacci.

senses.note: Invariable: il clown, i clown. The native word is il pagliaccio.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English club.

senses.note: An English loanword. It doesn't change in the plural: i club.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English coach.

senses.note: Does not change in the plural: i coach. The native Italian word is allenatore.

etymology: Borrowed from French cocaïne.

senses.note: Stressed on the i: co-ca-Ì-na.

etymology: From Latin cōda, monophthongized variant of cauda.

fact.text: English borrowed coda, the closing passage of a piece of music, straight from Italian. It is literally the piece's 'tail'.

senses.note: Also means queue: fare la coda = to stand in line.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin cōdicem.

fact.text: Latin codex (earlier caudex) meant 'tree trunk, block of wood'. Its meaning moved to wooden writing tablets, then to books, and later to books of laws.

senses.note: Codice fiscale = Italian tax ID code; codice postale = postcode.

etymology: From Latin colligere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin colligere, 'to gather together', which is also the source of English collect.

senses.note: cogliere l'occasione = to seize the opportunity. Also means to pick (flowers, fruit). Irregular: colgo, colto.

etymology: From Late Latin cōleōnem, derived from Latin cōleus (“sack, scrotum”).

fact.text: Its literal meaning is 'testicle', from Latin coleus (sack, scrotum). That is also why 'rompere i coglioni' (to annoy someone) is so rude.

senses.note: Strong insult. The feminine is cogliona. Literally means 'testicle'.

etymology: From Latin cognātus (“related by blood”), from cum (“with”) + nātus (“born”).

fact.text: From Latin cognatus 'related by blood' (co- 'with' + natus 'born'). That's ironic, since in-laws are related by marriage, not blood.

senses.note: Sister-in-law: cognata.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cognomen.

fact.text: From Latin cognomen, con- 'with' + nomen 'name'.

senses.note: Nome = first name; cognome = family name.

etymology: From coincidere + -enza (compare Latin coincidentia).

senses.note: Also a train or flight connection: perdere la coincidenza = to miss your connection.

fact.text: Made from co- + involgere, 'to wrap up', which comes from Latin involvere, the source of English 'involve'. Being involved literally means being wrapped up in something.

senses.note: Irregular: coinvolsi, coinvolto. Essere coinvolto in = to be involved in.

etymology: From Latin collātiōnem (“putting together, meeting”). Originally it was the name of the meal that monks ate after the evening meeting. Doublet of collazione.

fact.text: From Latin collatio ('meeting'). It was first the name of the light meal monks ate after their evening meeting.

senses.note: Fare colazione = to have breakfast.

etymology: From Latin cholera, from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra), from χολή (kholḗ, “bile”).

fact.text: From Greek kholē, 'bile'. The same root also gave Italian collera, 'anger', because people once thought too much bile made you angry.

senses.note: Masculine despite ending in -a: il colera. Don't confuse it with la collera (anger).

etymology: From colo + -ino (diminutive suffix).

senses.note: A small kitchen sieve; a large pasta colander is usually lo scolapasta.

etymology: From collaborare + -tore.

fact.text: A 'collaboratore di giustizia' is a criminal who cooperates with investigators, such as a former Mafia member who testifies. They are popularly called pentiti.

senses.note: Feminine: collaboratrice. Often means a co-worker or assistant.

etymology: From collo.

fact.text: Comes from collo, 'neck' (Latin collum). That is the same root as English 'collar': both are things worn around the neck.

senses.note: Also means a book series from a publisher (collana editoriale).

etymology: From Latin collēga.

senses.note: il/la collega; plural i colleghi (m), le colleghe (f).

etymology: From Latin colligāre.

fact.text: From Latin colligare: com- 'together' + ligare 'to tie'. The same root gives Italian legare (to tie) and English ligament.

senses.note: collegare A a B = to connect A to B; collegarsi (a Internet) = to log on.

ignored: English loanword spelled the same as the English, so it would make no useful flashcard.

senses.note: Anglicism: il college, invariable. Means a British-style boarding school or a US college.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin collēgium.

fact.text: Usually not 'college' in the American sense. A collegio is typically a boarding school; going to college or university is andare all'università.

senses.note: Also an electoral district: collegio elettorale.

etymology: From collezione + -are.

senses.note: Used for collecting stamps, coins and so on (also figuratively: collezionare errori). Gathering things = raccogliere.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin collēctiōnem.

senses.note: Fare collezione di francobolli = to collect stamps; also a fashion collection.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin collīna, from the feminine of Latin collīnus, from collis (“hill”) + -ina, from Proto-Indo-European *kl̥Hnís (“top, hill, rock”).

senses.note: in collina = in the hills

etymology:
From Latin collum, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷolsom, derived from the root *kʷel- (“to turn”).
Cognate with French cou, Galician and Portuguese colo, Sicilian coḍḍu, Spanish cuello.

fact.text: Comes from Latin collum, 'neck', which also gave Latin collare, 'neck band'. That is the source of English collar.

senses.note: Also a parcel or piece of luggage (i colli). Don't confuse colli with the plural of colle (hill).

etymology: From collocare + -mento.

senses.note: ufficio/centro di collocamento = job centre. Can also mean the placing or arrangement of things.

etymology: From co- + -loquio, from Latin colloquium.

fact.text: From Latin colloquium, 'a talking together' (con- + loqui 'to speak'), the same root as English colloquial. Careful: it means a formal talk or interview, not a casual chat.

senses.note: Colloquio di lavoro = job interview. Also a formal talk or meeting.

etymology: From colonna + -ello (diminutive suffix).

fact.text: English colonel comes from this word, meaning 'little column': the officer who led a column of soldiers. The French variant coronel explains why English says 'kernel'.

etymology: From Latin colōrāre.

senses.note: Transitive: colorare un disegno = to color in a drawing.

etymology: From Latin colōrem, from Old Latin colos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱel- (“to hide, conceal”).

fact.text: Latin color goes back to a root meaning to hide or conceal. Colour was thought of as what covers a surface. English conceal shares this root.

senses.note: Masculine despite the -e ending: il colore, i colori.

etymology: Inherited from Latin culpa, from Proto-Italic *kʷolpā (“wrong, mistake”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷolp-eh₂ (“bend, turn”), from *kʷelp-.

fact.text: From Latin culpa, 'fault'. It is the root of English 'culpable' and of the Latin phrase 'mea culpa' ('through my fault'), which English uses to admit a mistake.

senses.note: È colpa mia = it's my fault. Dare la colpa a qualcuno = to blame someone.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin culpābilis.
By surface analysis, colpa + -evole.
Doublet of colpabile, which is borrowed.

senses.note: colpevole di = guilty of. Opposite: innocente.

etymology: From colpo + -ire.

fact.text: It is built from colpo 'blow', which goes back through Latin colaphus to Greek kolaphos 'a punch'. French coup, as in coup d'etat, has the same origin.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: colpisco, colpisci, colpisce. It can also mean to impress someone.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin colpus, from Latin colaphus from Ancient Greek κόλαφος (kólaphos). Doublet of golfo.

fact.text: Comes from Greek kólaphos 'a slap, punch' via Late Latin colpus, the same source as French coup, as in coup d'état (Italian: colpo di stato).

senses.note: Colpo di stato = coup; colpo di fulmine = love at first sight; di colpo = suddenly.

etymology: From Latin cultellus (“small knife, dagger”), diminutive of culter (“knife”).

fact.text: From Latin cultellus 'little knife', a diminutive of culter 'knife'. English 'cutlery' comes from the same root, by way of French.

etymology: Contracted from Vulgar Latin *eccum illui, (genitive-)dative masculine singular of *eccum ille, under the influence of Latin cui (“to whom”). Compare French celui. and Romanian acelui.

fact.text: Comes from Vulgar Latin eccum illui, roughly 'behold, him'. The same eccum 'behold' is hidden in quello and questo.

senses.note: Almost always followed by che: colui che = he who. Feminine: colei; plural: coloro.

etymology: From comandare.

senses.note: Also the captain of a ship or plane.
Also means leadership (essere al comando) and headquarters. I comandi = the controls of a vehicle.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *combattere, from Latin cum + battuō.

senses.note: combattere contro qualcuno = to fight against someone. For everyday arguing, use litigare.

etymology: From combattere + -mento.

senses.note: Also a boxing match. fuori combattimento = knocked out (KO).

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin combīnāre.

senses.note: Colloquial: Che hai combinato? = What have you done / been up to? (often mischief).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin quōmodo et.

senses.note: Come stai? = How are you? Before è it shortens to com'è.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin quōmodo et.

senses.note: Also means 'like/as': come te = like you. Come stai? = How are you?

ignored: Come is not a pronoun; its 'how' meaning is studied on the adverb card for come.

senses.note: Com'è…? = What is … like? / How is …?

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cominitiāre.

fact.text: Comes from Vulgar Latin cominitiare, which also gave French commencer and so English 'commence'. 'Initiate' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Takes avere with a person as subject (ho cominciato) and essere when something starts (il film è cominciato).

etymology: Derived from Latin cōmoedia.

fact.text: Dante named his poem simply Commedia because it ends happily and is written in everyday language. Boccaccio later called it 'divina', which gave the title Divina Commedia.

senses.note: Also figurative 'an act, a sham': è tutta una commedia = it's all an act.

etymology: From Latin commentārī.

senses.note: Transitive, with no preposition: commentare una notizia = to comment on a piece of news.

etymology: From Latin commentum.

senses.note: Also commentary, e.g. il commento della partita (match commentary).

etymology: From Latin commercium.

fact.text: From Latin commercium: con- (together) plus merx (merchandise). Merx is also the root of English merchant, mercantile and market.

senses.note: Commercio estero = foreign trade; essere in commercio = to be on the market.

etymology: From Latin commissus.

fact.text: From Latin commissus, 'entrusted', the past participle of committere, which also gave English 'commit' and 'commission'. A commesso is someone entrusted with the shop.

senses.note: Female: la commessa. In the US: sales clerk.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin commissiōnem.

senses.note: Also a fee (commission) and an errand: fare commissioni = to run errands.

etymology: From French commode + -ino.

fact.text: A 'little commode': it comes from French commode (a chest of drawers, literally 'convenient') plus the diminutive -ino. In English, 'commode' later came to mean a chamber-pot cabinet.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin commoditātem.

fact.text: Not an English 'commodity'. It means convenience or comfort. A tradeable commodity is 'merce' or 'materia prima' in Italian.

senses.note: Per comodità = for convenience. Also means 'comfort' (le comodità di casa).

etymology: From Latin commodus.

fact.text: From Latin commodus 'convenient, fitting', the same root behind English 'accommodate' and 'commodity'.

senses.note: Also 'convenient, handy': mi fa comodo = it suits me. Of clothes: loose-fitting.

etymology: Derived from older compagna (assimilated to -ia), from Vulgar Latin *compānia. By surface analysis, compagna (“companion”) + -ia (abstract noun-forming suffix).

fact.text: Like English 'company' and 'companion', it goes back to Latin com- (with) + panis (bread). Your company were originally the people you shared bread with.

senses.note: Also a firm in some set phrases: compagnia aerea (airline), compagnia di assicurazioni.

etymology: From Late Latin compāniō (nominative form), a calque of Proto-West Germanic *gahlaibō. Doublet of compagnone, which came via the Latin accusative compāniōnem.

fact.text: Late Latin companio literally means 'one who shares bread with you', from com- 'with' and panis 'bread'. It was a calque of a Germanic word, and English companion has the same origin.

senses.note: Also classmate (compagno di classe), partner or comrade. Feminine: compagna.

etymology: From Latin compīlāre.

fact.text: Its everyday meaning is to fill in a form, not just 'to compile'. The Latin source compilare meant 'to plunder, rob', which later became 'to gather material from others'.

senses.note: Compilare un modulo = to fill in a form. Also 'to compile, draw up'.

etymology: Deverbal from compitare (“to spell; to enunciate”) + -o.

fact.text: Stress changes the meaning. Còmpito, stressed on the first syllable, is a task. Compìto, stressed on the second, is an adjective meaning polite or well-mannered.

senses.note: Stress on the first syllable: còmpito.

etymology: Partial calque of Spanish cumpleaños and adapted to fit Italian anno (“year”) and perhaps compiere.

fact.text: Modelled on Spanish cumpleaños and adapted to Italian anno ('year'). It literally means 'completing the year', the day you complete another year of life.

senses.note: Buon compleanno! = Happy birthday! compiere gli anni = to have one's birthday.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin complēmentum. Doublet of complimento.

fact.text: From Latin complementum, 'something that completes'. Italian complimento and English compliment go back to the same root, which is why the two are so easy to confuse.

senses.note: In grammar, complemento oggetto = direct object.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin complexus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin complexus, 'woven together', from com- (together) and plectere (to weave or braid). As a noun, un complesso can also mean a music band, as in a 1960s pop group.

senses.note: Also means intricate. 'Nel complesso' = on the whole, overall.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin complexus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin complexus, 'woven together', from com- (together) and plectere (to weave or braid). As a noun, un complesso can also mean a music band, as in a 1960s pop group.

senses.note: Complesso di inferiorità = inferiority complex. Also a group of buildings or a music band.

etymology: From completo + -mente.
Borrowed from Latin completus.

fact.text: As a noun, 'un completo' is a suit or matching outfit: a complete set of clothes.

senses.note: On a hotel or parking sign, 'completo' means full, no vacancies.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin completus.

fact.text: As a noun, 'un completo' is a suit or matching outfit: a complete set of clothes.

senses.note: A matching outfit or set, e.g. completo da uomo (men's suit). Also an adjective: complete, full.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin complicāre.

senses.note: Reflexive complicarsi = to get complicated: la situazione si complica.

etymology: Borrowed from Spanish cumplimiento. Doublet of complemento.

fact.text: 'Non fare complimenti!' means 'don't stand on ceremony, help yourself!' Hosts say it when offering food. In the plural the word also means fuss or formality.

senses.note: 'Complimenti!' = congratulations, well done!

etymology: From comportarsi + -mento.

senses.note: Plural 'comportamenti' often means 'behaviors' or 'actions'.

etymology: From Latin comportāre.

fact.text: Without -si it does not mean 'to behave'. That is the reflexive comportarsi. Plain comportare means 'to entail', as in Questo comporta dei costi.

senses.note: Subject is usually a thing: comporta dei rischi = it involves risks. 'To behave' is comportarsi.

fact.text: Without the reflexive -si, comportare means something different: 'to involve' or 'to entail', as in 'comporta dei rischi', it involves risks.

senses.note: Comportati bene! = Behave yourself! Takes essere.

ignored: This is an imperative + pronoun form, not a lemma. Study it on the comprare card.

senses.note: compra (tu imperative of comprare) + lo (it).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“to prepare, procure, get, purchase, obtain”), from cum + parō. Compare Portuguese and Spanish comprar, Romanian cumpăra.

senses.note: Comprare qualcosa a qualcuno = to buy something for someone.

etymology: From Latin comprendere, variant of comprehendere.

fact.text: The verb also means 'to include'. That's why 'servizio compreso' on an Italian menu means the service charge is already included in the price.

senses.note: Slightly more formal than capire. Also means 'to include'. Past participle: compreso.

etymology: From Latin comprōmittō.

senses.note: Conjugates like mettere: compromesso. 'To reach a compromise' is trovare un compromesso.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English computer.

senses.note: Invariable English loan: il computer, i computer (no -s in the plural).

etymology: From Latin commūne, noun use of the neuter form of commūnis.

fact.text: Italy is divided into nearly 8,000 comuni, from big cities like Rome down to villages with a few dozen people. Each one has its own mayor (sindaco).

senses.note: Also the town hall or council: andare in Comune. As an adjective, comune means 'common'.

etymology: From Latin commūnicāre.

senses.note: Often means 'to inform': comunicare qualcosa a qualcuno.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin commūnicātiōnem (“sharing, communication”).
Borrowed from Latin commūnitātem.

senses.note: Invariable: le comunità. Also used for residential care communities, e.g. for rehabilitation.

etymology: From come (“how”) + -unque (indefinite suffix).

fact.text: Built from come ('how') plus the indefinite suffix -unque, which works like English '-ever'. The same suffix gives chiunque (whoever), dovunque (wherever) and qualunque (whatever).

senses.note: As a conjunction + subjunctive it means 'however, no matter how': comunque vada = however it goes.

etymology: From come (“how”) + -unque (indefinite suffix).

fact.text: Built from come ('how') plus the indefinite suffix -unque, which works like English '-ever'. The same suffix gives chiunque (whoever), dovunque (wherever) and qualunque (whatever).

ignored: Duplicate: 'anyway' is studied on the adverb card for comunque.

senses.note: Takes the subjunctive: comunque vada = however it goes.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cum (“with”), from Proto-Italic *kom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“next to, at, with, along”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin cum 'with', which survives in English co-/con- words. A companion is literally someone you share bread (panis) with.

senses.note: Joins with il/i to make col/coi, mostly in speech.

etymology: Borrowed from French concentrer.

senses.note: To concentrate mentally is reflexive: concentrarsi su qualcosa.
Also 'concentrated' (succo concentrato). Concentrati! is the imperative of concentrarsi.

etymology: Deverbal from concertare + -o.

fact.text: In Italian this is any concert, but English borrowed it only for a piece for soloist and orchestra. It comes from concertare 'to bring into agreement'.

senses.note: Any live music show, including a rock gig.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin conclūdere.

senses.note: Concludere un affare = to close a deal; non concludere niente = to get nothing done. Past participle: concluso.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin conclūsiōnem.

senses.note: In conclusione = in conclusion. Can also mean completion.

etymology: From concorrere + -enza.

fact.text: Literally a running together (Latin concurrere), as rivals race for the same customers.

senses.note: Commercial rivalry or competitors. A contest is una gara or un concorso.

etymology: From Latin concursus.

fact.text: In Italy, most public-sector jobs, including teaching posts, are filled through a 'concorso pubblico', a competitive national exam that can draw huge numbers of candidates.

senses.note: Concorso pubblico = competitive exam for public-sector jobs.

etymology: From Late Latin condamnāre, from Latin condemnāre (“I condemn, convict, sentence”), from con- + damnō (“to discredit, find fault, disapprove, reject; to sentence someone to a punishment, declare guilty, condemn, doom, convict”), from damnum (“damage, injury, loss”).

fact.text: From Latin condemnare, built on damnum (damage, loss). The same root gives English 'damn' and 'damage', and the Italian danno (harm).

senses.note: condannare qualcuno a dieci anni = to sentence someone to ten years. Also: to condemn (morally).

etymology: From con- + dividere.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle condiviso. Also 'to share' an opinion: condivido la tua idea.

etymology: From condizione + -are.

senses.note: Il tempo ha condizionato la gara. Aria condizionata = air conditioning.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin conditiōnem.

senses.note: a condizione che + subjunctive = on condition that.

etymology: From condolersi + -anza.

senses.note: Almost always plural: Condoglianze! = My condolences. Fare le condoglianze a qcn.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin condominium (17th century).

fact.text: From Latin con- 'together' + dominium 'ownership', from dominus 'master of the house' (related to domus 'house'). So a condominium is literally a building that people own together.

senses.note: Also means the residents' association: riunione di condominio = residents' meeting.

etymology: Inherited from Latin condūcere (“to lead, bring or draw together”), from con- + dūcō (“lead”). By surface analysis, syncopic form of (archaic) conducere.

fact.text: From Latin conducere, 'to lead together' (con- + ducere, 'to lead'). English 'conduct', 'conductor' and 'duke' all come from the same Latin roots.

senses.note: Irregular: conduco, condussi, condotto, condurrò. Tradurre and produrre follow the same pattern.
Also very often a lecture or public talk: tenere una conferenza = to give a lecture.

etymology: From Latin cōnfirmāre.
From Latin cōnfīnis.

fact.text: Comes from Latin confinis, 'sharing a boundary', from con- (together) + finis (end, limit). Finis also gives English 'finish', 'final' and 'confine'.

senses.note: Used for national borders and for figurative limits: i confini della ragione.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin cōnfrontāre.

fact.text: Watch out: this verb usually means to compare, not to confront, and un confronto is a comparison. To confront someone or a problem is usually affrontare.

senses.note: confrontare A con B = to compare A with B. Noun: il confronto (comparison).

etymology: Deverbal from confrontare + -o.

fact.text: Looks like 'confrontation', but in everyday use it means 'comparison'. In confronto a means 'compared to'.

senses.note: In confronto a = compared to. It can also mean a confrontation or a match.

etymology: From Latin cōnfūsus.

senses.note: Can also mean muddled (ideas, speech) or hazy (memories). Also the past participle of confondere.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin congēlāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin congelare (con- + gelare, 'to freeze'), the same source as English 'congeal'. The root gel- also gives Italian gelo (frost) and gelato.

senses.note: Transitive (congelare il pesce, takes avere); for 'to freeze up / get frozen', congelarsi (takes essere) is more common.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin congrātulātiōnem, from congrātulor.

senses.note: Almost always plural: Congratulazioni! = Congratulations!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin coniugāre.

fact.text: Latin coniugare meant 'to yoke together' (con- + iugum, yoke). That is why the word can also mean 'to marry', and it shares a root with English 'conjugal'.

senses.note: Transitive: coniugare un verbo. Can also mean 'to combine' (coniugare qualità e prezzo).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin coniugem.

fact.text: From Latin coniux, 'one joined together' (con- 'together' + iungere 'to join', related to iugum 'yoke'). English 'conjugal' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Used in official and bureaucratic language. The article shows the gender (il/la coniuge). I coniugi = the married couple.
Connettersi a Internet / al Wi-Fi. Transitive connettere = to connect something.

etymology: From Late Latin cognōscentia, from Latin cognōscēns.

senses.note: Also an acquaintance: fare la conoscenza di = to meet. perdere conoscenza = to faint.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin conōscere, variant of Latin cognōscere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cognoscere, source of English cognition and recognize. English know goes back to the same ancient Indo-European root.

senses.note: Conoscere = be familiar with people or places; sapere = know facts. Ho conosciuto = I met.

etymology: Probably from a Vulgar Latin *conquisitāre, derived from Latin conquisitus, perfect passive participle of conquirō. Cf. also conquista. Compare Occitan, Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish conquistar.

senses.note: Also 'to win over' a person: l'hai conquistato? = did you win him over?

etymology: Deverbal from consegnare + -a.

senses.note: fare/effettuare le consegne = to make deliveries. From consegnare (to deliver, hand in).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnsignāre and adapted to native Italian segnare.

senses.note: Also 'to hand in/over': consegnare i compiti = to hand in homework.

ignored: Compound form of consegnare plus the pronoun lo; study it on the consegnare card.

senses.note: consegnare + lo

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnsequentia.

senses.note: Di conseguenza = consequently, as a result.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnsīderāre.

senses.note: Considerare qualcuno + adjective = to regard someone as: lo considero bravo.

etymology: From Latin cōnsīderātiōnem.

senses.note: prendere in considerazione = to take into account; fare una considerazione = to make a remark.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cōnsiliārī. By surface analysis, consiglio + -are.

features.construction: consigliare qualcosa a qualcuno; consigliare a qualcuno di + infinitive

senses.note: Ti consiglio di partire presto = I advise you to leave early.

etymology: From Latin cōnsilium.

fact.text: From Latin consilium, which also gave English 'counsel'. Italian keeps the other sense too: a consiglio can be a council, as in the Consiglio dei Ministri (cabinet).

senses.note: Countable: un consiglio = a piece of advice, consigli = advice. To give advice = dare un consiglio.

etymology: From Latin consulatus.
Borrowed from Latin cōnsonantem (“consonant”).
From Latin cōnsūmere.

senses.note: Consumarsi = to wear out, burn down. In a bar, consumare = to have something to eat or drink.

etymology: From contare. Compare French comptant (“cash”).

fact.text: Comes from contare, 'to count': cash is money you can count out on the spot. French comptant ('cash') comes from the same idea.

senses.note: Usually plural: i contanti. Pagare in contanti = to pay in cash.

etymology: From Latin computāre. Compare the doublets computare and compitare.

fact.text: From Latin computare, which also gave English both 'count' and 'compute'. The related raccontare means 'to tell': counting and recounting a story share one root.

senses.note: Contare su = to count on (ci stavo contando = I was counting on it). Also 'to matter'.

etymology: From contatto + -are.

senses.note: Takes a direct object with no preposition: contattare qualcuno.

etymology: From Latin contactus.

senses.note: Mettersi in contatto con = to get in touch with. Restare in contatto = to stay in touch.

etymology: From contemporaneo + -mente.

fact.text: This means 'at the same time', not 'in a modern way'. That matches the original meaning of English 'contemporary', from Latin con + tempus: 'existing at the same time'.

etymology: From Latin contemporāneus.

fact.text: The adverb contemporaneamente is very common and means 'at the same time, simultaneously', not 'in a modern way'.

senses.note: Also 'simultaneous'. Contemporaneamente = at the same time.

etymology: From Latin continēre.

senses.note: Conjugated like tenere: contengo, contiene, contenni. Contenersi = to restrain oneself.

etymology: From Latin contentus, perfect passive participle of contineō (“to contain”), whence Italian contenere.

fact.text: Same root as English 'content' (satisfied), from Latin contentus, 'held in, contained': someone whose wishes stay within limits. Watch out: the 'contents' of a box are il contenuto.

features.construction: contento di + inf.; contento che + subj.

senses.note: Takes the subjunctive after 'che' (contento che tu sia venuto) or 'di' + infinitive (contento di vederti).

etymology: From continuo + -mente.

senses.note: Covers both 'continuously' and 'continually, constantly'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin continuāre, from continuus.

senses.note: Continuare a + infinitive = to keep doing. Uses avere for people, essere for things: la festa è continuata.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin continuus, derived from contineō (“to hold together”).

senses.note: Also 'continual, constant': continue interruzioni = constant interruptions.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *contu(s), *comptu(s), from Latin computus. Doublet of computo and compito.

fact.text: Comes from Latin computus, 'calculation', like English 'count' and 'account'.

senses.note: Il conto, per favore = the bill, please. Also means a bank account: conto in banca.

etymology: Deverbal from contornare.

fact.text: On Italian menus contorni have their own section: a meat or fish secondo usually comes plain, so you order vegetables or potatoes separately.

senses.note: Usually vegetables or potatoes served with the main course. Also means 'outline'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin contrārius.

senses.note: al contrario = on the contrary; in caso contrario = otherwise. Also an adjective (contrary).

etymology: From Latin contractus.

senses.note: Firmare un contratto = to sign a contract.
In the plural, often grants or subsidies, or social-security contributions.

etymology: Inherited from Old Italian contra, from Latin contrā.

senses.note: Before personal pronouns, use 'contro di': contro di me, contro di noi.

etymology: Borrowed from French contrôler.

fact.text: Comes from Medieval Latin contrarotulum, a 'counter-roll': a duplicate register kept to check accounts against. So controlling first meant checking against a copy.

senses.note: Mainly means to check or inspect; 'to control' is a secondary sense. Controllarsi = to control oneself.

etymology: Borrowed from French contrôle.

fact.text: Comes, like English control, from French contrerole, a 'counter-roll': a duplicate register kept to check accounts against the original.

senses.note: sotto controllo = under control. It often means 'check, inspection': controllo passaporti.

etymology: Inherited from Latin convenīre, from cum + veniō.

fact.text: The related adjective conveniente is a false friend: it usually means good value or cheap, not convenient (that's comodo).

senses.note: Used impersonally with essere: ti conviene partire = you'd better leave; mi è convenuto.

etymology: From Latin conversātiōnem.

senses.note: Fare conversazione = to chat, make conversation.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin convincere.

fact.text: From Latin con- plus vincere, 'to conquer, to win', the root of Italian vincere and English 'victory'. To convince someone was literally to defeat them in argument.

features.construction: transitive: convincere qualcuno (a fare / di qualcosa)

senses.note: convincere qualcuno a fare qualcosa = to persuade someone to do something. Past participle: convinto.
il/la convivente: an unmarried partner you live with. Common in official and legal language.

fact.text: Cooperatives are a big part of Italian life. Coop, one of Italy's largest supermarket chains, is a network of consumer cooperatives, and many wineries and farms sell through co-ops.

senses.note: Also an adjective form: società cooperativa

etymology: Substantivized feminine of the adjective coperto.

fact.text: Literally 'the covered (thing)', from coprire 'to cover'. On a ship it also means the deck, so 'sotto coperta' means 'below deck'.

senses.note: Don't confuse with 'il coperto', the cover charge in restaurants.

etymology: From Late Latin coopertūra, from Latin coopertus.

senses.note: Also a roof, financial or military cover, and phone-network or insurance coverage.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōpia (“abundance”).

fact.text: Latin copia meant 'abundance', the root of English copious and cornucopia ('horn of plenty'). The meaning 'copy' grew in medieval Latin, from the idea of multiplying texts.

senses.note: Una copia del documento. Also a copy of a book or newspaper. Brutta copia = rough draft.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *cōpla, from Latin cōpula. Doublet of copula, which was borrowed. Compare Sicilian cucchia.

fact.text: Like English 'couple', it comes from Latin copula, 'a bond or link'.

senses.note: For 'a couple of' (a few) use un paio di, not coppia.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cooperīre. For the past historic stem copers- compare perdere: pers-, morire: mors-, etc.

fact.text: Its past participle coperto also names the cover charge on Italian restaurant bills, paid per place setting at the table.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: coperto. Coprirsi = to cover up or wrap up warm.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan coratge, Old French corage.

fact.text: It comes from the same Old French word as English 'courage'. Both go back to Latin cor, 'heart', because courage was thought to live in the heart.

senses.note: Used to encourage someone. The noun il coraggio = courage.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan coratge, Old French corage.

fact.text: It comes from the same Old French word as English 'courage'. Both go back to Latin cor, 'heart', because courage was thought to live in the heart.

senses.note: Coraggio! = Come on! / Chin up! Avere il coraggio di = to dare to. Che coraggio! can mean 'What nerve!'

etymology: Inherited from Latin chorda (“cord”), from Ancient Greek χορδή (khordḗ, “string of gut, the string of a lyre”).

fact.text: Goes back to Greek khordē 'gut', since early lyre strings were made of gut. English cord comes from the same word.

senses.note: Also a string of an instrument or racket. Corde vocali = vocal cords.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cordiālis. Noun meaning via French.

fact.text: From Latin cor, cordis 'heart', just like English cordial, so a cordial greeting is one from the heart. Italian emails often end with 'Cordiali saluti'.

senses.note: Cordiali saluti = Kind regards (letter closing).

etymology: From cordiale + -mente.

fact.text: Rooted in Latin cor, cordis 'heart', so it literally means 'from the heart'. The same root is behind English 'cordial' and, via French, 'courage'.

senses.note: Common sign-off in letters and emails, like 'Cordiali saluti'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin corpus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrep-. Doublet of the borrowing corpus.

fact.text: From Latin corpus, which also gave English corpse, corps and corporal. It is a distant cousin of Old English hrif 'belly', still heard in midriff.

senses.note: Can also mean a corpse. corpo a corpo = hand-to-hand.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin corrigere but adapted to the inherited reggere.

fact.text: A 'caffè corretto' is an espresso that has been 'corrected' with a shot of grappa, sambuca or brandy. Correcting a drink means spiking it.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle corretto, passato remoto corressi. Also used for marking exams.
The participle correlato often just means 'related': non sono correlati.

etymology: Inherited from Latin currentem.

fact.text: From Latin currens, 'running', the present participle of currere 'to run'. English current comes from the same root, as do courier and course.

senses.note: Also a noun: la corrente = current, draught; also electricity (manca la corrente = the power's out).

etymology: Inherited from Latin currentem.

fact.text: From Latin currens, 'running', the present participle of currere 'to run'. English current comes from the same root, as do courier and course.

senses.note: Also 'draught': c'è corrente = there's a draught. Adjective too: acqua corrente = running water.

etymology: Inherited from Latin currere, from Proto-Italic *korzō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱr̥s-é-ti, zero-grade thematic present of *ḱers- (“to run”).

fact.text: From Latin currere 'to run', which also gave English 'current', 'course', 'courier', 'occur' and 'currency', money that 'runs' from hand to hand.

senses.note: Uses avere for the activity (ho corso un'ora) and essere with a destination (sono corso a casa).
Adjective (also past participle of correggere). The adverb is correttamente, meaning 'correctly'.

etymology: From correre. Compare Spanish, Portuguese, and Catalan corredor. Compare also Vulgar Latin *curritōrius and *curritor, from currō.

fact.text: English 'corridor' came through French from Italian, and goes back to correre, 'to run'. A corridor was originally a passage for running along.

senses.note: Also the aisle of a train, plane or theatre.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin correspondēre, from Latin cum + respondeō.

senses.note: Takes a: corrispondere a qualcosa. Transitive use: to pay (a fee) or return (love).

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of correre (“to run”).

fact.text: From the past participle of correre 'to run'. Its old meaning 'privateering' produced corsaro, which became English 'corsair'.

senses.note: Also 'race' or 'ride' (bus, taxi). di corsa = in a hurry

etymology: From Latin cursus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cursus, 'a running', from currere, 'to run'. English course, current and cursor share the same root.

senses.note: Also the course of a river or of events. In corso = in progress.

etymology: From Latin cōrtem, shortened version of Latin cohors (“court; enclosure”). Doublet of the borrowing coorte.

fact.text: Latin cohors first meant an enclosed yard. It gave English both 'court' and 'cohort', and Italian also has coorte (cohort).

senses.note: fare la corte a = to court someone. A tennis court is un campo da tennis.

etymology: From cortese + -ia.

fact.text: Comes from cortese 'courteous', which comes from corte 'court'. Courtesy was first the polished behaviour expected at a royal court, the same story as in English.

senses.note: per cortesia = please; fare una cortesia = to do a favour.

etymology: From corte (“courtyard”) + -ile. Compare Sicilian curtigghiu.

fact.text: Built from corte ('court'), which comes from Latin cohors, 'enclosure'. That is the same source as English court, so a cortile really is a courtyard.

senses.note: Also the school playground; animali da cortile = farmyard animals.

etymology: From Latin curtus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-.

fact.text: Latin curtus, 'cut short', comes from an Indo-European root meaning 'to cut'. That root is distantly related to English short and shirt.

senses.note: Opposite of lungo. For a short person, Italians usually say basso.

etymology: Inherited from Latin causa. Doublet of the borrowing causa. The pronoun is a clipping of che cosa.

fact.text: It comes from Latin causa, 'cause, reason, lawsuit', so it is a cousin of English 'cause'. Italian later borrowed causa again, separately, to mean 'cause'.

senses.note: Also used to mean 'what?': Cosa fai? (short for che cosa).

etymology: Inherited from Latin causa. Doublet of the borrowing causa. The pronoun is a clipping of che cosa.

fact.text: It comes from Latin causa, 'cause, reason, lawsuit', so it is a cousin of English 'cause'. Italian later borrowed causa again, separately, to mean 'cause'.

senses.note: Short for che cosa; che alone also works. Cosa è → cos'è?

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnscientia.

fact.text: One Italian word covers both English 'conscience' and 'consciousness': avere la coscienza pulita = to have a clear conscience, but prendere coscienza = to become aware.

senses.note: Also consciousness or awareness: prendere coscienza di = to become aware of.

etymology: Masculine form of cosa.

senses.note: Masculine form of cosa. Used for people too: Coso = what's-his-name.

etymology: Inherited from Latin costa. Cognate with French côte, Romanian coastă, and Spanish cuesta.

fact.text: Latin costa meant 'rib' or 'side'. A coast is the side of the land. English coast came from it through Old French coste.

senses.note: Also rib (in anatomy usually costola), hillside, or the spine of a book.

etymology: From Latin cōnstāre. Doublet of constare, a borrowing.

fact.text: English cost comes from the same Latin verb, constare ('to stand firm, to be fixed'), by way of Old French couster. The idea is a price that stands fixed.

senses.note: Takes essere: è costato tanto. Quanto costa? = How much is it?

etymology: From costa (“coast”) + -iero.

senses.note: Strada costiera = coastal road. Derived from costa (coast).

etymology: Deverbal from costare (“to cost”) + -o.

senses.note: A ogni costo / a tutti i costi = at any cost, at all costs.

etymology: From costare + -oso.

senses.note: Means the same as caro, which can also mean 'dear'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin cōnstringere.

fact.text: Inherited from Latin constringere, 'to bind tightly', which is also the source of English 'constrain' and 'constrict'. The past participle costretto is related to English 'strict'.

senses.note: Costringere qualcuno a fare qualcosa. Irregular: costrinsi, costretto.

etymology: From Latin cōnstruere, probably a borrowing.

senses.note: -isc- verb: costruisco, costruisci. Past participle: costruito.

ignored: This is just costruire with the pronoun lo attached, so it belongs on the costruire card.

senses.note: costruire + lo: object pronouns attach to the end of the infinitive.

ignored: This is costruire with an attached pronoun, and the verb costruire has its own card.

senses.note: Costruire + mi: an infinitive with an attached object pronoun.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cōnstrūctiōnem.

senses.note: Both the act and the structure: in costruzione = under construction. A plain 'building' is often edificio.

etymology:
PIE word
 *ḱóm
 PIE word
 *swé
Inherited from Latin consuētūdinem. Doublet of consuetudine, which was borrowed.

fact.text: Comes from Latin consuetudo, 'custom'. English custom and costume are therefore the same word, and Italian still uses it for both a habit and an outfit.

senses.note: Also swimsuit (costume da bagno) and custom: usi e costumi = customs and traditions.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *eccum sīc. By surface analysis, ecco + sì. Closely parallel to Dalmatian coisa, Friulian cussì, Istriot cussèi, Sardinian gósi (bosìe, deàsi, etc.), Venetan cusì. Compare also Catalan així, French ainsi, Portuguese assim, Spanish así, Romanian așa, Sicilian accussì.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin eccum sic, 'behold, thus'. It is ecco (here is) fused with sì in its old sense of 'thus'. Spanish así is a cousin.

senses.note: Così così = so-so. Così tanto = so much. Fai così = do it like this.

etymology: Borrowed from Arabic قُطُن (quṭun); see cotton for more.

fact.text: Like English 'cotton', it comes from Arabic quṭun. The word reached Europe along with the cotton trade through the Arab Mediterranean.

senses.note: Di cotone = made of cotton. Cotone idrofilo = cotton wool.

etymology: A southern variant of coccia.

fact.text: Originally a southern word. Mussels are 'muscoli' in Liguria and 'peoci' in Venice. In slang, the word is also an unkind term for an unattractive woman.

senses.note: Impepata di cozze: mussels steamed with lots of black pepper, a Neapolitan classic.

etymology: If not direcly inherited, then a latinization of older criare (a more securely native form), from Latin creāre.

senses.note: Also 'to cause': creare problemi = to cause problems.

etymology: Derived from Late Latin creātūra, from Latin creō.

senses.note: In southern Italy it can also mean a baby or small child.

etymology: Inherited from Latin crēdere (“to believe”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin credere 'to believe', which also gave English credit, creed, credible and incredible.

features.construction: credere a/in qualcosa; credere che + congiuntivo

senses.note: credere a qualcuno = believe someone; credere in = believe in; credo che + subjunctive.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin crēditum.

fact.text: From Latin creditum, 'something entrusted', from credere, 'to believe'. Giving someone credit literally means believing they will pay you back. Italian credere still means 'to believe'.

senses.note: Also used for phone top-up credit and university credits.

etymology: Borrowed from French crème.

fact.text: Asking for crema in your coffee won't get you dairy cream: that is panna. Crema means skin cream, custard, or the golden foam on top of an espresso.

senses.note: Dairy cream is panna. Crema means a lotion, a creamy soup or sauce, or the foam on an espresso.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cremāre. First attested in the 19th century.

Inherited from Latin crepāre (“to rattle, creak, crack”).
The informal sense of 'die' is shared with both the French and Romanian cognates crever and crăpa.

fact.text: From Latin crepare, 'to rattle, crack', which is also behind English decrepit and crevice. The French relative crever also means 'to die'.

senses.note: Rude when said of people: Crepa! = Drop dead! Crepare dal ridere = to die laughing.

etymology: From Latin crēscere, from Proto-Italic *krēskō, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱreh₁- (“to grow, become bigger”).

fact.text: Its gerund crescendo, 'growing', became the musical term for getting louder. The crescent moon is also named from Latin crescere: it is the growing moon.

senses.note: Intransitive takes essere (sono cresciuto). Transitive with avere = to raise (children).

etymology: From Latin crista.

fact.text: Fare la cresta (sulla spesa) means secretly keeping some of the money you were given to go shopping, a bit like skimming off the top.

senses.note: Also a rooster's comb, the crest of a wave and a mohawk hairstyle.

etymology: From Late Latin or Juridical Latin criminālis (“criminal”), from Latin crīmen (“verdict; crime”).

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il criminale / la criminale.

etymology: From criminale + -ità.

senses.note: Crime as a social phenomenon: tasso di criminalità = crime rate. A single crime is un reato or un crimine.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin crīmine.

senses.note: Means a serious crime; any legal offence is usually 'reato'.
Medical term for a fungal infection. Invariable: le criptococcosi.

etymology: From Latin crisis, from Ancient Greek κρίνειν (krínein, “to decide”).

fact.text: From Greek krinein 'to decide'. A crisis was the turning point of an illness, when it was decided whether you lived or died. English critic and criterion share the root.

senses.note: Invariable plural: le crisi.

etymology: From Latin Christus, from Ancient Greek Χριστός (Khristós), proper noun use of χριστός (khristós, “the anointed one”), a calque of Hebrew מָשִׁיחַ (māšīaḥ, “anointed”) (see also messia).

fact.text: From Greek Khristós, 'the anointed one', a direct translation of Hebrew māšīaḥ, the source of messia (messiah). Both words mean the same thing.

senses.note: Capitalized for Jesus. 'Un povero cristo' = a poor wretch. Used as a curse, which many find offensive.

etymology: From critica + -are.
From Latin criticus.

senses.note: Female form: la critica, which also means 'criticism'.

fact.text: Built on croce 'cross', from ships crossing back and forth over the sea. English cruise likewise comes from Dutch kruisen 'to cross'.

senses.note: Fare una crociera = to go on a cruise.

etymology: From Latin chronica.

fact.text: Italian newspapers sort the news by colour: 'cronaca nera' (black) is crime news, 'cronaca rosa' (pink) is celebrity gossip and 'cronaca bianca' (white) covers everyday local events.

senses.note: Today it often means news reporting: fatti di cronaca = news stories. Also 'cronaca in diretta' = live commentary.

etymology: Inherited from Latin crusta, from Proto-Indo-European *krustós (“hardened”), from *krews- (“to form a crust, begin to freeze”).

fact.text: Latin crusta also gave English 'crust'. Its Indo-European root meant 'to harden, freeze' and is related to Greek krystallos, 'ice', the source of 'crystal'.

senses.note: Also crust (of bread, cheese) or the Earth's crust: la crosta terrestre.

etymology: From Latin crūdus (compare French cru, Spanish crudo). Doublet of cru.

fact.text: In Italy, prosciutto crudo is cured, uncooked ham like Parma ham, while prosciutto cotto is cooked ham. If you ask only for 'prosciutto', you may get either.

senses.note: Opposite of cotto (cooked). Also harsh or blunt: la cruda verità.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin cochleārium, derived from cochlear, from cochlea (“snail”), which perhaps was an instrument used to eat eggs and snails. It's also possible that it derives from the use to which it was put, the concave shape, or perhaps originally it was made with the shell of a snail.
Cognate with Sicilian cucchiara, French cuillère, Portuguese colher, Catalan cullera and Spanish cuchara.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cochlea, 'snail'. The Roman cochlear may have been a small tool for eating snails and eggs, or it may simply have been named for its shell-like shape.

senses.note: Teaspoon = cucchiaino.

etymology: From Late Latin cocīna, from earlier coquīna.

fact.text: English 'kitchen' comes from the same Late Latin word, cocina. Old English borrowed it as cycene, so the two words are long-lost relatives.

senses.note: Also means cooking or cuisine (la cucina italiana), and a cooker or stove.

etymology: From Late Latin cocīnāre, from Latin coquīnāre. The slang sense is a semantic loan from English cook.

fact.text: From Latin coquinare, from coquina 'kitchen'. English kitchen comes from the same Latin word, through Old English cycene.

senses.note: La cucina means both 'kitchen' and 'cuisine': la cucina italiana.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French cosin, cousin, from Latin cōnsobrīnus. Doublet of consobrino.

fact.text: Came from Old French cosin, the same word that gave English cousin. Both go back to Latin consobrinus, which first meant a child of your mother's sister.

senses.note: A female cousin is la cugina. I cugini can mean cousins of mixed sex.

etymology: From Latin cūlus (“anus”).

fact.text: In slang it also means luck: 'avere culo' is to be lucky and 'che culo!' means 'what luck!' It's vulgar but very common among friends.

senses.note: 'Farsi il culo' means to work your butt off. 'Che culo!' means 'what luck!'

etymology: From Latin cultūra.

senses.note: Also means learning or knowledge: una persona di cultura = a cultured person.

etymology: From Late Latin cocere, from Latin coquere.

fact.text: Latin coquere is the root of English cook and kitchen. Biscotti are literally 'twice-cooked': bis + cotto, the past participle.

features.construction: transitive (ho cotto la pasta); intransitive with essere (la pasta è cotta)

senses.note: Means to cook food by heat (boil, bake). Cucinare means to prepare meals. Irregular: cuocio, cotto, cossi.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *corem m, from Latin cor n.

fact.text: Comes from Latin cor (heart), which also gives English 'cordial', 'courage' and 'record' (from Latin recordari, to call back to the heart, i.e. remember).

senses.note: Also used figuratively: 'di cuore' = sincerely; 'nel cuore della notte' = in the dead of night.

etymology: From Latin cūra, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeys- (“to heed”).

fact.text: Also means medical treatment, not necessarily a cure. Fare una cura means undergoing treatment. Getting healed is la guarigione.

senses.note: Prendersi cura di = to take care of. Con cura = carefully.

etymology: From Latin cūrāre.

fact.text: Latin cūrāre, 'to care for', also gave English cure and curator. On Italian book covers, 'a cura di' means 'edited by'.

senses.note: Used for patients and illnesses: curare una malattia. Also 'to look after': curare il giardino.

etymology: From curare + -si.

senses.note: Also 'to get treatment'. Curarsi di qualcosa = to care about/bother with something.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin cūriōsus.

senses.note: Can mean both 'inquisitive' and 'odd, strange' (una cosa curiosa).

fact.text: Latin for 'the course of life'. Curriculum first meant a running or a racecourse, from currere, 'to run'.

senses.note: Often shortened to curriculum or CV. In everyday use the plural usually stays the same: i curriculum.

etymology: Nominalized feminine singular of curvo (“curved”, adjective).

fact.text: In football, la Curva is the curved stand behind each goal, where the most passionate fans (the ultras) sit. Curva Nord and Curva Sud are famous names at many Italian stadiums.

senses.note: Used for road bends and for curves in maths and graphs, e.g. curve di livello (contour lines).

etymology: Derived from Latin curvus (“bent”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to turn; to bend”).

senses.note: Also 'stooping' when describing a person: curvo per l'età.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French coissin or Old Occitan coisin, from Vulgar Latin *coxīnum, *cossīnum, from Latin coxa (“hip; thigh”).

fact.text: Shares its origin with English 'cushion'. Both come through Old French from Latin coxa, 'hip, thigh', because the first cushions were seat pads to sit on.

senses.note: Also means a cushion, e.g. on a sofa.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin custōdia, a noun derived from custōs (“guardian”).

senses.note: Also: a protective case (custodia degli occhiali = glasses case). custodia cautelare = pre-trial detention.

etymology: From Latin dē (“from”) + ā/ab (“of, from”). In the meaning of “at, near, by”, da probably comes from Latin unde + ad.

fact.text: With the present tense it means 'for' or 'since': Vivo qui da due anni = I have lived here for two years. English speakers often wrongly use the past tense here.

senses.note: Also 'at someone's place' (da Mario) and 'by' (passive). Merges with articles: dal, dalla, dai.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin damnātiōnem. Equivalent of dannare + -zione.

senses.note: Often used as an exclamation: Dannazione! = Damn it!

etymology: Inherited from Latin damnum, from Proto-Italic *dapnom, from Proto-Indo-European *dh₂pnóm (“expense, investment”), derived from *deh₂p- (“to sacrifice”).

fact.text: From Latin damnum, 'loss' or 'harm'. Its verb damnare gave English 'damn' and 'condemn', and 'indemnity' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Often plural: i danni = the damage. Also 'harm'. Risarcire i danni = to pay damages.

etymology:
Univerbation of da + per + tutto.
Compare French partout, Catalan pertot and Spanish por todas partes for similar constructions.

fact.text: Fused from da + per + tutto, roughly 'from through all'.

senses.note: Synonym: ovunque.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dō, from Proto-Italic *didō, from Proto-Indo-European *dédeh₃ti, from the root *deh₃- (“give”).

fact.text: Latin dare gave English data, meaning 'things given'. It also gave date: Roman letters ended with 'data...', meaning 'given (on this day)'.

senses.note: dare qualcosa a qualcuno. Note the accent in dà (he gives), which tells it apart from da (from).

etymology: From dare + -si.

fact.text: The everyday expression può darsi means 'maybe' or 'it could be'. Literally it is 'it can give itself', in the sense of 'it can happen'.

senses.note: Darsi a qualcosa. Also: darsi da fare = to get busy; può darsi = maybe.

etymology: From Late Latin data, from Latin datus.

fact.text: False friend: Italian data is a calendar date, not information. Both come from Latin data, 'given', as in letters dated 'data Romae' (given at Rome). English data is i dati.

senses.note: Data di nascita = date of birth. A romantic date is un appuntamento; English 'data' is i dati.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin datum.

fact.text: English data is the Latin plural of datum, meaning 'something given', from dare (to give). In Italian, dato is still literally 'given', the past participle of dare.

senses.note: Mostly plural: i dati = data. Dato is also the past participle of dare (given).

etymology: From older davante. Presumably di + avante.

senses.note: davanti a = in front of: davanti alla stazione.

etymology: From older davante. Presumably di + avante.
ignored: Nominalized use (il davanti); the ordinary meaning is studied on the adverb card davanti.

senses.note: Invariable noun: il davanti della maglia = the front of the sweater.

etymology:
Univerbation of da + vero.
The pronunciation with -vv- is due to the word's spelling being fossilized with the syntactic gemination of the traditional (Tuscan) pronunciation of da. The pronunciation with a single -v- reflects the regional and now standard pronunciation of da. Compare Spanish de veras, de a de veras (“for real”)

fact.text: Literally 'from true': da + vero fused into one word. The double v is a frozen trace of the Tuscan habit of doubling the consonant after da.

senses.note: Also a reply on its own: Davvero? = Really?

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēbitum, noun use of the neuter form of dēbitus, perfect passive participle of dēbeō (“to owe”).

fact.text: English debt comes from the same Latin debitum, but it reached English through French as 'dette'. Scholars later added the silent b to make it look like the Latin.

senses.note: Avere debiti = to be in debt.

etymology: From Latin debilis.

fact.text: Comes from Latin debilis, 'weak', which also gave English 'debilitate'.

senses.note: Also used for faint light or sound. Same form for masculine and feminine; plural deboli.

etymology: From Latin dēcīdere, from dē + caedō.

fact.text: From Latin decidere, 'to cut off' (de + caedere, 'to cut'). Deciding is literally cutting off the other options. The same root gives homicide and incision.

senses.note: decidere di + infinitive: Ho deciso di partire. Past participle: deciso.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēcīsiōnem.

senses.note: Italians 'take' decisions: prendere una decisione = to make a decision.
Opposite of crescente. Luna decrescente = waning moon.

etymology: di (preposition) + il (article)

senses.note: di + il, used before masculine singular nouns. Also partitive 'some': del pane = some bread.

etymology: From Latin dēlicātus.

senses.note: Also means sensitive (a delicate matter), gentle (a mild flavour) or tactful.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēlīctum, from dēlinquō (“to transgress, err”); probably a semi-learned borrowing.

fact.text: Comes from Latin delictum, 'offence'. English uses the same word in the legal phrase 'in flagrante delicto', meaning caught red-handed. 'Delinquent' shares its root.

senses.note: A serious crime, often murder: delitto passionale (crime of passion).

etymology: From Late Latin dēliciōsus.

senses.note: Also 'delightful, charming' for places or people.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēlūdō.

fact.text: Looks like English 'delude' and shares its Latin root deludere (to mock, deceive), but it means to disappoint or let down. 'To delude oneself' is illudersi.

senses.note: Irregular: deluso, delusi. Essere deluso da = to be disappointed by.

etymology: From Latin dēlūsiōnem.

fact.text: Not a 'delusion' in the English sense. It means disappointment. A false belief is an illusione, and a psychiatric delusion is a delirio.

senses.note: Che delusione! = What a letdown!

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin democratia, from Ancient Greek δημοκρατίᾱ (dēmokratíā). By surface analysis, demo- + -crazia.
Inherited from Latin dēnārius, via a non-Tuscan dialect where Latin /rj/ yields /r/.

fact.text: From Latin denarius, a Roman silver coin. The same coin gave Arabic dinar, and its d was the abbreviation for the penny in the old British £sd system.

senses.note: Usually singular and uncountable. Soldi is the everyday word; denaro sounds a bit more formal.

etymology: From Latin dentem. Doublet of zanna.

fact.text: Pasta cooked 'al dente' is literally cooked 'to the tooth': firm enough that you still feel it when you bite. The word comes from Latin dentem, like English 'dentist'.

senses.note: lavarsi i denti = to brush one's teeth.

etymology: From Latin dentifricium.

fact.text: From Latin dentifricium: dens 'tooth' + fricare 'to rub', so literally 'tooth rub'.

etymology: From dente + -ista.

senses.note: il/la dentista; plural i dentisti (m), le dentiste (f)

etymology: From Late Latin dē intrō.

senses.note: Also a preposition: dentro la scatola / dentro alla scatola. Opposite: fuori.

etymology: Deverbal from denunciare + -a.

fact.text: This is less dramatic than 'denunciation'. Italians routinely 'fanno la denuncia' at the police station after a stolen wallet or lost passport, a simple official report.

senses.note: fare/sporgere denuncia = to report something to the police. Plural: denunce.

fact.text: Usually stronger and more concrete than English 'denounce': it normally means filing a police report. Ti denuncio! means 'I'll report you to the police!'

senses.note: Denunciare un furto = to report a theft. Also: to denounce, to expose; to declare (income).

ignored: Infinitive plus clitic pronoun; study the verb denunciare instead.

senses.note: denunciare + ti.
Same form for masculine and feminine; plural deprimenti.

etymology: From Latin dēprimō.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle depresso, passato remoto depressi. Deprimersi = to get depressed.

etymology: Borrowed from French dérober.

fact.text: Goes back to the Frankish word *raubōn. That is the same Germanic root that gave English the verb rob.

senses.note: The object is the victim: derubare qualcuno (di qualcosa) = to rob someone (of something).

etymology: From Latin dēscrībere (“to describe”).

senses.note: Irregular past participle: descritto (like scrivere → scritto).

etymology: From the older form diserto, from Latin dēsertum, substantivized neuter form of dēsertus, perfect passive participle of dēserō (“to forsake, abandon”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin desertum, 'something abandoned', from deserere, 'to forsake'. A desert is literally a deserted place, from the same root as English 'deserter'.

senses.note: Also an adjective: deserto = deserted, empty (una strada deserta = an empty street).

etymology: From an alteration of the older disiderare, from Latin dēsīderāre (“to long for, desire, feel the want of, miss, regret”). Doublet of desirare, taken from Old Occitan.

fact.text: From Latin desiderare, which also gave English 'desire' via French. It is often linked to sidus 'star', as if 'missing the stars', but that origin is debated.

senses.note: In shops, 'Desidera?' means 'What would you like?'. Can take an infinitive: desidero partire.

etymology: From an alteration, based on its Latin root, of the older disidero, desidero, from Latin dēsīderium.

fact.text: Latin desiderium is often traced to sidus 'star', as if it meant missing the stars or waiting for them. This is a popular theory, but scholars debate it.

senses.note: Esprimere un desiderio = to make a wish. Plural: desideri.
Masculine, invariable French loan: il dessert, i dessert. Also common: il dolce.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin destinātārius and French destinataire.

senses.note: Feminine: destinataria. The opposite is il mittente (sender).

etymology: From Latin dēstinātiōnem.

senses.note: Arrivare a destinazione = to reach one's destination.

etymology: Deverbal from destinare + -o.

senses.note: Can also mean destination: a destino = at its destination.

etymology: From Latin dextra or dextera. Compare French dextre, Portuguese destra.

fact.text: From Latin dextra, the right hand. The same root gives English 'dexterous' (handy, because most people favour the right hand) and 'ambidextrous', meaning 'right-handed on both sides'.

senses.note: a destra = on/to the right; la destra can also mean the right hand or the political right.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English detective.

senses.note: Invariable: il/la detective, i/le detective. Native synonym: investigatore.

etymology: From Latin dētestārī.
From French détail.

fact.text: Borrowed from French détail, from Old French taillier 'to cut': a detail is literally a small piece cut off. The same root gives English tailor and Italian tagliare.

senses.note: nei dettagli = in detail; al dettaglio = retail.

etymology: From Latin dictātus, dictātum.

senses.note: Also the past participle of dettare (to dictate).

etymology: From Latin dē. Cognate with English to. For etymology 1, preposition sense 11, compare French delà, deçà and deci delà.

senses.note: Merges with the article: del, dello, della, dei, degli, delle. Often d' before a vowel: d'oro.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dialectos.

fact.text: Many Italian 'dialects', such as Neapolitan or Sicilian, are not versions of standard Italian. They are separate Romance languages that grew directly out of Latin.

senses.note: Parlare in dialetto = to speak the local dialect.

etymology: From Latin dialogus, from Ancient Greek διάλογος (diálogos).

fact.text: The Greek prefix dia- means 'through', not 'two'. It comes from dialegesthai 'to converse', so a dialogue can have any number of speakers.

senses.note: Plural: dialoghi (with h).

etymology: From Late Latin diamantem, from Latin adamantem, from Ancient Greek ἀδάμας (adámas, “invincible, untamed; hard substance”), from ἀ- (a-, “un-”) + δαμάζω (damázō, “to overpower, tame, conquer”), from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂-.

fact.text: From Greek adámas, 'untameable, invincible', a name for the hardest substance. The same Greek word gave English adamant.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin diārium.

fact.text: Italian schoolchildren all carry a 'diario', a school planner for homework and notes to parents. Decorated diaries are a big back-to-school purchase every September.

senses.note: Tenere un diario = to keep a diary.

etymology: From Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin diabolus (possibly semi-learned), itself from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos).

fact.text: Comes from Greek diabolos, meaning slanderer (literally one who throws things across). English 'devil' and 'diabolical' come from the same word.

senses.note: Also used in exclamations: che diavolo...? = what the devil...?

etymology: From Latin Decembrem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin decem, 'ten'. December was the tenth month of the early Roman calendar, which began in March.

senses.note: Italian months are not capitalised: a dicembre = in December.

etymology: From Latin dēclārāre.

senses.note: Niente da dichiarare? = Anything to declare? Dichiararsi = to declare one's love.

etymology: From dichiarare + -zione, based on Latin dēclārātiōnem.

fact.text: Two everyday phrases with it: 'dichiarazione dei redditi' is your annual tax return, and 'dichiarazione d'amore' is a declaration of love.

senses.note: Fare una dichiarazione = to make a statement.

etymology: Inherited from Latin decem ac novem (“ten and nine”). Compare Venetan disinove.
From Latin decem ac septem (“ten and seven”). Compare Venetan dixisete.
Inherited from Latin decem.
ignored: Secondary noun use of the numeral; studied on the numeral card dieci.

senses.note: As a noun: il dieci (a grade, shirt number, etc.). Invariable.

etymology: Inherited from Latin decem.
From Latin diaeta (“diet, regimen”), from Ancient Greek δίαιτα (díaita, “way of living”).

fact.text: Goes back to Greek díaita, 'way of living'. The word first meant a whole lifestyle and only later narrowed to what you eat.

senses.note: Essere a dieta = to be on a diet. Fare la dieta = to diet.

etymology: From an earlier Italian form drieto, from Late Latin dē retrō, from Latin dē + retrō. Compare French derrière and Sicilian darreri

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin de retro, 'from behind', the same source as French derrière. English borrowed derrière as a polite word for the backside.

senses.note: Also a preposition: dietro la casa, dietro di me (with di before pronouns).

etymology: From Latin dēfendere.

senses.note: Irregular: difesi, difeso. Difendersi = to defend oneself.

etymology: From Late Latin dēfēnsa, from the feminine of Latin dēfēnsus, perfect passive participle of dēfendō.

senses.note: Used in military, legal and sports contexts. Legittima difesa = self-defence.

etymology: From Latin defectus.

senses.note: Also used for personal faults. Essere in difetto = to be in the wrong.

etymology: From Latin differentem.

senses.note: Diverso is the more common everyday synonym.

etymology: From Latin differentia.

senses.note: La differenza tra A e B = the difference between A and B.

etymology: From Latin difficilis.

fact.text: Literally 'not easy': Latin dis- plus facilis, 'easy'. That second part lives on in Italian facile (easy) and English 'facilitate'.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural difficili.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin difficultātem.

senses.note: Invariable: le difficoltà. Essere in difficoltà = to be in trouble.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dismenticāre.

fact.text: Built on mente, 'mind' (Latin mens): to forget is literally to let something 'drop out of the mind', the same mente that Italian uses today.

senses.note: Dimenticare qualcosa, or dimenticarsi di qualcosa (with essere).

etymology: From Latin dīminuō.

fact.text: The musical term diminuendo, meaning gradually getting softer, is just this verb's gerund: 'diminishing'.

senses.note: Takes essere when intransitive (i prezzi sono diminuiti) and avere when transitive.

etymology: From Latin dēmōnstrāre.

fact.text: Built on Latin monstrare, to show, which comes from monstrum, a warning sign or portent. That same monstrum gave English the word monster.

senses.note: Also 'to prove'. Dimostra 30 anni = he looks 30.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dēmōnstrātiōnem, or from dimostrare + -zione.

senses.note: Also a proof in maths/logic, or a public demonstration (protest).

fact.text: Alfred Nobel patented dynamite in 1867. He named it after Greek dynamis, 'power', the same root as dynamic and dynasty.

senses.note: Also used figuratively for something explosive or amazing: è dinamite!

etymology: From Latin deus, from earlier *dẹ̄vos, from Old Latin deivos, from Proto-Italic *deiwos, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós, derived from the root *dyew- (“sky, heaven”).

fact.text: Comes from the ancient root *dyew-, 'sky', which also gave Latin dies ('day') and Jupiter. The gods were originally the 'sky ones'.

senses.note: Capitalised Dio for God. Irregular plural: gli dèi (not i dei); feminine dea, dee.
A university or government department. A department store is un grande magazzino.

fact.text: Literally 'one who depends', from dipendere (to depend): an employee depends on an employer. As an adjective it means dependent or addicted.

senses.note: Dipendente da = dependent on; can also mean addicted. As a noun: employee.

fact.text: Literally 'one who depends', from dipendere (to depend): an employee depends on an employer. As an adjective it means dependent or addicted.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il/la dipendente.

etymology: From dipendere (“to depend”) + -enza. Doublet of dependance.

senses.note: Dipendenza da (droghe, gioco…) = addiction to. It also means 'dependence'.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *dēpendĕre, from Classical Latin dēpendēre. By surface analysis, di- + pendere.

fact.text: Literally 'to hang down from', from Latin de + pendere ('to hang'). It shares a root with English 'pendant' and 'pendulum'.

senses.note: Used with 'da': 'dipende da te' means 'it's up to you'. Takes essere. Past participle: dipeso.

etymology: From Latin dēpingō. Compare English depict.

fact.text: From Latin dēpingere, which is also the source of English 'depict'. So a dipinto (painting) is literally something depicted.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle dipinto, passato remoto dipinsi. Un dipinto = a painting.

etymology: From dipingere (“to paint”). Possibly corresponds to a Vulgar Latin *dēpinctus for Latin dēpictus.

fact.text: Comes from dipingere 'to paint', from Latin depingere. Its past participle depictus gave English 'depict', so a dipinto is literally something depicted.

senses.note: Also the past participle of dipingere: 'painted'.

etymology: From Ancient Greek δίπλωμα (díplōma).

fact.text: Greek díplōma meant a folded paper, from diploûn 'to double'. Official documents were folded in two.

senses.note: Masculine despite the -a ending: il diploma, i diplomi. Often means the high-school diploma (maturità).

features.construction: reflexive: mi diplomo, mi sono diplomato

senses.note: Usually for a school diploma (e.g. high school); for a university degree Italians say laurearsi.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dīcere, from Proto-Italic *deikō, from Proto-Indo-European *déyḱeti (“to show, point out”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin dicere 'to say', the source of English dictate, diction, dictionary and verdict (literally 'true saying').

senses.note: dire qualcosa a qualcuno. Past participle: detto.

etymology: From diretto + -mente.
From Late Latin dīrēctōrem, from Latin directus.

senses.note: Feminine: direttrice. Also an orchestra conductor or newspaper editor. A film director is regista.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dīrēctiōnem.

senses.note: In direzione di = towards. Also means management or head office.
A senior manager or executive. The article shows the gender (il/la dirigente). Also used for a political leader.
