etymology: From Latin dīrigere (“to steer, direct”), probably borrowed in this form.

fact.text: English 'direct' comes from Latin directus, the past participle of dirigere. Italian kept both: the verb dirigere and its participle diretto, which also means 'direct'.

senses.note: Also to conduct an orchestra. Irregular: diressi, diretto.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *dērēctus or *dirictus, both assimilated forms from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of diretto.

fact.text: From Latin directus 'straight', also the source of English direct. French droit and Spanish derecho share the same idea that a right is what is straight.

senses.note: Avere il diritto di + infinitive = to have the right to. Diritti umani = human rights.

etymology: From dis- + abile.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural disabili. Also used as a noun: un/una disabile.

etymology: From dis- + abile.
ignored: This is the adjective used as a noun, and the context uses the adjective, which has its own 'disabile' (adj) card.

senses.note: Un/una disabile. Today 'persona con disabilità' is often preferred.

fact.text: Only means disabled in the tech sense: a feature or account that has been turned off. For a person, Italian uses disabile or persona con disabilità.

senses.note: For devices, accounts and settings. A person with a disability is disabile.

etymology: From dis- + Latin astrum (“star”); compare Piedmontese disastr.

fact.text: Literally means 'bad star' (dis- + Latin astrum), from the astrological idea that a misfortune came from an unlucky star. English 'disaster' came from this Italian word through French.

senses.note: Sono un disastro = I'm hopeless, I'm a mess.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of discendere (“to go down, descend”). Cognate with Piedmontese dissèisa. Displaced Latin dēscēnsus.

senses.note: in discesa = downhill. In skiing, discesa libera is the downhill race.

etymology: From Latin disciplīna.

senses.note: Also means a school subject or a sports event: le discipline olimpiche.

etymology: From Late Latin discursus, from Latin discurrō.

fact.text: Comes from Latin discurrere, 'to run to and fro', from currere 'to run'. A speech is words running back and forth. English 'discourse' has the same origin.

senses.note: Also 'talk, conversation': Che discorsi! = What kind of talk is that!

etymology: From disco + -teca.

fact.text: Formed like biblioteca (library): disco (record) plus -teca (collection). It first meant a record library, a sense it still has, before it came to mean a club.

senses.note: Andare in discoteca = to go clubbing.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin discussiōnem.

senses.note: Can also mean an argument or quarrel: avere una discussione con qualcuno.

etymology: From Latin discutiō.

fact.text: Latin discutere meant 'to shake apart, break up', from dis- + quatere (to shake). Discussing a topic was once pictured as breaking it into pieces.

senses.note: Irregular forms: discussi (past remote), discusso (past participle). Discutere di = to talk about; used alone it can mean 'to argue'.

etymology:

Latin designō
Latin designāre
Italian disegnare
From Latin designāre. Doublet of designare.

fact.text: Shares its Latin root, designare, with English 'design' and 'designate'. Renaissance critics set Florentine disegno (drawing) against Venetian colore (colour).

senses.note: Also 'to design'. Un disegno = a drawing.

etymology: From disgusto + -oso.

fact.text: It is built on gusto 'taste', so something disgusting is literally against your taste. English disgust comes from the same Latin word, gustus.

etymology: From dis- + occupato; cognate with Piedmontese disocupà.

senses.note: Also a noun: un disoccupato / una disoccupata = an unemployed person.

etymology: From Latin dehonestus. By surface analysis, dis- + onesto. Cognate with Piedmontese disonest.

senses.note: Usually an adjective, meaning dishonest (disonesto/a/i/e). Feminine noun: disonesta.

etymology: From Medieval Latin or Late Latin dīspēnsa, feminine past participle of dīspendō, from Latin dis- + pendō.

senses.note: Le dispense also means lecture notes or course handouts at university.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dēsperāre.

fact.text: Literally 'un-hope': Latin de- + sperare, to hope. Italian still uses sperare for 'to hope', and English despair and desperate share the root.

senses.note: Disperare di farcela = to despair of making it. The reflexive disperarsi = to be distraught.

etymology: From dis- + piacere.

features.construction: indirect object + dispiacere (mi dispiace, ti dispiace)

senses.note: Works like piacere: mi dispiace = I'm sorry (lit. 'it displeases me'). Auxiliary essere.

etymology: From Latin dispōnere.

senses.note: Conjugated like porre (dispongo, disposto). Disporre di = to have at one's disposal.

etymology: From Latin distantia.

senses.note: a distanza = remotely, from a distance

etymology: From Latin distīnctus, perfect passive participle of distinguō.

fact.text: Formal Italian letters and emails often close with 'Distinti saluti', which works like 'Yours faithfully' or 'Kind regards'.

senses.note: Can also mean 'distinct, separate', e.g. due problemi distinti.
Full form: distributore automatico. Also petrol station (distributore di benzina).

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *destrugere, from Classical Latin dēstruō, from dē- (“un-, de-”) + struō (“to build”).

fact.text: From Latin destruere, literally 'to un-build' (de- plus struere, 'to build'). The same root gives English structure and construct.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle distrutto, passato remoto distrussi. Transitive, takes avere.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin disturbāre.

senses.note: Non disturbare = do not disturb. Scusi il disturbo = sorry to bother you.

etymology: Deverbal from disturbare + -o. Cognate with Piedmontese disturb. Compare also Medieval Latin disturbium, Spanish disturbio, Portuguese distúrbio.

senses.note: Scusi il disturbo = sorry to bother you. In medicine it means disorder (disturbo alimentare).

etymology: From Latin digitus, from Proto-Indo-European *deyǵ- (“to show, point out, pronounce solemnly”).

fact.text: From Latin digitus, which also gave English 'digit'. Numbers are called digits because people counted on their fingers.

senses.note: Irregular plural: le dita (feminine). A toe is il dito del piede.

etymology: Variant of detta, feminine past participle of dire, referring to the name of the company.

fact.text: A variant of detta, 'said' (from dire). It referred to the name the business was called by, as in 'the said firm'.

senses.note: Often a small or family business. Other words: azienda, società.

etymology: Borrowed from Arabic دِيوَان (dīwān), from Persian دیوان (dêvân), ultimately from Sumerian 𒁾 (dub).

fact.text: Persian divan first meant a register, then an office or council, whose rooms had cushioned benches, hence 'sofa'. The same word gave Italian dogana, 'customs'.

senses.note: Divano letto = sofa bed.

etymology: From a verbal derivative of Latin dēventum, perfect passive participle of dēveniō (“arrive, come”), possibly through a Vulgar Latin form *dēventāre as a frequentative of this verb.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono diventato. Also 'to turn': diventare rosso = to turn red.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dīversus.

fact.text: Word order changes the meaning: before a plural noun it means 'several' (diversi giorni = several days), but after it means 'different' (giorni diversi = different days).

senses.note: diverso da = different from.

etymology: Cognate with Piedmontese divertent.

fact.text: Related to the verb divertire (to amuse), from Latin divertere 'to turn aside'. English 'diverting', meaning entertaining, comes from the same root: fun turns your mind away from cares.

senses.note: Used for things and people: un film divertente, una persona divertente.

etymology: From divertire (“to amuse, to entertain”, from Latin dīvertere) + -mento (“-ment”); cognate with Piedmontese divertiment.

senses.note: Buon divertimento! = Have fun! The verb is divertirsi = to have fun.

etymology: From earlier divertere, from Latin dīvertere (“to turn away”).

fact.text: From Latin divertere, 'to turn away': amusing someone turns their mind away from their cares. English diversion keeps both senses.

senses.note: Divertirsi = to have fun: ci siamo divertiti molto. Not an -isc- verb: diverto.

fact.text: From Latin divertere, 'to turn aside'. Having fun means turning away from your cares, a sense English keeps in 'diversion' as a word for entertainment.

senses.note: Reflexive: mi diverto, ci siamo divertiti. Divertiti! = Have fun!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dīvidere (“to divide, to separate”).

senses.note: Also 'to share': dividere qualcosa con qualcuno. Irregular: diviso, divisi.

etymology: Deverbal from divietare + -o, from vietare (“to forbid”). Compare Piedmontese diviet.

fact.text: You will see it everywhere on Italian signs: 'divieto di sosta' means no parking, 'divieto di balneazione' no swimming, and 'divieto di accesso' no entry.

senses.note: Common on signs: divieto di sosta (no parking), divieto di fumare (no smoking).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin dīvīsiōnem.
From divorzio + -are; cognate with Piedmontese divorsié.

senses.note: Intransitive in Italian: divorziare da qualcuno = to divorce someone.

etymology: From Latin dīvortium (“separation, divorce”).

fact.text: Divorce only became legal in Italy in 1970. Voters confirmed it in a 1974 referendum, when about 59% chose to keep the law.

senses.note: chiedere il divorzio = to file for divorce.

etymology: Borrowed from Renaissance Latin dictiōnārium.

ignored: Stray initialism from a garbled context fragment.

senses.note: Often used like an adjective: vino DOC; un milanese doc = a true Milanese.

etymology: Probably a back-formation of doccione (“conduit, spout”), from Latin ductiōnem, from ducere, infinitive of dūcō (“lead, guide; draw, pull”), or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin root *ducea, ultimately from the same root. Compare Dozza, a borrowing from Emilian Dòza.

fact.text: Originally meant a pipe or spout. French borrowed it as douche, which then passed into English, so douche ultimately comes from Italian.

senses.note: fare la doccia = to take a shower.

etymology: From documento + -ario. Compare Piedmontese documentari.
Borrowed from Latin documentum.

fact.text: Comes from Latin documentum, built on docere, to teach. A document was first a lesson or proof. Doctor and doctrine come from the same verb.

senses.note: i documenti often means ID papers: 'Documenti, prego!'

etymology: From Latin duodecim.

From Sicilian Medieval Latin doana, dovana (attested from the end of the 12th century), from Andalusian Arabic *duwān, an alteration of the Arabic دِيوَان (dīwān, “administrative office”), borrowed from Persian دیوان (divân, “customs, divan”). Compare Piedmontese dogan-a.

fact.text: Came via Arabic dīwān, 'administrative office', from Persian divân. The same word gave English 'divan', the couch, and French douane.

senses.note: Passare la dogana = to go through customs.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dulcem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin dulcis, which gave English dulcet ('sweet-sounding'). It also appears in la dolce vita and dolce far niente, 'sweet idleness'.

senses.note: As a noun, il dolce = dessert or cake. Acqua dolce = fresh water.

etymology: From dolce + -ezza.

senses.note: Also gentleness and softness, and an endearment: ciao, dolcezza! = hi, sweetheart!

etymology: From English dollar.

fact.text: The English word dollar goes back to German Taler, short for Joachimsthaler: silver coins minted in the 1500s from silver mined at Joachimsthal in Bohemia.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dolor, from doleō + -or.

fact.text: From Latin dolor, from dolere 'to hurt'. It shares a root with English 'condolence' (from condolere, 'to suffer with someone').

senses.note: Also emotional pain or grief. Ho un dolore alla schiena = I have a pain in my back.

etymology: From domandare.

fact.text: Not mainly 'demand': domandare just means 'to ask'. To demand something forcefully is pretendere or esigere. In economics, though, domanda e offerta means 'supply and demand'.

senses.note: Fare una domanda = to ask a question. Fare domanda = to apply (for something).

etymology: From Latin dēmandāre, whence also Italian demandare (a borrowed doublet).

fact.text: Watch out: it normally means simply 'to ask', not 'to demand'. To demand something forcefully, Italians say esigere or pretendere. Una domanda is a question.

senses.note: domandare qualcosa a qualcuno. A common synonym of chiedere.

etymology: From Late Latin dē māne (“early in the morning”), from dē + Latin māne, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂- (“to ripen, mature”).

fact.text: From Late Latin dē māne, 'early in the morning'. The idea of 'in the morning' gradually shifted to mean 'the next day'.

senses.note: A domani! = See you tomorrow! Il domani (noun) = the future.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin [diēs] Dominica (literally “day of the Lord”).

fact.text: From Latin dies Dominica, 'the Lord's day', which Christians used in place of the pagan 'day of the Sun'. It is the only Italian weekday that is feminine.

senses.note: Not capitalised. la domenica = on Sundays.

etymology: From Late Latin domna, shortened variant of Latin domina (“lady, mistress of an estate or household”), from dominus (“master”), from domus (“home”). Doublet of dama. Cognate with Sicilian donna.

fact.text: Comes from Latin domina, 'mistress of the house', from domus 'home'. Madonna is literally 'my lady', and prima donna means 'first lady' of the opera.

senses.note: Also used for 'wife' in some contexts, and for the queen in cards and chess.

etymology: From Latin dōnum (“gift”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin donum (gift), the same root as English donate, donor and donation.

senses.note: More formal than regalo; also a talent: avere il dono della parola = to have the gift of the gab.

etymology: From earlier dopoi, dipoi, inherited from Vulgar Latin dē post.

senses.note: Adverb: ci vediamo dopo = see you later. Also a preposition: dopo cena = after dinner.

etymology: From dopo- + domani.
From Latin duplus, whence also duplo (a borrowed doublet).

fact.text: English coffee menus borrowed it: a 'doppio' is a double espresso. In Italy you would usually ask for 'un caffè doppio'.

senses.note: Camera doppia = double room. Feminine is doppia, as in 'in doppia' (in a double).

etymology:

Inherited from Latin dormīre, from Proto-Italic *dormiō, from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥m-yé-ti, from *drem- (“to sleep”) + *-yéti.

fact.text: From Latin dormire 'to sleep', the root of English dormant and dormitory (a place for sleeping).

senses.note: Dormire come un ghiro = to sleep like a log (literally 'like a dormouse').

etymology: From Vulgar Latin dossum, from Latin dorsum. Doublet of the borrowed dorso.

fact.text: The common word addosso, 'on (oneself)', is literally a + dosso, 'on the back'. Dosso and dorso (back) both come from Latin dorsum.

senses.note: Also 'back' in set phrases: togliersi di dosso = to take off (clothes) or get rid of.

fact.text: In Italy, anyone with a university degree can be called dottore or dottoressa. A research doctorate (dottorato di ricerca) is a separate degree that comes later.

senses.note: Dottorato di ricerca = PhD.

etymology: Inherited from Latin doctōrem.

fact.text: In Italy anyone with a university degree may be addressed as dottore or dottoressa, so the 'doctor' you meet may not be a physician at all.

senses.note: Feminine: la dottoressa. Also used as a title for any university graduate.

etymology: From Latin dē ubi (“from where, whence”), or from a strengthening of the older form ove with a prothetic d-. Compare Piedmontese doa, French d'où.

fact.text: Not a bird! It means 'where' and is pronounced DOH-veh. The Italian for dove (the bird) is colomba.

senses.note: Dov'è...? = Where is...? Di dove sei? = Where are you from?

fact.text: Not a bird! It means 'where' and is pronounced DOH-veh. The Italian for dove (the bird) is colomba.

ignored: Same word as the adverb dove ('where'), which has its own card.

senses.note: Dov'è? = Where is it/he/she?

etymology: Inherited from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”). Cognate with Sicilian duviri.

fact.text: Comes from Latin debere 'to owe', like English debt, debit and due. It can still mean 'to owe', and as a noun il dovere means 'duty'.

senses.note: fare il proprio dovere = to do one's duty. Same word as the verb dovere (must).

etymology: Inherited from Latin dēbēre (“to owe”). Cognate with Sicilian duviri.

fact.text: Comes from Latin debere 'to owe', like English debt, debit and due. It can still mean 'to owe', and as a noun il dovere means 'duty'.

senses.note: Followed by an infinitive: devo andare. As a modal it often takes the auxiliary of the next verb.

etymology:
From dove (“where”) + -unque (indefinite ending).
Compare Spanish dondequiera for a similar construction.

senses.note: When it means 'wherever', it takes the subjunctive: dovunque tu vada = wherever you go.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English drink.

senses.note: An English loanword, usually invariable: i drink. For a general drink, use bevanda or bibita.

etymology: Contraction/syncopation of diritto, from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus (or from Late Latin drictus; compare French droit, Catalan dret, Romanian drept, Sicilian drittu), from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of diretto.

fact.text: A shortened form of diritto, from Latin directus. It is a doublet of diretto, so both words come from the same Latin word.

senses.note: A shorter form of diritto. Often used as an adverb: vai sempre dritto = go straight ahead.

etymology: Contraction/syncopation of diritto, from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus (or from Late Latin drictus; compare French droit, Catalan dret, Romanian drept, Sicilian drittu), from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of diretto.

fact.text: A shortened form of diritto, from Latin directus. It is a doublet of diretto, so both words come from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Adverb. 'Vai sempre dritto' = keep going straight on.

etymology: Attested from the 1560s; ultimately from Middle Dutch drôge (“dry”), perhaps through Middle French drogue (c. 1462); see etymology at drug.

fact.text: Probably from Middle Dutch droge, 'dry', referring to dried herbs and spices. That old 'spice' sense survives in drogheria, a grocer's shop.

senses.note: Means narcotics. A medical drug is un farmaco or una medicina.
Can sound pejorative; the neutral term is tossicodipendente. Also an adjective: 'drugged, high'.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dubium.

fact.text: Latin dubius, meaning 'doubtful', is linked to duo, 'two'. To doubt is to be torn between two options, like English 'in two minds'.

senses.note: senza dubbio = without a doubt. avere un dubbio = to be unsure about something.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin dubitāre.

fact.text: Latin dubitare probably goes back to a root meaning 'two', as in being torn between two options. German Zweifel ('doubt') is built the same way from zwei, 'two'.

features.construction: dubitare di qualcosa / dubitare che + congiuntivo

senses.note: Dubitare di qualcosa; dubitare che + subjunctive.

etymology: Inherited from Latin duae ~ duas, feminine plural of duo, from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. Attempts at gender distinction are still found in Old Italian, but the different forms soon became interchangeable variants. The victory of due may be due to its being the phonetically intermediate form.
ignored: Using the number as a noun is a secondary use; the numeral due is studied on its own card.

etymology: Inherited from Latin duae ~ duas, feminine plural of duo, from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. Attempts at gender distinction are still found in Old Italian, but the different forms soon became interchangeable variants. The victory of due may be due to its being the phonetically intermediate form.
From due (“two”) + cento (“hundred”).

From Vulgar Latin *dunquam, a cross of Late Latin dunc and Latin unquam (“ever”), with the former itself being a cross of Latin tunc (“then”) with dum (“while”). The final /-e/ may reflect an older form */ˈdonkwas/, with adverbial /-s/, for which cf. Middle French doncques.

senses.note: Also 'so' or 'well then'. Often opens a sentence: Dunque, dove eravamo?

etymology: Inherited as a shortening of Latin domus ecclēsiae (“meeting-house, house of the assembly”, a calque of Ancient Greek οἶκος τῆς ἐκκλησίας (oîkos tês ekklēsías), designating a private house placed at the disposal of the Christian community) and later domus Dominī (“house of our Lord”) or Deī (“of God”); from Proto-Italic *domos, from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm, derived from the root *dem- (“to build”).

fact.text: English dome comes from this word, via French dôme. The Italian word goes back to Latin domus 'house', short for 'house of the Lord'. A duomo was God's house, not a dome.

senses.note: A city's main church, e.g. il Duomo di Milano. Formally also called cattedrale.

fact.text: Originally the present participle of durare, 'to last'. English 'during' formed the same way, from an old verb 'dure', meaning to last.

senses.note: Used directly before a noun: durante il viaggio = during the trip.

etymology: Inherited from Latin dūrāre, from Proto-Indo-European *dewǝ- (“to run forward”).

fact.text: English 'duration', 'durable' and 'endure' come from the same Latin verb, durare. Durata means 'duration'.

senses.note: Compound tenses take essere or avere: è durato / ha durato. Essere is more common.

etymology: From Latin dūrus, from Proto-Italic *dūros, from Proto-Indo-European *duh₂-ró-s (“long”), from *dweh₂- (“far, long”). Cognate with Ancient Greek δηρός (dērós, “long”), Sanskrit दूर (dūrá, “distant, far, long”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin durus 'hard'. Something hard lasts, which is why English durable and endure share the same origin.

senses.note: Hard as in 'not soft', and also 'tough': è dura = it's tough. For 'difficult' you usually use difficile.

etymology: From Latin et.

fact.text: It comes from Latin et, the same word as in 'etc.' (et cetera). The ampersand '&' started out as the letters e and t joined together.

senses.note: Often ed before a vowel, especially e: io ed Elena. Don't confuse it with è (is).

fact.text: It comes from Latin et, the same word as in 'etc.' (et cetera). The ampersand '&' started out as the letters e and t joined together.

ignored: Misspelling of è; essere and the conjunction e have their own cards.

senses.note: Misspelling of è (he/she/it is).

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English e-mail.

senses.note: Usually feminine: un'e-mail, often just la mail. Invariable plural. Formal: posta elettronica.

etymology: From Latin excellentem (“distinguished”, “excellent”), present active participle of excellō (“to elevate, raise up”).

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural eccellenti.

etymology: From Latin excessus.

senses.note: eccesso di velocità = speeding; in eccesso = in excess, surplus.

etymology: Phonetic spelling of Latin et cētera (“and the rest” or “and so forth”).

senses.note: Often abbreviated to 'ecc.' in writing. In speech you can also say 'e così via'.

etymology: From Latin exceptus, the past participle of excipere.

senses.note: Synonym of tranne. eccetto che = except that / unless.

etymology: From eccezione + -ale.

senses.note: Often just means 'great, amazing' in speech: una cena eccezionale.

etymology: From Latin excitāre (“to rouse, awaken, summon”).

fact.text: Careful: 'sono eccitato' often sounds sexual to Italians. To say you're excited about something, use 'sono emozionato', 'sono entusiasta' or 'non vedo l'ora'.

senses.note: Eccitarsi = to get excited, but it often suggests sexual arousal. Use it with care.

etymology: Inherited from Latin eccum, from ecce + eum.

fact.text: Comes from Latin eccum, a contraction of ecce eum, 'behold him'. Ecce is the 'behold' in Ecce homo, 'Behold the man'.

senses.note: Pronouns attach to it: eccolo = here he/it is; eccomi = here I am.

etymology: Inherited from Latin eccum, from ecce + eum.

fact.text: Comes from Latin eccum, a contraction of ecce eum, 'behold him'. Ecce is the 'behold' in Ecce homo, 'Behold the man'.

senses.note: Takes attached pronouns: eccomi (here I am), eccoti, eccoli (here they are).
senses.prompt: here it is! / there you go!

etymology: Inherited from Latin eccum, from ecce + eum.

fact.text: Comes from Latin eccum, a contraction of ecce eum, 'behold him'. Ecce is the 'behold' in Ecce homo, 'Behold the man'.

senses.note: Invariable; used for both singular and plural. Takes attached pronouns: eccolo (here it is), eccomi (here I am).
senses.prompt: here is / here are / there it is

etymology: From ecologia + -ico.

fact.text: Ecology comes from Greek oikos, 'house, household'. The German biologist Ernst Haeckel coined the term (Ökologie) in 1866 for the study of living things' 'home'.

senses.note: Also 'eco-friendly': un villaggio ecologico. Plurals: ecologici, ecologiche.

etymology: Derived from Latin oeconomia, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομία (oikonomía).

fact.text: From Greek oikonomia, 'household management': oikos (house) + nomos (law). The economy started out as the rules for running a home.

senses.note: Also means economics as a subject: studiare economia.

etymology: From Latin oeconomicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκονομικός (oikonomikós, “skilled with household management”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek oikonomikos, 'good at running a household' (oikos = house, nomos = rule). That is why it means both 'economic' and 'cheap', as in thrifty.

senses.note: Also means 'economic' (la crisi economica). Unlike English 'cheap', it doesn't suggest poor quality.

etymology: From Latin aedificium.

fact.text: This is the same word as English 'edifice'. Both come from Latin aedificare, 'to build'. 'Edify' shares the root: it originally meant to build someone up morally.

senses.note: More formal than 'palazzo', which is the everyday word for an apartment building.

etymology: From Latin ēditōrem.

fact.text: False friend: an editore mainly publishes books and does not edit them. Someone who edits texts is usually called a redattore or curatore.

senses.note: Feminine: editrice. A text editor is usually il redattore or il curatore.

ignored: This is a clitic compound (educare + lo); study it on the educare card.

senses.note: educare + lo (him/it).

fact.text: False friend: it means polite or well brought up, not educated in the academic sense. A well-educated person is istruito; a rude one is maleducato.

senses.note: Not 'educated'. That is istruito or colto. Maleducato = rude.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēducātiōnem.

fact.text: Careful: in everyday Italian this word often means manners or politeness. A 'persona maleducata' is rude, not uneducated. Schooling is more often called 'istruzione'.

senses.note: Often means good manners: 'che educazione!'. School learning is often 'istruzione'.

etymology: From Latin effectus.

senses.note: In effetti = in fact; effetti personali = personal belongings.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin effectuāre.

senses.note: Typical of official language: effettuare una consegna, un pagamento, una prenotazione.

etymology: From ego- + -ista.

senses.note: Same form for both genders in the singular; plurals egoisti/egoiste. Also a noun: un egoista.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēgregius.

fact.text: From Latin egregius, from e grege, 'out of the flock': someone who stands out from the herd. English 'egregious' comes from the same word but now means outstandingly bad.

senses.note: Common at the start of formal letters: Egregio Signor Rossi = Dear Mr Rossi.
Used as a tag ('…, eh?' = right?) or to show hesitation or resignation.
Used to get someone's attention.

etymology: From ehi + là.

fact.text: Built from ehi (hey) + là (there), so it matches English 'hey there' word for word.

senses.note: A cheerful greeting, or a way to get someone's attention.

etymology: From Latin ēlegantem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin elegans, related to eligere 'to choose'. So an elegant person is someone who chooses carefully, and the word shares its root with English 'elect' and 'select'.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural eleganti.
Le elementari (scuola elementare) = primary school.
Same form for both genders: l'elettricista. Plurals: gli elettricisti (m), le elettriciste (f).

fact.text: Ultimately from Greek elektron, 'amber'. People noticed that rubbed amber attracts small objects, so static electricity was named after amber.

senses.note: Feminine and invariable (stressed final -à). Elettricità statica = static electricity.

etymology: From elettronico (“electronic”), on the model of English electronics.

senses.note: Singular in Italian: l'elettronica è... (unlike English 'electronics are').

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ēlectiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin eligere, 'to pick out'. Through French, the same verb also gave English 'elite', meaning the 'chosen' ones.

senses.note: Often plural: le elezioni = the elections (e.g. le elezioni politiche).

etymology: Borrowed from French hélicoptère.

fact.text: Coined in French in 1861 by Gustave de Ponton d'Amécourt from Greek helix (spiral) + pteron (wing). So it splits as helico-pter, not heli-copter.

etymology: From Latin ēlīmināre.

fact.text: Latin eliminare literally meant 'to put out of the house'. It comes from ex (out) + limen (threshold), the same root as English 'subliminal'.

senses.note: Also used for deleting files and for knocking teams out of a competition.

etymology: From emergere + -enza; cf. Medieval Latin ēmergentia, from Latin ēmergentem.

senses.note: In caso di emergenza = in case of emergency.

etymology: From French émotion.

fact.text: Italians use it more widely than English uses emotion. 'Che emozione!' means 'How exciting!', so it often means a thrill rather than just a feeling.

senses.note: Often means excitement or thrill: Che emozione! = How exciting!

etymology: Borrowed from French endémique. By surface analysis, endemia + -ico.

senses.note: Plural: endemici / endemiche.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin energia, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia).

fact.text: Greek energeia is en, 'in', plus ergon, 'work', so it literally means 'being at work'. The same ergon is in English ergonomics.

senses.note: The stress falls on the -i-: energìa.

etymology: From Latin ēnormem.

fact.text: Latin enormis meant 'out of the norm': ex- (out of) + norma, a carpenter's square or rule. So something enormous is literally off the scale.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural enormi.
Feminine: entrambe. As an adjective it takes the article: entrambi i ragazzi. Also a pronoun.

etymology: From earlier intrare, from Latin intrāre (“to enter”).

senses.note: Takes essere and needs 'in': sono entrato in un bar = I went into a bar.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of entrare (“to go in, to enter”). Already found in Medieval Latin intrāta.

senses.note: Ingresso is a synonym; the opposite is uscita (exit). In the plural, le entrate can also mean income.

etymology: Inherited from Latin intrō.

senses.note: Entro venerdì = by Friday; entro un'ora = within an hour.
A feminine noun: un'epidemia di colera = a cholera epidemic.

etymology:
From Ancient Greek ἐπεισόδιον (epeisódion) "parenthetic addition, episode", neuter of ἐπεισόδιος (epeisódios) "following upon the entrance".
Cognate with Piedmontese episòdi.

fact.text: From Greek epeisodion, 'a coming in besides'. In Greek tragedy, an episode was the part of dialogue that came between two choral songs.
From Greek epokhē, 'a stop, a pause', so originally a fixed point in time from which a period was counted. It is the same word as English 'epoch'.

senses.note: All'epoca = at the time; d'epoca = vintage or period (auto d'epoca).

etymology: Borrowed from French équipage.

fact.text: Borrowed from French équipage. The verb équiper, also the source of English 'equip', is usually traced to Old Norse skipa, 'to fit out a ship', which is related to 'ship'.

etymology: From Latin herba, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreh₁- (“to grow, become green”).

fact.text: Latin herba also gave English herb, herbal and herbivore. Italian still uses erba for both grass and herbs.

senses.note: Also 'herb' (erbe aromatiche = herbs) and, in slang, marijuana.

etymology: From Latin hērēditāre.

fact.text: From Latin hereditare, from heres 'heir'. English heir, heredity and heritage all come from the same root, and so does Italian erede 'heir'.

etymology: From Latin heroem (“hero”).

fact.text: The feminine 'eroina' means both heroine and heroin. The drug's name comes from Bayer's trademark Heroin, from Greek heros 'hero', reportedly because it made users feel heroic.

senses.note: Feminine: l'eroina (heroine), which also means the drug heroin.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin errōrem. Sense 2 is built from the original Latin sense of errō (“to wander”). By surface analysis, errare + -ore.

fact.text: From Latin errare 'to wander', so a mistake was first a straying from the path. In poetry errore can still mean 'wandering', like English 'knight-errant'.

senses.note: fare un errore = to make a mistake; per errore = by mistake.
Also used as an exclamation: Esagerato! = You're overdoing it! / Come on, that's too much!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exāmen. Doublet of sciame, which was inherited.

fact.text: Latin examen meant both 'swarm' and the pointer on a pair of scales, hence weighing up and testing. The inherited form became sciame 'swarm'.

senses.note: Dare/fare un esame = to take an exam. Superare un esame = to pass it.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exāmināre.

fact.text: From Latin examinare 'to weigh', from examen, the pointer on a pair of scales. To examine something was originally to weigh it carefully.

senses.note: Also 'to test' a candidate: esaminare uno studente.

etymology: From Latin exactus.

senses.note: On its own, Esatto! means 'Exactly!' or 'That's right!'

etymology: From Latin ēsca.

fact.text: In Latin, esca meant 'food'. Because it also means tinder in Italian, 'dare esca a' means to add fuel to something, such as a quarrel or a rumour.

senses.note: Also figurative (a lure, a decoy). Another meaning is tinder.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exclūdere. Compare the inherited doublet schiudere.

fact.text: Latin ex (out) + claudere (to shut), so literally 'to shut out'. The same claudere gave Italian chiudere and English close.

senses.note: Irregular forms: escluso, esclusi. Also means to rule out, as in escludere un'ipotesi.

etymology: From earlier esemplo, essemplo, probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin exemplum, derived from Latin eximō (“to take out, take away”). Compare the inherited doublet scempio.

fact.text: From Latin exemplum, the source of English 'example' and also of 'sample', which is a shortened form of Old French essample.

senses.note: ad esempio / per esempio = for example. Dare il buon esempio = to set a good example.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exercitus.

fact.text: From Latin exercitus, past participle of exercere 'to train, exercise'. An army was literally 'a trained (exercised) body' of men, which links it to English 'exercise'.

senses.note: Stress on the second syllable: e-SER-ci-to.

etymology: From Latin exercitium.

senses.note: 'Fare esercizio' = to exercise. 'Esercizio commerciale' = a shop or business.

etymology: From Latin exsistere.

senses.note: Takes essere: è esistito. Non esiste! is also slang for 'No way!'

etymology: From Latin experientia.

fact.text: Shares the Latin root experiri 'to try, test' with English experiment. Galileo used 'sensate esperienze' to mean experiments based on the senses.

etymology: From Latin expertus.

senses.note: Feminine: l'esperta. Also an adjective: esperto di vini = expert in wines.

fact.text: Latin explodere originally meant to drive an actor off the stage by clapping and hissing (ex 'out' + plaudere 'to clap'). The sense of bursting with a bang came much later.

senses.note: Irregular past: esploso, esplose. Takes essere when intransitive: la bomba è esplosa.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin explōsiōnem, derived from to eject” ← “to drive out by clapping.

fact.text: Latin explodere (ex + plaudere 'to clap') first meant to drive an actor off the stage by clapping and hissing. The 'bang' meaning came much later.

senses.note: Also figurative: un'esplosione di rabbia = an outburst of anger.

etymology: Borrowed from French explosif. By surface analysis, esploso + -ivo.

senses.note: Also an adjective: esplosivo/a, 'explosive'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin expositiōnem.

senses.note: esposizione a sud = south-facing. Also means exhibition (m2).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin expressiōnem (“a pressing out”).

senses.note: Covers a facial expression, a phrase or idiom, and expressing feelings.

etymology: Past participle of esprimere; borrowed from Latin expressus.

fact.text: This is the past participle of esprimere, 'to press out'. The coffee is usually explained as being 'pressed out' by forcing hot water through the grounds. The word also means an express train or an express letter.

senses.note: In Italy you just order 'un caffè'; by default that is an espresso.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exprimere. Compare the inherited doublet spremere.

fact.text: Its past participle is espresso, and the coffee's name is often linked to being 'pressed out'. The same Latin exprimere also gave spremere, 'to squeeze', as in spremuta (fresh juice).

senses.note: Irregular: past participle espresso, passato remoto espressi. Esprimersi = to express oneself.

etymology: From essere + -ci.

senses.note: c'è + singular, ci sono + plural: 'C'è un problema', 'Ci sono due gatti'.
senses.prompt: to be there; there to be

etymology: Inherited from Latin sum, esse. The infinitive form is attested already from Early Medieval Latin essere. The past participle stato, shared with the verb stare, is from Latin stātus.

fact.text: A patchwork verb: sono goes back to the same ancient root as English 'is', past forms like fui share a root with English 'be', and the participle stato is borrowed from stare.

ignored: The list means the verb essere ('(we) are'), which is studied on the verb card; this is the noun made from it.

senses.note: Example: un essere umano = a human being.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sum, esse. The infinitive form is attested already from Early Medieval Latin essere. The past participle stato, shared with the verb stare, is from Latin stātus.

fact.text: A patchwork verb: sono goes back to the same ancient root as English 'is', past forms like fui share a root with English 'be', and the participle stato is borrowed from stare.

senses.note: Highly irregular: sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono. Also the auxiliary for many verbs of motion and change.

fact.text: Essere is the verb 'to be', used here as a noun meaning 'a being', just like English 'being' in 'human being'.

senses.note: Plural: gli esseri umani. Also l'uomo in the general sense of humankind.

ignored: A bad parse that merges the two verbs essere and stare, which share the past participle stato.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ipsum.

fact.text: From Latin ipsum, meaning 'itself'. It's the same root as in the Latin phrase 'ipso facto' and is also hidden inside stesso ('same'), which comes from Latin iste + ipsum.

senses.note: Mostly used in writing for things; forms: essa, essi, esse. In speech the subject pronoun is usually left out.

etymology: Borrowed from French est, from Old English ēast.

fact.text: Borrowed from French est, which comes from Old English ēast.

senses.note: Invariable. A est di = east of.

etymology: Latinizing modification of state, inherited from Latin aestātem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eydʰ- (“burn; fire”).

fact.text: Not an English 'estate' (that is tenuta or proprietà). It comes from Latin aestas 'summer', from a root meaning 'to burn'.

senses.note: D'estate / in estate = in summer. Feminine: l'estate calda.

etymology: From Latin externus.

senses.note: As a noun, l'esterno = the outside. All'esterno = outside, outdoors.

etymology: From Latin externus.

senses.note: All'esterno = outside, on the outside. Also an adjective: external.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exterus, from exter (“of another country”).

fact.text: The plural gli Esteri means foreign affairs: Italy's foreign minister is usually just called il ministro degli Esteri.

senses.note: all'estero = abroad (going or living); dall'estero = from abroad.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin exstinctor.
Borrowed from Latin aestīvus.

senses.note: Una giornata estiva = a summer's day. The noun 'summer' is estate.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin extrāneus (“external, foreign; strange”), whence also Italian strano (an inherited doublet).

fact.text: Latin extraneus gave Italian both estraneo and strano. Through Old French estrange it also gave English 'strange' and 'stranger', so it fits that un estraneo is a stranger.

senses.note: Estraneo a = unrelated to. As a noun, un estraneo = a stranger or outsider.
Also used as a noun: un estroverso = an extrovert.

fact.text: Italians buy cheese and cold cuts by the etto rather than the kilo. It is short for ettogrammo, and the etto- part comes from Greek hekaton, 'hundred'.

senses.note: Standard unit at the deli: un etto di prosciutto, due etti di formaggio.

etymology: Inherited from Latin aetātem.

fact.text: English age comes from the same Latin word, aetas, via Old French aage. Aetas comes from aevum 'lifetime', which also gave English eternal.

senses.note: Invariable: l'età, le età. Che età hai? = How old are you? (Quanti anni hai? is more common.)

etymology: Borrowed from English euro, from eurocurrency.

fact.text: In standard Italian the word never changes in the plural: 20 euro, not 20 euri. You may hear 'euri' as a joke or in careless speech.

senses.note: Invariable: un euro, cinque euro. 'Euri' is nonstandard.

etymology: From Latin ēvidentem.

fact.text: Watch out for the related noun evidenza: it means obviousness or prominence (mettere in evidenza = to highlight). Evidence in a court case is 'prova'.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural evidenti.

etymology: From Latin ēvidentia.

fact.text: Partly a false friend. It mainly means obviousness: è un'evidenza means 'it's obvious'. Evidence in court is la prova, though evidenze scientifiche is spreading under English influence.

senses.note: mettere in evidenza = to highlight. Proof in court is usually 'prova'.

etymology: From Latin ēvītāre (“to avoid”), from ē- + vītō.

fact.text: Latin ēvītāre also gave English 'inevitable', which literally means 'unavoidable' (Italian: inevitabile).

senses.note: Takes a direct object or di + infinitive: evitare di parlare = to avoid talking.

etymology: From evolvere + -si.

senses.note: Reflexive: mi evolvo; past: si è evoluto.

etymology: From Latin fabrica (“workshop”), from faber (“forger, smith”). Compare French fabrique, German Fabrik. Doublet of forgia.

fact.text: Not the same as English fabric, which is tessuto in Italian. Comes from Latin fabrica, workshop, from faber, a smith. English fabricate shares the root.

etymology: From Latin facienda, neuter plural of faciendus (“that which is to be done”). Doublet of azienda. Cognate with Sicilian facenna.

fact.text: Comes from Latin facienda, 'things to be done'. The same Latin word also gave Italian azienda (company), much as English 'agenda' literally means 'things to be done'.

senses.note: Plural: le faccende (di casa) = household chores, as in fare le faccende.

etymology: From Late Latin facia, from Latin faciēs (“face”).

fact.text: 'Che faccia tosta!' literally means 'What a hard face!' but is used like 'What a nerve!'. A faccia tosta is someone with a lot of cheek.

senses.note: Faccia a faccia = face to face. Plural: facce, without the i.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin facilis (“easy”), from faciō (“to do, make”).

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural facili. È facile = it's easy.

etymology: From facile + -mente.
From Latin facultātem, probably a borrowing.

senses.note: Invariable plural: le facoltà. E.g. la Facoltà di Medicina. Also means a mental faculty or a right/power.

etymology: From Latin phalaena, from Ancient Greek φάλαινα (phálaina, “moth; whale”). The semantic shift from "whale" to "moth" occurred in Hellenistic Greek, likely due to an analogy between the fluttering movement of a moth's wings and the fins or spout of a whale. Doublet of balena (“whale”)

fact.text: Comes from Greek phalaina, which meant both 'moth' and 'whale'. The same word gave Italian balena (whale), so a moth and a whale are etymological twins.

senses.note: Moth in general. A clothes moth is usually la tarma.

etymology: From fallo + -are or falla + -are, from Vulgar Latin *falla, or from Late Latin fallāre, from Latin fallere.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin fallere, 'to deceive, to trip up'. English fail, fallible and fallacy come from the same root.

senses.note: Rare and literary; in everyday speech use sbagliare. Related: fallato = faulty, defective.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fallīre, from Latin fallere.

fact.text: English 'fail' comes from the same Latin root, fallere 'to deceive', via Old French faillir. So do 'fallible' and 'false'.

senses.note: For people: ha fallito. For plans: è fallito. Also means 'to go bankrupt': l'azienda è fallita.

etymology: Deverbal from fallare (“to make a mistake”) + -o. Compare Spanish fallo.
ignored: It comes from a bad parse: in the context this is fa' + lo (from fare), not the noun fallo.

senses.note: Fare fallo = to commit a foul. Cogliere in fallo = to catch someone out.

etymology: From Latin falsus, from fallere.

fact.text: From Latin falsus, past participle of fallere, 'to deceive'. The same verb lies behind English fallacy and, via French, fail.

senses.note: Also fake or forged; as a noun, un falso = a forgery.

etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek φανός (phanós).

fact.text: Comes from Greek phanós, 'torch, lantern', from a root meaning 'to shine'. The same root is behind English phantom and phenomenon.

senses.note: Invariable: il falò, i falò.

etymology: Inherited from Latin famem (“hunger”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *dʰH- (“to disappear”). Compare Galician fame, French faim, Portuguese fome and Romanian foame, Sicilian fami.

fact.text: False friend: this means hunger, not fame. The Italian for fame is fama.

senses.note: Avere fame = to be hungry (literally 'to have hunger'). Morire di fame = to starve.

etymology: Inherited from Latin familia (“servants, domestic staff, household”).

fact.text: Latin familia first meant a household's servants and slaves (famulus = servant). Only later did it come to mean relatives.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin familiāritātem.

senses.note: Avere familiarità con = to be familiar with. Invariable: le familiarità.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fāmōsus.

senses.note: Can also be ironic or mean notorious: il famoso ladro = the notorious thief.

etymology: Borrowed from English fan.

fact.text: This sense of the English word is short for fanatic, from Latin fanaticus, 'of a temple; inspired by a god'. It has nothing to do with the fan that blows air.

senses.note: Il/la fan. In standard Italian the plural is usually invariable: i fan.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fānāticus.

fact.text: Latin fanaticus meant 'of a temple, inspired by a god', from fanum 'temple'. English 'fan', as in a sports fan, is generally seen as a shortening of 'fanatic'.

senses.note: Feminine: la fanatica. Also an adjective: essere fanatico di = to be crazy about.

fact.text: A shortened form of (va') a fare in culo, roughly 'go do it up the backside'. The longer form vaffanculo keeps the 'va' (go) at the start.

senses.note: Very offensive. The full form is vaffanculo; mandare a fanculo = to tell someone to get lost.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin phantasma, or Ancient Greek φάντασμα (phántasma).

fact.text: Comes from Greek phantasma 'apparition', from phainein 'to show'. That root also gives English phantom, fantasy and phenomenon.

senses.note: Masculine even though it ends in -a: il fantasma, i fantasmi.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin phantasticus (“imaginary”), from Ancient Greek φανταστικός (phantastikós).

senses.note: Used like English 'great, terrific'. Plural: fantastici, fantastiche.

fact.text: The ci and la in farcela don't refer to anything specific. They are fixed parts of the idiom, so 'ce la faccio' is one set phrase for 'I can make it'.

features.construction: pronominal: farcela (ce la faccio, ce la fai…); farcela a + infinitive

senses.note: Ce la faccio! = I can do it! Ce l'ho fatta! = I made it! Non ce la faccio più = I can't take it anymore.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin fāre.

fact.text: It comes from Latin facere, which also gave English 'fact' and 'factory'. 'Affair' comes from French à faire, 'to do', so it is a relative too.

senses.note: Also 'to make': fare una torta. Irregular: faccio, fai, fa, facciamo, fate, fanno.

etymology: Inherited from Latin farīna (“flour, meal”), from far (“kind of grain”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin far, an ancient type of wheat (the source of Italian farro).

etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin pharmacia, from Ancient Greek φαρμακεία (pharmakeía, “the use of drugs”).

fact.text: Italian pharmacies are marked by a lit green cross. They take turns staying open at night and on holidays as the 'farmacia di turno'.

senses.note: The shop (chemist's, drugstore). The pharmacist is il/la farmacista.

etymology: From fare (“to do, make”) + -si (“oneself”).

senses.note: Si fa tardi = it's getting late; farsi male = to get hurt; farsi la doccia = to shower.

etymology: From Ancient Greek φάσις (phásis, “appearance”).

senses.note: Le fasi lunari = the phases of the moon. Essere fuori fase = to be out of sorts.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fastidium.

fact.text: This is not 'fastidiousness'! Both words come from Latin fastidium, 'loathing'. Italian kept the 'bother' sense, while English 'fastidious' drifted to mean 'very picky'.

senses.note: dare fastidio a qualcuno = to bother someone; ti dà fastidio? = does it bother you?

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fatīga, from Latin fatīgō (“to tire, weary”).

fact.text: The Twelve Labours of Hercules are known in Italian as le dodici fatiche di Ercole, which shows that the word means hard work as well as tiredness.

senses.note: Very common as 'effort': fare fatica = to struggle; a fatica = barely, with difficulty.

etymology: From fattore (“farmer”).

fact.text: Not a factory, which is fabbrica. It comes from fattore, the steward who once managed a landowner's estate.

senses.note: Fattoria didattica = educational farm for school visits.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fābula. Compare the doublets fiaba and fola.

fact.text: Latin fabula 'story' gave Italian both favola and fiaba (fairy tale), and also English fable and fabulous.

senses.note: Colloquially 'una favola' means something wonderful: è una favola!

etymology: From Latin favor.

senses.note: Per favore = please; fare un favore = to do a favor; a favore di = in favor of.

etymology: Borrowed from English fax.

fact.text: Short for facsimile, from Latin fac simile, 'make alike'.

senses.note: Invariable: il fax, i fax. Also used for the machine. Mandare un fax = to send a fax.

etymology: From Late Latin Febrārius, from Latin (mēnsis) Februārius. Compare Sicilian frivaru.

senses.note: Months are lowercase in Italian. In February = a febbraio / in febbraio.

etymology: Inherited from Latin febrem, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰegʷʰris, an extension of the root *dʰegʷʰ- (“to burn, warm”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin febris. English 'fever' and 'febrile' come from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Avere la febbre = to have a temperature.

etymology: From Latin fidem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ-.

fact.text: Italians also call a wedding ring la fede, the symbol of faithfulness. It comes from Latin fides, the root of English fidelity.

senses.note: Also means wedding ring (la fede nuziale). In buona fede = in good faith.

etymology: From Latin fidēlem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin fidelis, the root of English fidelity. The 'fi' in hi-fi (high fidelity) is the same word, meaning sound that is faithful to the original.

senses.note: Same form for both genders. As a noun, i fedeli = the faithful (churchgoers).

etymology: From earlier *fecato, from Late Latin fīcātum (“liver”), from Latin iecur fīcātum (“fig-stuffed liver, foie gras”).

fact.text: Romans fattened geese on figs and called the result iecur ficatum, 'fig-stuffed liver'. Over time the 'fig' part (ficatum) became the everyday word for liver itself.

senses.note: Figurative: avere fegato = to have guts (courage).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fēlīcem.

fact.text: Latin felix first meant 'fruitful, fertile'. It comes from an ancient root meaning 'to suckle', the same root as Latin femina (woman) and fetus. English 'felicity' comes from the same word.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural felici. 'Felice di + infinitive' = happy to…

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fēlīcitātem. By surface analysis, felice + -ità.

fact.text: Latin felix first meant 'fertile, fruitful', then 'lucky, happy'. It comes from a root meaning 'to suckle', the same root behind Latin femina, 'woman'. The name Felix means 'lucky'.

senses.note: Usually uncountable; the form doesn't change in the plural (le felicità).

etymology: Inherited from Latin fēmina.

senses.note: Used for animals and a baby's sex (è femmina); said of a woman it can sound crude. Use donna.

etymology: From Latin fēminīnus, with change of suffix by dissimilation. By surface analysis, femmina (“female”, noun) + -ile.

senses.note: Also 'women's': squadra femminile = women's team. Note the double m.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fēria.

fact.text: Ferragosto, Italy's 15 August holiday, comes from Latin Feriae Augusti, 'rest days of Augustus'. It shares a root with le ferie, your annual leave.

senses.note: Almost always plural: le ferie = annual leave. Andare in ferie = to go on holiday.

fact.text: Confusingly, ferie means holidays, yet a giorno feriale is a working day. Church Latin used feria for ordinary weekdays (feria secunda = Monday), hence the twist.

senses.note: giorno feriale = working day; orario feriale = weekday timetable. Opposite: festivo.

etymology: From Latin ferīre, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰerH-.

fact.text: From Latin ferire 'to strike'. Through Old French s'entreferir 'to strike each other', the same root gave English interfere.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: ferisco, ferisci. Ferirsi = to get hurt. Also figurative: to hurt someone's feelings.

fact.text: Comes from ferire 'to wound', from Latin ferire 'to strike'. The same verb is hidden in English 'interfere', from Old French s'entreferir, 'to strike each other'.

senses.note: Also injury in general. From ferire (to wound); ferito/ferita = wounded person.
Past participle of ferire. Also figurative: ferito nell'orgoglio = hurt in one's pride.

etymology: Inherited from Latin firmāre. Doublet of firmare.

fact.text: Comes from Latin firmare ('to make firm, fix'), so stopping something means fixing it in place. The same root gives English firm, affirm and even farm (once a fixed rent).

senses.note: fermare qualcuno = to stop someone. To stop yourself is fermarsi (with essere): ci fermiamo qui.
Reflexive, takes essere: mi sono fermato. Can also mean 'to stay' a while: fermarsi a cena.

etymology: From fermare (“to stop”).

senses.note: La fermata dell'autobus = the bus stop.

etymology: From Latin firmus, from Proto-Italic *fermos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer-mo-s (“holding”), from the root *dʰer- (“to hold”).

fact.text: From Latin firmus, the source of English 'firm'. The same root gives fermare (to stop) and fermata (a bus or tram stop).

senses.note: 'Stai fermo!' = keep still! 'Fermo!' on its own = Freeze! / Stop!

etymology: From Latin ferrum.

fact.text: For luck, Italians 'touch iron' (toccare ferro) where English speakers knock on wood.

senses.note: The appliance is il ferro da stiro; i ferri can also be knitting needles.

etymology: From Late Latin fēsta, from the plural of Latin fēstus (“festive”).

fact.text: From Latin festa, 'festive (days)', which is also the root of English 'feast', 'festival' and 'festive', and of Spanish fiesta.

senses.note: Fare una festa = to throw a party. Also holiday: Buone feste! A political party is un partito.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *festizāre. Derivable from festa + -eggiare.

senses.note: Used for birthdays, wins and parties: festeggiare un compleanno. For religious rites, celebrare is used.

etymology: Borrowed from English festival.

fact.text: In Italy 'il Festival' usually means the Sanremo song festival. It has run since 1951 and helped inspire the Eurovision Song Contest.

senses.note: Invariable loanword: il festival, i festival.

etymology: From Latin fēstīvus.

fact.text: Watch out: giorno feriale means a working day, even though ferie means holidays. Festivo is the holiday word, as on Italian bus timetables marked 'festivo'.

senses.note: Mainly giorno festivo = Sunday or public holiday. The opposite is feriale = weekday.

etymology: Uncertain; several possibilities exist. Probably ultimately from Latin findere, through an alteration of its past participle fissus into a form *fictus > *fectus, later becoming feminine. (Compare the change from fixus to fitto). An alternative may be a Vulgar Latin *offetta (“little piece”), diminutive of offa. Compare Galician and Portuguese fita, Dalmatian fiata, Sicilian feḍḍa, Sardinian fitta.

fact.text: Fette biscottate are a breakfast staple in Italy. These twice-baked, rusk-like slices are usually spread with jam or dipped in caffellatte.

senses.note: Una fetta di pane = a slice of bread. Fette biscottate = rusks (crispy toasted bread slices).

etymology: From fiamma (“flame”) + -ifero (“-iferous, producing”).

fact.text: Literally 'flame-bearer': fiamma (flame) plus -ifero (bearing). It is the same ending as in English 'coniferous', which means cone-bearing.

senses.note: Una scatola di fiammiferi = a box of matches.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French flanc (“flank, side”).

fact.text: Shares its source with English flank (Old French flanc). Italian regularly turned fl- into fi-, as in fiore (flower) and fiamma (flame).

senses.note: The plural i fianchi often means hips. di fianco a = next to; fianco a fianco = side by side.

etymology: From Latin ficus.

fact.text: In slang the word also means cool. Che fico! means How cool!, and it is often spelled figo. Be careful, though: the feminine fica is vulgar.

senses.note: Plural fichi. Means both the fruit and the tree.

fact.text: This is a false friend even though it was borrowed from English. Italians use 'la fiction' for TV drama series, such as the RAI series about Inspector Montalbano, not for novels.

senses.note: Invariable: le fiction. Literary fiction is 'narrativa'.

etymology: From fidanz(are) + -ato. Compare French fiancé.

fact.text: In everyday Italian, il fidanzato/la fidanzata usually just means boyfriend/girlfriend, not fiancé. The idea of a formal engagement is often not implied at all.

senses.note: Also the everyday word for boyfriend. Feminine: la fidanzata; i fidanzati = engaged couple.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fīdāre, from Latin fīdere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin fidere 'to trust', related to fides 'faith', which gave English fidelity and confide. The classic dog name Fido is Latin for 'I trust'.

senses.note: Almost always reflexive: fidarsi di qualcuno. Mi fido di te = I trust you. Takes essere: mi sono fidato.

etymology: From fidar(e) (“to entrust”) + -si (enclitic reflexive pronoun).

fact.text: A classic Italian proverb: Fidarsi è bene, non fidarsi è meglio, meaning 'Trusting is good, not trusting is better.'

senses.note: Takes di: mi fido di te = I trust you. Reflexive, so compound tenses use essere.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fīdūcia.

senses.note: Avere fiducia in qualcuno = to trust someone. Rarely used in the plural.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fīlia, from fīlius (“child, son”), from Old Latin fīlios, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Cognate to French fille, Portuguese filha, Galician filla, Romanian fie, Spanish hija, Sicilian figghia, Sardinian filla, Romansh feglia.

fact.text: Latin filia comes from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning 'to suck', so a child was originally 'a suckling'. English 'filial' and 'affiliate' come from the same Latin family.

senses.note: Masculine figlio = son; i figli = children or sons.

etymology: From Latin fīlius, from Old Latin fīlios, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeh₁y-li-os (“sucker”), a derivation from the verbal root *dʰeh₁(y)- (“to suck”). Cognate to French fils, Portuguese filho, Galician fillo, Romanian fiu, Spanish hijo, Sicilian figghiu, Corsican figliu, Sardinian fillu, Romansh fegl.

fact.text: Comes from Latin filius, which goes back to a root meaning 'to suck', so a son was first 'one who suckles'. The same Latin word gives English filial and affiliate.

senses.note: The plural figli also means 'children' in general (sons and daughters). A daughter is figlia.

etymology: From Latin fīliolus. By surface analysis, figlio (“son”) + -olo (diminutive suffix).

senses.note: Affectionate form of figlio; also used to address a boy (sonny). Old spelling: figliuolo.

fact.text: Careful with the feminine: figa is also a vulgar noun for female genitals. Fico also literally means fig.

senses.note: Che figo! = How cool! As a noun, un figo = a hot guy. Central/Southern variant: fico.

etymology: From Latin figūra, possibly borrowed.

fact.text: 'Fare bella figura' (making a good impression) and avoiding 'brutta figura' (embarrassing yourself) are well-known Italian ideas about how you look and behave in public.

senses.note: A number or digit is una cifra, not una figura. Fare bella figura = to make a good impression.

fact.text: Figurati! (or Si figuri! when speaking formally) is a very common reply to 'grazie', meaning 'don't mention it'. Literally it means 'imagine (that I'd mind)!'

senses.note: Usually reflexive: figurarsi. Figurati! = Just imagine! / Don't mention it!

etymology: Compare French se figurer.

fact.text: Its imperative is everywhere in daily Italian. Figurati! is the standard reply to grazie (don't mention it), and it also works as a sceptical as if! or no way!

senses.note: Reflexive: mi figuro. Figurati! / Si figuri! = don't mention it, or as if!

etymology: Probably from filo, or from Latin fila, plural of filum. Compare French file, Portuguese fila.

senses.note: fare la fila = to queue / stand in line; in prima fila = in the front row; di fila = in a row.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English file.

fact.text: Watch out: a native Italian word is spelled the same way. Le file (pronounced FEE-leh) is the plural of fila, 'row' or 'queue'. Only the article tells them apart in writing.

senses.note: Invariable: il file, i file. Pronounced as in English.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English film.

senses.note: Invariable: il film, i film.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fīlum.

fact.text: From Latin filum 'thread', which also gave English filament, fillet (a little strip) and file as in 'single file', meaning a line of people.

senses.note: Also wire (filo elettrico). The figurative plural le fila: tirare le fila = to pull the strings.

etymology: From Late Latin fīnālis, from Latin fīnis (“end; boundary, limit”), whence fine. By surface analysis, fine (“end; limit; goal”) + -ale.

senses.note: As a noun: la finale = the final (match), il finale = the ending (of a film or book).

etymology: From finale + -mente.

fact.text: This mostly means 'at last!', said with relief after waiting. When you list steps and mean 'finally' or 'lastly', Italians usually say infine instead.

senses.note: Expresses relief: Finalmente! = At last! For 'finally' at the end of a list, use infine.

etymology: From finanza + -ario.
Univerbation of fino (“fin(o)”) + che.

senses.note: Often with a redundant 'non': aspetta finché (non) torno. Can also mean 'as long as'.

etymology: From Latin fīnem.

fact.text: The gender changes the meaning: la fine is the end or conclusion, il fine is the aim or purpose. 'Il fine giustifica i mezzi' means 'the end justifies the means'.

senses.note: Alla fine = in the end. Il fine settimana = weekend. Il fine (masculine) = aim, purpose.

etymology: From Latin fenestra.
Inherited from Latin fingere (“to fashion, make up”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin fingere 'to shape, make up', the same root behind English 'feign', 'fiction', 'figment' and even 'effigy'. Pretending is literally shaping a story.

senses.note: fingere di + infinitive: finge di dormire. Past participle finto also means 'fake'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fīnīre.

senses.note: -isc- verb (finisco). Avere when transitive (ho finito), essere when intransitive (è finita).

ignored: It is a clitic compound (finisci + li) of finire, which belongs on the finire card.

senses.note: finisci (imperative of finire) + li (them).

etymology: From some such adjectival form as Vulgar Latin *fīnus, from Latin fīnis (“a boundary, limit”), whence Italian fine. The prepositional usage is directly paralleled in Latin fīne, fīnī (“up to, as far as”).

senses.note: Usually followed by a: fino a domani = until tomorrow; fino alla valle = as far as the valley.

etymology: From fino (“until”) + ora (“now”).

senses.note: Finora tutto bene = So far so good.

etymology: From the feminine of finto.

senses.note: Mostly used in fare finta (di) = to pretend. In sport, finta = a feint or dummy.

etymology: From Latin fictus, perfect passive participle of fingō, probably through a Vulgar Latin root *finctus, with a nasal infix. Compare French feint, Lombard fint and Piedmontese fint.

fact.text: The past participle of fingere, 'to pretend', from Latin fingere. English feign, fiction and figment come from the same root.

senses.note: fare finta di = to pretend to.

etymology: Inherited from Latin flōrem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin flos, which also gave English 'flower' and 'flour'. Flour was once 'the flower of the meal', meaning its finest part. Through the same ancient root, it is also related to English 'blossom'.

senses.note: The plural fiori is also the suit of clubs in cards. il fior fiore = the very best, the cream.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Latin firmoder.
Italian firmarebf.
Italian firma
Back-formation from firmare, from Latin firmāre, from firmus; cognates include English firm (adjective). Doublet of dharma.

fact.text: English firm, 'company', comes from this word: the signed name a business traded under. In Italian it means signature. A firm is una ditta or un'azienda.

senses.note: Mettere la firma = to sign. Verb: firmare.

etymology: From Latin firmāre, from firmus. Doublet of fermare.

fact.text: From Latin firmare, 'to make firm', so a signature firms up a document, as in English confirm. Its twin word fermare, from the same Latin verb, means 'to stop'.

senses.note: La firma = the signature. Firmare un contratto = to sign a contract.

etymology: From Latin physicus (“physical”, “natural”), from Ancient Greek φυσικός (phusikós).

fact.text: English physician shares this root, Latin physicus 'natural': medieval doctors were seen as experts in the natural world.

senses.note: As a noun: il fisico = physique/body or physicist; la fisica = physics.

etymology: Inherited from Latin flūmen.

fact.text: Comes from Latin flumen. Fiume is also the Italian name of the Croatian city Rijeka, and both names simply mean 'river'.

etymology: From Late Latin folia, from the plural of Latin folium (“leaf”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin folium 'leaf', which also gave English foliage, folio and portfolio. A folio was originally a leaf of paper.

senses.note: Don't confuse with il foglio, a sheet of paper.

etymology: From Latin folium.

fact.text: Comes from Latin folium 'leaf', like English foil, folio and foliage. Italian kept both: foglia (f.) is a leaf, while foglio (m.) is a sheet of paper.

senses.note: Don't mix it up with la foglia (leaf). A bed sheet is il lenzuolo.

etymology: Deverbal from follare + -a. Compare Sicilian fuḍḍa.

fact.text: It comes from follare, to full (press and beat) cloth, from Latin fullo, the source of English 'fuller'. A crowd is people pressed tightly together.

senses.note: C'era una gran folla = there was a big crowd. The plural folle looks like the adjective folle (mad).

fact.text: Comes from folle, 'mad', from Latin follis, 'bellows' or 'windbag'. English fool and folly come from the same root via French, so a fool is literally a windbag.

senses.note: Fare follie = to do crazy things or splurge. Plural follie can mean extravagances.

etymology: From Latin fundus (“deep”).

fact.text: From Latin fundus 'bottom; piece of land'. The same word gave English 'fund' and 'fundamental'. In Italian, fondo still means both the bottom of something and a fund.

senses.note: In fondo = at the bottom / after all. Plural fondi also means funds.

etymology: From Late Latin fontāna, from Latin fontānus, from fōns. The meaning of fountain, as an artificial installation, may be partly derived from or influenced by the Old French equivalent.

fact.text: Comes from Latin fons, 'spring'. The same root gives English fountain and the baptismal font in a church.

senses.note: La Fontana di Trevi is Rome's most famous one.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fontem m, of Proto-Indo-European origin.

fact.text: From Latin fons, fontis 'spring'. That's also where English fountain and the baptismal font come from.

senses.note: Also a spring of water. Masculine in il fonte battesimale (baptismal font).

fact.text: Italians rarely use this loanword. Their own name for the sport is calcio, 'kick', taken from calcio fiorentino, a rough Renaissance ball game still played in Florence every June.

senses.note: Invariable. The everyday word is il calcio; football americano = American football.

etymology: From forca (“gardening fork”) + -etta (diminutive suffix). Compare French fourchette. Sense four is calqued from French.

fact.text: This is a diminutive of forca, a pitchfork, so a table fork is literally a 'little pitchfork'. Someone who loves eating is called una buona forchetta, 'a good fork'.

senses.note: essere una buona forchetta = to be a hearty eater.

etymology: Derived from Early Medieval Latin foresta. Documented since the thirteenth century.

fact.text: Medieval Latin foresta probably comes from silva forestis, 'the outside wood' (from foris, 'outside'). It meant royal hunting land that lay outside the common, fenced land.

senses.note: A smaller wood is usually un bosco; foresta suggests a large, wild forest.

etymology: Inherited from Latin fōrma.

fact.text: Formaggio (cheese) comes from Latin formaticus, meaning made in a mould (forma). French fromage has the same origin, and a whole wheel of Parmesan is still called una forma.

senses.note: Also means form or mould. Essere in forma means to be fit.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French formage, from Medieval Latin fōrmāticum, from Latin fōrma (“mould/mold”). Compare modern French fromage.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin formaticum, cheese pressed into a forma (mould). French fromage comes from the same word, with the letters shuffled.

etymology: From Latin formāre.

senses.note: formarsi = to take shape; also to be trained or educated (la formazione = training).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fōrmātiōnem.

fact.text: In football it means the team lineup. La formazione titolare is the starting eleven, and newspapers print the probabili formazioni (likely lineups) before a match.

senses.note: Also means formation, and a sports team's lineup.

etymology: From forno + -ello (“diminutive suffix”), or from Vulgar Latin *furnellus, from Latin furnus. Compare French fourneau, Sicilian furneddu, Catalan fornell, Romansh furnel, Sardinian furredhu, Occitan fornèl, Portuguese fornilho, Spanish hornillo.

fact.text: Literally a 'little oven': forno 'oven' + the diminutive -ello. French fourneau and Spanish hornillo are formed the same way.

senses.note: Also a single burner on a cooker. Stare ai fornelli = to be cooking.

etymology: From fornire + -tore.

senses.note: Feminine: la fornitrice. Fornire = to supply.

etymology: From Latin furnus, from Proto-Italic *fornos, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷʰr̥-nós, from *gʷʰer- (“warm, hot”).

fact.text: From Latin furnus 'oven'. Its close relative fornax gave English furnace, and both go back to a root meaning 'warm, hot'.

senses.note: Al forno = baked (pasta al forno). Can also mean a bakery.

etymology: Inherited from Latin forsit.

fact.text: From Latin forsit, a shortening of fors sit, roughly 'be it by chance'. Latin fors (chance) is also the root of fortuna, which gave English 'fortune'.

senses.note: Usually takes the indicative: Forse ha ragione.

etymology: From Latin fortem

fact.text: In music forte means 'loud'. The piano's full name, pianoforte, means 'soft-loud', because it could play both depending on touch.

senses.note: Also 'loud'. As an adverb: parla più forte = speak louder. Slang: che forte! = how cool!

etymology: From Latin fortūna, from fors (“chance, luck”).

fact.text: Fortuna was the Roman goddess of luck, often shown with a wheel. Her name comes from Latin fors, 'chance'.

senses.note: Per fortuna = luckily; Buona fortuna! = Good luck! Also means 'fortune' (wealth, fate).

etymology: From fortunato + -mente.
From Latin fortūnātus.

senses.note: Essere fortunato = to be lucky (the person is lucky, not 'has luck').

etymology: From Late Latin fortia, a noun derived from the neuter plural of Latin fortis (“strong”).

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin fortia, originally the neuter plural of fortis 'strong, brave', as in fortia facta 'brave deeds'. English 'force' and 'fortitude' share the root.

senses.note: Also an interjection: Forza! = Come on! / Go on! (cheering)

ignored: Infinitive plus clitic pronoun; study the verb forzare instead.

senses.note: forzare + mi.

etymology: Clipping of fotografia.

fact.text: It ends in -o but is feminine because it is short for la fotografia. La moto (motocicletta) and la radio work the same way.

senses.note: Feminine and invariable: la foto, le foto.

etymology: From foto- + -grafia.

senses.note: Often shortened to la foto (plural le foto). fare una foto = to take a photo.

etymology: From Latin futuere (“to fuck”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰew- (“to hit”).

fact.text: Comes straight from the Latin swear word futuere, which also gave French foutre. Romans used it just as crudely.

senses.note: Also 'to screw over, con'. Me ne fotto = I don't give a damn. Fregare is a milder word.
Fottiti! = Fuck off! / Screw you! Fottersene = not to give a damn.
Vulgar intensifier, usually placed before the noun: quel fottuto sogno.

etymology: From Latin īnfrā, which stems from inferus.

fact.text: Fra and tra mean exactly the same. Italians pick whichever sounds smoother, so they say tra fratelli rather than fra fratelli, and fra tre rather than tra tre.

senses.note: Interchangeable with tra; also means 'among'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fragilem.

fact.text: English 'frail' is a twin of fragile: both come from Latin fragilis, from frangere 'to break'. The same verb gives English fracture and fraction.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural fragili. The stress falls on the first syllable: FRA-gi-le.

etymology: From Latin fragrantia.

senses.note: Often used for food, e.g. la fragranza del pane appena sfornato (freshly baked bread).

etymology:
From Francia + -ese.
Borrowed from Old French franceis.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. Same form for masculine and feminine; plural francesi.

etymology: From franco- (“free from duty”) + bollo (“stamp”).

fact.text: Made from franco (free of charges) and bollo (seal). Literally it is a seal showing that the postage is already paid.

senses.note: For an ink or rubber stamp, Italian uses timbro.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).

fact.text: Looks like English 'phrase', but it usually means a whole sentence. Fare una frase = to make a sentence.

senses.note: A full sentence. Can also mean a phrase or expression.

etymology: From Latin frātellus, a diminutive of Latin frāter, from Proto-Italic *frātēr, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰréh₂tēr.

fact.text: Comes from a diminutive of Latin frater, which shares an Indo-European root (*bhrehter) with English 'brother'. The Latin form also gave English 'fraternal' and 'fraternity'.

senses.note: Plural fratelli = brothers, or siblings of mixed sex: Hai fratelli? = Do you have siblings?

fact.text: Made from fra ('between') + tempo ('time'), so nel frattempo is literally 'in the between-time'.

senses.note: Used almost only in the phrase nel frattempo.

etymology: Inherited from Latin frīgidus (“cold”) (through a syncopated Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form frigdus, fricdus, attested in the Appendix Probi, or fridus, found in a Pompeian inscription), itself from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sríHgos. Doublet of frigido, a later borrowing.

fact.text: Watch the taps in Italy: C stands for caldo, which means HOT. The cold tap is marked F for freddo. Freddo comes from Latin frigidus, the root of English frigid.

senses.note: Fa freddo = it's cold (weather). Ho freddo = I'm cold.

etymology: Inherited from Latin frīgidus (“cold”) (through a syncopated Vulgar Latin or Late Latin form frigdus, fricdus, attested in the Appendix Probi, or fridus, found in a Pompeian inscription), itself from frīgeō (“to be cold”), from frīgus (“cold, coldness”), from Proto-Indo-European *sríHgos. Doublet of frigido, a later borrowing.

fact.text: Watch the taps in Italy: C stands for caldo, which means HOT. The cold tap is marked F for freddo. Freddo comes from Latin frigidus, the root of English frigid.

senses.note: Ho freddo = I'm cold; fa freddo = it's cold. A cold (illness) is il raffreddore.

etymology: Borrowed from English freezer.

senses.note: Invariable: i freezer. A native alternative is il congelatore.

etymology: From earlier *frecàre, from Latin fricāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin fricare 'to rub', the same root as English 'friction'. The slang sense 'to cheat' grew out of this basic meaning of rubbing.

senses.note: Mi hanno fregato = I've been had. Literal sense: to rub. Fregarsene = not to give a damn (me ne frego).

etymology: From fregarsi + -ne. Coined or popularized by Gabriele d'Annunzio as a translation of the English to not give a fuck.

fact.text: 'Me ne frego!' was the motto of Gabriele d'Annunzio's legionnaires at Fiume in 1919. Mussolini's Fascists later adopted it, so the phrase still carries some political history.

senses.note: Me ne frego = I don't give a damn. Rather blunt; use 'non m'importa' in polite settings.

etymology: From freno + -are, or possibly from Latin frēnāre.
