fact.text: Comes from freno, from Latin frenum (bridle), so to brake was first to rein in a horse.

senses.note: Transitively also 'to curb, hold back': frenare l'inflazione, frenare le lacrime.

etymology: Inherited from Latin frēnum.

fact.text: From Latin frenum 'bridle, bit'. English refrain (to hold back) comes from Latin refrenare, which literally meant to rein in with a bridle.

senses.note: Freno a mano = handbrake. Figuratively: a curb or restraint.

etymology: From Latin frequentāre.

fact.text: Don't say attendere for 'attend': in Italian it means 'to wait'. To attend a school or course is frequentare.

senses.note: Frequentare l'università. Also: to frequent a place, to hang out with someone.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *friscum.

fact.text: English fresco comes from the Italian phrase a fresco, 'on the fresh', meaning painting on plaster that is still wet.

senses.note: Used for food, air and so on: pane fresco = fresh bread.

etymology: Deverbal from frettare + -a.

senses.note: Avere fretta = to be in a hurry. In fretta = quickly. Non c'è fretta = there's no rush.

etymology: Inherited from Latin frīgere, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰer-.

fact.text: A colourful brush-off: 'Va' a farti friggere!' (literally 'go get yourself fried') means 'Get lost!'

senses.note: Irregular: past participle fritto (as in fritto misto), passato remoto frissi.

etymology: Clipping of frigorifero.

senses.note: Short for il frigorifero. Invariable: i frigo.

etymology: Word build upon the model of the French calorifère (“heater, radiator”), as an adaptation made using Latin frigor (“coldness”) + -fer (“-bearing, -carrying, -bringing”).

fact.text: Literally means 'cold-bringer': Latin frigus, frigoris (cold) plus -fer (bearing).

senses.note: In everyday speech it is usually shortened to il frigo.

etymology: From fritto + -are.
ignored: A rare dialectal verb; the context's 'fritta' comes from friggere, so study that card instead.

senses.note: Dialectal; standard Italian uses friggere (past participle fritto).

etymology: From fritto (“fried”) + -ata.

fact.text: 'Ho fatto una frittata!' means 'I've messed up!' The image is broken eggs: once they're cracked, you can't undo it.

senses.note: Idioms: fare una frittata means to make a mess of things; girare la frittata means to twist the argument.

etymology: Inherited from Latin frontem (“forehead”). For noun 1 sense 2 compare the Latin etymon and derivatives in Italian like sfrontato (“shameless”). Cognate with Sicilian frunti.

fact.text: The gender changes the meaning: la fronte is your forehead, but il fronte is a front line in war or a weather front.

senses.note: Feminine here. Masculine il fronte = (battle/weather) front. di fronte a = opposite.

etymology: From frullare + -tore.

senses.note: From frullare, 'to whisk, blend'. Un frullato = a milkshake or smoothie.

etymology: From Late Latin fructa, from Latin fructus.

fact.text: Italian has two words here: la frutta is fruit as food in general, and il frutto is one fruit or a figurative 'fruit' of work. Frutti di mare (fruits of the sea) means seafood.

senses.note: Collective and usually singular: mangio la frutta. A single piece of fruit is un frutto.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *focīlis [petra], derived from Latin focus. Compare French fusil, Friulian fusîl, Piedmontese fusil.
Borrowed from Latin fuga. Compare the inherited doublet foga.

fact.text: The musical fugue comes from this word, because the voices seem to chase each other. The same Latin root gives English fugitive and refuge.

senses.note: Also: fuga di gas = gas leak; in music, a fugue.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fugīre, from Latin fugere, from Proto-Italic *fugiō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewg-. Cognate with Sicilian fùjiri.

fact.text: Comes from Latin fugere, 'to flee', the same root behind English fugitive, refuge and centrifugal (literally 'fleeing the centre').

senses.note: Takes essere when intransitive: sono fuggito. fuggire da = to flee from.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fugitīvus and adapted to Italian fuggire.

senses.note: Often used as a noun: un fuggitivo = a fugitive. Related to fuggire (to flee).

ignored: The context form is the past participle of fulminare; the chemistry noun is too rare to study.

senses.note: Chemistry term for an explosive salt, e.g. fulminato di mercurio.

etymology: From Latin fulmen.

fact.text: Love at first sight is 'un colpo di fulmine', literally a lightning strike.

senses.note: Countable: 'un fulmine' = a bolt of lightning.

etymology: From Latin fūmāre.

senses.note: Vietato fumare = No smoking. Il fumo = smoke.

etymology: From fumo + -etto.

fact.text: Literally 'little puff of smoke' (fumo + -etto). The name came from speech bubbles, which look like puffs of smoke, and then spread to the whole comic.

senses.note: Means comics in general or a comic book; also a speech bubble.

etymology: From Latin fūmus, from Proto-Italic *fūmos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós.

fact.text: An Italian saying, 'tanto fumo e poco arrosto' (lots of smoke and little roast), describes something all show and no substance.

senses.note: Also smoking: 'Il fumo fa male'. In slang it means hashish.

etymology: From Late Latin fūnerālis (“pertaining to a funeral”), from Latin funus.

senses.note: Often used in the plural for a single funeral, especially in formal use: i funerali.

etymology: Borrowed from French fonctionner. Cognate with Piedmontese funsioné.

fact.text: Italian splits English 'work' in two: lavorare is to work at a job, and funzionare is for things that work. 'Non funziona!' means 'It doesn't work!'

senses.note: Used for things that function: il telefono non funziona. For working at a job use lavorare.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin fūnctiōnem.

senses.note: Also a church service; in funzione di = depending on.

etymology: From Latin focus (“hearth”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin focus, 'hearth'. Kepler used focus for the burning point of a lens, which gave English 'focus'. In Italian, mettere a fuoco still means 'to bring into focus'.

senses.note: fuochi d'artificio = fireworks; also a stove burner. Hai da accendere? = Got a light?

etymology: From Latin forīs.

fact.text: From Latin forīs, 'out of doors', related to foris, 'door'. Through Late Latin foranus and Old French, the same root gave English 'foreign', which literally means 'from outside'.

senses.note: Fuori! = Get out! Cenare fuori = to eat out.

etymology: Borrowed from French fourgon. Cognate with Piedmontese furgon.

fact.text: Came through French fourgon from Vulgar Latin *furicare 'to rummage', which is linked to Latin fur 'thief'. That same root gives English 'furtive'.

senses.note: furgone dei traslochi = removal van; furgone funebre = hearse.

etymology: From Latin fūrtum, derived from fūr (“thief”).

fact.text: From Latin furtum, from fur (thief). The same root gives English 'furtive', meaning sneaky or done in secret.

senses.note: Furto con scasso = burglary.

etymology: From fuso + -ibile; cognate with Piedmontese fusibil.

fact.text: Literally 'the meltable thing', from fuso (melted), because the wire inside melts to break the circuit.

senses.note: È saltato un fusibile = a fuse has blown.

etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

fact.text: The name comes from fuso, 'spindle'. Traditionally the pasta was made by winding strips of dough around a thin rod or spindle to get the spiral shape.

senses.note: Used in the plural (singular fusillo, rare): i fusilli.

etymology: From Latin futūrus (future participle of esse).

fact.text: From Latin futurus, the future participle of esse, 'to be'. It literally means 'about to be'.

senses.note: In futuro = in the future. In grammar it also means the future tense.

etymology: Archaic variant of galea (“galley”) used in the nautical sense, from which the primary modern usage derives.

fact.text: It first meant 'galley', the oar-driven ship. Convicts were often sentenced to row in galleys, so the ship's name came to mean prison itself.

senses.note: Informal: andare in galera = to go to jail. Carcere and prigione are more neutral.

etymology: From Medieval Latin galeria (“gallery”), perhaps an alteration of galilea (“church porch”), probably from Latin Galilaea (“Galilee”), region of Israel. More at Galilee.

fact.text: Probably from Medieval Latin galilea, a church porch, named after Galilee, the region of Israel. The link to the place name is likely but not certain.

senses.note: Also means a shopping arcade, a road or rail tunnel, and the balcony or circle in a theatre.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin gamba. Cognate with Sicilian gamma ~ jamma.

fact.text: From Late Latin gamba, from Greek kampe, 'bend'. 'Essere in gamba' means to be smart or capable.

senses.note: essere in gamba = to be smart, capable.

fact.text: A signature word of Tuscan, and especially Florentine, speech: 'che ganzo!' means 'how cool!'. Its older meaning as a noun was a secret lover.

senses.note: Typically Tuscan slang. Elsewhere, figo is more common.

etymology: Uncertain. Possibly borrowed from Arabic غارة (ḡāra), whence also Spanish algara.

senses.note: Any contest or race. Fare a gara = to compete with each other.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French garage.

senses.note: Invariable: i garage. Pronounced the French way, with the stress on the last syllable.

fact.text: The 17th-century Flemish chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont made the word up, basing it on Greek 'chaos'. It is one of the few scientific words with a known inventor.

senses.note: Invariable: il gas, i gas. una perdita di gas = a gas leak.

etymology: From gatto (“cat”) + -ino (diminutive suffix).

senses.note: Diminutive of gatto. Also used affectionately for a person: ciao, gattino.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cattum.

senses.note: A female cat is la gatta.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English gay.

senses.note: Invariable English loan: un gay, una gay, i gay. Very common as an adjective too.

etymology: From Latin gelātus, derived from gelū (“frost, chill”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“cold”). By surface analysis, gelo (“frost, cold”) + -ato (past participle suffix). Literally, “frozen.” Akin to Russian моро́женое (moróženoje).

fact.text: It literally means 'frozen', from Latin gelu 'frost'. The same root gives English congeal, gelatin and, through French gelée, jelly.

senses.note: Prendo un gelato = I'll have an ice cream. The shop is la gelateria.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin gelidus, derived from gelū, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *gel- (“cold”).

fact.text: From Latin gelu, 'frost'. The same root gives Italian gelato and English gelatin and jelly (via French gelée), all things that set or freeze.

senses.note: Can also be used for an attitude: uno sguardo gelido = an icy stare.

etymology: From Latin generālis.

senses.note: 'In generale' = in general. Same form for both genders; plural generali.

etymology: From generale + -mente.

senses.note: Synonyms: di solito, in genere.

etymology: From Latin generātiōnem.

senses.note: Per generazioni = for generations.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin generis.

fact.text: English gender, genre, general and generic all go back to Latin genus, 'kind, race', from a root meaning 'to beget'.

senses.note: Also means kind or type, and genre. In genere = generally.

etymology: From Latin generum, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵm̥ros, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵem-.

fact.text: Careful: don't confuse it with genere, which means 'gender' or 'genre'. Genero comes from Latin gener, 'son-in-law'.

senses.note: Daughter-in-law is la nuora.

etymology: From Latin generōsus.

senses.note: vino generoso = a strong, full-bodied wine.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin genius.

fact.text: In Latin a genius was the guardian spirit each person was born with. Despite the English word genie, it is not related to the Arabic jinn.

senses.note: Plural geni. andare a genio = to be to one's liking; il Genio = army engineers.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin genitōrem, from genitus, from participle of gignere.

fact.text: From Latin genitor 'begetter', from gignere 'to beget'. It shares a root with English progenitor, genitive and gene.

senses.note: Usually plural: i miei genitori = my parents.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin ienuārius, from Latin Iānuārius.

fact.text: From Latin Ianuarius, the month of Janus. Janus was the two-faced Roman god of doorways and beginnings, looking back at the old year and forward to the new one.

senses.note: Months are lowercase and normally take no article: a gennaio = in January.

etymology: Inherited from Latin gentem, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵénh₁tim. Doublet of genesi via Ancient Greek, and compare etymology 1.

fact.text: Comes from Latin gens, 'clan, family', which also gave English gentle and genteel, both once tied to being of good family.

senses.note: Grammatically singular: la gente è... (people are...). Genti means 'peoples, nations'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin gentīlis.

fact.text: Mainly means kind or polite rather than English 'gentle'. Both come from Latin gentilis, 'of the same clan (gens)', which later became 'well-born, noble'.

senses.note: Gentile Signora/Signore = Dear Madam/Sir in formal letters. Grazie, molto gentile!

etymology: From Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).
From Latin gypsum, from Ancient Greek γύψος (gúpsos).

fact.text: It comes via Latin gypsum from Greek gypsos, so it is related to English 'gypsum'.

senses.note: Also plaster, or a plaster cast: ha la gamba nel gesso (his leg is in a cast).

etymology: Back-formation from gestione.

fact.text: This looks like English gesture, but it almost always means to manage or run something. The gesturing sense is rare; to gesticulate is usually gesticolare.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: gestisco, gestisci. Also means to run or handle (a business, a situation).

etymology: Inherited from Latin gestus.

fact.text: From Latin gerere, 'to carry or perform'. English jest shares this root: Old French geste meant tales of heroic deeds, from Latin gesta.

senses.note: Plural gesti. Don't confuse it with le gesta, meaning heroic deeds or exploits.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin iectāre, from Latin iactāre. Cognate with Sicilian jittari.

fact.text: From Latin iactāre, 'to throw'. Through Old French jeter it also gave English jet and jettison, which means throwing cargo overboard.

senses.note: Gettare via = to throw away. Gettare la spugna = to throw in the towel.

etymology: Calque of French glacier as ghiaccio + -aio.

fact.text: Built from ghiaccio ('ice') plus -aio, much like French glacier (from glace, 'ice'), the word English borrowed.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *glacium/a, from Latin glaciēs. Doublet of ghiaccia. Compare Sicilian chiatru.

fact.text: From Latin glacies, 'ice', the same root as English 'glacier' and 'glacial'. Italian changed the Latin gl- sound to ghi-.

senses.note: Usually uncountable. Plural i ghiacci = ice sheets or ice fields. Ghiacciaio = glacier.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French jaque.

fact.text: Comes from Old French jaque, the same source as English jacket. The word is usually traced to the name Jacques, a nickname for French peasants.

senses.note: giacca e cravatta = jacket and tie. Plural: giacche.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French jalne (variant of jaune), from Latin galbinus. Crime fiction sense is in reference to the yellow covers of a series of mystery novels published by Mondadori from 1929.

fact.text: Italians call a crime novel or thriller 'un giallo' (a yellow) because from 1929 the publisher Mondadori printed its mystery series with yellow covers.

senses.note: As a noun, un giallo is a crime or mystery story.

etymology: Borrowed from French jardinage. By surface analysis, giardino + -aggio.

fact.text: Borrowed from French jardinage. French jardin is Germanic in origin (Frankish *gard, 'enclosure'), which makes it a cousin of English yard and garden.

senses.note: Uncountable in practice: fare giardinaggio = to do some gardening.

etymology: Borrowed from French jardin, of Germanic origin (compare Franconian gardo, German Garten).

fact.text: Borrowed from French jardin, of Germanic origin (*gardō, an enclosure). It is related to English 'garden', and Old English ġeard, from the same Germanic root, became 'yard'.

senses.note: giardino zoologico = zoo; giardini pubblici = public gardens, park.

etymology: From Latin [ars] gymnastica (“gymnastic [art]”).

fact.text: Goes back to Greek gymnos, 'naked', because athletes in ancient Greece trained without clothes. English gym and gymnasium share the same root.

senses.note: Also general exercise and school PE: fare ginnastica = to work out or exercise.

etymology: From Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵónu.

fact.text: Comes from Latin genuculum, 'little knee', from genu. That word shares an Indo-European root with English 'knee'.

senses.note: Plural is usually feminine: le ginocchia ('in ginocchio' = kneeling). 'I ginocchi' also exists.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iocārī. By surface analysis, gioco (“game”) + -are. Cognate with Sicilian jucari.

fact.text: From Latin iocari, 'to jest', from iocus, 'joke', which is also where English joke and jocular come from.

senses.note: Giocare a calcio = to play football. For instruments use suonare.

etymology: From giocare + -tore. Compare French joueur, Piedmontese giugador and giugheur, Portuguese jogador, Romanian jucător, Spanish jugador.

senses.note: Feminine: la giocatrice. A musician is not a giocatore; use suonatore or musicista.

etymology: Diminutive of gioco (“game”).

senses.note: Negozio di giocattoli = toy shop.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iocus. Compare English joke.

fact.text: Comes from Latin iocus, 'jest', which also gave English 'joke' and 'jocular'. In Italian the meaning moved from joking to playing.

senses.note: Also 'play'. prendersi gioco di = to make fun of; in gioco = at stake.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French joie, from Late Latin gaudia, from Classical Latin gaudium. Doublet of gaudio. Cognate with Sicilian gioja.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old French joie, the same word that gave English 'joy'. Both go back to Latin gaudia, a plural of gaudium 'joy' that was later treated as a feminine singular.

senses.note: Also an affectionate form of address: 'Ciao, gioia!' = 'Hi, darling!'

etymology: From Latin diurnālis (with influence from giorno (“day”)), from Latin diurnus, from Latin diēs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). Originally an adjective meaning "daily" (modern giornaliero) as a modifier for foglio giornale.

fact.text: Built on giorno (day), from Latin diurnalis 'daily'. English journal and journey come from the same root; a journey was first a day's travel.

senses.note: 'Giornalaio' or 'edicola' = newsagent/newsstand.

etymology: From giornale + -ista.

fact.text: Built from giornale 'newspaper', which comes from giorno 'day'. English 'journal' and 'journey' (originally a day's travel) share this Latin root, diurnalis 'daily'.

senses.note: Singular is the same for both genders: il/la giornalista. Plurals: giornalisti (m), giornaliste (f).

etymology: Borrowed from Old French jornee. Documented from 1230–50. Derivable from giorno + -ata.

fact.text: A close relative of Old French jornee, the word that became English journey, which first meant a day's travel or a day's work. Journal comes from the same root.

senses.note: Giornata is the day as it is lived (buona giornata!). Giorno is the day as a calendar unit.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin diurnum. Doublet of diurno, a borrowing.

fact.text: From Latin diurnum 'daily (thing)'. The same word reached English via French as journal (a daily record) and journey (originally a day's travel).

senses.note: Buongiorno = good morning/hello. Giornata stresses the whole length of a day.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iuvenis. Cognate with Sicilian jùvini.

fact.text: Comes from Latin iuvenis, which gave English 'juvenile'. English 'young' and 'youth' go back to the same Indo-European root.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine: giovane, plural giovani. Also used as a noun: i giovani = young people.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iuvenis. Cognate with Sicilian jùvini.

fact.text: Comes from Latin iuvenis, which gave English 'juvenile'. English 'young' and 'youth' go back to the same Indo-European root.

senses.note: il/la giovane; i giovani = young people. Also an adjective (young).

etymology: Inherited from Latin Jovis diēs or Iovis diēs, variant of diēs Iovis (“day of Jupiter”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin Iovis dies, 'Jupiter's day'. English Thursday is 'Thor's day', so both languages named the day after a thunder god.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. Invariable. Il giovedì = on Thursdays.

etymology: From Latin gȳrāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin gyrare, from Greek gyros, meaning circle. The same root gives English 'gyrate' and 'gyroscope', and the Greek gyros, meat turning on a spit.

senses.note: Also: girare a destra (turn right), girare un film (shoot a film), girare per la città (wander about).

etymology: From Latin gȳrus, from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros).

fact.text: Comes from Greek gûros, 'ring, circle', the same root as English gyroscope and gyrate. The word also names the Giro d'Italia cycling race.

senses.note: fare un giro = go for a walk/ride; in giro = around.

etymology: Reminescence of the Central Italian verb gire (“to go”), derived from Latin īta, feminine of ītum, ultimately from Latin īre. Cognate with Sicilian juta. Cf. the regional use of gimo (“we go, let's go”).

fact.text: Comes from the old Central Italian verb gire 'to go', from Latin ire. So a gita is literally 'a going'.

senses.note: fare una gita; gita scolastica = school trip. For a longer journey use viaggio.

etymology: From Latin jūdicāre, iūdicāre (“to pass judgement”).

senses.note: Also 'to consider': lo giudico onesto = I consider him honest.

etymology: From Latin iūdicem.

fact.text: In medieval Sardinia the island was split into four kingdoms called giudicati, and each one was ruled by a monarch with the title giudice, meaning judge.

senses.note: Il/la giudice, depending on the person. Giudice di gara = referee or umpire in sport.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin jūdicium, iūdicium.

fact.text: A wisdom tooth is a dente del giudizio, a 'tooth of judgment'. Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel fresco of the Last Judgment is Il Giudizio Universale.

senses.note: Mettere giudizio = to start being sensible. Also verdict or assessment.

etymology: Inherited from Latin Iūnius.

fact.text: From Latin Iunius, the month traditionally said to be named after the goddess Juno, although the Romans themselves proposed other explanations.

senses.note: Italian months are not capitalised. A giugno / in giugno = in June.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iungere (“to join”), from Proto-Italic *jungō, from Proto-Indo-European *yunégti ~ *yungénti, from the root *yewg-, whence also Romanian ajunge.

fact.text: From Latin iungere, 'to join', related to English join, junction and yoke. The meaning shifted from joining to arriving, as if you join your destination.

senses.note: More formal than arrivare. Takes a: giungere a destinazione. Irregular: giunsi, giunto.

etymology: From Latin jūrāre, iūrāre (“to swear or take an oath”), itself from the root *h₂yew- (“justice”, “law”).

fact.text: From Latin iurare 'to take an oath', which is related to ius 'law'. English jury, jurist and justice share the same roots.

senses.note: To promise under oath, not to curse. Lo giuro! = I swear!

etymology: Borrowed from French jury, from English jury. Same etymon as giurì.

fact.text: A round trip: English jury came from Anglo-Norman, ultimately from Latin iurare 'to swear'. Italian then borrowed it back via French.

senses.note: Also a panel of judges in contests, e.g. la giuria di Sanremo.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin iūstitia. Doublet of giustezza.

senses.note: Also means the law or the courts: farsi giustizia da sé = to take the law into your own hands.

etymology: Inherited from Latin iūstus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin iustus, 'just, lawful', which is also where English gets just, justice and justify. So un uomo giusto is a just man, not only a correct one.

senses.note: Also means 'fair, just'. At the end of a sentence, 'giusto?' works like 'right?' to ask for agreement.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin iam (“already, now”).
Cognate with Portuguese já and Spanish ya.

senses.note: On its own, Già! means 'Yeah, right / Indeed' in conversation.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin iūsum~iōsum, from Classical Latin deorsum.

senses.note: Su e giù = up and down. Essere giù = to feel down. Also means 'downstairs'.

ignored: This is only an elided spelling of glielo/gliela; it is studied on the glielo card.

senses.note: Elided glielo/gliela before a vowel: gliel'ho detto.

etymology: Univerbation of glie + lo.

senses.note: Gli + lo. The same form covers to him, to her, to them and formal Lei: glielo do = I give it to him/her.
senses.prompt: it to him / it to her

etymology: From globalizzare + -zione.
Learned borrowing from Latin glōria.
Uncertain.

fact.text: English 'goof' may be related. Etymonline traces it, tentatively, to dialect goff 'foolish clown', from French goffe 'awkward', from this Italian word.

senses.note: Also awkward socially: un tentativo goffo = a clumsy attempt.

etymology: From Latin gula, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷel- (“throat”).

fact.text: From Latin gula, meaning throat. English 'gullet' comes from the same word through Old French goulet, which meant 'little throat'. In Italian, gola also names the sin of gluttony.

senses.note: mal di gola = sore throat. Also means gluttony and a mountain gorge.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English golf.

fact.text: Careful: un golf is also a jumper or cardigan. Mettiti il golf means 'put your sweater on', not 'grab your clubs'.

senses.note: Invariable. Giocare a golf = to play golf.

etymology: From Late Latin gumma, from Latin cummi, gummi, from Ancient Greek κόμμι (kómmi).

fact.text: Goes back through Latin gummi to Greek kómmi, which is probably borrowed from Egyptian. The same ancient word gave English gum.

senses.note: Also means rubber in general; gomma da masticare = chewing gum.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin gunna (“leather garment”).

fact.text: Nothing to do with 'going to'! It comes from Late Latin gunna, a fur or leather garment, which also gave English the word 'gown'.

etymology: From the city in Milan called Gorgonzola.

fact.text: Named after Gorgonzola, a town just outside Milan. It is one of Italy's oldest blue cheeses and has protected (DOP) status.

senses.note: Masculine (il formaggio) and invariable.

etymology: From Latin gubernātōrem.

fact.text: Comes via Latin gubernator from Greek kubernan, 'to steer a ship'. A governor was first a helmsman. The same Greek root later gave English 'cybernetics'.

senses.note: Il governatore della Banca d'Italia = the Governor of the Bank of Italy.

etymology: From the verb governare or from Latin gubernum. Compare Portuguese governo, Spanish gobierno.

fact.text: Comes from Latin gubernare, which was borrowed from Greek kybernan, meaning to steer a ship. Greek kybernan is also the source of English cybernetics, and through that, the cyber- prefix.

etymology: From gracchio (“chough”) + -are. Compare with Spanish grajear (“to caw”) from the same Latin root.

senses.note: Used of crows and magpies; also of a crackling radio or a croaking voice.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *grātīre, from Latin grātus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin gratus, 'pleasing, thankful'. That is the same root as English grateful, gratitude and gratis. An ospite gradito is a welcome guest.

senses.note: Polite offers use the conditional: Gradirebbe un caffè? = Would you care for a coffee?
senses.prompt: to care for, to like to have

etymology: From Latin gradus.

fact.text: Latin gradus meant 'step'. The same word gives English grade, gradual and graduate, and also degree, which came through French.

senses.note: Not a university degree (that's la laurea). Essere in grado di = to be able to.

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic *krapfo, from Proto-West Germanic *krappō.

fact.text: Related to 'graffiti': Italian graffito, 'a scratched mark or inscription', comes from graffiare, 'to scratch'.

senses.note: Verb: graffiare = to scratch.

etymology: From Latin gramma from Ancient Greek γράμμα (grámma, “a twenty-fourth of ounce”).

fact.text: From Greek gramma, which meant 'something written, a letter' and also a tiny weight. That makes it a relative of 'grammar' and 'telegram'.

senses.note: Abbreviated g; un etto = 100 grammi, a common amount at the deli counter.

etymology: Inherited from Latin grandem, of unclear origin.

fact.text: Comes from Latin grandis, a word whose origin is unclear. In spoken Latin it pushed out the classical word for big, magnus, which survives in English only in words like magnitude.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine (plural grandi). Often shortened to gran before a noun: un gran caldo.

etymology: Borrowed from Proto-West Germanic *krappō (“hook”).

fact.text: It is made from pomace, the grape skins, seeds and stems left over from winemaking. An espresso with a splash of it is called a caffè corretto, a 'corrected' coffee.

senses.note: Distilled from pomace. Often drunk after a meal, or added to espresso.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin grassus. Doublet of crasso.

fact.text: Martedì grasso, 'fat Tuesday', is the Italian name for Shrove Tuesday, the same idea as French Mardi Gras: one last feast before Lent.

senses.note: Also fatty or greasy (of food). Noun: il grasso = fat, grease.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin grātīs.

fact.text: Latin gratis was a contraction of gratiis, 'for thanks', meaning done only for thanks and not for payment. It comes from gratia, which also gives grazie.

senses.note: Invariable. Entrata gratis = free entry. A more formal word is gratuito.

etymology:

Inherited from Latin gravis. Doublet of greve.

fact.text: It comes from Latin gravis, 'heavy', which also gave English gravity and grief. A distant relative is Sanskrit guru, which literally means 'heavy, weighty' and so 'venerable'.

senses.note: Used for serious crimes, illnesses and injuries (ferito grave). Also means heavy, or low-pitched.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin gravitātem. By surface analysis, gravi- + -ità.

senses.note: Used for physics and for seriousness: la gravità della situazione = the seriousness of the situation.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin grātia (“favour/favor; goodwill; charm”).

fact.text: Grazie (thank you) is just the plural of this word: literally 'graces, favours', from Latin gratias agere (to give thanks). English grace and gratitude share the root.

senses.note: The plural grazie also means 'thank you'.

etymology: Plural of grazia (“grace”), from Latin grātia, as used in the phrase grātiās agō (“to thank; to express thanks”). Compare Sicilian grazzi and Spanish gracias.

fact.text: Literally 'graces', the plural of grazia. It comes from the Latin phrase gratias ago, 'I give thanks'. English grace and gratitude share the root.

senses.note: Grazie mille = thanks a lot. The usual reply is prego.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *crītāre with irregular voicing.

fact.text: English 'cry' comes from the same Vulgar Latin root: *critare passed into Old French as 'crier' and then into English. So gridare and cry are cousins.

senses.note: Noun: il grido (pl. le grida or i gridi). Gridare aiuto = to shout for help.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French or Old Occitan, both from Frankish *grīs, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz (“grey”). Akin to Old High German grīs (“grey”) (German greis) and Dutch grijs (“grey”). More at grizzle. Cognate with Sicilian grisu/griciu.

fact.text: It comes from Frankish *grīs, meaning grey. The same root gave English 'grizzled' and the grizzly bear, named for its grey-tipped fur.

senses.note: Feminine plural grigie. Also figurative: una giornata grigia = a dull, gloomy day.

etymology: From Latin grossus.

fact.text: This means big, not disgusting. English 'gross' comes from the same Latin grossus and first meant large or thick. That older sense survives in 'gross weight' and 'a gross' (144).

senses.note: Stresses physical bulk or size (un grosso cane). Grande is the more general word for big.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *cruppus, (cf. Renaissance Latin grupus).

senses.note: Also used for a music band: un gruppo rock.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *wadaniāre, of Germanic origin; from Frankish *waiþanōjan, *waiþanōn (“to hunt, graze”) (a calque of Latin petere). Compare French gagner, Catalan guanyar, Portuguese ganhar, Galician gañar, Galician ganar, Galician gadaña, Galician gadañar, cf. also Spanish ganar and Spanish guadañar.

fact.text: Comes from Frankish *waidanjan, 'to hunt, graze'. Through Old French gaaignier, the same root gave French gagner and English 'gain'.

senses.note: Also 'to gain/win': guadagnare tempo = to gain time.

etymology: Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *wai (“expression of grief”). Alternatively from Ancient Greek οὐαί (ouaí), from the verse in Revelation 8:13. Compare English woe, German Weh, Latin vae.

fact.text: May be related to English 'woe' and Latin vae, a cry of grief. The exclamation 'Guai!' still works much like 'woe!'.

senses.note: Essere nei guai = to be in trouble. Guai a te! = Woe betide you!

etymology: From Old Occitan, from Old French guant, from Frankish *want, from Proto-Germanic *wantuz (“glove, mitten”), from Proto-Indo-European *wondʰnú- (“glove”), from the root *wendʰ- (“to wind, wrap”). Cognates include French gant, Catalan guant, Sicilian nguanta and Spanish guante.

fact.text: From Germanic *wantuz. Italian often turned Germanic w- into gu-, the same change seen in guerra (war) and guardare (compare ward).

senses.note: Usually plural: un paio di guanti = a pair of gloves.

etymology: From guardando + -li.
ignored: Gerund of guardare with an attached pronoun; the verb belongs on the guardare card.

senses.note: guardando + li: the pronoun attaches to the end of the gerund.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin wardāre.

fact.text: Comes from Medieval Latin wardare, which was borrowed from Germanic. That is the source of English guard, and also of regard, which means to look at.

senses.note: Takes a direct object, with no word for 'at': guardo la TV. Guarda! = Look!
Guardarsi allo specchio = to look in the mirror. Guardarsi da = to beware of.

etymology: From guardare, of Germanic origin, possibly corresponding to Frankish *warda or Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐍂𐌳𐌾𐌰 (wardja), all ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to watch, notice, give heed”). Compare French garde, Spanish guarda.

fact.text: From a Germanic root meaning 'to watch', which also gave English ward and warden. English guard came from that same root by way of French.

senses.note: Always feminine, even for a male guard: la guardia. Di guardia = on duty.

etymology:
From Frankish *warjan, possibly through the intermediate of a Late Vulgar Latin *warīre, *uarīre.
Compare French guérir, Occitan garir, Catalan and Spanish guarir.

fact.text: A Germanic loan, from Frankish *warjan, 'to protect'. Germanic w- became gu- in Italian, just as in guerra (war) and guardare (compare 'ward').

senses.note: Intransitive with essere (la ferita è guarita); transitive 'to cure' takes avere.

etymology: From the short past participle of guastare (“to ruin”) in Tuscan; compare the Standard Italian participle guastato. Cognate with Piedmontese guast.

senses.note: C'è un guasto = there's a fault. As an adjective: broken, out of order (la lavatrice è guasta).

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin werra, from Frankish *werʀu (“confusion; quarrel”).

fact.text: It comes from Frankish *werru, 'quarrel', the same Germanic source as English war. Romance languages dropped Latin bellum, perhaps because it sounded like bellus, 'beautiful'.

senses.note: Also used figuratively: guerra dei prezzi = price war.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French guerrier.

fact.text: From guerra 'war', which comes from Frankish *werra. That Germanic word is also the source of English war.

senses.note: Feminine: la guerriera. Also an adjective: popolo guerriero = warlike people.

etymology: From guidare. Compare French guide, Spanish guía. Doublet of ghia.

senses.note: Always feminine, even for a male guide (Marco è una brava guida). Also means 'driving': patente di guida.

etymology: From Old Occitan guidar, of Germanic origin; e.g. Frankish *witan, Proto-Germanic *witaną, possibly through a Medieval Latin intermediary. Compare French guider, Spanish guiar.

senses.note: Also means to guide or lead. 'Patente di guida' = driving licence.

etymology: From Latin gustāre. Compare gusto.

fact.text: It is related to gusto ('taste'), which English borrowed from Italian. When you do something 'with gusto', you are doing it with relish.

senses.note: Often means to savour or enjoy: gustare un buon vino.

etymology: From Latin gustus (“taste”), from Proto-Italic *gustus, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵéwstus.

fact.text: English borrowed gusto from Italian, but in Italian the everyday meaning is taste or flavour. 'With gusto' is con gusto or di gusto.

senses.note: Che gusti vuoi? = Which (ice-cream) flavours do you want? Also taste in style: avere buon gusto.

ignored: This is the feminine form of handicappato, used here as an adjective; study the base word handicappato instead.

senses.note: Dated and can sound offensive; persona con disabilità is preferred.
Dated and can offend. Prefer disabile or persona con disabilità. Feminine: handicappata.

ignored: An English first name or a technical unit name with no Italian dictionary data, so not a useful card.
A hesitation noise found in subtitles, not a real Italian word to learn.
A filler sound that is the same in English, so there is nothing to translate.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English hobby.

senses.note: Invariable English loanword: l'hobby, gli hobby.

etymology: Borrowed from French hôtel, from Middle French hostel (“hostel”, “inn”), from Old French ostel (“shelter”), from Latin hospitālis (“pertaining to hospitality”). Doublet of ospedale and ospitale.

fact.text: Borrowed from French hôtel, which comes from Latin hospitalis. That makes it a sibling of ospedale, 'hospital', and English hostel.

senses.note: Invariable: gli hotel. Synonym: albergo.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ictus (“a blow”), from the expression ictus apoplecticus.

fact.text: Latin ictus means a blow, just like English 'stroke'. The medical term is a shortened form of ictus apoplecticus.

senses.note: Invariable. Avere un ictus = to have a stroke.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin idea, from Ancient Greek ἰδέα (idéa, “notion, pattern”), from εἴδω (eídō, “to see”).

fact.text: Came via Latin from Greek idéa, from a verb meaning 'to see'. An idea is literally something the mind 'sees'.

senses.note: Plural idee. Common: Che bella idea! / Non ne ho idea.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin ideālis.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural ideali. Also a noun: l'ideale = the ideal.

etymology: From Renaissance Latin identicus + -ficare.

senses.note: identificarsi con = to identify with.

etymology: inherited from Latin identitās

senses.note: Invariable plural. Carta d'identità = ID card.

etymology: From ideo- + -logia.

fact.text: Coined in French (idéologie) by the philosopher Destutt de Tracy in 1796. It first meant 'the science of ideas' and only later took on its political sense.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).

fact.text: From Greek idiōtēs, 'private person, layman', from idios 'private'. It first meant someone who was not in public life or had no special skill, and only later meant a fool.

ignored: These contexts use the noun 'idiota' (sei un idiota), which gets its own noun card.

senses.note: Plurals idioti (m) / idiote (f). More often a noun: sei un idiota.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin idiōta, from Ancient Greek ἰδιώτης (idiṓtēs, “layman”) from ἴδιος (ídios, “private”).

fact.text: From Greek idiōtēs, 'private person, layman', from idios 'private'. It first meant someone who was not in public life or had no special skill, and only later meant a fool.

senses.note: Same singular for both sexes (un/un'idiota). Plural is idioti (m) or idiote (f). Insulting.

etymology: From Latin hydraulicus, from Ancient Greek ὑδραυλικός (hudraulikós, “of a water organ”), from ὕδραυλις (húdraulis, “water organ”), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”) + αὐλός (aulós, “pipe”). Cognate with Piedmontese idràulich.

fact.text: Goes back to Greek hydraulis, a water organ, from hydor 'water' + aulos 'pipe'. The same root gives English 'hydraulic'. A plumber is basically a water-pipe person.

senses.note: As an adjective, idraulico means 'hydraulic'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin heri.

fact.text: From Latin heri. It goes back to the same Indo-European root as the 'yester-' in English 'yesterday', so the two words are distant relatives.

senses.note: l'altro ieri = the day before yesterday; ieri sera = last night.

etymology: From Ancient Greek ὑγιεινή (hugieinḗ).

fact.text: From Greek hugieine, meaning the art of health. It is related to Hygieia, the Greek goddess of health and cleanliness.

senses.note: Usually singular: l'igiene personale = personal hygiene.

etymology: From earlier 'l, a reduced form of lo. The initial i- is a svarabhakti vowel added in order to make the pronunciation easier. Proof of this is De scriptura nigra (a work in Old Lombard) only employing il to mean “the”, and el to mean “he/him”. Also, works in 1400’s Tuscan showing both “il” and “el”, yet with no forms such as “de Roma” instead of “di Roma” appearing, prove that il does not originate as a pretonic evolved form of el. Compare, by the way, Sicilian lu ~u, representing both the definite masculine singular article, and also iḍḍu (“he”) ḍḍu (“that”) and chiḍḍu (“that”); all cognates from the same source.

fact.text: Like lo, la and French le, it comes from Latin ille, 'that'. Latin had no word for 'the', so Romance languages made one out of a word for pointing at things.

senses.note: Used before most consonants: il libro. Use lo before s+consonant, z, gn, ps (lo zio) and l' before vowels.
Irregular plural: le dita dei piedi. The big toe is 'l'alluce'.
Often just 'il gruppo' or the loanword 'la band' (invariable plural: le band).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin illūmināre (“to illuminate”). Compare alluminare.

senses.note: Means to shine light on. To light a fire is 'accendere' (accendere un falò).

etymology: From Latin illustris (“bright, shining, brilliant, lustrous; clear, lucid; illustrious, distinguished, famous”), from illūstrō (“to illustrate”).

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural illustri. Also used ironically: un illustre sconosciuto (a total nobody).

etymology: From imballare + -aggio.

senses.note: Covers both the act of packing and the material, e.g. boxes and wrapping.

fact.text: Built from in + bosco (wood): hiding in the woods to attack. English ambush comes from the same idea through Old French, literally 'in the bush'.

senses.note: Tendere un'imboscata = to set an ambush.

etymology: From Latin imitārī.

senses.note: Also to forge or counterfeit: imitare una firma.

etymology: From Latin imāginārī (“to imagine, to conceive”), from imāginem (“a copy, likeness, image”).

senses.note: Immagino che... = I suppose that... (usually + subjunctive). Immagina! = Just imagine!

etymology: From Latin imāginem (“image, imitation”), from Proto-Italic *imā (“copy”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eym- (“copy”). Doublet of imago, and also the now-archaic mania.

senses.note: Double m in Italian: immagine. Feminine: l'immagine, le immagini.

etymology: From immediato + -mente.

senses.note: A common synonym is subito.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin immōbilis (“immobile, immovable”).

fact.text: Literally 'immovable'. Italian law calls land and buildings beni immobili and movable goods beni mobili, which is why furniture is i mobili.

senses.note: A building or piece of land. As an adjective, immobile = motionless. Agenzia immobiliare = estate agency.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *imparāre, from in- + parāre. Compare French emparer (“to seize”).

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin in- + parare ('to prepare'), the same parare found in English 'prepare'. Learning is, in a sense, getting yourself ready.

senses.note: Imparare a + infinitive: imparo a nuotare = I'm learning to swim.

etymology: From im- + pasta + -are.

fact.text: Formed from im- + pasta + -are, so it literally means 'to make into dough'. The pasta inside it originally meant any dough or paste.

senses.note: Also to mix cement, plaster, etc. Related noun: l'impasto (dough, mixture).

etymology: From Latin impatientem.

senses.note: Impaziente di fare qualcosa = eager to do something.

etymology: From im- + pazzo (“crazy, mad”) + -ire.

fact.text: Mayonnaise can go mad too: when it splits or curdles, Italians say la maionese è impazzita.

senses.note: Takes essere and the -isc- pattern: impazzisco, sono impazzito. Da impazzire = incredibly.

etymology: Inherited from Latin impedīre.

fact.text: From Latin impedire, literally 'to shackle the feet' (in- + pes, pedis, 'foot'). English 'impede' has the same origin, but the Italian verb is the everyday word for 'prevent'.

senses.note: Impedire a qualcuno di fare qualcosa = to prevent someone from doing something.

etymology: From im- + pegno + -are.

fact.text: Built from pegno, 'pledge' or 'pawn'. The literal first meaning is to pawn something, then to pledge your word, then to commit or keep someone busy.

senses.note: Not commettere (commit a crime). Impegnarsi = to make an effort; essere impegnato = to be busy.

etymology: Deverbal from impegnare + -o.

senses.note: Ho un impegno = I have a prior engagement. Con impegno = with dedication.

etymology: From im- + pensabile; cognate with Piedmontese impensàbil.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural impensabili.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin impermeābilis. Compare Piedmontese impermeàbil.

fact.text: This is the adjective 'impermeable' used as a noun: an impermeable coat. English made a similar move with 'mac', short for the Macintosh waterproof coat.

senses.note: As an adjective it means 'waterproof': una giacca impermeabile.
impianto elettrico = wiring; impianto di riscaldamento = heating system; impianti sciistici = ski lifts.
Usually a white-collar or office employee. Feminine: l'impiegata.

etymology: From importare + -ante.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural importanti.

etymology: From Medieval Latin importantia.

senses.note: Avere importanza = to matter. Non ha importanza = it doesn't matter.

etymology: From Latin importāre.

fact.text: Latin importare meant 'to bring in, carry'. Both languages kept the 'carry weight' idea: compare English importance and 'a matter of great import'.

senses.note: Non importa = never mind. Non m'importa = I don't care. With avere it means 'to import'.

etymology: From Late Latin impossibĭlis, im- + possibile.

senses.note: Also used of people, as in English: sei impossibile! = you're impossible!

etymology: From imprendere + -tore.

fact.text: Built from imprendere, to undertake, + -tore. It is put together just like French entrepreneur (from entreprendre), the word English borrowed: literally an undertaker of ventures.

senses.note: Feminine: imprenditrice. Related: impresa = business, enterprise.

Cognate with Sicilian mprisa.
Compare French entreprise for a similar construction.

fact.text: English borrowed impresario from Italian, where it meant the person who runs an impresa: a theatrical or operatic undertaking.

senses.note: Also means business or company: piccole e medie imprese = small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

etymology: From Latin impressio, impressionis from impressus

fact.text: Watch out: 'fare impressione' often means to be upsetting or give you the creeps, e.g. il sangue mi fa impressione, 'blood makes me squeamish'.

senses.note: avere l'impressione che + subjunctive = to have the feeling that.

etymology: From im- + prevedibile.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural imprevedibili.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin improbābilis. By surface analysis, in- + probabile.

senses.note: È improbabile che + subjunctive: È improbabile che venga.

etymology: From improntare.

senses.note: impronte digitali = fingerprints; impronta (del piede) = footprint.

etymology: From improvviso + -mente.

fact.text: Comes from improvviso, from Latin improvisus, meaning unforeseen. English improvise has the same root, by way of Italian improvvisare: to do something without preparing for it.

senses.note: Synonyms: all'improvviso, di colpo.

etymology: From Latin improvisus (“unforeseen”).

fact.text: English 'improvise' came through French from Italian improvvisare, which comes from this word. To improvise is to do something unforeseen, without preparing.

senses.note: All'improvviso = suddenly. Note the double v.

etymology: Inherited from Latin in.

senses.note: Merges with the article: nel, nella, nei… Used with countries and transport: in Italia, in treno.

etymology: From in- + affidabile.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural inaffidabili.

etymology: From inaspettato + -mente.
Deverbal from incaricare.

senses.note: affidare un incarico a qualcuno = to give someone a task. Also an official post or mandate.

etymology:
From Late Latin incastrāre, likely derived from castrum (“fortress”). Cognate with French encastrer, Spanish encastrar.
Unrelated to Italian castrare (“to castrate”).

senses.note: Also 'to frame' someone. Incastrarsi = to get stuck or to fit together (puzzle pieces).
senses.prompt: to fit in, to wedge in

fact.text: Formed from in- + cazzo (a vulgar word for penis) + -are. That is why it is too rude for polite talk. Arrabbiarsi is the neutral way to say 'to get angry'.

senses.note: Mostly used as incazzarsi (with essere) = to get pissed off. Incazzato = furious.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin incendium.

fact.text: Comes from Latin incendere, 'to set on fire'. English gets 'incendiary' from it, and also 'incense', literally 'something burnt'.

senses.note: A destructive fire (house, forest). Fire in general or a campfire is il fuoco.

fact.text: Watch out: this usually means an accident or crash, not just an 'incident'. A minor English 'incident' is more often un episodio or un fatto.

senses.note: incidente stradale = road accident, car crash.

etymology: From Latin incīnctus, past participle of incingō. Compare French enceint, Spanish encinto.

fact.text: Comes from Latin incinctus. Ancient writers such as Isidore of Seville explained it as 'ungirded', because pregnant women loosened their belts. Not everyone accepts that explanation.

senses.note: Used almost only in the feminine: incinta, plural incinte. Essere incinta = to be pregnant.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin inclūdere. Doublet of inchiudere, which was inherited.

senses.note: Irregular past: inclusi, incluso. Incluso also means 'included'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin inclūsus. Cf. chiuso.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun. Used like 'including': incluso me = me included; IVA inclusa = VAT included.

fact.text: Built on colpa 'fault, guilt', from Latin culpa. English culprit and culpable come from the same root, as does the Latin phrase mea culpa.

senses.note: Incolpare qualcuno di qualcosa = to blame someone for something.

etymology: From in- + cominciare.

senses.note: Same as cominciare. Uses avere with an object, essere without one: Il film è incominciato.

etymology: Derived from Late Latin incontrā. By surface analysis, incontro (adverb) + -are. Compare Portuguese and Spanish encontrar, French rencontrer.

senses.note: Meet or run into someone. For 'get to know someone' use conoscere.

etymology: Deverbal from incontrare + -o.

senses.note: Also a sports match. Andare incontro a = to go towards someone or to meet them.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin incrēdibilis. By surface analysis, in- + credibile.

senses.note: The same form is used for masculine and feminine; the plural is incredibili.
A crossroads: al prossimo incrocio gira a destra. It can also mean a cross between breeds.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin incubus.

fact.text: From Latin incubus, a demon believed to lie on sleepers' chests. It comes from incubāre, 'to lie upon', which also gave English incubate.

senses.note: Stress on the first syllable: ìncubo.

etymology: From Latin indāgō (“investigation”).

senses.note: Police investigations are often plural: le indagini. Also means a survey.

etymology: From Latin indicāre.

senses.note: Also 'to indicate, show': indicare la strada = show the way.
senses.prompt: to point at, to point out

etymology: From in- + dietro. Compare Romanian îndărăt, and Sicilian 'n 'arreri.

senses.note: Tornare indietro = to go back; stare indietro = to stay back; essere indietro = to be behind.
Mi è indifferente = I don't mind / it's all the same to me.

etymology: From in- + dimenticabile.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural indipendenti. Note the -i- spelling.

etymology: Deverbal from indirizzare + -o.

senses.note: Indirizzo email = email address. A formal speech is un discorso, not un indirizzo.

etymology: From in- + dispensabile.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural indispensabili. Lo stretto indispensabile = the bare essentials.

etymology: From in- + dosso + -are.

fact.text: Built from in + dosso ('back', from Latin dorsum) + -are, so it literally means 'to put on your back'. Dorsum is also where English 'dorsal' comes from.

senses.note: Also means to put on. In everyday speech portare is very common: porto gli occhiali.

etymology: From in- + Latin divināre.

fact.text: Built on Latin divinare, 'to foresee or prophesy', which shares a root with English 'divine'. Guessing was literally divining the answer.

senses.note: Indovina! = Guess! Related: indovinello = riddle, indovino = fortune-teller.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin industria.

fact.text: Latin industria meant diligence or hard work. English 'industrious' still has that original sense of being hard-working.

etymology: From Latin īnfantia.

fact.text: From Latin infantia. Its root, infans, literally meant 'not speaking' (in- + fari, 'to speak'), which is also where English infant comes from.

senses.note: Scuola dell'infanzia = nursery school, preschool.

etymology:
Univerbation of in + fatti, literally “in facts”.
Compare similar constructions with French en fait (literally “in fact”) and English in fact.

fact.text: Watch out: it confirms or explains, like 'indeed' or 'that's why'. It never corrects someone the way English 'in fact, no…' can. For that, Italians say in realtà.

senses.note: Confirms what was just said. 'Infatti!' on its own = Exactly!

fact.text: Watch out: it confirms or explains, like 'indeed' or 'that's why'. It never corrects someone the way English 'in fact, no…' can. For that, Italians say in realtà.

senses.note: Confirms what was said: Infatti! = Exactly! For 'actually' (contradicting), use in realtà.

etymology: From Latin īnferiōrem, comparative form of īnferus (“low, deep”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(H)n̥dʰér.

fact.text: It shares its Latin root inferus ('below') with inferno. Hell was simply 'the place down below'.

senses.note: Often literal: il piano inferiore = the floor below; il labbro inferiore = the lower lip.

etymology: From infermo (“invalid”, “infirm”) + -iere (“-er”, “-or”).

fact.text: Built on infermo, 'sick', from Latin infirmus, 'not strong'. That is the same root as English infirm and infirmary.

senses.note: Female form: l'infermiera. Plural infermieri can cover a mixed group.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin īnfernus, īnfernum (“the depths of the earth”), noun use of īnfernus (“of the lower regions”), derived from īnferus (“low”).

fact.text: English borrowed 'inferno' from Italian, helped by Dante's Inferno, the first part of the Divine Comedy. It goes back to Latin infernus 'of the lower regions', from inferus 'low'.

senses.note: Vai all'inferno! = Go to hell!

etymology:
Borrowed from Latin in fīne.
By surface analysis, univerbation of in + fine.

fact.text: Don't mix it up with finalmente. 'Infine, aggiungi il sale' marks the last step (lastly), while 'Finalmente sei arrivato!' expresses relief (at last!).

senses.note: Marks the last step or item. For relieved 'at last!' use finalmente.

etymology: From Latin īnfōrmāre.

senses.note: informare qualcuno di qualcosa. The reflexive informarsi means to find out or make enquiries.
Feminine: informatrice.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin īnfōrmātiōnem (“idea, concept”).

fact.text: Unlike English, Italian can count it: one informazione, many informazioni. To ask for directions or details, you 'chiedere informazioni', which is plural.

senses.note: Countable in Italian: un'informazione = a piece of information; usually plural: informazioni.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnfortūnium.

fact.text: Looks like 'misfortune', and Latin infortunium did mean that, but in modern Italian it usually means an accident or injury, e.g. a footballer's injury.

senses.note: Injury from an accident or sport: infortunio sul lavoro = workplace accident. A wound is 'ferita'.

etymology:
From ingegno + -ere (agentive suffix).
Compare French ingénieur.

fact.text: Built on ingegno, talent or ingenuity, from Latin ingenium. That Latin word also gave English engine and ingenious.

senses.note: Also a title that drops the final -e before a name: l'ingegner Rossi. The feminine ingegnera is increasingly used.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French engleis.

fact.text: Italian does not capitalize nationalities or languages: inglese, italiano, francese. Writing Inglese mid-sentence is a typical English speaker's mistake.

senses.note: Written in lowercase. Also a noun: l'inglese = the English language.

etymology: From Latin ingressus.

senses.note: Also the hall of a flat. 'Ingresso libero' = free admission.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin initiāre. Cf. also cominciare.

features.construction: iniziare qualcosa / iniziare a + infinitive; essere when intransitive

senses.note: Ho iniziato il libro (avere with an object); il film è iniziato (essere with no object). iniziare a + infinitive.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin initium.

fact.text: From Latin initium, literally 'a going in' (in + ire 'to go'). The same word gives English initial and initiate.

senses.note: all'inizio = at the beginning; dall'inizio = from the start.
Takes di: mi sono innamorato di te = I fell in love with you.

etymology: From innamorare. Compare Portuguese namorado.

senses.note: innamorato di qualcuno = in love with someone. innamorarsi = to fall in love.

etymology: Univerbation of innanzi + tutto.

fact.text: A fusion of innanzi ('before, ahead') and tutto ('everything'), so literally 'before everything'.

senses.note: Also written innanzi tutto. Synonym: prima di tutto.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin innoc|ēns, ~entis (“harmless, inoffensive”). Cognate with Sicilian nnucenti.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural innocenti. Also used as a noun: un innocente.

etymology:
From Latin in ultrā.
By surface analysis, univerbation of in + oltre.
Compare French en outre.

fact.text: Made from in + oltre, literally in beyond. Italian oltre (beyond) comes from Latin ultra, the same word behind English prefixes like ultraviolet. French has the matching phrase en outre.

senses.note: Also means moreover, besides or in addition.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin inquilīnus.

senses.note: Feminine: l'inquilina. The landlord is il padrone di casa.

etymology: From inquinare + -mento.

senses.note: From inquinare (to pollute). inquinamento atmosferico = air pollution.

etymology: From insalato, which is an adjective derived from the verb insalare (“to salt”).

fact.text: Literally 'salted', from insalare, 'to salt'. Early salads were greens seasoned with salt, and English 'salad' comes from the same salty root.

senses.note: Also means lettuce. Insalata mista = mixed salad.
Same form for men and women: l'insegnante. From insegnare, 'to teach'.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin īnsignāre (also present in Medieval Latin), from Latin signāre. For sense 3 compare Spanish enseñar.

fact.text: Comes from Latin insignare, 'to mark with a sign', so it is related to English 'sign' and 'insignia'. The idea is pointing something out to someone.

features.construction: insegnare qualcosa a qualcuno; insegnare a + infinitive

senses.note: insegnare qcs a qcn; insegnare a + infinitive (mi ha insegnato a nuotare).

etymology: From Latin īnsequī, remodeled after Italian seguire (“to follow”).

senses.note: Also figurative: inseguire un sogno = to chase a dream.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *īnsemel, which is a combination of Latin īnsimul and semel. See also French ensemble, Catalan ensems and Neapolitan nzieme.

fact.text: Shares its Vulgar Latin root *insemel with French ensemble, which English borrowed for a group performing together.

senses.note: insieme a / insieme con = together with. As a noun, l'insieme = the whole.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnsipidus (“tasteless”), from in- (“not”) + sapidus (“savory”).

fact.text: From Latin in- 'not' + sapidus 'tasty', from sapere 'to taste, to be wise'. That same verb gave Italian sapere 'to know'.

senses.note: Of food lacking salt or flavour; figuratively, dull (una persona insipida).

etymology: From Latin īnsistere, from in + sistō.

features.construction: insistere su qualcosa; insistere a/per + infinitive; insistere perché + subjunctive

senses.note: insistere su qualcosa = to insist on something; insistere a fare = to keep on doing

etymology:
Univerbation of in (“in”) + somma (“sum; essence”), a calque of Latin in summā.
Compare French en somme.

fact.text: Literally 'in sum': in + somma, copied from Latin 'in summa'. It is the same idea as English 'in sum' and French 'en somme'.

senses.note: Also a colloquial 'so-so' (Come va? Insomma...) or an impatient 'come on!'.

ignored: Infinitive plus clitic pronoun; study the verb insultare instead.

senses.note: insultare + mi.

etymology: Univerbation of in + tanto.

senses.note: Can also mean 'for now / to begin with': Intanto siediti = For now, sit down.
Used for drains, noses and traffic: strade intasate = jammed roads.
Same form for masculine and feminine; plural intelligenti.

etymology: Inherited from Latin intendere.

fact.text: Latin intendere literally meant 'to stretch toward' (in + tendere, 'to stretch'). English 'intend' comes from the same verb, as if your mind reaches out toward a goal.

senses.note: Non intendevo te = I didn't mean you. Also intendere + infinitive = to intend to.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin intentiōnem.

senses.note: Avere intenzione di + infinitive = to intend to: ho intenzione di partire.
Same form for masculine and feminine; plural interessanti.

etymology: From interesse + -are.

senses.note: Mi interessa = I'm interested in it. Interessarsi di/a = to take an interest in.
Mi interesso di arte. Also: to see to or look after something (me ne interesso io).
Interessato a qualcosa = interested in something. It can also mean self-interested.

fact.text: Originally a Latin verb: interesse, 'to be between', and so 'to matter'. The infinitive was turned into a noun, and English borrowed the idea as interest.

senses.note: Also financial: gli interessi = interest on money. Plural can mean business affairs.
For the door-entry phone of a building, Italians usually say citofono.

etymology: From inter- + nazionale.

fact.text: The Milan football club Inter is short for Internazionale. It was founded in 1908 by members who broke away from AC Milan because they wanted to accept foreign players.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural internazionali.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English internet.

fact.text: Italians usually drop the article with this word: 'l'ho trovato su internet' (I found it on the internet).

senses.note: Usually used without an article: su internet, navigare in internet.

etymology: From Latin internus.

fact.text: In Italian addresses, 'int.' (interno) gives the apartment number, as in Via Roma 5, int. 3. The Ministero dell'Interno is Italy's interior ministry.

senses.note: Also a noun: l'interno = the inside; all'interno = inside.

etymology: From Latin internus.

fact.text: In Italian addresses, 'int.' (interno) gives the apartment number, as in Via Roma 5, int. 3. The Ministero dell'Interno is Italy's interior ministry.

senses.note: All'interno = inside. Also means a phone extension or a flat number in an address.

etymology: Inherited from Latin integrum (“whole, entire”). Doublet of integro, a later borrowing.

fact.text: It comes from Latin integer, 'untouched' (in- 'not' + tangere 'to touch'). That makes it a cousin of English integer, integrity and entire.

senses.note: Latte intero = whole milk. Per intero = in full.

etymology: From Latin interrumpere.

fact.text: From Latin inter 'between' + rumpere 'to break'. Italian rompere has the past participle rotto, and English 'bankrupt' comes from Italian banca rotta, 'broken bench'.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle interrotto; passato remoto interruppi.

ignored: Fragment: infinitive interrompere plus the clitic mi; study the verb interrompere instead.

senses.note: interrompere + mi; Non interrompermi! = Don't interrupt me!

etymology: From Latin intervenīre (“to intervene”).

fact.text: Its noun, intervento, often means a surgical operation or a speech at a conference. 'Ho subito un intervento' means I had an operation.

senses.note: Conjugates like venire, takes essere: sono intervenuto. Intervenire in una discussione.
Also very common for a surgical operation, or a speech/contribution at a meeting.

etymology: Calque of English interview, from inter- + vista. Compare Spanish and Portuguese entrevista.

fact.text: A calque of English 'interview' (inter + vista). English had itself taken the word from French entrevue, so the idea came back to Romance languages in a roundabout way.

senses.note: Fare un'intervista = to conduct an interview. A job interview is usually un colloquio.

etymology: Inherited from Latin intēnsus. Doublet of intenso.

senses.note: Past participle of intendere. Inteso? / Siamo intesi? = Got it? / Agreed?

etymology: From in + torno.

senses.note: Adverb: qui intorno (around here). As a preposition use intorno a: intorno al tavolo.

etymology: Borrowed from French entrevoir, from Vulgar Latin *intervidēre.

fact.text: Like French entrevoir, it literally means 'to see between'. English interview comes from the related French entrevue, so both words are built on 'see between'.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: intravisto. The spelling intravvedere also exists.

fact.text: Built on treccia, 'braid' or 'plait'. Things that intertwine are literally being braided together.

senses.note: Reflexive form of intrecciare (to braid, to weave). Le nostre vite si intrecciano.
Can also be used as a noun: un introverso = an introvert.

etymology: From Latin inūtilis, from in- + ūtilis.

senses.note: È inutile + infinitive = it's no use / pointless (È inutile piangere).

etymology:
Univerbation of in + vece.
Compare Venetan invéze.

fact.text: Originally 'in vece', 'in the place (of)', from Latin vicis 'turn, place'. The same root gives English vice-president and vicar, someone acting in another's place.

senses.note: invece di + noun/infinitive = instead of. Also used to contrast: 'whereas, on the other hand'.

fact.text: Originally 'in vece', 'in the place (of)', from Latin vicis 'turn, place'. The same root gives English vice-president and vicar, someone acting in another's place.

ignored: Same meaning as the adverb card for invece, so this conjunction label would only duplicate it.

senses.note: Invece di + noun/infinitive = instead of: invece di uscire = instead of going out.

etymology: From Latin inventum, the supine form of inveniō (“find, discover”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin invenire, 'to come upon, find'. To invent was first to 'find' something. English 'inventory', a list of what is found, comes from the same verb.

senses.note: Also means to make up (a story, an excuse): Te lo sei inventato!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin inventiōnem.

fact.text: From Latin invenire, 'to come upon, find' (in + venire, to come). An invention was originally something you found or discovered, not something you built.

senses.note: Can also mean a fabrication or made-up story.

etymology: From Late Latin hībernum, reanalyzed as in- + verno, for which cf. Emilian invêren, Sicilian mmernu, Spanish invierno, Portuguese inverno.

fact.text: From Late Latin hibernum '(time) of winter', the same root as English hibernate: animals that hibernate are 'wintering'.

senses.note: In inverno / d'inverno = in winter.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin investīre.

fact.text: Careful in the news: un pedone investito is not a funded pedestrian but one hit by a car. Investire also means 'to run over'.

senses.note: Investire in qualcosa = to invest in something. Also: to run over, as in è stato investito = he was hit by a car.

etymology: From Late Latin inviāre, which is derived from Latin via (“path, road”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese enviar, French envoyer.

fact.text: Built on Latin via, 'road', so it roughly means 'to put on the way'. Its French cousin envoyer gave English envoy, a person sent on a mission.

senses.note: More formal than mandare; common for emails, letters and parcels.

etymology: From Late Latin invīsibilis.
Borrowed from Latin invītāre.

senses.note: Invitare qualcuno a cena / a fare qualcosa. Noun: l'invito (invitation).

etymology: Deverbal from invitare.

senses.note: Related verb: invitare (ti invito a cena = I'm inviting you to dinner).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin eo, from Classical Latin egō̆.

fact.text: Comes from Latin ego 'I', the same word English took over for the 'ego', your sense of self.

senses.note: Usually left out because the verb shows the subject (sono = I am). Not capitalised, unlike English I.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ironia, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνεία (eirōneía).

fact.text: Comes via Latin from Greek eironeia, meaning dissimulation or feigned ignorance. Socrates was famous for this: pretending not to know so he could expose what others didn't know.

senses.note: Set phrase: ironia della sorte = irony of fate, as luck would have it.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin irrītāre.

senses.note: Also used for skin: il sapone mi irrita la pelle. Reflexive irritarsi = to get annoyed.

etymology: From iscrivere + -si.

senses.note: Used with 'a': iscriversi all'università, a un corso, in palestra (at the gym).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin īnscrīptiōnem. By surface analysis, inscrivere + -zione.

senses.note: Iscrizione all'università/in palestra. It can also mean an inscription carved on a monument.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *isula, from classical Latin īnsula.

fact.text: English isolated came via French from Italian isolato, literally 'made into an island'. Its Latin source insula also gave English insulate and peninsula.

senses.note: isola pedonale = pedestrian zone

etymology: From Latin īnspectōrem.

senses.note: Feminine: l'ispettrice. Ispettore di polizia = police inspector.

etymology: From Latin īnstantem, from īnstō.

senses.note: All'istante = instantly, at once. Un istante! = just a moment!

etymology: From Latin īnstitūtum.

senses.note: Istituto tecnico = a type of technical secondary school.
Medical term. Italian drops the h: isto- = histo-. Invariable plural.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin italiānus (“Italian”). By surface analysis, Itàlia (“Italy”) + -àno (“-an”, derivational suffix).

fact.text: Unlike English, Italian does not capitalize adjectives of nationality or names of languages: un film italiano, parlo italiano.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. As a noun: l'italiano = the Italian language; gli italiani = Italians.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin italiānus (“Italian”). By surface analysis, Itàlia (“Italy”) + -àno (“-an”, derivational suffix).

fact.text: Unlike English, Italian does not capitalize adjectives of nationality or names of languages: un film italiano, parlo italiano.

senses.note: Languages are lowercase in Italian: parlo italiano.

ignored: An English loanword with no dictionary data, taken from a fragmentary context.

senses.note: English loanword; invariable plural.

ignored: A personal name with no dictionary meaning, not an Italian word.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English killer.

senses.note: Invariable English loan: il killer, i killer. Mostly means a hired killer; also any murderer.

etymology: From Latin illa(m), feminine form of ille.

senses.note: Before feminine singular nouns: la casa; becomes l' before a vowel (l'amica). Also a pronoun: her/it.
Often shortened to 'la camera'. Plural: le camere da letto. 'Camera' alone means room, not camera.
False friend: 'la camera' means room. Plural: le macchine fotografiche.

etymology: Inherited from Latin labrum, related to labium, from the Proto-Indo-European root *leb- (“to hang down”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin labrum, which may share an Indo-European root, *leb- ('to hang down'), with English lip. Its relative labium gave English labial.

senses.note: Irregular plural: le labbra (feminine) for lips; i labbri for rims or edges.

etymology: From Latin labōrātōrium.

fact.text: From Latin laboratorium, from laborare 'to work', the same root as labour. A lab is literally a place for working.

senses.note: Can also mean a workshop, e.g. a craftsman's workroom or a hands-on class.

etymology: From Latin lacrima.

fact.text: Old Latin had dacrima, which later shifted from d to l. It comes from the same Indo-European root as English 'tear' (the drop from your eye) and Greek dakry.

etymology: From earlier latro, from Latin latrō (“mercenary; thief; robber”) (nominative form). Doublet of ladrone, from the Latin accusative latrōnem.

fact.text: Latin latro first meant a hired soldier or mercenary, and only later a robber. Italian also kept a twin word, ladrone, from the Latin form latronem.

senses.note: Feminine: la ladra. Al ladro! = Stop, thief!

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English lady.
ignored: Unadapted English loanword identical to the English, so it can't be tested from an English prompt.

senses.note: Unadapted English loan, invariable: la lady, le lady.

etymology: Univerbation of là + giù.

senses.note: From là + giù. The opposite is lassù (up there). Can also mean 'over there'.

etymology: Inherited from Old Italian laco, from Latin lacus (“lake”), from Proto-Indo-European *lókus (“lake, pool”).

senses.note: Plural laghi keeps the hard g sound with -ghi.

ignored: This is just lamentarsi with the pronoun mi attached; study it on the lamentarsi card.

senses.note: lamentare + mi; the infinitive of lamentarsi used with io.

fact.text: Related to English 'lament', from Latin lamentum. In English, lament suggests deep grief, but in Italian it covers everyday grumbling about the weather or traffic.

senses.note: Lamentarsi di qualcosa = to complain about something. Past: mi sono lamentato/a.

etymology: From Latin lampada, from lampas.

senses.note: Literally 'little lamp' (lampada + -ina).

etymology: From Latin lāna.

fact.text: Straight from Latin lana. English 'lanolin', the grease taken from sheep's wool, gets its name from the same word.

senses.note: di lana = woollen: un maglione di lana.

etymology: From Late Latin lanceāre, from Latin lancea. Compare Catalan llançar, French lancer, Occitan and Portuguese lançar, Spanish lanzar, English launch (via Northern Old French).

fact.text: From Latin lancea 'lance', so it originally meant to hurl a spear. English launch comes from the same root, through Northern Old French.

senses.note: Also 'to launch' (a product, a rocket). Lanciarsi = to throw oneself, to dive in.

etymology: From lanciare.

fact.text: Comes from lanciare, which comes from lancia, 'lance'. English launch comes from the same source through Old French lancier: originally, to hurl a lance.

senses.note: Used for a throw in sport, a parachute drop, and the launch of a rocket or product.

etymology: From Latin lapidāre (“to stone”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin lapis, 'stone'. English shares the root in lapis lazuli, the blue gemstone.

senses.note: Also used figuratively: to tear someone apart with criticism.

ignored: This is the unchanged English loanword, so the card would test nothing. The usual Italian word is portatile.

senses.note: Invariable plural: i laptop. Italians more often say il (computer) portatile.

etymology: From Latin largus.

fact.text: False friend: this means wide, not large. 'Large' or 'big' is grande. Farsi largo means to make way, and al largo means offshore.

etymology: Inherited from Latin laxāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin laxare, 'to loosen', which also gave English relax. Through French it produced laissez-faire ('let do') and, via Anglo-Norman, English lease.

senses.note: Also 'to let': lascia fare a me = let me do it. Leaving a place is usually partire or andarsene.

etymology: Univerbation of là + su.

senses.note: Opposite: laggiù (down there). Also used for heaven.

etymology: From Latin laterālis.

senses.note: Often translates as 'side': porta laterale = side door. Same form for masculine and feminine.

etymology:
From Latin lātus (“side”, “flank”).
Compare Spanish lado and Portuguese lado.

fact.text: Comes from Latin latus, 'side, flank'. That is the source of English lateral, bilateral and collateral.

senses.note: Di lato = sideways. D'altro lato = on the other hand.

etymology: From Late Latin lactem, accusative of Late Latin lactis.

fact.text: If you order 'a latte' in Italy you will likely get a plain glass of milk. Ask for a caffellatte or a latte macchiato instead.

senses.note: Usually uncountable. Caffellatte = coffee with milk.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin laurea.

fact.text: From Latin laurea, 'laurel crown' (from laurus, laurel). Italian graduates still wear a laurel wreath on graduation day, the same symbol behind the English word 'laureate'.

senses.note: Prendere la laurea = to graduate; laurearsi = to graduate (from university).

fact.text: Comes from laurea, Latin for a laurel wreath. Italian graduates still wear a laurel crown on graduation day, much like ancient victors and poets.

senses.note: Used for a university degree: laurearsi in medicina. For finishing high school, say diplomarsi.

etymology: From the town of Lavagna, near Genoa, known for slate quarries in the nearby mountains.

fact.text: Named after Lavagna, a town near Genoa. Its nearby quarries supplied the slate that school boards were once made of, and lavagna also means 'slate'.

senses.note: Also used for a whiteboard. alla lavagna = at the board.

etymology: From lavanda + -eria.

fact.text: English 'laundry' comes from the same root. Middle English lavendrie came from Old French lavanderie, which goes back to Latin lavare, 'to wash'.
