senses.note: The shop or room where clothes are washed. Washing to be done is il bucato. Lavanderia a gettoni = laundromat.
Used for both the kitchen sink and the bathroom washbasin.

etymology: From Latin lavāre (“to wash”), from Proto-Indo-European *lewh₃- (“to wash”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin lavare, meaning 'to wash'. The same root gave English lavatory, and laundry through Latin lavanda, 'things to be washed'.

senses.note: lavare i piatti = to do the dishes.
Reflexive, uses essere. lavarsi i denti = to brush one's teeth; lavarsi le mani = wash one's hands.

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of lava (“to wash”) + stoviglie (“dishes, crockery”).

fact.text: Literally means 'washes-crockery', from lava (washes) and stoviglie (dishes). Italian makes many verb-plus-noun compounds like this, such as portafoglio (wallet) and apriscatole (can opener).

senses.note: Invariable: la/le lavastoviglie. A person who washes dishes is a lavapiatti.

etymology: From lavare + -trice.

fact.text: Made from lavare (to wash) + -trice, the feminine ending for someone or something that does an action, as in attrice (actress). Literally 'the washer'.

senses.note: Fare la lavatrice = to do a load of washing.

etymology: From Latin labōrāre.

fact.text: From Latin laborare 'to toil', the same root as English labor, laboratory and laborious.

senses.note: Il lavoro = work/job. Also used of machines: non lavora = it doesn't work.
giorno lavorativo = working day; orario lavorativo = working hours; esperienza lavorativa = work experience.

etymology: From Latin labōrātōrem. By surface analysis, lavorare + -tore. Compare Portuguese lavrador, Spanish labrador, cf. also Aromanian lãlãtoari.

senses.note: Feminine: la lavoratrice. Built from lavorare (to work) + -tore.

etymology: Deverbative from lavorare; perhaps corresponding to Latin labor.

fact.text: Comes from lavorare, from Latin laborare 'to toil'. That is the same root as English labour and laboratory, which is literally a place for work.

senses.note: Uncountable sense: ora di lavoro = working hour. Plural lavori also means 'works' (lavori in corso).

etymology: From Latin illas, which is the accusative plural feminine of ille. Cognate with Sicilian li~i.

senses.note: Used before all feminine plural nouns: le case, le amiche. Also an object pronoun: them (f.), to her.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English leader.

senses.note: il/la leader; invariable plural: i leader. Pronounced as in English.
Una leccata = a single lick. Figuratively also flattery or bootlicking.

etymology: From Latin ligāmen (“bandage, band, tie”). Compare Sicilian ligama.

fact.text: Comes from Latin ligamen, meaning 'band, tie', from ligare 'to bind'. English 'ligament' comes from the same root: the tissue that ties bones together.

senses.note: Used for emotional ties, connections between things, and chemical bonds.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ligāre.

fact.text: From Latin ligare 'to bind', which also gave English ligament and oblige. A ligament is literally a tie between bones.

senses.note: Legare con qualcuno = to get on with someone. Legarsi = to bond.

etymology: From Latin lēgem.

fact.text: Funny coincidence: 'legge' also means 'he/she reads' and 'leggi' means 'you read' (from leggere), so 'Lui legge le leggi' means 'He reads the laws'.

senses.note: Plural: le leggi. Studiare legge = to study law.

etymology: See the etymology of the corresponding lemma form.

fact.text: Comes from Latin legere 'to read, to gather'. The same root gives English lecture, legible and legend (literally 'things to be read').

senses.note: Irregular past participle: letto (ho letto un libro).

etymology: Inherited from Latin legere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin legere 'to read, to gather'. The same root gives English lecture, legible and legend (literally 'things to be read').

senses.note: Irregular: past participle letto (ho letto), passato remoto lessi.

etymology: From leggero + -ezza; cognate with Piedmontese legerëssa.

fact.text: Lightness is the first of Italo Calvino's Six Memos for the Next Millennium, his lectures on literary values. He praised the art of making heavy things feel light.

senses.note: Also means carelessness: con leggerezza = thoughtlessly; una leggerezza = a careless slip.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French legier, from Vulgar Latin *leviārius, from Latin levis.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old French legier, the source of modern French léger, rather than inherited directly from Latin. The native Italian word from Latin levis is lieve.

senses.note: Also 'slight' (un leggero errore). Musica leggera = pop music.

etymology: Inherited from Latin lignum. Cognates include Spanish leño, Romanian lemn.

senses.note: Firewood is la legna (feminine). A wood/forest is il bosco.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin illaei.
The formal address Lei appears in the 16th century in connection with Signoria (“Lordship”), Eccellenza (“Excellency”), Santità (“Holiness”) and Magnificenza, alongside Voi.

fact.text: Formal 'you' is literally 'she'. In the 16th century people were addressed through feminine titles such as Vostra Signoria (Your Lordship), and the pronoun for 'she' stayed after the titles were dropped.

senses.note: Subject pronoun, also used after prepositions (con lei = with her). Often left out before the verb.

etymology: From lento (“slow”) + -mente.
Inherited from Latin lentus.

fact.text: Musicians already know this word: 'lento' on a score means play slowly. Its Latin ancestor lentus first meant 'pliant, flexible' before it came to mean sluggish.

senses.note: Can also mean loose or slack: una vite lenta (a loose screw).

etymology: From Latin linteolum, from linteum, nominal form of linteus (“linen”), from linum (“linen; flax”).

fact.text: Masculine in the singular but usually feminine in the plural: il lenzuolo, le lenzuola. It works like il braccio, le braccia and l'uovo, le uova. Lenzuoli is used for sheets counted one by one.

senses.note: Plural is usually le lenzuola (f.) for a bed's set of sheets; i lenzuoli counts single sheets.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin leōnem.

fact.text: The winged lion of Saint Mark is the symbol of Venice, which is why the top prize at the Venice Film Festival is called the Golden Lion.

senses.note: Also the zodiac sign Leo: sono del Leone.

etymology: From Latin littera.

senses.note: Lettere (plural) also means humanities, as in Facoltà di Lettere.

etymology: From Latin litterātūra.
From Latin lectus (“bed”). Compare French lit, Galician and Portuguese leito and Catalan llit.

fact.text: Letto is also the past participle of leggere (ho letto = I have read). That's a coincidence: Latin lectus 'bed' comes from a root meaning 'lie down', related to English 'lie'.

senses.note: Andare a letto = to go to bed. A letto! = Off to bed!

etymology: Inherited from Latin levāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin levare, 'to raise, lighten', the root of English 'lever' and 'elevate'. The Levant (Italian levante) is the east, where the sun rises.

senses.note: Common in speech: levare le scarpe (take off your shoes). Levarsi = to get up / take off.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin lectiōnem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin lectio, 'a reading', because teaching once meant reading texts aloud. English lesson comes from the same word.

senses.note: Also a university class or lecture: andare a lezione = to go to class.

etymology: From Latin illī, nominative masculine plural of ille.

fact.text: Don't mix up li (them) with lì (there): the accent changes the word. In compound tenses the participle agrees with li: li hai fatti?

senses.note: Direct object for male or mixed groups (feminine: le). Comes before the verb: li vedo = I see them.

etymology: From Latin lībra.

fact.text: It comes from Latin libra, which is why pounds are abbreviated 'lb' and why the £ sign is a stylised L.

senses.note: Only for weight. The British currency is la sterlina.

fact.text: 'Liberaci dal male' is the closing line of the Italian Lord's Prayer (Padre Nostro): 'deliver us from evil'.

ignored: Imperative of liberare plus the pronoun ci, not a headword; study it on the liberare card.

senses.note: libera (tu imperative of liberare) + ci (us). 'Liberaci dal male' = deliver us from evil.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin līberāre. See also Old Italian liverare, livrare (“to finish”).

senses.note: Liberare la stanza = to vacate the room; liberarsi di = to get rid of.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₁lewdʰ-
Proto-Indo-European *-teros
Proto-Indo-European *h₁léwdʰeros
Proto-Italic *louðeros
Old Latin loeber
Latin līberumlbor.
Italian libero
Learned borrowing from Latin līberum.

fact.text: In football, a libero, or sweeper, is the defender who is free of any marking duties. It comes from the same Latin root as 'liberty'.

senses.note: Also means unoccupied or available (sei libero?). For free of charge, gratis or gratuito is more usual.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin lībertātem.

senses.note: Invariable: le libertà in the plural.

etymology: From libro + -eria.

fact.text: False friend: it is not a library (that is biblioteca). It means a bookshop or a bookcase, the places where you buy books or keep them.

senses.note: Also means 'bookshop'. A library is una biblioteca.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin librum (“book”).

fact.text: Latin liber first meant the inner bark of a tree, which was used as an early writing material. English 'library' comes from the same word.

etymology: From Latin licentia.

fact.text: A driving licence is la patente, not la licenza. Licenza is for permits such as a trading or fishing licence. It comes from Latin licet, 'it is allowed', which also gives English illicit.

senses.note: Also military leave (in licenza) and the school certificate licenza media.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin licentiāre. Compare French licencier.

fact.text: Don't be fooled by the look of it: this almost never means 'to license'. It means to fire someone, because it comes from 'licenza', permission to leave. Licenziarsi means to quit your job.

senses.note: Licenziarsi = to quit or resign. Essere licenziato = to be fired.

etymology: From Latin Lycēum.

fact.text: Named after the Lyceum, the Athens site where Aristotle taught. It took its name from a nearby shrine of Apollo Lykeios.

senses.note: An academic upper secondary school (ages about 14–19), e.g. liceo classico or liceo scientifico.

etymology: From Latin līmitem.

fact.text: From Latin limes, which first meant a path or strip of land between fields. Later it came to mean the fortified frontier of the Roman Empire.

senses.note: Essere al limite = to be at the limit, at breaking point.

etymology: From Arabic لَيْمُون (laymūn).

fact.text: Comes from Arabic laymun. English 'lemon' comes from the same Arabic word through Old French limon, so both languages borrowed the fruit's name from Arabic.

senses.note: Means both the fruit and the tree. Succo di limone = lemon juice.

etymology: From Latin līnea (“line, thread”), from līnum (“flax”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin linea, a linen thread, from linum (flax). So English 'line' and 'linen' are related: the first lines were threads of flax.

senses.note: Also a phone line or transport line. 'Mantenere la linea' means to keep your figure.

etymology: From earlier lengua, from Latin lingua.

fact.text: Old Latin had dingua. The d- may have turned into l- because people linked it with lingere, 'to lick'. Latin lingua is also where English language and linguist come from.

senses.note: lingua madre = mother tongue; le lingue straniere = foreign languages.

etymology: From Latin liquidus.

senses.note: Also a noun: il liquido = the liquid.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin lyricus, from Ancient Greek λυρικός (lurikós).

fact.text: From Greek lyrikos 'of the lyre', because such poems were sung to the lyre. In Italian it also means operatic: la lirica is opera, and a cantante lirico is an opera singer.

senses.note: Also 'operatic': cantante lirico = opera singer. La lirica = lyric poetry or opera.

etymology:
From Vulgar Latin *līsius, from Ancient Greek λισσός (lissós, “smooth”). Or, from *lixus, derived from *lixāre (“to clean, boil”), presumably related to lixa (“lye”).
Compare Portuguese and Spanish liso, French lisse, Catalan llis, Sicilian lisciu, Friulian, Lombard, and Provençal lis, Romansh glisch.

fact.text: Useful at the bar: whisky liscio means a whisky served neat, and acqua liscia is still water, as opposed to frizzante (sparkling).

senses.note: Andare liscio = to go smoothly. Capelli lisci = straight hair.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *lista, of Germanic origin, from either Frankish *līsta or Lombardic līsta, both from Proto-West Germanic *līstā.

fact.text: From a Germanic word meaning 'strip, border'. A list was first a strip, such as a strip of paper with names on it, which is why Italian still uses it for 'stripe' too.

senses.note: Lista della spesa = shopping list. Elenco is a common synonym.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin lītigāre. Compare Spanish lidiar and Portuguese lidar.

fact.text: Not 'to litigate'. Italians litigare whenever they argue, for example over the remote or with a sibling. To sue someone is fare causa a qualcuno.

senses.note: Litigare con qualcuno = to argue with someone. Passato prossimo: ho litigato.

etymology: From French litre.

fact.text: Came in through French litre, from Greek litra, which was a Sicilian coin and a unit of weight.

etymology:
Deverbal from livellare (“to level, to make level”) + -o.
Alternatively, from Vulgar Latin *lībellus.

fact.text: Related to English 'level', which comes from Latin libella, a small balance or plumb level. Libella is a diminutive of libra 'scales', the root of the £ sign.

senses.note: curve di livello = contour lines; a livello di = at the level of

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *(il)lu, from Latin illum, illud, by dropping il- and -m. Cognate with Sicilian lu.

senses.note: Used before z, s+consonant, gn, ps, x, y: lo zaino, lo studente. The plural is gli.

etymology: From Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus. Cognate with Sicilian lucali.

fact.text: Comes from Latin locus, 'place', which is also the root of English local, location, locate and locomotive.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine: polizia locale. As a noun, il locale = a venue, bar or room.

etymology: From Late Latin locālis, from Latin locus. Cognate with Sicilian lucali.

fact.text: Comes from Latin locus, 'place', which is also the root of English local, location, locate and locomotive.

senses.note: Also means 'room' in property ads (un appartamento di tre locali). As an adjective, locale means 'local'.
Doesn't change in the plural (le località). Località turistica = holiday resort.

etymology: From Latin logicus.

senses.note: È logico! = Of course! / It's obvious!

etymology: From the Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longe; cognate with French lointain, Sicilian luntanu, Friulian and Romansch lontan, Dalmatian luntun.

senses.note: Agrees as an adjective: lontano/a/i/e. Lontano da = far from.

etymology: From the Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longe; cognate with French lointain, Sicilian luntanu, Friulian and Romansch lontan, Dalmatian luntun.

senses.note: lontano da = far from. As an adjective it agrees: una città lontana.

etymology: Borrowed from English lord.

fact.text: Italian borrowed this from English. The English word goes back to Old English hlafweard, 'loaf-keeper': a lord was originally the head of a household, who guarded its bread.

senses.note: Invariable: i lord. The Lord (God) is il Signore.

etymology: Uncertain; often suggested to be from derived from Latin lūridus (“sallow, pale”), via Late Latin lurdus, making it a doublet of lurido.

fact.text: Literally 'dirty'. Gross weight is the 'dirty' total that includes packaging, while netto (net) literally means 'clean'.

senses.note: The opposite is netto. Stipendio lordo = gross salary. Its older meaning is 'dirty'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin illōrum, genitive plural of ille, illud (“that”).

fact.text: From Latin illorum 'of those', a genitive plural. That is why it can also mean 'their' and never changes for gender or number.

senses.note: Also 'their/theirs' (il loro libro), which never changes form. Capitalised Loro is a very formal 'you' (plural).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin lucta, from Latin lūctāre (“to wrestle”). Compare French lutte. By surface analysis, lottare (“to fight”) + -a.

fact.text: Comes from Latin luctari, 'to wrestle'. English 'reluctant' comes from reluctari, 'to struggle against', so a reluctant person is literally wrestling back.

senses.note: Also the sport of wrestling: lotta libera = freestyle wrestling. Verb: lottare.

etymology: Inherited from Latin luctārī.

senses.note: lottare per/contro qualcosa. Also 'to wrestle'; la lotta = struggle or wrestling.

etymology: From Old French lot, from Frankish *hlot, from Proto-Germanic *hlutą.

fact.text: English borrowed lotto from this Italian word, which came via French from a Germanic word related to English lot, as in 'drawing lots'.

senses.note: Il Lotto is Italy's traditional numbers lottery; a lottery in general is la lotteria. Also 'lot, batch'.

etymology: From Latin lūcem (“light”), from Proto-Italic *louks, from the Proto-Indo-European root *lewk- (“bright; white”). Doublet of the borrowed lux.

fact.text: Italians say 'dare alla luce' (to give to the light) for giving birth. It comes from Latin lux, the root of English lucid.

senses.note: Accendere/spegnere la luce = to turn the light on/off. Also colloquially 'electricity'.

etymology:
From Latin iūlius, through a process of dissimilation; compare also the obsolete regional variant form giuglio. Alternatively, derived from a Vulgar Latin root *lūlius, along with other Italo-Romance and Rhaeto-Romance cognates; compare Corsican lugliu, Neapolitan lùglio, Sicilian lugghiu, Venetan lujo, Romansh lügl, Friulian Lui, Ladin lugio, Ligurian lûggio, Emilian and Romagnol lój, Lombard luj. Gallo-Roman town name Juliobona (nowadays in Normandy, France) evolved into its modern French name Lillebonne following the same process.
Doublet of Giulio.

fact.text: Named after Julius Caesar, from Latin Iulius. Over time the initial sound changed to l-, so Iulius became luglio. The name Giulio is its doublet.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian and usually no article: a luglio = in July.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin illui.

senses.note: Also 'him' after prepositions (con lui). In speech it replaces the formal egli. Often left out.

etymology: From Luna, from Latin lūna, from Old Latin losna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂, derived from the root *lewk- (“bright”). Cognates include Armenian լուսին (lusin), Spanish luna, Portuguese lua, Romanian lună, Russian луна́ (luná).

fact.text: Latin luna gave English lunar and lunatic, since madness was once blamed on the moon. Its root *lewk- meant 'bright', the same root that gave English light and lucid.

senses.note: luna di miele = honeymoon; avere la luna storta = to be in a bad mood

etymology: From Latin Lūnae dīēs, variant of dīēs Lūnae (“day of the Moon”).

fact.text: From Latin Lunae dies, 'day of the Moon'. English Monday comes from 'Moon day' too, so both languages name it after the Moon.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. Il lunedì = on Mondays; lunedì = this Monday.

etymology: From Latin longus (“long, extended”), from Proto-Indo-European *dlongʰos (“long”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin longus, from the same Indo-European root as English 'long', since both descend from PIE *dlonghos.

senses.note: Forms: lungo, lunga, lunghi, lunghe. Also a preposition: lungo il fiume = along the river.

etymology: From earlier luoco < loco, from Latin locus.

fact.text: From Latin locus, the root of 'local' and 'location'. Un luogo comune is a cliché, matching English 'commonplace', which comes from Latin locus communis.

senses.note: Avere luogo = to take place. In primo luogo = in the first place.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *lūpum, from Latin lŭpum. Doublet of lupus and lovo.

fact.text: Italians wish good luck with 'In bocca al lupo!' (into the wolf's mouth). You don't say thank you. The traditional reply is 'Crepi!' (may it die!).

senses.note: Feminine: la lupa (she-wolf). Plural: i lupi.

etymology:
From Latin illāc. Compare Spanish allá, Portuguese lá, French là, Sicilian ḍḍà.
The original geminated -ll-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in most regional Italian varieties.

senses.note: The accent tells it apart from la (the/her). Là and lì both mean 'there'.

etymology:
From Latin illic. Compare Spanish allí, Portuguese ali.
The original geminated -ll-, though lost in the standard language, is still found in most regional Italian varieties.

senses.note: Keep the accent: li without it means 'them'. là also means 'there', usually a bit vaguer or farther away.

etymology: Inherited from Latin magis.

fact.text: Comes from Latin magis, 'more', which shifted to 'rather' and then to 'but'. The same word gave French mais 'but' and Spanish más 'more'.

senses.note: At the start of a sentence it can just add emphasis: Ma dai! = Come on!

etymology: Plural of maccherone, of uncertain origin.

fact.text: In 18th-century England a 'macaroni' was a flashy young man who had picked up continental fashions. That's why Yankee Doodle 'called it macaroni' when he stuck a feather in his cap.

senses.note: Plural noun: i maccheroni. Singular: il maccherone.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula. Doublet of macula, a borrowing.

fact.text: A caffè macchiato is literally a 'stained' coffee: espresso marked with a spot of milk.

senses.note: Also a spot or patch. Separately, la macchia is Mediterranean scrubland.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin machina (“engine, device, mill”), from Ancient Greek μαχανά (makhaná). Compare the inherited doublet macina (“grindstone”).

fact.text: Shares its Greek root (makhana, 'device') with English machine and mechanic. Italians just started calling the car 'the machine'.

senses.note: Also means 'machine'. Macchina fotografica = camera. Auto(mobile) is a synonym.

etymology: From Latin mea domina (“my lady”).

fact.text: Literally means 'my lady', from Latin mea domina. In the same way, French ma dame gave English 'madam', and domina is also behind 'dame'.

senses.note: Madonna! = 'Good heavens!' Usually capitalized for the Virgin Mary. As an old title it meant 'my lady'.

etymology: From the older form matre, from Latin mātrem, from Proto-Italic *mātēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.

fact.text: Comes from the same Indo-European word as English mother. Its Latin parent mater also gave English maternal and matrix.

senses.note: In everyday speech Italians usually say mamma.

etymology: From Latin magistrum. Doublet of mastro.

fact.text: Comes from Latin magister, built on magis 'more': 'the greater one'. Its opposite was minister, from minus 'less'. English 'master' and 'mister' come from the same word.

senses.note: Feminine: la maestra. Secondary-school teachers are professori. Also means 'master' of an art.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin maiestātem.

fact.text: In art history a Maestà is a painting of the Madonna enthroned with the Christ Child. The best known is Duccio's great altarpiece in Siena, finished in 1311.

senses.note: Invariable. Sua Maestà = His/Her Majesty.

etymology:
Borrowed from Greek μακάρι (makári, “I wish”), which is derived from Ancient Greek μακάριος (makários, “blessed, happy”).
Compare Sicilian macari, Portuguese macar (“although”, conjunction), Spanish maguer (“although”, conjunction) and Romanian măcar (“even”, adverb).

fact.text: From Greek makári 'I wish', from ancient makários 'blessed'. That is why 'Magari!' still means 'If only!'.

senses.note: Said on its own, 'Magari!' means 'I wish! / If only!'. Magari + subjunctive = if only...

etymology:
Etymology tree
Arabic خَزَنَ (ḵazana)der.
Arabic مَخْزَن (maḵzan)
Arabic مَخَازِن (maḵāzin)bor.
Italian magazzino
From Arabic مَخَازِن pl (maḵāzin), plural of مَخْزَن (maḵzan, “storeroom, storehouse”), noun of place from خَزَنَ (ḵazana, “to store, to stock, to lay up”). Compare Sicilian magasenu.

fact.text: Not a magazine (that's una rivista)! Both words come from Arabic makhazin, 'storehouses'. English magazine first meant a store, then a 'storehouse' of articles.

senses.note: grandi magazzini = department store. 'In magazzino' = in stock.

etymology: From Latin Maius.

senses.note: Months are lowercase in Italian. In May = a maggio / in maggio.

etymology: From Latin maiōrem /majjoːrɛ̃/, accusative case of maior, from Proto-Italic *magjōs, from Proto-Indo-European *m̥ǵh₂yós, from *méǵh₂s (“big”, “great”).

fact.text: English 'major' and 'mayor' both come from the same Latin word, maior, meaning 'greater'.

senses.note: Comparative of grande. Fratello maggiore = older brother. La maggior parte = most.

etymology: From Late Latin magia, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).

fact.text: Comes from Greek mageía, the art of the magoi, the Persian priestly caste. Their name also gave us the Magi, the three wise men of the Nativity story.

senses.note: Also a magic trick or spell (fare una magia). Adjective: magico.

etymology: From maglia + -etta.

fact.text: A diminutive of maglia (jersey, knitwear). In cycling, the leader of the Giro d'Italia wears the maglia rosa, the famous pink jersey.

etymology: From maglia + -one.

fact.text: Literally a 'big maglia': maglia (a knitted top, or a sports jersey like the Giro d'Italia's maglia rosa) plus the augmentative suffix -one.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin magnificus.

fact.text: From Latin magnus 'great' plus -ficus 'making', so roughly 'doing great things'. Lorenzo de' Medici, ruler of Renaissance Florence, is known as il Magnifico.

senses.note: Also used to mean wonderful or superb: una giornata magnifica.

etymology: From Latin macrum, from Proto-Indo-European *mh₂ḱrós.

fact.text: Comes from Latin macer (thin), which also reached English through French as meagre. Emaciated comes from the same root.

senses.note: Of food it means lean or low-fat: carne magra, yogurt magro.

etymology: From ma (“but”).

senses.note: Shows doubt or resignation and often comes with a shrug. Mah, vedremo = well, we'll see.

etymology: Inherited from Latin magis.

senses.note: After the verb it needs non: non lo vedo mai. In questions it means 'ever': sei mai stato...?

etymology: From Latin maiālis, from the goddess Maia.

fact.text: Latin maialis is linked to the goddess Maia, to whom pigs were sacrificed in ancient Rome. Her name is also behind the month of May.

senses.note: Also a colloquial insult for a dirty or lecherous person.

etymology: Borrowed from Spanish maíz.

fact.text: It is a Taíno word from the Caribbean, borrowed by Spanish as maíz after Columbus. English maize comes from the same source.

senses.note: Invariable noun. Corn on the cob is pannocchia; popcorn is popcorn.

fact.text: From Latin maiusculus, 'rather large', a diminutive of maior.

senses.note: Short for lettera maiuscola. In maiuscolo = in capitals.

ignored: This is just the shortened form of male (as in mal di pancia), so it belongs on the male card.

senses.note: Shortened form used before di: mal di pancia = stomach ache, mal di testa = headache.

ignored: A fragment of the adverbial phrase 'a malapena', not a standalone noun.

senses.note: Only used in the adverbial phrase a malapena (also a mala pena) = barely, hardly.
Also a noun: il malato / la malata = sick person, patient.

etymology: Cognate with Catalan malaltia, English malady, French maladie, Sicilian malatìa, Portuguese maladia.

fact.text: Related to English malady. Both come from Latin male habitus 'in bad condition', which gave Italian malato 'sick'.

senses.note: Essere in malattia = to be on sick leave.

etymology: From Latin male.

fact.text: Has nothing to do with English 'male' (that is maschio). It comes from Latin male 'badly', from malus 'bad', the root of English malice and malfunction.

senses.note: Opposite of bene. Stare male = to feel ill; fare male = to hurt.

etymology: From Latin maledictiōnem.

senses.note: As an exclamation, Maledizione! means 'Damn!' or 'Blast!'. The opposite is benedizione.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mamma.

senses.note: Warm, everyday word; madre is the neutral word. Mamma mia! = My goodness!
An affectionate diminutive of mamma, mostly used by children.

etymology: Borrowed from English manager.

fact.text: Italian borrowed this from English, but English 'manage' came from Italian maneggiare, 'to handle (horses)', from mano 'hand'. So the word went out and then came back home.

senses.note: English loanword. It does not change in the plural (i manager), and you say la manager for a woman.

etymology: From mancare.

senses.note: Mancanza di = lack of. Sentire la mancanza di qualcuno = to miss someone.

etymology: From manco (adjective) + -are, or from a Vulgar Latin *mancāre, from Latin mancus.

fact.text: Italian flips the English: 'I miss you' is Mi manchi, literally 'you are lacking to me'. The thing or person missed is the subject, so 'we miss Rome' is Ci manca Roma.

senses.note: Works backwards: the person missed is the subject. Mi manchi = I miss you (lit. you are lacking to me).

etymology: Probably from Old French manche (“sleeve”).

fact.text: Probably from Old French manche 'sleeve'. In the Middle Ages a lady might give a knight her sleeve as a token or gift, and the word later came to mean a small gift of money.

senses.note: Lasciare la mancia = to leave a tip. Plural: mance.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mandāre.

fact.text: From Latin mandare, 'to entrust, to order', the same root as English mandate and command. To send someone was originally to give them an order.

features.construction: transitive: mandare qualcosa/qualcuno a qualcuno/in un luogo

senses.note: mandare qualcosa a qualcuno = to send something to someone. mandare via = to send away.

etymology: From mandare + -gli.
ignored: This is just mandare with the pronoun gli attached; study it on the mandare card.

senses.note: mandare + gli (to him).

etymology: From Latin mandātum.

senses.note: mandato d'arresto = arrest warrant.

etymology: Diminutive of mandola.

fact.text: English 'mandolin' comes from this word via French; it is a diminutive of mandola. The Neapolitan mandolin was developed in 18th-century Naples and became a classic, much-teased symbol of Italy.

etymology: From mano + -etta.

fact.text: Literally means 'little hand': mano (hand) plus the diminutive suffix -etta.

senses.note: Almost always plural: le manette. 'Mettere le manette a qualcuno' = to handcuff someone.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French mangier, from Latin mandūcāre (“to chew, (coll.) eat”). Doublet of manducare, manicare, and manucare.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old French mangier, from Latin mandūcāre, 'to chew'. That comes from mandere, 'to chew', which is also the root of English 'mandible', the jawbone.

senses.note: Il mangiare can mean 'food'. In chess and draughts, mangiare = to take a piece.

etymology: Inherited from Latin manica.

fact.text: From Latin manus 'hand'. Italians call the English Channel 'la Manica', the Sleeve, after its shape, just as the French call it 'la Manche'.

senses.note: in maniche di camicia = in shirtsleeves; un altro paio di maniche = a different matter

etymology: Borrowed from Old French maniere, from manere.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old French maniere, the same word that gave English 'manner'. It ultimately goes back to Latin manus 'hand', so it is literally your way of handling things.

senses.note: Le buone maniere = good manners; in maniera + adj = in a … way.

etymology: Inherited from Latin manus (whence also English manual, etc.), from Proto-Italic *manus, perhaps from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂-r̥ ~ *mh₂-én-, derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meh₂- (“to beckon”), or perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *mon-u- (see the Proto-Italic entry).

fact.text: From Latin manus 'hand', which also gave English manual, manicure and manuscript (written by hand). It stays feminine like the Latin word, even with its -o ending.

senses.note: Feminine even though it ends in -o: la mano, le mani. Dare una mano = to lend a hand.

etymology: From Late Latin manūtenēre (“to support”), from Latin manū (“with the hand”) + teneō (“to hold”). By surface analysis, mano + tenere. Compare French maintenir, Spanish mantener, Portuguese manter.

fact.text: Literally 'to hold in the hand', from Latin manu (by hand) + tenere (to hold). English 'maintain' came from the same Latin source by way of French maintenir.

senses.note: Conjugated like tenere: mantengo, mantieni, mantenni, manterrò. Also: to support someone financially.

etymology: Disputed, maybe from a pre-Latin (possibly Illyrian) root. Compare Albanian mëz, and Romanian mânz, Aromanian mãndzu, which might be from the same source.

fact.text: Its origin is disputed. It may come from a pre-Latin Balkan root, possibly Illyrian, related to Albanian mëz and Romanian mânz (both meaning 'foal').

senses.note: The meat. Usually uncountable: carne di manzo, manzo bollito (boiled beef).

etymology: From Latin mappa, of possibly Semitic origin.

fact.text: Latin mappa meant 'napkin, cloth', because maps were drawn on cloth (mappa mundi). Through French nappe, the same word gave English 'napkin'.

senses.note: For road or tourist maps, 'cartina' is also very common.

etymology: Of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *marką or Proto-Germanic *markō.

fact.text: Of Germanic origin and related to English mark and march (a border land). The Italian region Le Marche is named after medieval 'marche', frontier territories.

senses.note: Di marca = branded. Marca da bollo = revenue stamp.

etymology: From marcare + -tore.

senses.note: For a marker pen, pennarello is more common. In sport, marcatore means goalscorer.

etymology: From marcia + piede.

fact.text: A compound of marcia (march, walking) and piede (foot), so it is literally the place where you walk on foot.

senses.note: Also used for a railway station platform.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mare, from Proto-Italic *mari, from Proto-Indo-European *móri.

fact.text: From Latin mare, the source of English 'marine' and 'maritime'.

senses.note: Andare al mare = to go to the seaside or beach.

etymology: Inherited from Latin marītus.

fact.text: From Latin maritus ('husband'). English 'marital' and 'marry' (from Latin maritare via French) come from the same word.

senses.note: Mio marito = my husband (no article with a singular family word).

etymology: Originally Tuscan, from Byzantine Greek μάραον (máraon, “sweet chestnut”), ultimately from Proto-Celtic *māros (“great”), referring to the size of the nut, related to Welsh mawr and Cimbrian môr, a borrowing.

fact.text: The colour is named after a nut: marrone is a large sweet chestnut, like French marron in marron glacé.

senses.note: Plural marroni (occhi marroni). As a noun, il marrone also means a large chestnut.

etymology: From the toponym Marsala, from Arabic.

fact.text: This fortified wine is named after the Sicilian town of Marsala, whose name comes from Arabic. An English merchant, John Woodhouse, made it popular in Britain in the 1770s.

senses.note: Masculine, like most wines: il marsala. Used in cooking, e.g. scaloppine al marsala.

etymology: From Latin Martis dīēs, variant of dīēs Martis (“day of Mars”).

fact.text: Means 'day of Mars', the Roman war god. English Tuesday is named after Tiw, a Germanic war god, so both languages name the day after a god of war.

senses.note: Lowercase and invariable. Il martedì = on Tuesdays; martedì = this Tuesday.

etymology: Inherited from Latin (mēnsis) mārtius.

fact.text: From Latin Martius, the month of Mars, Roman god of war. It was the first month of the early Roman calendar, when military campaigns started again.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian and usually without an article: a marzo, in marzo = in March.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Late Latin mascara
Latin *mascra
Proto-Indo-European *mesg-der.
Proto-Germanic *maskwǭ
Proto-West Germanic *maskābor.
Latin masca
Italian maschera
Inherited from Late Latin mascara, *mascra, masca. Doublet of mascara.

fact.text: English got 'mask' (via French masque) and 'masquerade' from this word. 'Mascara' comes from the same source, through Spanish máscara and Italian maschera.

senses.note: Also a commedia dell'arte stock character (Arlecchino) and a theatre usher.

etymology: From maschio.

senses.note: Also 'men's': squadra maschile = men's team. For people and animals, maschio is common.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin masclus, contracted form of Latin masculus. Doublet of mascolo and masculo.

fact.text: It can also mean a castle keep. Naples' famous Castel Nuovo is popularly called the Maschio Angioino, the 'Angevin keep'.

senses.note: Also used as an adjective: un gatto maschio. Opposite: femmina.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin maximus.

senses.note: Il massimo = the best, the most (È il massimo! = It's the best!).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin maximus.

senses.note: Al massimo = at most. È il massimo! = it's the best!

fact.text: In Italy a 'master' is usually a postgraduate professional course. The degree that matches an English master's is the laurea magistrale.

senses.note: Invariable English loan: due master. Often a postgraduate course, not the laurea magistrale.

fact.text: Goes back to Greek máthēma, 'something learned, a lesson'. Italian uses the singular (la matematica), while English adds an -s: mathematics.

senses.note: Singular in Italian: la matematica è difficile. It can also mean a female mathematician.

etymology: Latinization of older matera, from Latin māteria.

fact.text: Latin materia is usually linked to mater, 'mother'. It first meant the hard inner wood of a tree, the 'mother' substance that things are built from. English material comes from the same word.

senses.note: Also means a school subject: la mia materia preferita = my favourite subject.

etymology: From Latin māteriālis.

senses.note: Also an adjective: material, physical (danni materiali).

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin māternitātem.

senses.note: Also 'maternity ward'. Essere in maternità = to be on maternity leave. Invariable plural.

etymology: From ematite (“hematite”). Rods of hematite ore were once used as pencils.

fact.text: Comes from ematite (hematite), an iron ore. Rods of hematite were once used for drawing and writing, before graphite pencils.

etymology: From Latin mātrimōnium.

fact.text: Latin matrimonium is built on mater, 'mother', so it originally meant the state of motherhood. Patrimonium, from pater, meant 'inheritance' instead.

etymology: From Latin [hōra] mātūtīna.

fact.text: Comes from Latin hora matutina, 'the early hour', linked to Matuta, the Roman goddess of dawn. English 'matinee' and 'matins' share the root.

senses.note: Di mattina = in the morning; stamattina = this morning. Mattino (m.) is a synonym.

etymology: From Latin matutinus (“early”).

fact.text: From Latin matutinus 'of the morning', linked to Matuta, the Roman goddess of dawn. The same root gave the French-borrowed English 'matinee'.

senses.note: La mattina means the same thing and is more common in speech. Le 9 del mattino = 9 a.m.

etymology: From Late Latin mattus (“drunk, intoxicated”), itself either from a contraction of a form *madĭtus (as a past participle of Latin madeō), or madidus (“drunk, tipsy”). Cognate to French mat (“matte, pale”).

fact.text: From Late Latin mattus, 'drunk', probably from madere, 'to be wet'. So the word went from soaked, to drunk, to crazy.

senses.note: Andare matto per = to be crazy about. Matto da legare = completely mad.

etymology: The origin is uncertain, perhaps from Latin maltha (“cement”).

fact.text: In Italian finance news, il mattone ('the brick') means real estate. Investing in bricks is seen as the classic safe choice of Italian savers.

senses.note: Colloquially un mattone is also a heavy, boring book or film.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin mātūritātem.

fact.text: For Italian teenagers, 'la maturità' mostly means the final high-school exam. Students take it every June, and newspapers publish the essay topics on the morning of the first written paper.

senses.note: Invariable. La maturità is also Italy's high-school leaving exam (esame di maturità).

etymology: From Latin mē.

senses.note: Used after prepositions and for emphasis: con me, per me. The unstressed form is mi.
Also an adjective, 'mechanical'. La meccanica = mechanics, the science.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin media.

fact.text: Careful: la media means 'the average', not 'the media'. For newspapers and TV, Italians say i media, often pronounced 'mìdia' as in English.

senses.note: In media means 'on average'. 'The media' is i media (masculine, invariable), and le medie is middle school.

etymology: From Latin medicina.

senses.note: Both the drug and the science. Plural le medicine = medicines.

etymology: Inherited from Latin medicus. Compare Neapolitan miedeco.

fact.text: Florence's famous Medici family has a name that is simply the plural of this word, so it literally means 'doctors'.

senses.note: Doctors are usually addressed as 'dottore/dottoressa'. Medico di base/di famiglia = GP.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin medius, whence also Italian mezzo (an inherited doublet).

fact.text: From Latin medius, 'middle', which shares an ancient root with English mid and middle. Italian mezzo, 'half', is an inherited twin of the same Latin word.

senses.note: Dito medio = middle finger; scuola media = middle school; in media = on average.

etymology: From Latin melius. Cognate with Sicilian megghiu.

senses.note: Adverb, comparative of bene; the adjective is migliore. il meglio = the best.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin mēla, from mēlum, from Latin mālum, likely from Doric Greek μᾶλον (mâlon, “apple”); compare Attic μῆλον (mêlon).

fact.text: It comes from Latin mēla, a form of mālum 'apple', which looked almost identical to malum 'evil'. That pun is often cited as the reason the forbidden fruit of Eden became an apple.

senses.note: The fruit. The tree is il melo (masculine).

etymology: From Latin membrum (“member; limb”), from Proto-Indo-European *memso-, *mems-ro (“flesh”).

fact.text: Has two plurals with different meanings: i membri are members of a group, while le membra (feminine) are the limbs of a body, a leftover from the Latin neuter plural membra.

senses.note: Plural i membri for people; le membra means the limbs of the body.

etymology: Inherited from Latin memoria.

senses.note: 'A memoria' = by heart. In the plural, memorie can also mean memoirs.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin mendicāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin mendicare. A beggar in Italian is un mendicante.

senses.note: Mendicare (qualcosa) = to beg (for something); it can also be figurative: mendicare affetto.
Medical -ite = English -itis (bronchite, artrite), and these words are always feminine.

etymology: Derived from Latin minus.

senses.note: Meno male! = thank goodness! Also 'minus': le tre meno un quarto = quarter to three.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin mēnsa (“table”), although some sources disagree.

fact.text: From Latin mensa, 'table'. The high-IQ society Mensa took the same Latin word as its name, to suggest a round table where equals meet.

senses.note: A school, university or workplace cafeteria: mangiare in mensa.
Also an adjective: mensile = monthly (stipendio mensile)

fact.text: From Latin mensula, 'little table', a diminutive of mensa 'table', which also gives Italian mensa (canteen).

senses.note: A wall shelf. A bookcase or set of shelves is uno scaffale.

etymology: From Latin mentem, from Proto-Indo-European *méntis (“thought”).

fact.text: The Italian adverb ending -mente comes from this word: Latin clara mente meant 'with a clear mind' and became chiaramente, 'clearly'. English mental comes from the same Latin mens.

senses.note: Feminine despite ending in -e. Avere in mente = to have in mind.

etymology: From Latin mentīrī.

fact.text: From Latin mentiri, built on mens, 'mind', the same root as English 'mental'. Lying was seen as inventing something in the mind.

senses.note: Mentire a qualcuno: le ho mentito. Not 'lie down' (sdraiarsi). La menzogna = a lie.

etymology:
Inherited from Late Latin dum interim (“while”).
Akin to Spanish mientras.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin dum interim, roughly 'while in the meantime', which wore down over the centuries into one short word. Spanish mientras comes from the same source.

senses.note: In contrasts it also means 'whereas': io lavoro, mentre tu dormi.
Also spelled menu. It doesn't change in the plural: i menù.

etymology: From meraviglia + -oso.

fact.text: Built on meraviglia 'wonder', from Latin mirabilia 'wondrous things'. The same Latin word gave English marvel and marvellous through French.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mercātus.

fact.text: Both this word and English market come from Latin mercatus. It shares a root with merchant, mercantile and commerce.

senses.note: 'Al mercato' = at the market. 'A buon mercato' = cheap.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mercem (“merchandise”, “goods”).

fact.text: From Latin merx (goods), the root of English 'merchant', 'commerce' and 'mercantile'. Some scholars link it to Mercury, the Roman god of trade.

senses.note: Often plural: le merci. Treno merci = freight train.

etymology: From Latin Mercuriī diēs, variant of diēs Mercuriī (“day of Mercury”).

fact.text: Latin for 'Mercury's day'. English Wednesday is 'Woden's day', because Germanic peoples matched their god Woden with the Roman Mercury.

senses.note: Lowercase. Il mercoledì = on Wednesdays; mercoledì = this Wednesday.

etymology: Inherited from Latin merda, from Proto-Italic *(s)merdā, from Proto-Indo-European *smerd-h₂- (“stench”).

fact.text: In 1961 the artist Piero Manzoni sealed 90 tins labelled 'Merda d'artista' (Artist's Shit), priced by their weight in gold. Today they sell for large sums at auction.

senses.note: Also an exclamation (Merda!). 'Di merda' after a noun = crappy, lousy: una casa di merda.

etymology: From Latin merenda (“light evening meal”). Compare Galician and Portuguese merenda, Spanish merienda.

fact.text: The afternoon merenda is a ritual for Italian kids. The Latin word merenda comes from merere 'to earn, deserve', so it is the snack you've earned. Compare Spanish merienda.

senses.note: Usually the mid-afternoon snack, especially for children.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin merīdiōnālis. Cf. also the older Italian meriggionale.

fact.text: From Latin meridies 'midday', because at noon the sun stands due south. For the same reason, Southern Italy is also called il Mezzogiorno, literally 'midday'.

senses.note: Usually an adjective, meaning southern: l'Italia meridionale = Southern Italy.

etymology: From Latin meritāre, from meritus.

senses.note: Often used with the reflexive in speech: te lo meriti! = you deserve it!

etymology: From Latin meritum (“merit”, “deserts”), from a noun use of the neuter form of meritus.

senses.note: È merito tuo = it's thanks to you; in merito a = regarding.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin misculāre, derived from Latin miscēre (“mix”). Doublet of mischiare.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin misculare, which also gave Old French medler. That is the source of English 'meddle' and 'medley', so to meddle is literally to mix yourself in.

senses.note: Also 'to stir' or 'to shuffle' (cards). Mescolarsi means 'to mingle'.

etymology: From Latin mēnsem (“month”). Compare Catalan mes, French mois, Portuguese mês, Romansh mais, Spanish mes.

fact.text: Comes from Latin mensis. It shares an ancient Indo-European root with English 'moon' and 'month', because months were counted by the moon.

senses.note: Al mese = per month; il mese prossimo = next month.

etymology: From Late Latin missa, from Latin missum.

fact.text: Probably named after the Latin closing words Ite, missa est ('Go, it is the dismissal'), which the priest said to send the congregation home.

senses.note: andare a messa = to go to Mass. Also used in phrases like messa in scena (staging).

etymology: Borrowed from Old French message, from Early Medieval Latin missāticum, derived from Latin mittere (“send”).

senses.note: Also a text message: mandare un messaggio = to send a text.

etymology: From Latin metallum (“metal, mine, quarry, mineral”), from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, “mine, quarry, metal”).

fact.text: Greek métallon first meant 'mine, quarry', so the material was named after the place it was dug from. English medal also comes from the same Latin metallum.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin methodus, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).

fact.text: Comes from Greek methodos, made of meta 'after' and hodos 'way, road'. A method was literally the act of following a path.

senses.note: Stress on the first syllable: MEtodo.

etymology: From Latin metrum (“a measure”), from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron).

fact.text: Two words in one. Il metro (the unit) comes from Greek métron, 'measure', as in English metric and symmetry. La metro (the train) is short for metropolitana, 'metropolitan railway'.

senses.note: Il metro, plural i metri. Also means a measuring tape or ruler.

etymology: From Latin mētropolis.

fact.text: Via Latin from Greek mētēr 'mother' + polis 'city': literally a 'mother city', originally the parent city of a Greek colony.

senses.note: Feminine and invariable: la metropoli, le metropoli.

etymology: From metterci + -la.

senses.note: Usually mettercela tutta: ce la metto tutta = I'll give it my all.
senses.prompt: to put one's all into it

etymology: Inherited from Latin mittere, probably from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to exchange, remove”). Cognate with French mettre, Spanish meter, Occitan metre, and English mission.

fact.text: Comes from Latin mittere, 'to send'. Latin then gave English mission, emit, transmit and message. Over time the Italian verb's meaning drifted from sending to putting.

senses.note: Irregular: misi, messo. Mettersi = to put on (clothes); metterci = to take (time).

etymology: From mettere + -si.

senses.note: Mi metto la giacca. Mettersi a + infinitive = to start doing: si è messo a piovere.

etymology: From Late Latin medietātem, from Latin medius. Compare medietà, a borrowed doublet.

fact.text: Watch the accent: metà (stress on the last syllable) means half, but meta without the accent is a different word meaning goal or destination.

senses.note: Invariable: la metà, le metà. 'A metà' = halfway.

etymology: From mezza (“half; mid”) + notte (“night”), or directly from Latin mediam noctem.

fact.text: Just as mezzogiorno (noon) also means south, mezzanotte once also meant north, because at midnight the sun is on the opposite side, below the northern horizon.

senses.note: Rare plural mezzenotti: both parts change.

etymology: From Latin medius, whence also Italian medio (a borrowed doublet).

fact.text: English borrowed it in mezzo-soprano, a voice halfway between soprano and contralto. Mezzanine also comes from Italian mezzanino, a half floor.

senses.note: mezzo chilo, mezza pizza. Telling time: le due e mezzo (or mezza). mezzogiorno = noon.

etymology: From Latin medius, whence also Italian medio (a borrowed doublet).

fact.text: English borrowed it in mezzo-soprano, a voice halfway between soprano and contralto. Mezzanine also comes from Italian mezzanino, a half floor.

senses.note: per mezzo di = by means of. mezzi (di trasporto) = means of transport, public transport.

etymology: From mezzo- + giorno. Compare Catalan migjorn, Romanian miazăzi.

fact.text: Literally 'mid-day'. Because the sun stands in the south at noon, the word also means south, and il Mezzogiorno with a capital M is the usual name for southern Italy.

senses.note: a mezzogiorno = at noon

etymology: Inherited from Latin mē and, as an indirect object pronoun, possibly in part from Latin mihi.

senses.note: Unstressed and placed before the verb: mi vede. Also means 'to me' and 'myself': mi lavo.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mīlliārium.

fact.text: Like centinaio (about a hundred), this word is masculine in the singular but becomes feminine in the plural (le migliaia). This is a leftover of the Latin neuter plural ending -a.

senses.note: Plural is feminine: le migliaia. Migliaia di persone = thousands of people.

etymology: Back-formation from the plural miglia, from Latin mīlia n pl (“thousand”) in the phrase mīlia passuum (“thousand paces”). Doublet of mille.

fact.text: Comes from Latin milia passuum, 'a thousand paces', the Roman mile, which is also where English mile comes from. It shares its root with mille (thousand).

senses.note: Irregular feminine plural: le miglia. Miglio also means millet (pl. migli).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin meliōrāre, a verb based on Latin meliārī (“better”). By surface analysis, migliore + -are.

fact.text: Built on Latin melior, 'better', which also gives Italian migliore.

senses.note: Get better: è migliorato (essere). Improve something: ho migliorato il testo (avere).

etymology: Inherited from Latin meliōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *mélyōs, from *mel- (“strong, big”).

senses.note: Comparative of buono. With the article it means 'the best': il/la migliore.

etymology: From Milano (“Milan”) + -ese.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. Same form for men and women (il/la). Also an adjective: cotoletta alla milanese.

fact.text: Don't translate English billion as bilione: in standard Italian bilione means a million million (10^12). A thousand million is un miliardo.

senses.note: Takes di before a noun: un miliardo di euro.

fact.text: Literally 'a big thousand': mille plus the augmentative suffix -one. English million was borrowed from this Italian word, through French.

senses.note: Takes di before a noun: un milione di euro.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin mīlitāris.

senses.note: Also an adjective meaning 'military'. Fare il militare = to do military service.

etymology: From Latin mīlle, from Proto-Italic *smīɣeslī, from Proto-Indo-European *smih₂ǵʰéslih₂ (“one thousand”). Doublet of miglio.
From mille + uno.
From milli- (“a thousandth”) + metro (“metre”).

senses.note: Abbreviated mm.

etymology: From Latin minācia (“threat”), a noun based on mināx (“threatening”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin minacia 'threat', from minax 'threatening'. English 'menace' comes from the same source through Old French.

senses.note: Plural minacce (no i). Verb: minacciare, to threaten.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mināciāre, from Latin minācia, from mināx (“threatening”). Or, by surface analysis, minaccia + -are.

fact.text: Same family as English 'menace'. Both go back to Latin minax, meaning threatening.

senses.note: minacciare qualcuno; minacciare di fare qualcosa = to threaten to do something.

etymology: From minestrare (“to serve, prepare (as in soup)”), from Latin ministrāre.

fact.text: From minestrare, 'to serve (food)', from Latin ministrare, a relative of English minister and administer. The proverb 'o mangi questa minestra o salti dalla finestra' means take it or leave it.

senses.note: Usually a broth-based soup, often with pasta or rice. Zuppa is thicker and is often served with bread.

etymology: Derived from Latin minimus.

senses.note: Superlative of piccolo. Non ho il minimo dubbio = I haven't the slightest doubt.

etymology: Derived from Latin minimus.

senses.note: Come minimo / al minimo = at the very least. Il minimo indispensabile = the bare minimum.

etymology: From Latin ministrum.

fact.text: Latin minister meant 'servant', literally 'the lesser one', from minus. Its opposite was magister, 'the greater one', from magis, which gave English 'master'.

senses.note: A female minister is now often called 'la ministra'.

etymology: From Latin minōrem.

fact.text: Straight from Latin minor, 'smaller'. Its neuter form minus gave English 'minus', and the related verb minuere, 'to lessen', lies behind 'diminish' and 'minute'.

senses.note: Comparative of piccolo. Also younger: il fratello minore = younger brother. Plural: minori.

fact.text: Related to English 'minuscule', from Latin minusculus 'rather small'. In typography, minuscule still means lowercase script.

senses.note: Opposite: la maiuscola (capital letter). 'In minuscolo' = in lowercase.
Also means lowercase (lettera minuscola); the opposite is maiuscolo (capital).

etymology: From Latin minūtus. Doublet of menu.

fact.text: From Latin minutus, 'made small'. The same root gives English 'minute' (tiny) and 'menu', originally a small, detailed list.

ignored: The contexts use the noun il minuto (minute of time), which has its own card; the adjective is a rarer secondary use.

senses.note: Also 'fine, detailed'. Al minuto = retail.

etymology: From Latin minūtus. Doublet of menu.

fact.text: From Latin minutus, 'made small'. The same root gives English 'minute' (tiny) and 'menu', originally a small, detailed list.

senses.note: Un minuto! = Just a moment! As an adjective, minuto means tiny.
Agrees with the thing owned: mio, mia, miei, mie. Usually takes the article: il mio libro.

etymology: From Old Italian meo, from Latin meus, from Proto-Italic *meos.

senses.note: Agrees with the thing owned: mio/mia/miei/mie. Article dropped with singular family: mia madre.

etymology: From Old Italian meo, from Latin meus, from Proto-Italic *meos.

senses.note: Usually takes an article: il mio, la mia, i miei, le mie. È mio = It's mine.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin mīrāculum, from mīror.

fact.text: From Latin miraculum, from mirari 'to wonder at'. The same root gives English admire, marvel and mirror (an object you gaze at).

senses.note: Per miracolo = by a miracle, only just.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin miseria (“misery”). By surface analysis, mìsero + -èria.

fact.text: 'Porca miseria!', literally 'pig misery', is one of the most common mild Italian curses, roughly 'Damn it!' or 'For heaven's sake!'.

senses.note: Mainly means extreme poverty: vivere in miseria. Also 'a pittance': costa una miseria.

fact.text: Italy's national beauty pageant began in 1939 as '5000 lire per un sorriso' (5000 lire for a smile) and only took the English-style name Miss Italia after the war.

senses.note: English loanword, la miss (invariable): the winner of a beauty contest, e.g. Miss Italia.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin missiōnem.
Borrowed from Latin mītem (“mild, mature”).

fact.text: From Latin mitis 'mild', the same root found in English mitigate (literally 'to make mild'). It has nothing to do with the tiny English bug.

senses.note: Used for people (meek), climate (un clima mite) and prices. Same form for m/f; plural miti.

etymology: From mito + -logia.
From Latin mittentem, present active participle of mittō.

fact.text: From Latin mittere, 'to send', the same root behind English mission, missile, transmit and dismiss.

senses.note: Used with il or la for a man or a woman. The opposite is destinatario (recipient).

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin mōbilis.

fact.text: Furniture is literally the 'movable' goods, from Latin mobilis. Buildings and land are beni immobili, and an estate agency is an agenzia immobiliare. Compare French meuble and German Möbel.

senses.note: Plural mobili = furniture (uncountable in English): non ci sono mobili = there's no furniture.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin mōbilitātem.

senses.note: Stress on the final -à. persona a mobilità ridotta = person with reduced mobility.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin modus, 'manner, measure'. That is also the root of English 'mode', 'model' and 'modern'. Fashion is simply the current way of doing things.

senses.note: di moda / alla moda = fashionable; fuori moda = out of fashion.

etymology: From a variant of Late Latin modulus.

fact.text: From a diminutive of Latin modus 'measure'. The same root gave English model, module and, through Old French, mould.

senses.note: Also model, template or (sewing) pattern. For a decorative pattern, use motivo.

etymology: From Late Latin modernus; from Latin modo (“just now”).

fact.text: Built on Latin modo 'just now', so modern originally meant simply 'of just now'. The ending was modelled on hodiernus 'of today'.

etymology: From Latin modus, from Proto-Indo-European *modós, derived from the root *med- (“to measure”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin modus 'measure, manner', from a root meaning 'to measure'. It is related to English mode, model, modest and moderate.

senses.note: In questo modo = this way; non c'è modo = there's no way.

etymology: From Latin modulus.

fact.text: In everyday Italian this is mostly the paperwork form you fill in, not a 'module'. It comes from Latin modulus, 'little measure', which also gave English module and model.

senses.note: Compilare un modulo = to fill in a form. Not forma (shape).

etymology: Inherited from Latin mulier (nominative). The alternative forms reflect the Latin accusative mulierem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin mulier, which simply meant 'woman'. Over time the Italian word narrowed to mean a man's wife.

senses.note: Irregular plural: le mogli. Possessives usually drop the article: mia moglie.

etymology: From molle (“soft”) + -are.

fact.text: Built from molle, 'soft': letting go means loosening your grip. 'Non mollare!' (don't give up!) is a classic Italian cry of encouragement.

senses.note: Informal: mollare qualcuno = to dump someone. Non mollare! = Don't give up!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin multiplicāre.

senses.note: moltiplicare per: 3 moltiplicato per 4 = 3 times 4. Moltiplicarsi = to multiply, to increase.

fact.text: From Latin multus (much, many), the same root as English multi-, multiply and multitude.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun: molto tempo, molta acqua, molti libri. As an adverb 'very' it does not change: molto bello.

etymology: Derived from Latin multus, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare Portuguese muito, Romanian mult, Catalan molt.

fact.text: From Latin multus (much, many), the same root as English multi-, multiply and multitude.

senses.note: As an adverb it never changes: molto bella, lavora molto. As an adjective it agrees: molte case.

etymology: Derived from Latin multus, from Proto-Indo-European *ml̥tos (“crumbled, crumpled”, past passive participle). Compare Portuguese muito, Romanian mult, Catalan molt.

fact.text: From Latin multus (much, many), the same root as English multi-, multiply and multitude.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun: molto pane, molti soldi, molte cose. As an adverb it never changes: molto bello.

etymology: From Latin mōmentum.

fact.text: From Latin mōmentum, from movēre, 'to move'. It first meant a tiny movement, or the weight that tips a scale. English gets both 'moment' and 'momentum' from it.

senses.note: Un momento! = just a moment! / hold on! Al momento = at the moment.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin monachus.

fact.text: Comes from Greek monakhos, 'solitary', from monos, 'alone'. That is the same mono- as in monologue and monopoly: a monk was first someone who lived alone.

senses.note: Plural monaci. A nun is una monaca.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mundus (“world”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin mundus, 'world', which is also the source of English 'mundane'. 'Mundane' originally meant 'worldly' rather than 'dull'.

senses.note: Il mondo. In tutto il mondo = all over the world. Also used to mean people or society.

etymology: From Latin monēta. Compare Spanish moneda and Portuguese moeda.

fact.text: Named after Juno Moneta, whose temple in ancient Rome housed the mint. Latin moneta also gave English both money and mint.

senses.note: Also 'currency'. 'Money' in general is usually soldi or denaro.

etymology: From mono- + locale.

senses.note: In property ads: bilocale = two rooms, trilocale = three rooms.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem.

senses.note: in montagna = in/to the mountains.

etymology: From Latin monumentum, possibly a borrowing.

fact.text: From Latin monere 'to remind', so a monument is literally a reminder. The same root appears in English admonish and monitor.

etymology: Inherited from Latin morbidum (“sick”), from Latin morbus (“disease, illness”); as sickness makes one feeble, in Italo-Romance the meaning evolved into “limp, flabby”, and thence into “tender”, “delicate”.

fact.text: It means soft, not morbid! It comes from Latin morbidus 'sick', and over time the meaning drifted to 'soft'.

senses.note: Soft to the touch (cheese, pillow, skin). 'Morbid' in Italian is morboso.

etymology: Inherited from Latin morbidum (“sick”), from Latin morbus (“disease, illness”); as sickness makes one feeble, in Italo-Romance the meaning evolved into “limp, flabby”, and thence into “tender”, “delicate”.

fact.text: It means soft, not morbid! It comes from Latin morbidus 'sick', and over time the meaning drifted to 'soft'.

ignored: Rare noun use; the context ('aghi morbidi') uses the adjective morbido 'soft', which has its own card.

senses.note: Rare noun use; the adjective morbido means soft.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mordĕre, from Latin mordēre.

fact.text: Latin mordere gave English two words: 'morsel' (literally a little bite, from morsus) and 'remorse' (from remordere, 'to bite back', meaning guilt that keeps gnawing at you).

senses.note: Irregular: past participle morso, passato remoto morsi. Il morso = a bite.

etymology: Inherited from Latin morī(rī).

senses.note: Irregular: muoio, muori, muore; past participle morto. Morire di fame = to starve.

etymology: From Latin mortālis.

senses.note: Also means 'fatal' (incidente mortale = fatal accident). As a noun, i mortali = mortals.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mortem, from Proto-Indo-European *mér-tis (“death”), from *mer- (“to die”).

fact.text: It shares its Latin root with English mortal and mortgage. Mortgage comes from Old French and literally means 'dead pledge'.

senses.note: Plural: le morti (deaths). But i morti (masculine) means 'the dead'.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mortus, from Classical Latin mortuus, from Proto-Italic *mortwos, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, derived from the root *mer- (“to die; to disappear”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin mortuus, 'dead', which gives English mortuary. English mortgage is Old French for 'dead pledge'.

senses.note: Also the past participle of morire: è morto = he died. Sei morto! = you're dead (threat).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mortus, from Classical Latin mortuus, from Proto-Italic *mortwos, from Proto-Indo-European *mr̥twós, derived from the root *mer- (“to die; to disappear”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin mortuus, 'dead', which gives English mortuary. English mortgage is Old French for 'dead pledge'.

senses.note: In news reports, i morti = the dead, fatalities: 102 morti. Il giorno dei morti = All Souls' Day (2 Nov).

etymology: From Latin musca, from Proto-Indo-European *mus-. Compare Spanish mosca.

fact.text: Comes from Latin musca, from the Indo-European root *mus- (fly). English midge, and midget, which literally meant a little midge, come from the same root.

senses.note: Idiom: restare con un pugno di mosche = to end up empty-handed.

etymology: From mosso.

senses.note: Fare una mossa = to make a move. Comes from mosso, past participle of muovere.

etymology: Deverbal from mostrare + -a.

senses.note: Una mostra d'arte = an art exhibition. Mettere in mostra = to show off or display.

etymology: Inherited from Latin mōnstrāre (“to show”). Cognate with Spanish mostrar, Occitan muishar and French montrer.

fact.text: Comes from Latin monstrare 'to show', which gave English demonstrate. Monstrare itself comes from monstrum, a warning sign, the source of English monster.

senses.note: Mostrare qualcosa a qualcuno: Ti mostro la casa = I'll show you the house.

etymology: From the older form monstro, from Latin mōnstrum.

fact.text: Latin monstrum first meant an omen or divine warning. It comes from monere 'to warn', the same root as English 'admonish' and 'monitor'.

senses.note: Don't confuse with mostri = 'you show' (from mostrare). Also used for a genius: un mostro di bravura.

etymology: From Late Latin mōtīvus.

senses.note: Per quale motivo? = For what reason? Also motive, motif, or tune.

etymology: Shortened form of motocicletta.

fact.text: The gender changes the meaning: la moto is a motorbike, short for motocicletta, while il moto means motion or exercise, as in fare moto, 'to get some exercise'.

senses.note: Short for motocicletta, so it is feminine and has no separate plural: le moto. Il moto (masc.) means 'motion'.

etymology: From moto- + (bi)cicletta.

fact.text: A blend of moto- 'motor' + bicicletta 'bicycle', so literally a 'motor bicycle'. The short form moto stays feminine and does not change in the plural: le moto.

senses.note: In everyday speech usually shortened to la moto (feminine, invariable: le moto).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin mōtōrem.

senses.note: Also motor. Motore di ricerca = search engine.

etymology: From motore + -ino (diminutive suffix).

senses.note: Everyday word for a moped or small scooter; can also mean a small motor.

etymology: From muovere + -mento, perhaps based partly on Medieval Latin mōvimentum, from Latin moveō. Compare French mouvement.

senses.note: Also 'motion', 'bustle' and a musical movement. Fare movimento = to get some exercise.

etymology: Diminutive of mozza (“a type of cheese”), related to the verb mozzare. Originally of southern Italian origin. Compare Neapolitan muzzarella.

fact.text: The name is a diminutive of mozza, linked to the verb mozzare (to cut off). The cheese is made by pulling the stretched curd and cutting it into balls by hand. It comes from southern Italy.

etymology: Uncertain, possibly from Alemannic German Mugg, itself derived from or related to the verb muggire (“to moo, low”).

senses.note: The everyday word. 'Vacca' is the older/technical term and is also used as an insult.

etymology: From Latin mūtulus, syncopated to *mutlus, or from cumulus, transposed to a Vulgar Latin form *muculus > *muclus. Based on the first etymology, mutulo is a doublet, and based on the second, cumulo and cumolo are.

senses.note: Colloquial: un mucchio di = a lot of, loads of (un mucchio di soldi).
Medical term, usually in the plural: le mucose (nasali).

etymology: Of Germanic origin, perhaps borrowed from Lombardic *muff.

senses.note: Also 'mold' in US English. 'Fare la muffa' = to go mouldy.

etymology: From Late Latin molīnum, from molīnus, from Latin molō.

fact.text: From Latin molere 'to grind'. English mill shares this root, and so do your molars, the grinding teeth (from mola, millstone).

senses.note: Mulino a vento = windmill; mulino ad acqua = watermill.

etymology: From Latin multa.

fact.text: Despite its look, it is not related to molto. Latin multa ('penalty') is an old Italic word of unknown origin, also found in Oscan.

senses.note: prendere una multa = to get a fine or ticket; fare la multa a qualcuno = to fine someone

etymology: Borrowed from Latin multāre. By surface analysis, multa + -are.

fact.text: Has nothing to do with multi- (many). It comes from Latin multa, a fine or penalty, which Italian kept as la multa.

senses.note: La multa = fine, (parking/speeding) ticket. Prendere una multa = to get a ticket.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin mungere, from Classical Latin mulgēre (“to milk”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₂melǵ-.

fact.text: From Latin mulgere 'to milk'. It goes back to the same Proto-Indo-European root as English milk.

senses.note: Irregular: munsi (passato remoto), munto (past participle). Figuratively, to fleece someone.

etymology: From Latin municipium.

fact.text: From Latin municipium, from municeps, a citizen who 'took on duties' (munus 'duty' + capere 'to take'). English municipal comes from the same source.

senses.note: Also means the town council. In Rome, a municipio is also an administrative district.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *movĕre, from Latin movēre.

senses.note: Muoversi = to move (oneself), with essere. Muoviti! also means 'hurry up!'.
Muoviti! = Hurry up! Compound tenses use essere: mi sono mosso/a.

fact.text: Muro has two plurals with different meanings: i muri are the walls of a house or room, and le mura are the defensive walls around a city, as in le mura di Lucca.

senses.note: Feminine plural of il muro, used for city walls; the walls of a room or building are i muri.

etymology: From Late Latin mūrāre (“to provide or surround with walls”). By surface analysis, muro + -are.
ignored: Bad parse: the context's 'mura' is the plural of the noun muro (walls), not the verb murare.

senses.note: murare vivo qcn = to wall someone up alive.

etymology: From murare + -tore.

fact.text: Built from muro 'wall' (via murare). A Freemason is a libero muratore, literally a 'free bricklayer', although massone is the more common word.

senses.note: The construction worker who builds walls; also translates 'mason'.

etymology: From Latin mūrus, from Old Latin *moerus, *moiros, from Proto-Indo-European *mey- (“to strengthen”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin murus 'wall', which also gave English mural, a painting done on a wall. Old city walls get their own feminine plural: le mura.

senses.note: I muri = walls of a building; le mura (feminine) = city walls or fortifications.

etymology: From muscolo (“muscle”) + -are, or borrowed from Medieval Latin musculāris.

fact.text: English muscular covers two Italian words: muscolare means relating to muscles (dolore muscolare), while a person with big muscles is muscoloso.

senses.note: Used in technical phrases: spasmi muscolari. A muscly person is muscoloso.

fact.text: Goes back through Latin to Greek mouseion, a shrine of the Muses, the goddesses of the arts. The most famous one was the great centre of learning in ancient Alexandria.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin mūsica, from Ancient Greek μουσική (mousikḗ, “of a Muse”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek mousikē, 'art of the Muses'. The Muses were goddesses of the arts, and the same root gives English 'museum'.

etymology: From Medieval Latin mūsicālis, derived from Latin mūsica.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural musicali.

fact.text: Comes from Latin mutanda, 'things to be changed', from mutare 'to change'. In other words, underwear is literally your change of clothes.

senses.note: Almost always plural: le mutande. The singular mutanda is rare.

etymology: From Latin mūtus.

senses.note: film muto = silent film; restare muto = to be left speechless; la h è muta = h is silent.

etymology: From Latin mūtuum (“loan”), from a noun use of the neuter form of mūtuus (“lent”, “borrowed”).

fact.text: From Latin mutuum, 'loan', from mutuus, 'lent, exchanged'. English mutual has the same root, and the Italian adjective mutuo still means mutual, as in mutuo soccorso (mutual aid).

senses.note: Accendere un mutuo = to take out a mortgage.

etymology: Borrowed from Sanskrit नमस्ते (namastē, “hello, welcome”).
ignored: This is the Sanskrit greeting namaste, borrowed unchanged, so it is not useful Italian vocabulary for a card.

senses.note: Borrowed from Sanskrit; used in yoga contexts and as a playful greeting.

etymology: From Latin neāpolītānus, from Neāpolis (“Naples”), from Ancient Greek Νεᾱ́πολῐς (Neā́polĭs, literally “new city”).

fact.text: Naples was founded by Greek settlers as Neapolis, meaning 'new city'. The name napoletano still carries that ancient Greek origin.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. Feminine: napoletana. Also used for the Neapolitan language.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nascere.

fact.text: From Latin nāscī, whose past participle nātus means 'born'. This is the root of English 'native', 'nation', 'nature' and 'prenatal'.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono nato/a. Irregular past participle nato; passato remoto nacqui.

etymology: Cognate with Sicilian nàscita.

fact.text: Related to nascere, 'to be born', from Latin nasci. English 'nascent', 'native' and 'Renaissance' (rebirth) come from the same root.

senses.note: data di nascita = date of birth

etymology: From Late Latin inabscondere, from Latin abscondere.

fact.text: Comes via Late Latin inabscondere from Latin abscondere 'to hide away', the same root as English 'abscond', to run off and hide.

senses.note: Irregular: nascosi, nascosto. Nascondersi = to hide (oneself).

etymology: Inherited from Latin nāsus, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s.

fact.text: Comes from Latin nasus, and English nose is a true cousin: both go back to Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s. Latin nasus also gave English nasal.

senses.note: Ficcare il naso = to poke your nose into something.

etymology: From Old High German nestila (“belt, strap, thong”), from Proto-West Germanic *nastilu.

senses.note: Also means tape, as in nastro adesivo (sticky tape). Verme a nastro means tapeworm (also tenia).

etymology: From Latin nātālis (“natal”).

fact.text: From Latin natalis, 'of birth', short for the day of Christ's birth. It shares a root with English 'natal', and French Noël, which gave English 'Noel', comes from the same word.

senses.note: Capitalised for the holiday: Buon Natale! = Merry Christmas. A Natale = at Christmas.

etymology: From Latin nātūra.

senses.note: natura morta = still life (painting).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin nātūrālis.

senses.note: Acqua naturale = still water (vs. acqua frizzante = sparkling).

etymology: From Latin nāvem, from Proto-Italic *naus ~ *nāwis, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us, derived from the root *(s)neh₂- (“to swim, float”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin navis, the source of English navy, naval and navigate. The nave of a church is the same word, perhaps because its vaulted roof looks like an upturned hull.

senses.note: Nave spaziale = spaceship.

etymology: From Latin nāvigāre (“to sail, cruise”).

fact.text: Latin navigare comes from navis 'ship' + agere 'to drive', so it means steering a ship. Italians use the same verb for surfing the internet.

senses.note: Also navigare in Internet = to surf the web.

etymology: From Latin nāvigātōrem.

senses.note: Navigatore (satellitare) = satnav or GPS device. Also a seafarer or explorer.

etymology: From nazionale + -ità.

senses.note: Invariable: la/le nazionalità.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin nātiōnem.
From Latin inde (“thence, from that place; from that person, of them”). Compare French en (adverb, pronoun).

fact.text: Comes from Latin inde, 'from there, of them'. It is the same source as French en, as in j'en ai deux, which works just like Italian ne ho due.

senses.note: Replaces di + noun: Ne ho due = I have two (of them). Also 'from there': me ne vado.

etymology: Univerbation of né + anche.

fact.text: Made by joining né + anche, literally 'nor also'. Its twins nemmeno (né + meno) and neppure (né + pure) mean the same thing.

senses.note: Neanche io = me neither. Also 'not even': neanche un euro. Same as nemmeno and neppure.

etymology: From Latin nebula, through a contracted Vulgar Latin form *nebla. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud”). Compare Sicilian negghia, Venetan nebia, Spanish niebla, Romanian negură and Aromanian negurã. Doublet of nebula, which was borrowed.

fact.text: This comes from Latin nebula 'mist, cloud', the same word astronomers borrowed for nebulae. German Nebel 'fog' is a distant cousin.

senses.note: C'è nebbia = it's foggy.

etymology: From Latin necessārius.
