senses.note: è necessario + infinitive, or è necessario che + subjunctive. il necessario = the essentials.

etymology: From Latin negāre.

features.construction: negare qualcosa / di + inf. / che + congiuntivo

senses.note: negare di + infinitive; negare che + subjunctive (Nega che sia vero).

etymology: From Latin negātīvus.
Borrowed from Latin negōtium, possibly a semi-learned term. First attested 14th century.

fact.text: From Latin negotium, 'business', which is literally nec + otium, 'not leisure'. English 'negotiate' comes from the same word.

senses.note: Negozio di scarpe = shoe shop.

fact.text: Italian joins prepositions to the article that follows. In + il always becomes nel, never 'in il': nel paese (in the village), nel tuo nome (in your name). Its plural is nei: nei libri.

senses.note: in + il. Use nello before s+consonant, z, gn, ps (nello zaino) and nell' before a vowel.

etymology: From Latin inimīcus, with the loss of the first syllable.

fact.text: It comes from Latin inimicus, literally 'not a friend' (in- + amicus). Italian lost the first syllable.

senses.note: Also an adjective: un paese nemico (an enemy country). Feminine form: nemica.

etymology: Univerbation of né + meno, but may also continue Latin nē minimum (quidem) (literally “not even a little”), with the superlative replaced by the comparative, and nec minus (literally “nor any less, and just as much > and even”)).

fact.text: Formed from né 'nor' plus meno 'less', so it is literally 'nor less'.

senses.note: Takes non after the verb: non lo so nemmeno. Nemmeno io = me neither. Same as neanche and neppure.

etymology: From neo- + nato.

senses.note: Feminine: la neonata. Literally 'new-born' (neo + nato).

etymology: From Latin nigrum.

senses.note: Lavoro in nero = off-the-books work. Essere nero = to be furious (colloquial).

etymology: From Latin nervus. Doublet of nerbo.

fact.text: Comes from Latin nervus, which first meant tendon. It is related to Greek neuron.

senses.note: In the plural it can mean nerves or jitters. Avere i nervi = to be on edge, irritable.

etymology: From Latin nervōsus.

fact.text: Partly a false friend. Italians often use nervoso to mean irritable or cross, so mi fai venire il nervoso means 'you're getting on my nerves', not 'you make me anxious'.

senses.note: Often means irritable: sono nervoso can mean 'I'm on edge' or 'I'm in a bad mood'.

fact.text: Traditionally traced to Latin ne ipse unus, 'not even one'. In Italian versions of the Odyssey, Ulysses tells the Cyclops his name is Nessuno.

senses.note: Shortens like uno: nessun libro, nessuna idea. Singular only; needs non after the verb.

etymology: From Latin nē (“not”) + ipse (emphatic, literally “himself”) + ūnus (“one”), by surface analysis “not even one”. Cognate with Neapolitan nisciuno, Sardinian nisciunu, Friulian nissun, Ligurian nisciǜn, and Old French neisune. Compare Spanish ninguno and Romanian niciun.

fact.text: Traditionally traced to Latin ne ipse unus, 'not even one'. In Italian versions of the Odyssey, Ulysses tells the Cyclops his name is Nessuno.

senses.note: Before the verb there's no non: Nessuno viene. After it you need non: Non viene nessuno.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *nittus, a syncopation of Latin nitidus. Doublet of nitido, which is borrowed.

fact.text: Comes from Latin nitidus, meaning shining or clean. English net, as in net weight, comes from the same root through French net, meaning clean or with nothing extra.

senses.note: Un no netto = a flat no; un taglio netto = a clean cut. Also means net (peso netto = net weight).

etymology: Inherited from Latin nivem, from Proto-Italic *sniks, from Proto-Indo-European *snígʷʰs. Compare Portuguese neve, Spanish nieve.

fact.text: Shares a Proto-Indo-European root with English snow. Latin dropped the initial s- (nix, nivis) but Germanic kept it. Sierra Nevada means 'snowy range' in Spanish.

senses.note: Usually uncountable. The plural nevi is literary: le nevi del Kilimangiaro.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nivicāre, a verb based on Latin nivem (“snow”, noun). By surface analysis, neve + -icare. Cognate with Sicilian nivicari.

senses.note: Impersonal: nevica. Both è nevicato and ha nevicato are correct.

ignored: Elided form of niente, which is studied on its own card.

senses.note: Shortened niente before a vowel: nient'altro = nothing else.

etymology:
From an earlier neente, either from Latin ne gentem (“no person, no one”), nec entem, ne entem, or ne inde. Compare Old Catalan nient, Sicilian nenti, Piedmontese gnente, Occitan neient, French néant.
The regional pronunciation with initial self-gemination of /nj-/ is by speakers who try to correct the /ɲ-/ because of the orthography, but keep the syllable structure, and thus gemination, of the original /ɲ-/.

senses.note: After the verb it needs non: non ho visto niente. Synonym: nulla.

etymology: From Latin nepōtem, from Proto-Italic *nepōts, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *népōts. Compare French neveu, Romanian nepot, Catalan and Occitan nebot, Sicilian niputi and Persian نوه.

fact.text: From Latin nepos (grandson, nephew). English nepotism comes from Italian nepotismo, coined for Renaissance popes who gave powerful posts to their 'nephews'.

senses.note: Same word for both sexes: il nipote / la nipote. Context decides nephew vs grandchild.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nōn.

senses.note: At the end of a sentence it works as a tag question: È bello, no? = It's nice, isn't it?

etymology: Borrowed from English no.
ignored: Rare English-borrowed determiner (no-vax, no comment); the ordinary 'no' is studied on the adverb card no.

senses.note: Only in English loan expressions: no comment, no-vax, no logo. Invariable.

etymology: From Latin nōs, from Proto-Italic *nōs.

senses.note: Often left out because the verb ending shows the subject. Use it for emphasis or contrast.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan enojos.

fact.text: Came in through Old Occitan from Latin 'in odio' ('in hatred'), the same source as English 'annoy'.

senses.note: Can also mean 'annoying, tiresome', especially of people. Related noun: la noia (boredom).

etymology: From nolo (“hire”) + -eggiare.

senses.note: Typical for cars, bikes, boats, equipment; for flats and houses Italians usually say affittare.

etymology: From Latin nōmen.

senses.note: Often means first name; surname is cognome. In grammar it also means 'noun'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nōn.

senses.note: Goes before the verb: non parlo. Double negatives are normal: non vedo niente.

etymology: From Late Latin nonna.

fact.text: English 'nun' comes from the same Late Latin word, nonna. It was a respectful title for older women and nuns.

senses.note: i nonni = grandparents (or grandfathers).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin nonnus.

senses.note: Grandmother is la nonna.

etymology: Univerbation of non + ostante. Compare Portuguese não obstante, Spanish no obstante, French nonobstant.

fact.text: Literally non + ostante, 'not standing in the way', from Latin obstare (source of 'obstacle'). English 'notwithstanding' is built the same way: not + withstanding.

senses.note: Preposition: nonostante la pioggia. As a conjunction it takes the subjunctive: nonostante sia tardi.

etymology: Via Spanish and French, ultimately from Old English norþ.

senses.note: Invariable. Il Nord often means Northern Italy. A nord di = north of.

etymology: From Latin nōrmālis.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural normali.

etymology: Borrowed from New Latin nostalgia, coined from Ancient Greek νόστος (nóstos, “returning home”) + ἄλγος (álgos, “pain”).

fact.text: Coined in 1688 by the Swiss medical student Johannes Hofer from Greek nostos (homecoming) and algos (pain). He used it for an illness he saw in homesick Swiss soldiers.

senses.note: Also homesickness. Avere nostalgia di qualcuno = to miss someone.
Usually takes the article: il nostro, la nostra, i nostri, le nostre. Also means 'ours'.

etymology: From Latin nostrum, from Proto-Italic *nosteros.

senses.note: Agrees with the thing owned: nostro/a/i/e. Usually takes the article: il nostro amico.

etymology: From Latin nostrum, from Proto-Italic *nosteros.

senses.note: Usually with the article: il nostro, la nostra. After essere it often drops it: è nostro.
Used for written and musical notes. prendere nota = to take note. Also a bill or list.
Notare che… = to notice that… Also 'to note, point out'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin nōtitia.

fact.text: From Latin notitia 'knowledge, acquaintance', which also gave English notice (through French).

senses.note: Countable: una notizia = a piece of news; le notizie = the news. Una buona notizia = good news.

etymology: From the Latin nōtus (“known; notorious”).

fact.text: From Latin notus 'known', which is also the source of English notorious, notion and notify (through related words).

senses.note: è noto che... = it is well known that...

fact.text: Comes from Latin nox, which goes back to Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts, the same ancestor as English night. Latin nox also gives English nocturnal.

senses.note: Buona notte = good night, said when going to bed. Di notte = at night.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *nōvāgintā, from Latin nōnāgintā (blended with novem (“nine”)), from earlier *nūnāgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥(d)ḱomt (“nine tens”).
From novanta (“ninety”) + cinque (“five”).

etymology: From Latin novem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with Portuguese nove, Spanish nueve.
From nove (“nine”) + cento (“hundred”).
Inherited from Latin novembrem.

fact.text: From Latin novem, 'nine'. In the early Roman calendar the year began in March, so November was the ninth month.

senses.note: Months are lowercase in Italian: a novembre = in November.

etymology: From earlier novitade, novitate, from Latin novitātem (“newness, novelty”).

senses.note: Invariable: una novità, due novità. 'Ci sono novità?' = Any news?

etymology: From Latin nūbilis.

fact.text: From Latin nubilis, 'marriageable'. In Italian it is just the neutral official word for an unmarried woman.

senses.note: Only for women; an unmarried man is celibe. Typical on official forms.

etymology: From nucleo + -are.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural nucleari. E.g. energia nucleare, centrale nucleare.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nūlla, feminine singular and neuter plural (collective) of nūllus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin nullus, 'none', the same word behind English null, nullify and annul.

ignored: Duplicates the pronoun card nulla ('nothing'), where this meaning is studied.

senses.note: Like niente; needs non before the verb: non vedo nulla.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nūlla, feminine singular and neuter plural (collective) of nūllus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin nullus, 'none', the same word behind English null, nullify and annul.

senses.note: A synonym of niente. After a verb it needs non: Non cambia nulla.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin numerus, whence also Italian novero (an inherited doublet).

senses.note: Numero di telefono = phone number. Also means a shoe size or an issue of a magazine.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *nŏra, from Late Latin nura, from Classical Latin nurus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *snusós.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin nurus and Proto-Indo-European *snusós. Old English had a cognate, snoru (daughter-in-law), but modern English has lost it.

senses.note: Son-in-law is genero.

etymology:
From older notare, from Vulgar Latin *notāre, from Latin natāre. Compare Corsican nutà, Romanian înota.
The original Italian notare had no diphthong in the infinitive, but it did have conjugations such as nuota (“swims”), reflecting the regular diphthongization of Latin /ŏ/ in a stressed open syllable. Eventually the diphthong spread to all forms of the verb, including the infinitive.
Doublet of natare.

fact.text: It comes from Latin natare. The 'uo' began in stressed forms like nuota and later spread to the whole verb.

etymology: From nuotare.

senses.note: Usually uncountable: fare nuoto = to go swimming as a sport. Verb: nuotare.

etymology: Inherited from Latin novus, from Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, from the root *new-.

fact.text: Same word as English 'new'. Both come from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, which also gave Greek néos (as in neon) and Sanskrit náva.

senses.note: Before a noun it can mean 'another' (un nuovo lavoro). 'Di nuovo' = again.

etymology: Inherited from Latin nūtrīre.

fact.text: From Latin nutrire 'to suckle, nourish', the source of English nourish and nutrition. English nurse comes from the related nutrix 'wet nurse'.

senses.note: Means to nourish; for everyday feeding (e.g. a pet) dare da mangiare is more common. Also: nutrire speranza.

etymology: From a Latin nūbila, noun use of the feminine of nūbilus (“cloudy”), from nūbēs. Cognate with Sicilian nuvula. Compare Catalan núvol.

senses.note: nube is a more literary synonym.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin nūbilōsus, from Latin nūbilus. By surface analysis, nuvola + -oso.

senses.note: Opposite: sereno (clear). From nuvola, 'cloud'.

etymology: From Latin nec.

senses.note: né… né = neither… nor. The accent tells it apart from ne (of it, some).

etymology: From Latin aut.

senses.note: o... o... = either... or... Sometimes written od before a vowel.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin obligāre.

senses.note: obbligare qualcuno a fare qualcosa = to force someone to do something.
Also translates compulsory or obligatory. Note the double b.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin obiectīvus.

fact.text: This word also means a camera lens. Like the 'objective lens' in optics, it is the lens facing the object you photograph. A photographer is said to be davanti all'obiettivo, in front of the lens.

senses.note: raggiungere un obiettivo = to reach a goal. Also a camera lens. As an adjective it means objective or impartial.

etymology: From Latin obiectiōnem.

senses.note: Fare/sollevare un'obiezione = to raise an objection.

etymology: From Latin obsolētus.
Borrowed from Latin occāsiōnem, whence also Italian cagione (an inherited doublet).

fact.text: Italian shop signs reading 'occasione' are advertising a bargain, and 'un'auto d'occasione' is a second-hand car.

senses.note: cogliere l'occasione = to seize the opportunity; in occasione di = on the occasion of

etymology: From occhio (“eye”) + -ale.

senses.note: Almost always plural: gli occhiali. Occhiali da sole = sunglasses.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *oculāta, ultimately from Latin oculus (“eye”). Or by surface analysis, occhio + -ata.

senses.note: Dare un'occhiata = to take a look / have a glance.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin oclus, syncopated from Latin oculus, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃okʷ-, *h₃ekʷ- (“eye; to see”). Doublet of oculo, a borrowing.

fact.text: Italians say 'Occhio!' to mean 'Watch out!', often while pulling down the lower eyelid with a finger, a classic Italian hand gesture.

senses.note: Plural occhi. Occhio! = Watch out!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin occupāre.

senses.note: occupato = busy, taken or engaged (a seat, a phone line). occuparsi di = to take care of or deal with.
Followed by di: Me ne occupo io = I'll take care of it. Also 'to work in': si occupa di marketing.
senses.prompt: to take care of, to deal with

senses.note: Used for people and for things in use: phone line, toilet, seat (È occupato? = Is it taken?).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ōceanus, from the name of the deity Ōceanus, from Ancient Greek Ὠκεᾰνός (Ōkeănós).

fact.text: Named after Okeanos, the Greek god of a giant river that people believed flowed around the edge of the flat world.

etymology: From odio (“hatred”) + -are (1ˢᵗ conjugation verbal suffix).

fact.text: Built from odio 'hatred', which comes from Latin odium. English has the same root in odious.

senses.note: Regular -are verb: odio, odi, odia… Ti odio = I hate you.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin odium (“hate”), whence also uggia, inherited through Vulgar Latin.

fact.text: Comes from Latin odium 'hate', which also gave English the word odious.

senses.note: Don't confuse it with (io) odio, 'I hate', from odiare.

etymology: From Latin odōrāre (“to perfume, make fragrant”), derived from odor (“smell”).

senses.note: Also 'smell of': odorare di. Everyday speech often uses annusare or sentire l'odore.

etymology: From Latin odōrem, from an archaic form odōs, from Proto-Italic *odōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃édos, derived from the root *h₃ed- (“to smell, stink”). Doublet of aulore and olore.

fact.text: It comes from the same ancient root for smelling as Greek ozein ('to smell'). That Greek word gave English 'ozone', named for its sharp smell.

senses.note: In the plural, gli odori can also mean kitchen herbs (soup greens).

etymology: From the feminine of the past participle of offrire, or from Medieval Latin or Late Latin offerta, ultimately from Latin offerō. Compare Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan, and Sardinian oferta; Friulian ufierte; Romansh offerta; Sicilian ufferta.

senses.note: in offerta = on special offer; offerta di lavoro = job offer.
A legal offence is un reato, not un'offesa. Offesa is also the feminine of offeso, 'offended'.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *offerīre, from Latin offerre.

senses.note: Also 'to treat, to pay for': Offro io! = It's on me! Irregular past participle: offerto.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin obiectum.

fact.text: In Italian emails and business letters, the subject line is labelled 'Oggetto:', the way English uses 'Subject:' or 'Re:'.

senses.note: In emails and formal letters, 'Oggetto:' is the subject line.

etymology: Inherited from Latin hodiē.

fact.text: Comes from Latin hodie, a fusion of hoc die, 'on this day'. French aujourd'hui contains the same Latin word, hidden in the 'hui' at the end.

senses.note: Also 'nowadays': oggi i giovani… = young people nowadays…

etymology: From oggi (“today”) + giorno (“day”).

fact.text: Literally 'today-day': oggi comes from Latin hodie, 'on this day', and giorno is added on, so the word says 'day' twice.
Comes from Latin omnis 'all, every', the same root behind English omnibus, omnipotent and omnivore.

senses.note: Invariable. Always followed by a singular noun: ogni giorno = every day.

etymology: From ogni (“each, every”) + uno (“one”).

senses.note: Always takes a singular verb: ognuno ha. Feminine form: ognuna.

etymology: Onomatopoeic; compare Latin ō.

ignored: It is an English loanword with no dictionary data, so it isn't worth an Italian card.

senses.note: Italian equivalents: va bene, d'accordo.

etymology: From Latin olfactus, derived from olfaciō (“to smell, scent”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin olfacere 'to smell', literally 'to make a smell' (olere 'to smell' + facere 'to make'). English 'olfactory' comes from the same source.

senses.note: Somewhat technical; il senso dell'olfatto. Everyday verb: sentire l'odore.

etymology: From Latin oleum, from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).

fact.text: Comes from Latin oleum, from Greek elaion, which meant 'olive oil'. English 'oil' comes from the same Latin word, so oil originally just meant olive oil.

senses.note: Olio d'oliva = olive oil.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin ultra, from ulter.
Cognate with French outre, from Old French oltre.

fact.text: From Latin ultra 'beyond', which gave the English prefix ultra-, as in ultraviolet. Italian oltremare means 'overseas', the same idea as ultramarine.

senses.note: Oltre a = besides, in addition to: oltre a me = apart from me.

etymology: From Latin umbra, probably from Old Latin *omra, possibly from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂mr-u-, *h₂mrup-.

fact.text: In Venice, ombra also means a small glass of wine. It's said wine sellers in St Mark's Square moved their stalls to follow the bell tower's shadow to keep the wine cool.

senses.note: all'ombra = in the shade. In Venice, un'ombra is also a small glass of wine.

etymology: Variant of ombrella.

fact.text: English 'umbrella' was borrowed from Italian ombrella, a diminutive of ombra ('shade'). It was a 'little shade', first used as a sunshade rather than against rain.

senses.note: An ombrellone is a large beach umbrella or parasol.

etymology: Borrowed from French omelette.

fact.text: Goes back to Old French alemelle 'thin blade', from Latin lamella 'small thin plate'. The idea was the dish's flat, thin shape.

senses.note: Invariable French loan: l'omelette, le omelette. Italian 'frittata' is similar.

etymology: From Latin homicīdium.

fact.text: Comes from Latin homicidium, 'man-killing' (homo 'man' + caedere 'to kill'), which is also the source of English homicide.

senses.note: tentato omicidio = attempted murder; omicida = murderer.

ignored: Archaic/regional variant of uomo, which should be studied instead; the context is only a dialect name.

senses.note: Archaic/regional (Tuscan, Roman) form of uomo. Standard: l'uomo, gli uomini.

etymology: From Latin unda, from nasalized form of Proto-Indo-European *wódr̥ (“water”).

fact.text: Latin unda 'wave' also lies behind English undulate, inundate and abound. It's also behind redundant, which literally means 'overflowing'.

senses.note: Also radio/sound waves; andare in onda = to go on air.

etymology: From Latin honestus, from honor.

senses.note: Can also mean fair or reasonable: un prezzo onesto = a fair price.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin honestātem.

senses.note: Invariable noun.

etymology: Inherited from Latin honōrem.

senses.note: Fare gli onori di casa = to act as host.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin honōrābilis, remodelled with the suffix -evole. Doublet of onorabile.

fact.text: In Italy this is also the title for members of parliament: journalists say 'l'onorevole Rossi', and 'gli onorevoli' is a common way to refer to MPs.

etymology: Inherited from Latin opera.

fact.text: Latin opera was originally the plural of opus 'work', later reread as a feminine singular. English borrowed 'opera' from Italian: the musical work par excellence.

senses.note: A work or deed: un'opera d'arte. A job is il lavoro. Also means 'opera' (music).

etymology: From Latin operārius. By surface analysis, from operare + -aio

senses.note: Means a manual or blue-collar worker; feminine operaia. A worker in general is lavoratore.

etymology: From Latin operātiōnem.

senses.note: Used in every sense, including surgery (subire un'operazione), military operations and maths.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin opīniōnem.

senses.note: Secondo me / a mio parere = in my opinion.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin opportūnitātem.

senses.note: Invariable: le opportunità. Can also mean appropriateness (l'opportunità di una scelta).

etymology: From Latin opportūnus.

fact.text: Latin opportunus is traditionally explained as ob portum, 'toward the harbour', like a wind carrying ships into port. English 'opportunity' comes from the same word.

senses.note: È opportuno + infinitive = it's advisable to... Al momento opportuno = at the right moment.

etymology: Univerbation of o + pure; compare Lombard opur, Piedmontese opura.

senses.note: A stronger form of o, often between clauses. Can also mean 'or else'.

etymology:
Derived from Latin hōrā, ablative case of hōra (“hour”).
Compare Old French ore, Spanish ahora and Portuguese agora.

fact.text: From Greek hora via Latin, the same source as English 'hour'. 'Horoscope' contains it too: literally an 'hour-watcher', because it is read from the time of your birth.

senses.note: Same as adesso. The noun ora = hour/time: è ora di mangiare = it's time to eat.

etymology: Inherited from Latin hōra (“hour”), from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, “hour”).

fact.text: From Greek hora via Latin, the same source as English 'hour'. 'Horoscope' contains it too: literally an 'hour-watcher', because it is read from the time of your birth.

senses.note: Che ora è? / Che ore sono? = What time is it? The adverb ora means 'now'.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin hōrārium. Cognate with Piedmontese orari.

fact.text: As an adjective it means 'of the hours'. That is why clockwise is 'in senso orario' (in the direction of the hours) and anticlockwise is 'in senso antiorario'.

senses.note: Also means opening or working hours: orario d'ufficio = office hours.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ōrdināre.

senses.note: Covers ordering food or goods and giving commands. It can also mean to tidy or arrange.

etymology: From Latin ōrdinem.

fact.text: In a restaurant, the waiter takes your order with the word ordinazione, not ordine: 'Posso prendere l'ordinazione?'

senses.note: 'Fino a nuovo ordine' = until further orders. 'Dare un ordine' = to give an order.

etymology: From orecchia f.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin auricula, 'little ear', a diminutive of auris. Italian and French (oreille) kept the cute diminutive form. English 'auricle' comes from the same word.

senses.note: The plural is usually le orecchie (feminine); gli orecchi is also used. avere orecchio = to have an ear for music.

etymology: From Latin organicus.

senses.note: The food-waste category in Italian separate waste collection (raccolta differenziata).

etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin organizāre (“to organize”).

senses.note: Also 'to arrange, set up': organizzare una festa.
Reflexive of organizzare; uses essere: ci siamo organizzati = we got organized.

etymology: From organizzare + -zione.

senses.note: Means both the planning of something and an organized body (e.g. un'organizzazione no profit).

etymology: From Latin orīginālis.

senses.note: Same form for m/f; plural originali. Of a person it can also mean eccentric.

etymology: From orizzonte (“horizon”) + -ale.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine. Plural: orizzontali.

etymology: From ora (“now”) + mai (“ever, never”). Compare Piedmontese oramai, French désormais.

fact.text: Built from ora (now) + mai (ever), roughly 'now and from now on'. French désormais is a similar compound.

senses.note: Often sounds resigned: Ormai è troppo tardi = It's too late now.

etymology: From Latin aurum, from earlier ausum, from Proto-Italic *auzom, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éh₂usom (“glow”), derived from the root *h₂ews-.

fact.text: Latin aurum gives gold its chemical symbol Au. It probably comes from a root meaning 'to dawn, glow', the same root behind Aurora, goddess of the dawn.

senses.note: Plural gli ori = gold jewellery.

etymology: From Latin hōrologium, from Koine Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion).

fact.text: Comes from Greek hōrologion, 'hour-teller', via Latin horologium.

senses.note: One word for both wristwatch and clock. Orologio da polso = wristwatch.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin horribĭlis.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural orribili.

etymology: From Latin urtīca. Compare Sicilian ardìcula.

senses.note: gettare alle ortiche = to throw away, give up (a career, etc.).

etymology: From Late Latin ausāre, frequentative from Latin audēre.

fact.text: From Late Latin ausare, built on audere 'to dare'. Audere is the same root behind English audacious and audacity.

senses.note: Osare + infinitive, no preposition needed. Non osare! = Don't you dare!

etymology: From earlier *ospetale, from Late Latin hospitāle (“hospice, shelter, guesthouse”), substantivization of Latin hospitālis (“hospitable; pertaining to a host or guest”). Doublet of ospitale and hotel, which were borrowed from Latin and French respectively.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin hospitale, a guesthouse. The same source gave English hospital, hostel and hotel, all of them places that take in guests.

senses.note: in ospedale = in/to hospital. Plural: gli ospedali.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin hospitālitātem.

fact.text: Latin hospes meant both 'host' and 'guest'. It is the same root behind ospite, which in Italian can also mean either one.

senses.note: Invariable feminine noun ending in -tà.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin hospitāre (or hospitor, hospitārī), from Latin hospes. First attested 19th century.

fact.text: Comes from Latin hospes, which meant both 'host' and 'guest'. The same root gives English host, hospital, hostel, hotel and hospitality.

senses.note: Transitive: ospitare qualcuno = to have someone stay with you.

etymology: From Latin hospitem. Cognate to Italian oste (“innkeeper, landlord”).

fact.text: It means both guest and host, just like its Latin source hospes. That root also gives English host, hospital and hospitality.

senses.note: Same form for men and women: il/la ospite. It can also mean host, so context decides.

etymology: From Latin observāre.

senses.note: Also to remark or point out, and to keep or obey (osservare le regole).

etymology:
From Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst.
Compare Catalan, French, and Romanian os; Portuguese osso; Corsican, Sardinian, and Sicilian ossu; Spanish hueso.

fact.text: One of a few body words that switch gender in the plural: un osso becomes le ossa, just like il braccio becomes le braccia and il dito becomes le dita.

senses.note: Plural le ossa (feminine) for a skeleton's bones; gli ossi for separate bones, e.g. a dog's bones.

etymology: From Latin octāgintā, variant of octōgintā (“eighty”), from Proto-Indo-European *oktōḱomt, from earlier *oḱto(w)-dḱomt (“eight-ten”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + cinque (“five”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + due (“two”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + nove (“nine”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + quattro (“four”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + sei (“six”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + sette (“seven”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + tre (“three”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + otto (“eight”).
From ottanta (“eighty”) + uno (“one”).
From Latin obtinēre, probably a semi-learned borrowing.

senses.note: Conjugated like tenere: ottengo, ottieni, ottenni, otterrò. Ho ottenuto il lavoro = I got the job.

etymology: From French optimisme.

fact.text: From French optimisme, built on Latin optimum, 'the best'. It is the same root as Italian ottimo, 'excellent'. Voltaire's Candide, subtitled 'ou l'Optimisme', made the word famous.

senses.note: The -ista ending is the same for both genders in the singular. Plurals: ottimisti (m), ottimiste (f). Also means 'optimist'.

etymology: Calque of English optimize, from ottimo + -izzare.

fact.text: Modelled on English optimize and built from ottimo ('excellent, best', from Latin optimus) plus the verb ending -izzare.

etymology: From Latin optimus.

fact.text: Comes straight from Latin optimus, 'best', the source of English 'optimal' and 'optimist'. Like good/best in English, it is the irregular superlative of buono.

senses.note: Irregular superlative of buono (also buonissimo). Ottimo! = Great!

etymology: From Latin octō.

fact.text: From Latin octō, which is also behind English 'October', the eighth month of the old Roman calendar.

ignored: Using the number as a noun is a secondary use; the numeral otto is studied on its own card.

etymology: From Latin octō.

fact.text: From Latin octō, which is also behind English 'October', the eighth month of the old Roman calendar.

etymology: From Latin Octōbrem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin octo (eight). In the early Roman calendar the year began in March, which made October the eighth month.

senses.note: Italian month names are not capitalised: a ottobre = in October.

etymology: From otto (“eight”) + cento (“hundred”).
Borrowed from English outsider.

senses.note: English loanword, invariable: gli outsider. In sport it also means an underdog or dark horse.

etymology: From Medieval Latin ovālis.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin ovum, 'egg', so an oval is literally egg-shaped. Italian uovo, 'egg', comes from the same root.

etymology: Originated as an incorrect reading of a borrowing from French ouest, from Old English west. Doublet of vespro.

fact.text: Borrowed from French ouest, which comes from Old English west.

senses.note: Invariable. A ovest di = west of. Also called occidente.

etymology: From ove (“where”) + -unque (indefinite ending). Formed similarly to, and possibly influenced by, Latin ubīcumque.

senses.note: Also 'wherever' + subjunctive: ovunque tu vada. Synonym: dappertutto.

etymology: From ovvio + -mente.

fact.text: Ovvio, like English 'obvious', comes from Latin obvius, from ob viam, 'in the way'. Something obvious is literally lying right in your path.

senses.note: Often used alone as a reply meaning 'of course'.

etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin obvius.

fact.text: Like English obvious, it comes from Latin obvius, from ob viam, 'in the way'. Something obvious is literally right in your path.

senses.note: Ovvio! on its own means 'Of course!'

senses.note: Diminutive of pacco (parcel). Also a pack (pacchetto di sigarette) or a deal (pacchetto vacanze).

etymology: Borrowed from Middle Dutch pack (whence modern Dutch pak), from Old Dutch pac, *pakko, from Frankish *pakkō, from Proto-Germanic *pakkô (“bundle”).

fact.text: In slang it can also mean a con or swindle (fare il pacco a qualcuno), and 'tirare il pacco' means to stand someone up.

etymology: From Latin pācem (“peace”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ǵ-.

fact.text: Comes from Latin pax, pacem. Its old root meant 'to fasten', which is why English 'peace' and 'pact' are related: a peace was something agreed and fixed.

senses.note: 'Lasciare in pace' = to leave alone: Lasciami in pace! = Leave me alone!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pacificus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin pax (peace) + -ficus (making), so it literally means 'peace-making'. Magellan named the Pacific Ocean 'Mar Pacifico' after its calm waters.

senses.note: È pacifico che… = it's undisputed/obvious that… Plural: pacifici, pacifiche.

etymology: From earlier *patella, from Latin patella, diminutive of patera or patina.

fact.text: From Latin patella 'small dish', a diminutive of patina 'shallow pan'. English uses the same Latin word, patella, for the kneecap, which is shaped like a little dish.

senses.note: Dalla padella nella brace = out of the frying pan into the fire.

etymology: Derived from Old Italian patre, from Latin patrem, from Proto-Italic *patēr, from Proto-Indo-European *ph₂tḗr.

fact.text: English father shares its origin with Latin pater. In Germanic languages p became f, so pater and father are cousins.

senses.note: Parents = genitori, not padri. Also used as the title for priests: Padre Pio.

etymology: From earlier *patrone, from Latin patronus. Doublet of patron. Compare Sicilian patruni.

fact.text: From Latin patronus, from pater 'father', so it shares a root with English 'patron'.

senses.note: padrone di casa = landlord or host. Feminine: padrona. As 'boss' it can sound derogatory.

etymology: From paese + -aggio, based on French paysage. Compare also Spanish paisaje, Portuguese paisagem, Piedmontese paisagi, Sicilian pajisaggiu.

fact.text: Formed from paese (country) plus -aggio, on the model of French paysage. Spanish paisaje and Portuguese paisagem are built the same way.

senses.note: Also used for scenery or a view in general.

etymology: From Late Latin pāgēnsis (“inhabitant of a district”), from Latin pāgus (“village; district”). Compare Catalan, Portuguese, and Spanish país; French pays; Venetan pajès; Friulian paîs; Istriot and Piedmontese pais; Sicilian pajisi.

fact.text: From Late Latin pagensis, from pagus, a rural district. The same root gave English pagan, and through French pays it also gave peasant.

senses.note: Often capitalised for the nation: il Paese. Il Belpaese is a nickname for Italy.

etymology: Deverbal from pagare (“to pay”) + -a.

senses.note: Busta paga = pay slip; giorno di paga = payday. Plural: le paghe.

etymology: From pagare + -mento.

fact.text: The verb pagare comes from Latin pacare 'to pacify', from pax 'peace'. Paying a creditor calmed them down. English pay comes from the same word.

etymology: From earlier *pacare, inherited from Latin pacāre, from pax, pacis (“peace”). Doublet of pacare, a borrowing.

fact.text: Comes from Latin pacare 'to pacify', from pax 'peace', because paying a creditor calmed them down. English 'pay' comes from the same word via French payer.

senses.note: No 'per' needed: pagare il conto = to pay the bill; pagare la cena = to pay for dinner.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pāgina. Doublet of pania.

senses.note: a pagina 11 = on page 11.

etymology: From paglia (“straw”) + -accio. Originally in sense 3 exclusively, sense 1 developed as the traditional Italian character's outfit was made of the same fabric used to cover straw mattresses. Cognate with Piedmontese pajasso.

fact.text: Built from paglia 'straw'. It first meant a straw mattress. Clowns got the name because their costume was made from the same cheap cloth used to cover those mattresses.

senses.note: Also used as an insult: smetti di fare il pagliaccio = stop clowning around.

etymology: Back-formation as a masculine noun from the plural paia, from Latin paria (“even, equal”, neuter plural of pār). Cognate with Sicilian paru.

fact.text: The singular is masculine (il paio) but the plural is feminine (le paia). The plural comes from Latin paria, a neuter plural meaning 'equal things'.

senses.note: Plural turns feminine: un paio → due paia. Un paio di = a couple of / a pair of.

etymology: Inherited from Latin palātium (“palace, large residence”), from Palātium (“Palatine”), one of the seven hills of Rome. Cognate to English palace, French palais, Spanish palacio, Portuguese paço, palácio, see more at palātium.

fact.text: From Latin palatium, named after the Palatine Hill in Rome, where the emperors built their homes. English palace comes from the same hill.

senses.note: In everyday Italian it also means any large building or apartment block.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin palaestra, from Ancient Greek παλαίστρα (palaístra, “wrestling school”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek palaístra, a 'wrestling school'. Watch out: Italian ginnasio is not a gym. It is part of the classical secondary school (liceo classico).

senses.note: andare in palestra = to go to the gym.

etymology:
From Medieval Latin balla, palla, bala, from Frankish *ballu, from Proto-Germanic *balluz, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰoln- (“bubble”), from *bʰel- (“to blow, swell, inflate”).
Alternatively, via Lombardic *palla, from Proto-Germanic *ballô, from the same ultimate origin. Compare Sicilian baḍḍa.

fact.text: Che palle! (literally 'what balls!') is a very common, mildly vulgar way to say 'what a drag!'. Una palla also means something boring.

senses.note: Colloquially also 'a bore' or 'a lie' (raccontare palle). Plural palle is vulgar for testicles.

etymology: Calque of English basketball, from palla + canestro.

fact.text: A word-for-word translation of English 'basketball': palla (ball) + canestro (basket).

senses.note: Feminine because palla is feminine. In everyday speech Italians often say il basket.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pallidus, derived from palleō (“to be pale”).

fact.text: From Latin pallidus, from pallere, 'to be pale'. English got this word twice: 'pallid' directly from Latin, and 'pale' through Old French.

senses.note: Also figurative: una pallida idea = a faint idea.

fact.text: A chain of endings: palla (ball) becomes pallone (big ball, also a football), and then palloncino, literally a 'little big ball'.

etymology: From Latin panticem.

fact.text: English 'paunch' comes from the same Latin word, pantex ('belly'), by way of Old French panche.

senses.note: mal di pancia = stomach ache; a pancia in giù = face down.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pānem, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂- (“to feed, to graze”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin panis. English 'companion' literally means 'someone you share bread with' (com- 'with' + panis), and 'pantry' was once a bread store.

senses.note: Usually uncountable; pane tostato = toast.

etymology: From pane + -eria.

fact.text: Built on pane, bread, from Latin panis. The same root is in English companion, which literally means someone you share bread with.

senses.note: Many Italians also call the bakery il forno, literally the oven.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin panicus, from Ancient Greek πανικός (panikós, “pertaining to Pan”), from Πάν (Pán, “Pan”).

fact.text: Named after Pan, the Greek god of the wild. Sudden, groundless fear in lonely places was blamed on him, and English panic comes from the same Greek root.

senses.note: Common phrase: farsi prendere dal panico = to panic.

etymology: From pane (“bread”) + -ino (“small”).

fact.text: English treats 'panini' as one grilled sandwich, but in Italian panini is plural. Un panino is any filled roll, grilled or not. Literally 'little bread', from pane.

senses.note: Also a plain bread roll. Panini is the plural.

etymology: From Latin pannus (“cloth”).

fact.text: Italians put themselves in someone's clothes, not shoes: mettersi nei panni di qualcuno. And lavare i panni sporchi in famiglia means to keep your dirty laundry private.

senses.note: Plural panni = clothes or laundry. Nei panni di qualcuno = in someone's shoes.

etymology: From Latin papa, from Ancient Greek πάππας (páppas).

fact.text: Comes via Latin from Greek páppas, a baby word for 'father'. So the Pope is literally 'daddy', and papà (dad) shares the root. Only the stress tells them apart: PA-pa vs pa-PÀ.

senses.note: Stress on the first syllable: PA-pa. Don't confuse it with papà (dad), stressed on the last syllable.

fact.text: Stress changes everything: papà (stress on the end) is dad, but papa (stress on the first syllable) is the Pope.

senses.note: Invariable: i papà. Mind the accent: papa without it means pope.

etymology: From Latin paradīsus, from Ancient Greek παράδεισος (parádeisos).

fact.text: Via Greek parádeisos from an Old Iranian word for a walled enclosure or park. Paradise was originally a Persian royal garden.

senses.note: Heaven in the religious sense. Cielo is the sky (and also heaven).

etymology: Deverbal from parcheggiare + -o.

senses.note: Also a single parking space, or the act of parking.

etymology: From Old French parc. First attested in the 14th c.

fact.text: Watch out for a lookalike: the unrelated adjective parco means 'sparing, frugal' (parco nel mangiare, a light eater). It comes from Latin parcus, while the park comes from a Medieval Latin word for an enclosure.

senses.note: Plural parchi (with h). parco giochi = playground; parco nazionale = national park.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Latin pār. Doublet of pareglio and pariglio, both borrowed via Old French pareil. Compare Spanish parejo.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin pariculus 'little equal', from par 'equal', the root of English pair and par. The sense moved from 'similar' to 'a good amount of'.

senses.note: Adverb: ho dormito parecchio. As an adjective it agrees: parecchi libri = quite a few books.

etymology: From Latin parentem.

fact.text: This does not mean 'parent'! Your parents are i genitori. I parenti are relatives in general, such as cousins, aunts and uncles.

senses.note: il/la parente. Parents are i genitori, not i parenti.

etymology: From Late Latin parenthesis, from Ancient Greek πᾰρένθεσῐς (părénthesĭs).

senses.note: Plural doesn't change: le parentesi. Parentesi quadre = square brackets; graffe = curly braces.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pārēre, from Proto-Italic *pāzēō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s- (“watch, see”), s-present of *peh₂- (“protect”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin pārēre, 'to appear, be visible'. Add the prefix ad- and you get apparere, the source of English 'appear' and 'apparent'.

senses.note: A mio parere = in my opinion. More formal than opinione; used for expert or official opinions.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pārēre, from Proto-Italic *pāzēō, from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂-s- (“watch, see”), s-present of *peh₂- (“protect”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin pārēre, 'to appear, be visible'. Add the prefix ad- and you get apparere, the source of English 'appear' and 'apparent'.

features.construction: intransitive; often impersonal: (mi) pare che + subjunctive

senses.note: Mi pare che + subjunctive = I think that. Irregular: paio, pare; past participle parso.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin parētem, from Latin parietem m.

senses.note: Parete = the wall surface of a room or a rock face; muro = a wall as a structure, often outdoors.

ignored: Not Italian: an English name or brand with no dictionary meaning.
Imperative of parlare with an attached pronoun; the verb belongs on the parlare card.

senses.note: parla + ci: 'talk to us'. Parlaci di… = tell us about…

etymology: From parlare (“to speak”) + -mento (verbal action suffix).

fact.text: Built from parlare 'to speak' plus -mento, so a parliament is literally 'a talking'. English parliament comes from the same root, through Old French parlement.

senses.note: Italy's Parlamento has two chambers: the Camera dei Deputati and the Senato.

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin parabolāre.

fact.text: From Late Latin parabolare, from parabola 'parable, word'. The same root gave English parable, parley and parliament, which is literally a place for talking.

senses.note: parlare con/a qualcuno = to talk to someone; parlare di = to talk about.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *paraula, from Late Latin paravola, from Latin parabola (“comparison; later, speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of parabola, a borrowing. Compare with French parole, Catalan paraula, Sicilian palora and parola, Spanish palabra.

fact.text: From Latin parabola, 'comparison, parable', which later came to mean 'speech'. English 'parable' and 'parole' (release on a prisoner's word of honour) come from the same root.

senses.note: Also means 'word' as a promise: dare la propria parola = to give one's word.

etymology: Inherited from Latin partem, from Proto-Italic *partim.

senses.note: D'altra parte = on the other hand; dall'altra parte = on the other side.

etymology: From Latin participāre.

senses.note: Followed by a: partecipare a una riunione = to take part in a meeting.

etymology: From partire + -enza.

senses.note: in partenza = departing; punto di partenza = starting point

etymology: Borrowed from Latin particulāris.

senses.note: In particolare = in particular. Can also mean unusual or peculiar. As a noun, il particolare = detail.

etymology: From particolare + -mente.
Inherited from Latin partīre (“to divide”), from pars (“part”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin partire, 'to divide', from pars, 'part'. To leave was to part from someone. English depart has the same root.

senses.note: Takes essere. Partire per Roma = leave for Rome; partire da Milano = leave from Milan.

etymology: From partito, past participle of partire, from Latin partīre. Compare the similar development of French partie (“part; party, game”, etc.) from Old French partie (“party, gathering, group”, literally “part, section, division”), from Medieval Latin partīta.

fact.text: Freelancers in Italy talk about 'aprire la partita IVA', which means registering for a VAT number. Here partita means an accounting entry.

senses.note: Also a game of cards or chess: una partita a scacchi.

etymology: partire + -ito

fact.text: Comes from partire, which originally meant 'to divide' (Latin partire). A partito is a group that has split off. English 'party' and 'part' come from the same root.

senses.note: Only a political party. A party you celebrate at is una festa.

etymology: Borrowed from English partner.

senses.note: English loanword, invariable: il/la partner, i/le partner. Also means a business or dance partner.

etymology: From pascolo + -are.

features.construction: intransitive (also transitive: to put out to graze)

senses.note: Also transitive: pascolare le pecore = to graze the sheep. Noun: il pascolo = pasture.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pāscuum.

fact.text: From Latin pascere 'to graze, feed'. The same verb gave English pasture and pastor, which originally meant a shepherd leading his flock to graze.

senses.note: Also the act of grazing: portare le mucche al pascolo.

fact.text: From Latin pascha, via Greek, from Hebrew pesach 'Passover'. That is why the same word in Italian names both Easter and the Jewish Passover. Felice come una Pasqua means 'very happy'.

senses.note: Capitalised: Buona Pasqua! = Happy Easter. Pasquetta = Easter Monday.

etymology: From passare + -aggio, or from Old French passage.

fact.text: In everyday Italian, 'Mi dai un passaggio?' means 'Can you give me a lift?', so a passaggio is also a ride in someone's car.

senses.note: Passaggio pedonale = pedestrian crossing.

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of passa (“to pass”) + porto (“port”).

fact.text: Literally pass + port. It started as a permit to pass through a port or gate, and English passport has the same logic.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *passāre, derived from Latin passus (“step”, noun).

fact.text: Comes from Vulgar Latin *passare, from Latin passus 'a step'. Passus is also the source of English pace.

senses.note: Essere when intransitive (il tempo è passato), avere when transitive (ho passato l'esame).

etymology: From passare.

senses.note: In passato = in the past. Also past tense, and purée (passato di verdure).

etymology: From passo + -eggiare. Cognate with Sicilian passijari.

fact.text: The evening passeggiata is a cherished Italian ritual: people dress up and stroll slowly along the main street or piazza to see and be seen.

senses.note: A leisurely walk; camminare is the general verb for walking.
senses.prompt: to stroll, to take a walk

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of passeggiare (“to walk, stroll”). Cognate with Sicilian passijata.

fact.text: In many Italian towns people take a slow evening stroll along the main street or seafront to chat and be seen.

senses.note: Fare una passeggiata = to go for a walk. È una passeggiata! = It's a piece of cake!

ignored: In this context it is a form of the verb passare, not the noun 'strainer', so this is a bad parse.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin passiōnem.

fact.text: Latin passio meant 'suffering', from patior, 'to suffer'. That is why we speak of the Passion of Christ, and it is the root of English 'patient' too.

senses.note: Avere la passione per = to be passionate about, to love doing something.

etymology: From Latin passus (“a step”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin passus, a pace. The Romans measured distance in mille passuum, 'a thousand paces', and that phrase gave English the word mile.

senses.note: Tenere il passo = to keep pace; passo dopo passo = step by step.
