Inherited from Late Latin pasta, from Ancient Greek παστά (pastá).

fact.text: Goes back to Greek pastá, a barley porridge, from pássō, 'to sprinkle'. English 'paste', 'pastry' and 'pâté' come from the same root.

senses.note: Usually uncountable. The plural paste often means pastries or types of pasta.

etymology: From pasta (“pasta, dough”) + -iera (“-er, -or”).

fact.text: Naples' Easter classic: a shortcrust tart filled with ricotta, cooked wheat grains, candied fruit and orange-blossom water, with a lattice of pastry strips on top.

senses.note: Traditional Easter cake from Naples.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pāstus (“pasture, food”).

fact.text: From Latin pastus ('pasture, food'), from pascere ('to feed, graze'). It belongs to the same family as English 'pasture'.

senses.note: Don't confuse with pasta. Lontano dai pasti = between meals.

etymology: Borrowed from Spanish patata.

fact.text: Came via Spanish from Taíno batata, which actually meant the sweet potato. English potato has the same origin, while the Spanish word papa comes from Quechua.

senses.note: Patate fritte = chips/fries. Also a slang word for female genitals.

etymology: From Latin patentem.

fact.text: Not a patent, which is 'brevetto'. From Latin patens 'lying open', as in royal 'letters patent': open public documents that granted a right.

senses.note: prendere la patente = to get your driver's license.

etymology: From Latin patria (“fatherland”).

fact.text: Short for Latin terra patria, 'the father's land', from pater (father). English 'patriot' and 'patriotic' come from the same root.

senses.note: Has strong emotional or patriotic weight; for a neutral 'country' use paese.

etymology: From Latin patrōnus (“patron”).

fact.text: Every Italian town has a patron saint, and the saint's feast day is a local holiday. Milan celebrates Sant'Ambrogio on 7 December, and Rome celebrates Saints Peter and Paul on 29 June.

senses.note: Often appears as santo patrono. Can also mean patron or protector. Don't confuse it with padrone (owner, boss).

etymology: From Latin pactum from pacisci (“to make an accordance”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin pactum, from pacisci, to make an agreement. Its root is shared with Latin pax, peace, so a pact and peace are linguistic cousins.

senses.note: a patto che + subjunctive = provided that, on condition that

etymology:
Inherited from Latin pavor, with the ending replaced by -ura.
Compare French peur.

senses.note: avere paura di = to be afraid of; che paura! = how scary!

etymology: From Latin pausa.

senses.note: 'Pausa pranzo' = lunch break; 'fare una pausa' = to take a break.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pavīmentum. Doublet of Old Italian palmiento, inherited.

fact.text: False friend: this word means floor, not pavement. A British pavement (the US sidewalk) is il marciapiede. Pavimento and English pavement both come from Latin pavimentum, a rammed-down floor.

senses.note: The surface you walk on. A storey is piano.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin patientem, present active participle of patior (“to suffer”).

fact.text: From Latin patiens, from patior 'to suffer', so a patient is literally 'one who suffers'. English 'passion' comes from the same Latin verb.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il/la paziente, i/le pazienti. Also an adjective: 'patient'.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin patientia, derived from patiēns, present active participle of patior (“to suffer”).

fact.text: Said as an exclamation, Pazienza! is an everyday shrug meaning 'Oh well, never mind.' It comes from Latin patior, 'to suffer', since patience was originally the ability to endure.

senses.note: Pazienza! on its own means 'Oh well, never mind.'

etymology: From pazzo (“crazy”) + -esco.

senses.note: In casual speech it often means amazing: Una festa pazzesca! = An incredible party!

etymology:
Uncertain. Perhaps a Lombardic or Carolingian era borrowing from Old High German barrezzen (“to hate”) or maybe from French page (“page, serving boy”), probably via Neapolitan pazzo (compare French adage “être effronté comme un page”).
Alternatively from Latin patiēns (“suffering”). Compare Sicilian pacciu.

senses.note: Also a noun: un pazzo = a madman. Andare pazzo per = to be crazy about.

etymology:
Uncertain. Perhaps a Lombardic or Carolingian era borrowing from Old High German barrezzen (“to hate”) or maybe from French page (“page, serving boy”), probably via Neapolitan pazzo (compare French adage “être effronté comme un page”).
Alternatively from Latin patiēns (“suffering”). Compare Sicilian pacciu.
ignored: Noun use of the adjective pazzo (crazy), which is studied on the adjective card.

senses.note: Feminine: la pazza. Più comune come aggettivo: pazzo = crazy.

etymology: Inherited from Latin peccātum (“sin”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin peccatum 'sin', from peccare 'to sin'. English impeccable literally means 'unable to sin'.

senses.note: Plural peccati. The archaic plural peccata survives in old texts.

etymology: From pedo- + -iatra.

senses.note: Il pediatra (man) / la pediatra (woman); plural pediatri / pediatre. Same pattern as dentista.

etymology: From pedone + -ale.

fact.text: Built on pedone, which means both pedestrian and chess pawn. English pawn has the same source: via Old French, from Medieval Latin pedo, foot soldier.

senses.note: zona pedonale = pedestrian zone; strisce pedonali = zebra crossing. A pedestrian (person) is il pedone.

etymology: From Latin peius, from peior, peiōris.

fact.text: Comes from Latin peius, 'worse', the same root as English 'pejorative', a word that makes something sound worse than it is.

senses.note: Adverb, the comparative of male. The adjective is usually peggiore. Tanto peggio! = too bad!

etymology: From Late Latin peiōrāre (“worsen”), from Latin peiōrem (“worsen”). By surface analysis, peggiore + -are.

senses.note: Takes avere when transitive (to make worse) and essere when intransitive (to get worse): è peggiorato.

etymology: From Latin peiōrem, from Proto-Indo-European *ped-yōs (“to the ground, downward”).

senses.note: Il/la peggiore = the worst. The adverb 'worse' is peggio: sto peggio.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pellis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“to cover, wrap; skin, hide; cloth”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin pellis and is probably related to English 'pelt'. Italian pellicola (film) comes from Latin pellicula, which literally means 'little skin'.

senses.note: Also leather: una giacca di pelle (a leather jacket).

etymology: From Latin poena, from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ).

fact.text: Latin poena, borrowed from Greek poine ('blood money, fine'), is the source of English pain, penalty, penal and punish.

senses.note: Pena di morte = death penalty.

etymology: From penale + -ità.

senses.note: Invariable: la penalità, le penalità.

etymology: From pendere.

fact.text: Comes from pendere 'to hang, to lean', the same Latin root as English pendant, pendulum and depend.

senses.note: Plural pendii. Used for hillsides and ski slopes: un pendio ripido = a steep slope.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin pēnis.

fact.text: Latin pēnis first meant 'tail'. Its anatomical meaning began as a euphemism, and that is the meaning Italian and English both borrowed.

senses.note: Neutral anatomical term.

etymology: From Latin penna and pinna, from Proto-Italic *petnā, from Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ ~ pth₂én- (“feather, wing”).

fact.text: From Latin penna, 'feather'. The first pens were quills, and English 'pen' comes from the same word. Penne pasta is named after the slanted tip of a quill.

senses.note: Its first meaning is 'feather'.
English loanword used for the British coin.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pēnsāre (“weigh carefully”), frequentative of pendere. Doublet of pesare.

fact.text: From Latin pensare, 'to weigh carefully', so thinking is weighing. Its twin is pesare (to weigh). English pensive and even pansy (French pensée, thought) share the root.

features.construction: pensare a qc/qn; pensare di + inf.; pensare che + subj.

senses.note: pensare a = to think about. pensare di + infinitive. penso che + subjunctive.

etymology: Borrowed from Provençal pensier, from Latin pēnsāre. Compare Sicilian pinzeri.

fact.text: Came via Provençal from Latin pensare 'to weigh': thinking was seen as weighing things up. The same root gives English 'pensive'.

senses.note: stare in pensiero = to be worried; essere sopra pensiero = to be lost in thought

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pēnsiōnem. Doublet of pigione, which was inherited.

fact.text: From Latin pensio 'payment', from pendere 'to weigh out', because payments were once weighed. Its inherited twin is pigione, 'rent'.

senses.note: essere in pensione = to be retired; andare in pensione = to retire. Can also mean a small hotel or guesthouse.

etymology: From Late Latin (sē) paenitīre, from Latin paenitēre.

fact.text: From Latin paenitere, the root of English repent and penitent. A pentito, 'one who has repented', is a Mafia member who turns state's witness.

senses.note: Reflexive: mi pento di averlo detto. Non te ne pentirai = you won't regret it.

etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *pinta, alternative form of Latin picta (“painted [pot]”), feminine perfect passive participle of pingō (“to decorate; to paint”), from the custom of decorating crocks and pots by painting them.

fact.text: From Latin picta, 'painted (pot)', after the custom of painting crocks. It shares the root pingere with dipingere, 'to paint'.

senses.note: Saucepan or cooking pot. Pentola a pressione = pressure cooker.

etymology: From Latin piper, from Ancient Greek πέπερι (péperi, “pepper”), via Middle Persian from an Indo-Aryan source.

fact.text: Like English pepper, it goes back through Latin piper and Greek peperi to Sanskrit pippali, 'long pepper', after travelling the spice routes from India.

senses.note: Usually uncountable. Bell pepper (the vegetable) is 'il peperone'.

etymology: From Latin piper (“pepper”).

fact.text: False friend: if you order a pizza ai peperoni in Italy, you get bell peppers, not spicy sausage. The American 'pepperoni' salami is closer to salame piccante.

senses.note: peperoni ripieni = stuffed peppers. Chilli is peperoncino.

etymology: From Latin per, taking many roles from Latin pro.

fact.text: It shares an ancient Indo-European root with English 'for'. Its Latin parent per was also borrowed straight into English, as in 'per cent' and 'per day'.

senses.note: Also 'through' (per la strada) and 'in order to' before an infinitive (per vivere).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pira, from the plural of Latin pirum, reanalyzed as a feminine singular.

fact.text: Many fruits are feminine while their trees are masculine: la pera/il pero, la mela/il melo. Pera comes from the Latin plural pira, which was later taken for a feminine singular.

senses.note: The fruit is la pera; the tree is il pero.
Invariable; also written per cento or %: il dieci percento.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin perceptiōnem.

Univerbation of per (“for”) + che (“which”), probably inherited from Vulgar Latin. Compare Neapolitan pecché, Sicilian pirchì, and further Romance parallels such as Sardinian pro chite, French pourquoi, Spanish porque/por qué, Portuguese porque/por que.

fact.text: One word asks the question and gives the answer: Perché? Perché sì! (Why? Because!). It is per (for) + che (what), like French pourquoi.

senses.note: The same word answers too: Perché? – Perché sì! (Why? – Because!) Written with an acute accent: é.

etymology: Univerbation of per (“for”) + che (“which”), probably inherited from Vulgar Latin. Compare Neapolitan pecché, Sicilian pirchì, and further Romance parallels such as Sardinian pro chite, French pourquoi, Spanish porque/por qué, Portuguese porque/por que.

fact.text: One word asks the question and gives the answer: Perché? Perché sì! (Why? Because!). It is per (for) + che (what), like French pourquoi.

senses.note: Also means 'why?' in questions. With the subjunctive it means 'so that'.

etymology: Univerbation of per + ciò.

fact.text: Literally 'for that': per (for) plus ciò (that), fused into a single word. That is why it is stressed on the final ò.

senses.note: Introduces a consequence: Piove, perciò resto a casa.

etymology: Inherited from Latin percursus.

senses.note: Also a course or path (percorso a ostacoli = obstacle course) and, figuratively, a journey.

etymology: Inherited from Latin perdere. The variant past participle perso was created by analogy with preso, etc.

senses.note: Also 'to waste' (perdere tempo) and 'to miss' (perdere il treno). Past participle: perso or perduto.

etymology: From Latin perdita, the feminine of perditus. Compare French perte, Portuguese perda, and Spanish pérdida.

fact.text: Stress falls on the first syllable: PER-di-ta. It comes from perdere 'to lose', and the same word covers both a loss and a leak, since a leak is something being lost.

senses.note: una perdita di gas = a gas leak. Its main meaning is 'loss' (perdita di tempo = waste of time).

etymology: From Late Latin perdōnāre.

fact.text: Late Latin per + donare means 'to give completely'. English for-give is built the same way, and one of the two words may even be a calque of the other.

senses.note: Perdonami! = Forgive me! Also 'to pardon, excuse'.

etymology: Deverbal from perdonare (“to forgive”) + -o.

fact.text: Watch the stress: the noun is per-DO-no (forgiveness), while PER-do-no is 'they lose', from perdere.

senses.note: chiedere perdono = to ask for forgiveness.
Past participle of perdere. In everyday speech perso is more common; perduto sounds more literary.

etymology: From Latin perfectus.

senses.note: Perfetto! on its own = Great! / Perfect!

etymology: Univerbation of per + fino.

senses.note: Synonym of persino. Usually placed before the word it stresses: perfino lui = even him.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin perīculum. Doublet of the archaic inherited periglio.

fact.text: From Latin periculum, which also gives English peril and perilous. Signs reading 'Pericolo di morte' (danger of death) are common on Italian power lines.

senses.note: In pericolo = in danger. Adjective: pericoloso (dangerous).

etymology: Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin periculōsus. By surface analysis, pericolo + -oso.

fact.text: Built on pericolo, 'danger', from Latin periculum. The same Latin word gave English 'peril' and 'perilous'.

etymology: From peri- + feria.

fact.text: The same word as English 'periphery', from Greek periphéreia 'circumference': peri 'around' + pherein 'to carry'.

senses.note: Often suggests less well-off outer districts, unlike the leafy English 'suburbs'.

etymology: From Latin periodus, from Ancient Greek περίοδος (períodos, “circuit, period of time, path around”), from περι- (peri-, “around”) + ὁδός (hodós, “way”).

fact.text: Not the punctuation mark: the US 'period' (full stop) is punto in Italian. The word comes from Greek períodos, 'a way around', a cycle.

senses.note: In questo periodo = at this time, these days. In grammar it also means a complex sentence.

fact.text: Italians say 'Permesso?' politely as they step into someone else's home, and in crowds to ask people to let them pass.

senses.note: Also a permit or leave from work. 'Permesso?' = May I come in? / Excuse me, may I pass?

etymology: From Latin permittere.

fact.text: Its past participle permesso is also a polite word. Italians say 'Permesso?' when they enter someone's home or need to squeeze past people in a crowd.

senses.note: permettere a qualcuno di + infinitive. Irregular: permesso, permisi. Permettersi = to afford.

etymology: Univerbation of per + sino.

fact.text: Built from per + sino (an older form of fino, 'up to'), so it literally means 'up to'. That is the same idea as English 'going so far as'. The variant perfino is built the same way.

senses.note: Goes before the word it stresses: persino lui = even him. Same as perfino.

etymology: From Latin persōna (“person”), of Etruscan origin.

fact.text: Latin persona first meant an actor's mask and probably came from Etruscan. It gave English person, persona and personality.

senses.note: Always feminine, even when it refers to a man: è una brava persona.

etymology:
Borrowed from French personnage; persona + -aggio.
Compare Piedmontese përsonagi.

senses.note: Always masculine, even for women. Can also mean a public figure.

etymology: From Latin persōnālis.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine: problemi personali, vita personale.

etymology:
Borrowed from Late Latin persōnālitātem, from Latin persōna (“mask; character”), from Etruscan 𐌘𐌄𐌓𐌔𐌖 (φersu), from Ancient Greek πρόσωπον (prósōpon, “face; mask”).
Cognate with Piedmontese përsonalità.

fact.text: Built on Latin persona, an actor's mask. It is often traced to Etruscan phersu and Greek prosopon, face or mask, so a personality was once the mask you showed.

senses.note: Invariable. Also 'a public figure': una personalità della TV.

etymology: From personale + -mente.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin per hoc, 'through this', and first meant 'therefore'. Over time it shifted to 'but', the same meaning as its Spanish cousin pero.

senses.note: At the end of a sentence it works like English 'though'. It can also be a conjunction meaning 'but'.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin per hoc (“for this reason”, literally “through this”). The original meaning of però was “for this reason, therefore”. Cognate with Spanish pero, Old Franco-Provençal enperoi.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin per hoc, 'through this', and first meant 'therefore'. Over time it shifted to 'but', the same meaning as its Spanish cousin pero.

senses.note: Can also come later in the clause: È caro, è buono però. On its own, Però! means 'Wow, not bad!'
Same form for both genders. Colloquially, 'che pesante!' means 'what a bore!'

etymology: Inherited from Latin pēnsāre (“weigh, hang”), whence also the doublet pensare (“to think”). Compare French peser.

fact.text: Pesare and pensare (to think) both come from Latin pensare 'to weigh'. To think was to weigh things up. English ponder comes from Latin 'to weigh' too.

senses.note: Transitive: pesare la frutta. Intransitive: peso 70 chili = I weigh 70 kilos.

etymology: From Latin piscārī.

fact.text: The noun la pesca means 'fishing', but another word spelled la pesca means 'peach' (from Latin persica, 'Persian fruit'). The two are pronounced with a slightly different e.

senses.note: Andare a pescare = to go fishing. Also 'to catch' or 'to draw' (a card).

etymology: Inherited from Latin piscem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-.

fact.text: Latin piscem and English fish both go back to one Indo-European root. Latin p often matches English f, as in pater and father. The star sign Pisces is the same word.

senses.note: Pesce d'aprile = April Fool's joke.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pēsum, from Latin pēnsum.

fact.text: The peso currency is the same word in Spanish, meaning 'weight'. It was originally a coin of a set weight of silver, just as the pound began as a weight.

senses.note: Also gym weights: alzare pesi. Verb: pesare (to weigh).
Singular -ista is the same for both genders; plurals are pessimisti (m) and pessimiste (f). Also a noun: pessimist.

etymology: From Latin pessimus.

fact.text: From Latin pessimus, 'worst', which also gave English the word pessimist: someone who always expects the worst.

senses.note: Absolute superlative of cattivo. Peggiore = worse; pessimo = awful, very bad.

ignored: Not an Italian word; probably the English name Pete or a parsing fragment.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pectinem.

fact.text: From Latin pecten 'comb'. Scallops are called Pecten in biology because of their comb-like ridges, and in Italian pettine can also mean a scallop.

senses.note: Masculine despite the -e ending: il pettine, i pettini.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pectus, from Proto-Italic *pektos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peg- (“breast”). Compare Catalan pit, Portuguese peito, Romanian piept, Spanish pecho.

senses.note: Also breast meat: petto di pollo = chicken breast.

etymology: Variant of pezza.

fact.text: An important person is un pezzo grosso, literally 'a big piece', the Italian for a 'big shot' or 'bigwig'.

senses.note: Also a music track. Da un pezzo = for a while now.

fact.text: From German Föhn, a warm dry Alpine wind. AEG trademarked 'Fön' for its hairdryers in 1908.

senses.note: Invariable: i phon. Also spelled fon, which is the standard spelling.

etymology: Inherited from Latin placēre. Compare Romanian plăcea, French plaire, Occitan plaser.

fact.text: From Latin placēre, which also gave English please and pleasure. Mi piace la pizza literally means 'pizza is pleasing to me'.

senses.note: The thing liked is the subject: mi piace il caffè, mi piacciono i libri.

etymology: From piace(re) (“to be liked, to please”) + -evole.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine. Plural: piacevoli.

etymology: Derived from Late Latin planēta.

senses.note: Masculine despite the -a ending: il pianeta, i pianeti. La pianeta is a priest's chasuble.

etymology: Inherited from Latin plangō, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂k-. Compare Spanish plañir, Catalan plànyer, Romanian plânge, French plaindre.

fact.text: It comes from Latin plangere, 'to beat one's breast in grief'. The same root gives English plaintive and, through French, complain.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle pianto, passato remoto piansi. Used with an object it means 'to mourn': piangere un amico.

etymology: Inherited from Latin plānus. Compare Sicilian chianu.

fact.text: From Latin planus 'flat, smooth', the same root as English plain, plan and plane. The instrument is short for pianoforte, 'soft-loud', because it could play both quietly and loudly.

senses.note: Also 'softly, quietly': parla piano. Piano piano = little by little.

etymology: Inherited from Latin plānum, derived from plānus.

fact.text: From Latin planus 'flat, smooth', the same root as English plain, plan and plane. The instrument is short for pianoforte, 'soft-loud', because it could play both quietly and loudly.

senses.note: Also means floor/storey (al primo piano) and, as an adverb, slowly/softly (vai piano).

etymology: From Latin planta, from Proto-Italic *plāntā, from Proto-Indo-European *pléh₂-n̥t-eh₂, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat”).

fact.text: Latin planta also meant the sole of the foot, which is why the medical term is plantar fasciitis. In Italian, pianta del piede still means the sole of the foot.

senses.note: Also means a floor plan or map: la pianta della città.

etymology: From Latin plantāre. By surface analysis, pianta (“plant”) + -are. Compare Sicilian chiantari.

fact.text: Piantare in asso means to leave someone in the lurch. It probably started as piantare in Nasso, after Theseus abandoning Ariadne on the island of Naxos.

senses.note: Colloquially also 'to dump' someone (mi ha piantato). Piantarla = to stop it.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat”). Doublet of chiatto.

fact.text: Goes back to Greek platys, 'broad, flat', through Vulgar Latin *plattus. That is also where English 'plate' and 'platter' come from, and as an adjective piatto still means flat.

senses.note: As a noun, il piatto means 'plate, dish'. An apartment is un appartamento.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *plattus, from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “broad, flat”). Doublet of chiatto.

fact.text: Goes back to Greek platys, 'broad, flat', through Vulgar Latin *plattus. That is also where English 'plate' and 'platter' come from, and as an adjective piatto still means flat.

senses.note: Also a course or dish of food: primo piatto = first course. Lavare i piatti = to do the dishes.

etymology: From Latin platea, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa). Doublet of platea. Cognate with Portuguese praça, Spanish plaza, French place, German Platz.

fact.text: Comes from Greek plateia (hodos), 'broad way', via Latin platea. The same root gave English place, plaza and German Platz.

senses.note: Also 'market' or 'the public'. Scendere in piazza = to take to the streets.

etymology: Borrowed from Middle French, whence French piquant.

fact.text: From piccare, 'to prick, sting'. English 'piquant' and 'pique' come from the same root via French: spicy food pricks your tongue.

senses.note: Also strong (cheese: provolone piccante) and risqué (una battuta piccante).

etymology: Onomatopoeic, related to picca, piccare.

senses.note: picchiare qualcuno = to beat someone up; il sole picchia = the sun is beating down.

etymology: Borrowed from Neapolitan piccione, from Latin pīpiōnem. Doublet of pippione.

fact.text: From Latin pipio, 'chirping chick', which imitates the sound. The same word reached English through French as 'pigeon'.

etymology: From piccolo + -etto.

senses.note: Affectionate or teasing. Feminine: piccoletta.

etymology:
Uncertain. Possibly from:
* An onomatopoeic root or children's/nursery word *pikk-, *picc-.
* From Vulgar Latin *pikk (“little”), related to *piccāre (“to pierce”), from Proto-Indo-European *bew-, *bu- (“to make a dull, hollow sound”).
* From picca (“point”).
* From Vulgar Latin pittitus (“small, worthless”), which is linked to French petit and English piece.

fact.text: The tiny English flute called the piccolo is this word. It is short for Italian 'flauto piccolo', meaning 'small flute'.

senses.note: Can also mean young: da piccolo = as a child. Feminine: piccola.

etymology: From Latin pedem (“foot”), from Proto-Indo-European *pṓds. Compare Catalan peu, French pied, Piedmontese pé, Latvian pēda, Lithuanian pėdės, Portuguese pé, Sardinian pei, Spanish pie.

fact.text: Comes from Latin pes, pedis 'foot', the same root found in English pedal, pedestrian and pedicure.

senses.note: A piedi = on foot; in piedi = standing.

etymology: From earlier *piecare, from Latin plicāre, from Proto-Indo-European *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”).

fact.text: From Latin plicare 'to fold', the root behind English ply, pliable, complicate and explicit. Something complicated is literally 'folded together'.

senses.note: Piegare i vestiti = to fold clothes. Spelling: add h before e/i: pieghi, pieghiamo.

etymology: Inherited from Latin plēnus, from Proto-Italic *plēnos, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”). Compare Catalan ple, French plein, Portuguese cheio, Romanian plin, Sardinian prenu, Sicilian chinu, Spanish lleno.

fact.text: Comes from Latin plenus, meaning full. The same root gives English 'plenty'.

senses.note: Pieno di = full of. Fare il pieno = to fill up the tank. Pieno zeppo = jam-packed.

etymology: Inherited from Latin petra, from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, “stone, rock”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek petra, 'rock', the same word behind English 'petrify', 'petroleum' (rock oil) and the name Peter.

senses.note: Also stone as a material: un muro di pietra = a stone wall.

etymology: From Latin petrōsus or from pietra + -oso. Doublet of petroso.

senses.note: From pietra (stone) + -oso: terreno pietroso = stony ground.

etymology: Inherited from Old Italian pietade, pietate, from Latin pietātem (“piety”, “pity”). By surface analysis, pio (“pious”) + -età (“-ity”).

fact.text: English got both 'pity' and 'piety' from Latin pietas, and Italian keeps both meanings in this one word. English also borrowed it for art showing Mary holding the dead Christ, like Michelangelo's Pietà.

senses.note: Also religious piety. Avere pietà di qualcuno = to take pity on someone. Invariable: le pietà.

etymology: Borrowed from English pyjamas, pajamas, from Urdu پایجامه (pāyjāma)/Hindi पैजामा (paijāmā), from Persian پایجامه (pâyjâma), پاجامه (pâjâma, “leg garment”).

fact.text: Came into Italian through English from Hindi/Urdu, which took it from Persian pā-jāma, meaning 'leg garment'. It was originally loose trousers.

senses.note: Singular in Italian: il pigiama = a pair of pyjamas.

etymology: Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin pigrum. See also peritarsi, which was inherited from a derivative verb pīgritārī.
Borrowed from Latin pilula, pillula.

fact.text: From Latin pilula, 'little ball', a diminutive of pila ('ball'). Pila is said to be linked to pilus ('hair') because Roman balls were stuffed with hair, but that link is uncertain.

senses.note: La pillola on its own often means the contraceptive pill.

etymology: From earlier pedota, pedotta, from Byzantine Greek *πηδώτης (*pēdṓtēs, “helmsman”), from Ancient Greek πηδόν (pēdón, “oarblade, oar”). The pil- forms are probably influenced by pileggiare (“to sail, navigate”).

fact.text: Comes from Byzantine Greek for 'helmsman', based on Ancient Greek pedon, 'oar blade'. The first pilots steered ships, not planes.

senses.note: il/la pilota; plural piloti (m), pilote (f). Also means a racing driver.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *plo(v)ia. Doublet of ploia; piecewise doublet of piova.
Inherited from Latin plumbum.

fact.text: From Latin plumbum, which also gives the chemical symbol Pb and English 'plumber': Roman water pipes were made of lead.

senses.note: Uncountable as the metal. anni di piombo = the 'Years of Lead' (1970s terrorism in Italy)

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *plovere, from Classical Latin pluere.

senses.note: Impersonal: piove (it's raining). Past: è piovuto, or ha piovuto.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pipa, from Latin pipō (“to pip”).

fact.text: Comes from the same Vulgar Latin root *pipa as English pipe, but it only means the kind you smoke. A plumbing pipe is un tubo.

senses.note: Only a tobacco pipe. A water or gas pipe is un tubo.

etymology: Child speak, similar to French pipi.

senses.note: Childish/family word. Fare la pipì = to pee. Invariable.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin piscīna.

fact.text: Latin piscīna originally meant a fishpond, from piscis 'fish'. The meaning later shifted to any pool, and finally to the swimming pool.

senses.note: andare in piscina = to go to the pool.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pisellum, diminutive of Latin pisum, from Ancient Greek πίσον (píson).

fact.text: Both words go back to Latin pisum. English once said 'pease' for a single pea, then mistook it for a plural and created the new singular 'pea'.

senses.note: Usually plural: i piselli. Careful: it's also common slang for penis.

etymology: Variant of pesta (“footprint”), technical senses influenced by French piste.

senses.note: Also a ski run, runway, rink or dance floor (pista da ballo); seguire una pista = to follow a lead.

etymology: Borrowed from French pistole, from Czech píšťala (“firearm”, literally “tube, pipe”).

fact.text: Probably from Czech píšťala, 'pipe, whistle', the name Hussite fighters gave their tube-shaped firearms.

senses.note: A rifle is un fucile. Pistola ad acqua = water pistol.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pictōrem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin pictor, from pingere, 'to paint'. That is the same root as English picture, depict and pigment.

senses.note: Feminine: la pittrice. A house painter is un imbianchino.

etymology: From Latin pictūra.

senses.note: Also wall paint. A single painted picture is usually un quadro or un dipinto.

etymology: Univerbation of più + (archaic) tosto (adverb). Compare French plutôt and Catalan més aviat.

fact.text: Formed by joining più (more) and old tosto (soon), so it literally means 'sooner'. French plutôt (plus tôt) was built the same way.

senses.note: Piuttosto difficile = rather difficult. Piuttosto che = rather than.

etymology:
First attested in 1590, as Neapolitan pizza (Velardiniello, La storia de cient'anne arreto). Likely related to Byzantine Greek πίτα (píta, “cake, pie”) (12th century);
the origin of the Greek word is itself uncertain. Also possibly from Lombardic bizza (also pizza or bizzo (pizzo), which would rather suggest a north-to-south spread of the word. See the English and Greek entries for more detail.

fact.text: In colloquial Italian 'Che pizza!' means 'What a bore!'. A reel of film is also called a pizza, after its round flat can.

etymology: From pizza + -aiolo.

fact.text: In 2017 UNESCO added the art of the Neapolitan pizzaiuolo to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

senses.note: Feminine: pizzaiola. 'Alla pizzaiola' means cooked with tomato, garlic and oregano.

etymology: From pizza + -eria.
Deverbal from pizzicare + -o.

senses.note: un pizzico di sale = a pinch of salt. It can also be a pinch on the skin.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin plūs, from Old Latin *plous, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁-, *pelh₁u- (“many”).
The initial autogemination, though lost in standard pronunciation, is still found in most varieties of regional Italian. The gemination occurs predictably before the palatalization of the original liquid -l-, compare doppio, orecchio, etc.

fact.text: Comes from Latin plus, which is also the English word plus. In maths Italians say 'due più due' for 'two plus two'.

senses.note: il più = the most. non... più = no longer: non lavoro più.

etymology: From the adjective plastico (“plastic”), from Latin plasticus (“pertaining to moulding/molding or shaping”).

fact.text: Greek plastikós meant 'mouldable'. That's why plastic surgery means reshaping the body, not adding man-made material.

senses.note: Also short for plastic surgery; materie plastiche = plastics

etymology: Borrowed from Latin plūrālis.

senses.note: Also a noun: il plurale (the plural). Opposite: singolare.

etymology: From Latin pneumaticus, from Ancient Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikós, “relating to wind or air”), from πνεῦμα (pneûma, “wind, air, breath, spirit”), from πνέω (pnéō, “to blow, breathe”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek pneuma, meaning air or breath, because the tire is air-filled. English pneumatic and pneumonia come from the same Greek root.

senses.note: Standard article is lo/gli pneumatici, though il pneumatico is common in speech. Also gomma, colloquially.

fact.text: The short form po' takes an apostrophe, not an accent, because letters were dropped. Writing pò is a classic spelling mistake, even among Italians.

senses.note: Agrees: poco, poca, pochi, poche. Poche monete = few coins.

etymology: From Latin paucus, from Proto-Italic *paukos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂ukos, derived from the root *peh₂w- (“few”, “little”). Compare French peu, Portuguese pouco, Spanish poco.

fact.text: The short form po' takes an apostrophe, not an accent, because letters were dropped. Writing pò is a classic spelling mistake, even among Italians.

senses.note: un po' (short for un poco) = a bit: un po' di pane = a bit of bread.
'Poco' stays the same; 'profondo' changes to match the noun: acqua poco profonda.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin poesis.

fact.text: Greek poiesis simply meant 'making, production', so a poet was literally a 'maker'. The same Greek verb is behind English poem, poet and onomatopoeia.

senses.note: Also very common for a single poem: una poesia di Leopardi; le poesie = poems.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin poēta, from Ancient Greek ποιητής (poiētḗs).

fact.text: Comes from Greek poiētḗs, 'maker', from poiein 'to make'. To the Greeks a poet was literally a craftsman of words.

senses.note: Masculine even though it ends in -a: il poeta, i poeti. For a woman: la poetessa (or la poeta).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *pos, from Classical Latin post. Compare Portuguese pois, Spanish pues, French puis, and Romanian apoi / Romanian poi (archaic păi).

fact.text: Comes from Latin post 'after', the same root as English post- in postpone and postwar. Its cousins are French puis and Spanish pues.

senses.note: Used for sequence: prima... poi (first... then). Also 'later': ci vediamo poi.

etymology:
Univerbation of poi + che.
Compare French puisque.

fact.text: Built from poi 'after' and che 'that', it first meant 'after' and later 'because'. English since went through the same shift from time to cause.

senses.note: Causal and slightly formal. It often opens the sentence: poiché pioveva, siamo rimasti a casa.

etymology: Inherited from Latin polenta.

fact.text: In Latin, polenta was a porridge of hulled barley and other grains. The maize version Italians eat today only arrived after corn came over from the Americas in the 1500s.

senses.note: A staple of northern Italy; usually uncountable.
Also means 'policy'; the plural politiche means policies.

etymology: From Latin polīticus, from Ancient Greek πολιτικός (politikós).

senses.note: As a noun, il politico = politician; la politica = politics or policy.

etymology: From Late Latin polītīa, from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía).

fact.text: Comes from Greek politeía, meaning citizenship or government, from polis, 'city'. English 'police', 'policy' and 'politics' all share this root.

senses.note: Singular in Italian: la polizia è arrivata (the police have arrived).

etymology: From polizia + -otto.

senses.note: Feminine: la poliziotta.

etymology: From Medieval Latin apodissa (“receipt for money”), from a Byzantine Greek *ἀπόδειξα (*apódeixa), from Ancient Greek ἀπόδειξις (apódeixis, “proof”). Doublet of the learned borrowing apodissi.

fact.text: English 'policy' in the insurance sense came from this Italian word via French police. It goes back to Greek apódeixis, 'proof', and has no link to 'policy' meaning a plan, which comes from 'polis'.

senses.note: Only for insurance and similar contracts. A political or company policy is politica.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pollicem.

fact.text: The same word means 'thumb', because an inch was traditionally the width of a thumb. French pouce and Spanish pulgada work the same way.

senses.note: Its basic meaning is 'thumb'. Screens are measured in pollici.

etymology: From Latin pullus, from Proto-Indo-European *polH- (“animal young”).

fact.text: From Latin pullus, 'young animal'. Some trace it to the same Indo-European root as English foal and Greek polos (colt), though the origin is disputed.

senses.note: Slang: a sucker or dupe. Spennare il pollo = to fleece someone.

fact.text: Built from polpa ('flesh, pulp') plus the suffix -accio, so roughly 'big lump of flesh'.

senses.note: Only the leg muscle. A young cow is il vitello.

etymology: From poltro (“bed”).

fact.text: Politicians who cling to power are said to be 'attaccati alla poltrona', glued to the armchair. The related word poltrone means a lazybones.

senses.note: Also a seat in the front rows of a theatre and, figuratively, a cushy post.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pulverem, from Proto-Indo-European *pel- (“dust; flour”). Doublet of polve, from the Latin nominative pulvis. Akin to Sicilian prùvula.

fact.text: Comes from Latin pulvis/pulverem, meaning dust. This is the same root as English 'pulverize', literally to turn something into dust.

senses.note: Polvere da sparo = gunpowder. Fare polvere = to raise dust.

etymology: Inherited from Latin post merīdiem (“after noon”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin post meridiem, 'after midday'. That is the same phrase behind the English abbreviation p.m.

senses.note: Di pomeriggio = in the afternoon.

etymology:
Univerbation of pomo (“apple”) + d' (“of”) + oro (“gold”), literally “golden apple”. Possibly owing to the fact that the first varieties of tomatoes arriving in Europe and spreading from Spain to Italy and North Africa were yellow. Earliest attestation (of the archaic plural form pomi d'oro) goes back to Matthiolus (1544).
A red strain was later developed in Moorish Africa, which came to be known in Italy as pomo dei mori (“apple of the Moors”).

fact.text: Literally 'golden apple' (pomo d'oro), probably because the first tomatoes that reached Italy were yellow. The word is first recorded in 1544.

etymology: From pompa (“pump”) + -iere.

fact.text: From French pompier, built on pompe (pump), so firefighters are literally 'pump men', named after the water pumps they used to put out fires.

senses.note: I pompieri = the fire brigade. The official term is vigile del fuoco.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin pontem.
Compare French, Dutch, and Catalan pont, Romanian punte, Romansh punt, Portuguese ponte, Spanish puente.

fact.text: Italians fare il ponte, or make the bridge: if a holiday falls on a Thursday, they take Friday off to bridge it to the weekend.

senses.note: Also a ship's deck. Fare il ponte = take a long weekend.
An English loanword. It is also an adjective that never changes form: musica pop, gruppi pop.

etymology: From Latin populāris.

senses.note: Also 'of the people' or 'folk': musica popolare = folk music.

etymology: From Latin populus, from Proto-Italic *poplos (“army”).

fact.text: Latin populus goes back to Proto-Italic *poplos, which probably meant 'army'. English people comes from the same Latin word, through French.

senses.note: A people or nation (il popolo italiano). For 'people' meaning persons, use gente or persone.

etymology: From Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos.

fact.text: Comes from Latin porcus, 'pig', which reached English as 'pork' via French.

senses.note: Mostly in fixed exclamations that agree with their noun: porca miseria! (mild), porco cane! Some combinations are offensive.

etymology: Inherited from Latin porrigere.

senses.note: Slightly formal. porgere la mano = to hold out one's hand; porgere le scuse = to offer apologies. Past participle: porto.

etymology: Inherited from Latin pōnere (“to put, place”), with pōnō > *ponjo> *pogno > pongo subsumed to the 'L-pattern' of vengo (cf. Old Italian vegno, vegnamo, vegnono) in a much-debated process of 'velar allomorphy'. This is mirrored in Spanish pongo, vengo, but with an opposite outcome in Portuguese ponho, venho.

fact.text: From Latin ponere, to put. Its past participle positus gave English position, deposit and opposite, which is why the Italian past participle is posto.

senses.note: Porre una domanda = to ask a question. Irregular: pongo, poni, pone; past participle posto.

etymology: Inherited from Latin porta, from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to pass through”).

fact.text: From Latin porta, the source of English portal and porter (originally a doorkeeper). In football the porta is the goal, so a goalkeeper is a portiere.

senses.note: Also 'goal' in football; il portone = the main front door of a building.

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of porta (“to carry”) + foglio (“sheet of paper”).

fact.text: Literally a 'carry-sheet', from porta (carries) + foglio (sheet of paper). English borrowed this same word as portfolio, a case for carrying papers.

senses.note: Also means portfolio (ministerial or financial). Plural: portafogli.

etymology: Inherited from Latin portāre (“to bring, carry”), from Proto-Indo-European *per- (“go, traverse”).

fact.text: From Latin portare 'to carry', the same root as English porter, portable, transport, import and export.

senses.note: Also 'to take (someone somewhere)': portami in albergo = take me to a hotel. Also 'to wear'.

etymology: From Latin portus, from Proto-Italic *portus, from Proto-Indo-European *pértus (“crossing”), from the root *per- (“to go forth”, “to cross”).

fact.text: From Latin portus, which goes back to an ancient root meaning 'crossing'. English ford and Norse fjord come from the same root.

senses.note: Don't confuse with (io) porto = I bring/take, from portare.

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of posa (“to put, to lay”) + cenere (“ash”).

fact.text: A verb plus object compound: posa, 'puts down', + cenere, 'ash', so literally a 'put-ash'. Compounds like this are usually masculine and invariable.

senses.note: Invariable: il posacenere, i posacenere.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin pausāre, perhaps influenced in meaning by Latin pōnere. Compare French poser.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin pausare (to pause, rest), the source of French poser and English 'pose'. So 'pose' and 'pause' are related.

senses.note: posare mattoni = to lay bricks; posare per una foto = to pose for a photo.

etymology: From posare.

senses.note: Usually plural: le posate = cutlery.

etymology: From Latin positīvus.
From Latin positiōnem.

senses.note: Means a location and also a job: una posizione a Milano = a position (job) in Milan.

etymology: Inherited from Latin possidēre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin possidere, which is usually explained as pot- ('master, powerful') + sedere ('to sit'). To own something was to sit on it as its master.

senses.note: The stem changes: possiedo, possiedi, possiede, but possediamo, possedete. Conjugated like sedere.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin possibilis.

senses.note: il più possibile = as much as possible; prima possibile = as soon as possible.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin possibilitātem.

senses.note: Invariable plural. Also 'chance, opportunity': avere la possibilità di = to have the chance to.

etymology: Inherited from Latin posita, feminine singular of positus, past participle of pōnō (“to put”). Originally, "post for horses or for mooring ships", then "stopping place for coaches on a journey, way station". Doublet of posta (feminine past participle of porre).

fact.text: Comes from Latin posita, 'placed'. It first meant a relay station along a route where horses were kept ready, and later the service that carried letters between those stations.

senses.note: Also means 'post office' (andare alla posta); posta elettronica = email.

etymology: From posta + -ale.

senses.note: Ufficio postale = post office; codice postale = postcode; cassetta postale = mailbox.

etymology: From posta.

fact.text: Il Postino (1994), the film about a humble island postman who befriends the poet Pablo Neruda, won an Oscar for its score and made the word famous worldwide.

senses.note: Feminine: la postina. From posta (mail).

etymology: From Latin postus, from positus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin positus, 'placed', the past participle of ponere, 'to put'. English position, post and deposit come from the same Latin root.

senses.note: Also means 'seat' (posto libero?) and 'job' (un posto di lavoro).

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.

fact.text: As a noun, il potere means 'power'. It replaced Latin posse and shares a root with English potent and potential.

senses.note: Al potere = in power. Same form as the verb potere (can, to be able).

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin potēre, regularization of Latin posse.

fact.text: As a noun, il potere means 'power'. It replaced Latin posse and shares a root with English potent and potential.

senses.note: Followed by an infinitive: posso venire? As a modal it often takes the auxiliary of the next verb.

etymology: From Latin pauperem. Given that the expect native reflex would have been *popere, this form was likely among the early borrowings into Italian from Gallo-Italic.

senses.note: un uomo povero = a man without money; un povero uomo = a poor (pitiable) man

etymology: From Latin pauperem. Given that the expect native reflex would have been *popere, this form was likely among the early borrowings into Italian from Gallo-Italic.
ignored: This is just the adjective used as a noun, which the adjective card povero already covers.

senses.note: i poveri = the poor. Feminine: la povera.

etymology: From Latin paupertātem. By surface analysis, povero + -tà.

senses.note: Invariable: la povertà, le povertà.

etymology: From pranzo + -are.

senses.note: Intransitive, with avere: ho pranzato. From il pranzo, 'lunch'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin prandium, whence also Dalmatian prinz and Romanian prânz. Ultimately of Proto-Indo-European origin.

fact.text: Comes from Latin prandium, which may originally have meant 'first meal' or 'early meal'. In formal use pranzo can also be a main meal or banquet, hence sala da pranzo, dining room.

senses.note: Pranzare = to have lunch. Sala da pranzo = dining room.

etymology: Noun use of the feminine form of the adjective pratico.

fact.text: In offices it often means a bureaucratic file or case: sbrigare una pratica is to get some paperwork through, and le pratiche are the forms you chase at the town hall.

senses.note: fare pratica = to get practice; in pratica = basically, in practice.

etymology: From pratico + -mente.

senses.note: Also means 'almost'. In speech it is very often a filler, like 'basically'.

etymology: From Late Latin practicus, from Ancient Greek πρᾱκτῐκός (prāktĭkós, “pertaining to an action”), derived from πρᾱγ- (prāg-), the root of πρᾱ́σσω (prā́ssō, “to do”) + -τῐκός (-tĭkós, verbal adjective suffix).

senses.note: essere pratico di = to know well or be familiar with, e.g. non sono pratico della zona.

etymology: Inherited from Latin prātum (“meadow”).

senses.note: Also means a lawn: 'Non calpestare il prato' = keep off the grass.

etymology: From precedere with substantive senses under the influence of English precedent and French précédent.

senses.note: Also a noun: un precedente = a precedent; senza precedenti = unprecedented.

etymology: From precedere + -enza.

fact.text: On Italian roads the triangular 'give way' sign is called 'Dare precedenza', literally 'give precedence', which is the Italian way of saying yield.

senses.note: Also 'right of way' on the road: dare la precedenza = to give way / yield.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin praeferre, with a change in conjugation.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: preferisco. Preferire A a B = to prefer A to B. Preferirei = I'd rather.
Also the past participle of preferire (to prefer).

etymology: From Late Latin praefixum, from Latin praefixus.

senses.note: Also the telephone area/dialling code: il prefisso di Roma è 06.

etymology: From earlier precare, from Latin precārī.

fact.text: The everyday 'prego' (you're welcome, go ahead) literally means 'I pray/beg'. English pray comes from the same Latin precari, via Old French.

senses.note: Also 'to beg': ti prego = please. Prego = you're welcome / go ahead.

fact.text: Literally means 'I pray' or 'I beg', the io form of pregare (to pray). So the polite reply really means something like 'I beg you, don't mention it'.

senses.note: Also 'please, go ahead' when offering something, and 'Prego?' = 'Can I help you?'

etymology: From Late Latin praelevāre (prae- + levāre).

senses.note: Prelevare soldi al bancomat = to withdraw money at the ATM. Un prelievo = a withdrawal (also a blood test).

etymology: From Latin premere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin premere, past participle pressus. That participle is where English gets press, pressure, impress, express and depress.

senses.note: Premere il pulsante = press the button. Used intransitively, mi preme means it matters to me.

etymology: From Latin praemium.

fact.text: From Latin praemium, built from prae 'before' and emere 'to obtain', so roughly 'what you get ahead of others'. English 'premium' comes from the same Latin word.

senses.note: Also reward, bonus, or insurance premium. vincere un premio = to win a prize.

etymology: Inherited from Latin prēndere, from earlier prehendere, from prae- (“before”) + *hendere (“take, seize”) (not attested without a prefix), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰed-.

fact.text: From Latin prehendere 'to seize', the same root as English apprehend, comprehend and prison.

senses.note: Very broad: prendere il treno (take the train), prendere un caffè (have a coffee).
Non prendertela! = Don't take it badly! Prendersela con qlcu = to get angry at someone. Past: me la sono presa.
Prendersi cura di = to take care of; prendersi un caffè = to have a coffee.

etymology: From Latin praenotāre.

fact.text: From Latin praenotare, pre- plus notare: literally 'to note down beforehand', which is exactly what happens when you book. It shares its root with English 'note'.

senses.note: prenotare un tavolo / una camera. The noun is la prenotazione (booking, reservation).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin praeoccupāre.

fact.text: This is a false friend. Italian preoccupato means 'worried', not 'lost in thought' like English preoccupied. Sono preoccupato means 'I'm worried'.

senses.note: Preoccuparsi (di) = to worry (about), with essere: non preoccuparti!

fact.text: Watch out: Italian 'preoccupato' means worried, not 'preoccupied' in the English sense of lost in thought. Sono preoccupato = I'm worried.

senses.note: Preoccuparsi di/per qualcosa. Non preoccuparti! = Don't worry! The negative tu-command uses the infinitive.

fact.text: Not quite English 'preoccupied' (lost in thought). In Italian it normally means worried or anxious, and la preoccupazione is a worry.

senses.note: Essere preoccupato per qualcuno = to be worried about someone.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin praeoccupātiōnem.

fact.text: Careful: English 'preoccupation' usually means being absorbed in something, but the Italian word usually means worry or anxiety.

senses.note: Plural often means 'cares, troubles': avere molte preoccupazioni.

etymology: From Latin praeparāre (“to make ready in advance”), from prae- (“pre-”) + parō (“to make ready”).

senses.note: Prepararsi = to get ready: mi preparo per uscire.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin praepositiōnem.

senses.note: Preposizioni articolate combine with the article: di + il = del, in + la = nella.

etymology: From Latin praesentāre (“to present, show”).

senses.note: Also 'to introduce' (a person). presentarsi = to introduce oneself / to show up.

etymology: From presentare + -zione.

senses.note: Fare le presentazioni = to introduce people to each other.

etymology: Inherited from Latin praesentem.

senses.note: Students answer 'Presente!' at roll call. Il presente = the present (time or tense).

etymology: From Latin praesentia.

fact.text: Italian job ads long asked for candidates 'di bella presenza', meaning good-looking and well-presented. The phrase is now widely criticised as discriminatory.

senses.note: In presenza = in person (vs. online). Le presenze can also mean attendance.

fact.text: Comes from Latin praeses, 'one who sits in front', from praesidere. That is the same root as English 'preside' and 'president'.

senses.note: Il/la preside, the same form for a man or a woman. Can also mean the dean of a faculty.

etymology: From Latin praesidentem.

senses.note: Il/la presidente, plural i/le presidenti. It also means the chair of a board or committee.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin pressiōnem.

senses.note: On its own it often means blood pressure: misurare la pressione = to take someone's blood pressure.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *pressō, from Latin presse (“narrow, short”). Cognate with Walloon and French près.

fact.text: On Italian envelopes it works like English c/o (care of): Mario Rossi presso Bianchi. It is also standard for workplaces: lavora presso il Comune.

senses.note: Mostly a preposition: presso la stazione; lavoro presso una banca = I work at a bank.

etymology: Inherited from Latin praestāre (“to provide, supply, offer, bestow”).

fact.text: Italian has no single everyday verb for 'to borrow': people say prendere in prestito or farsi prestare (literally 'to get lent').

senses.note: prestare qcs a qcn. Also: prestare attenzione = to pay attention.
Prendere in prestito = to borrow; dare in prestito = to lend.

etymology: From Late Latin praestus, from the Latin praestō (“at hand”, adverb). Compare Catalan prest, French prêt.

fact.text: English took 'presto' as a music term for a very fast tempo. It also gave magicians' 'Hey presto!', said when something appears in an instant. The source is Latin praesto, 'at hand'.

senses.note: A presto! = See you soon! al più presto = as soon as possible.

etymology: From Latin praesūmō.

senses.note: Irregular: presunsi, presunto. Presunto also means 'alleged': il presunto colpevole.

etymology: From Old Italian preite, from Vulgar Latin *previter, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros). Compare French prêtre, Romanian preot.

fact.text: Comes from Greek presbyteros, 'elder'. English 'priest' and 'presbyterian' come from the same Greek word, so a priest was originally just 'an older man'.

senses.note: Everyday word. The more formal word is sacerdote.

etymology: From Latin praevidēre.

senses.note: prevedere di + infinitive. Main sense is also 'to foresee, forecast'. Conjugated like vedere: previsto.

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin praevīsiōnem, from Latin praevideō.

senses.note: le previsioni del tempo = the weather forecast (usually plural).

etymology: A syncope of earlier pretosemolo, with metathesis from petrosemolo, from a cross of Latin petroselīnum and sēmen (thus "stone seed") as in Sardinian perdusèmene. The Latin word borrowed from Ancient Greek πετροσέλῑνον (petrosélīnon), from πέτρα (pétra, “stone”) + σέλῑνον (sélīnon, “celery”).

fact.text: Both this word and English 'parsley' come from Greek petroselinon, 'rock celery'. Italians say someone who turns up everywhere 'è come il prezzemolo'.

senses.note: Usually uncountable: un po' di prezzemolo.

etymology: From Latin pretium, whence also Italian pregio, a doublet. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *préti (“back”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin pretium, 'price, value'. The same word gave English 'price', 'praise' and 'precious', and Italian pregio ('merit').

etymology: From earlier priscione, possibly via Old French prison, from Latin prehēnsiōnem (“the act of seizing”), from prehendō (“to seize, grab”). Doublet of prensione.

fact.text: English 'prison' has the same origin: Latin prehensio, 'the act of seizing', from prehendere 'to grab', probably passed on through Old French prison.

senses.note: 'In prigione' = in prison/jail. 'Carcere' (m.) is a common synonym.

etymology: See primo.

fact.text: English borrowed the same word in 'prima donna', literally 'first lady', meaning the lead female singer in an opera. It comes from primo, 'first'.

senses.note: Prima di + noun/infinitive; prima che + subjunctive. Prima o poi = sooner or later.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin prīma vēra (“early spring”), derived from vēr (“spring”). Compare Spanish primavera, French primevère.

fact.text: It comes from Late Latin prima vera, 'early spring', built on Latin ver, 'spring'. Informally, the plural counts years of life: 'ha venti primavere' means 'she is twenty'.

senses.note: in primavera = in spring. Seasons are not capitalised in Italian.

etymology: From Latin prīmus, from earlier prīsmos < *prīsemos < Proto-Italic *priisemos.

fact.text: On an Italian menu, 'il primo' is the first course, usually pasta, risotto or soup. It comes after the antipasto and before 'il secondo', the meat or fish course.

senses.note: Ordinal adjective that agrees with its noun: il primo giorno, la prima volta. Prima (adverb) = before, earlier.

etymology: Derived from Latin principālis. By surface analysis, principe + -ale.

fact.text: Careful: a school principal is not il principale but il preside or il dirigente scolastico. As an adjective it just means main, as in la strada principale.

senses.note: A bit dated; capo is more common today. As an adjective it means 'main'.

etymology: From Latin prīncipem (“chief”) (compare principio (“principle”) from the meaning "first").

fact.text: Latin princeps meant 'the one who takes first place' (primus + capere). Augustus chose it as a modest-sounding title for himself as Rome's first emperor.

senses.note: Feminine: principessa. Plural principi is the same as the plural of principio (principle).

etymology: From principe (“prince”) + -essa (“-ess”); compare French princesse, Sicilian principissa.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin priōritātem.

senses.note: Invariable: the plural is also 'le priorità'.

etymology: From Latin prīvātus.

senses.note: Also a noun: un privato = a private individual; in privato = in private.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin probābilis.

senses.note: È probabile che + subjunctive: È probabile che piova.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin probābilitātem. By surface analysis, probabile + -ità.

senses.note: Invariable. Con ogni probabilità = in all likelihood

etymology: From probabile + -mente.

Borrowed from Latin problēma, from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, “obstacle”), from προβάλλω (probállō, “to throw or lay something in front of someone, to put forward”), from prefix προ- (pro-, “in front of”) + βάλλω (bállō, “to throw, to cast, to hurl”).

fact.text: From Greek próblēma, literally 'something thrown in front', an obstacle in your path. Like other Greek -ma words (il tema, il sistema), it is masculine.

senses.note: Masculine despite the -a: il problema, i problemi.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōcēdere.

senses.note: Procedere con qualcosa = to go ahead with something. 'Come procede?' = How's it going?

etymology: From Latin processus, possibly borrowed.

fact.text: In Italian news this word usually means a court trial, not a process. Il processo Andreotti means the Andreotti trial. Context tells you which meaning is meant.

senses.note: Also very common for a court trial: il processo a qualcuno = someone's trial.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōclāmāre.

senses.note: Also: to declare someone something (proclamare qualcuno vincitore).

etymology: From Latin prōcūrātōrem.

senses.note: Also: procuratore della Repubblica = public prosecutor; a sports agent. Feminine: procuratrice.

etymology: From Latin productus.

senses.note: Also the past participle of produrre (to produce).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōdūcere.

senses.note: Irregular: stem produc- (produco, producevo); past participle prodotto.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōductōrem, from Latin prōductus.

senses.note: Feminine: produttrice. Used for farm produce, manufacturing and film.

etymology: From professione + -ista.

senses.note: il/la professionista. libero professionista = self-employed professional or freelancer.

ignored: A shortened form of professore used before names; study it on the professore card.

senses.note: Shortened form of professore used before a surname: il professor Rossi.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin prŏfessōrem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin professor, from profiteri, 'to declare publicly'. A professor was originally someone who publicly professed to be an expert in a subject.

senses.note: Used for secondary-school teachers too, often shortened to prof. Feminine: professoressa.

etymology: Deverbal from profilare.

senses.note: Side view of a face, outline, or a social-media/user profile.

etymology: From Latin profundus.

fact.text: From Latin profundus: pro- + fundus (bottom). English 'profound' is the same word, and fundus also gave us 'fund' and 'foundation'.

senses.note: Used literally and figuratively: un respiro profondo (a deep breath), il profondo sud (the deep south).

fact.text: Usually traced to Latin per fumum, 'through smoke', from scented incense smoke. English 'perfume' came via French from Italian perfumare.

senses.note: Also any pleasant smell: il profumo del caffè.

etymology: Borrowed from French projet, derived from projeter (“to plan”).

senses.note: Also a plan or design: il progetto di una casa = the design of a house.

etymology: From Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).

fact.text: Ends in -a but is masculine because it comes from a Greek neuter noun in -ma. The same goes for il problema, il sistema and il tema, which all take -i in the plural.

senses.note: Masculine despite the -a ending: il programma, i programmi.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōgressus.

senses.note: Often plural: fare progressi = to make progress.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prohibēre.

features.construction: proibire qcs a qcn; proibire a qcn di + infinitive

senses.note: -isc- verb: proibisco. Proibire a qualcuno di fare qualcosa.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōiectilis (“projectile”), from Latin prōiectus, perfect passive participle of prōiciō (“throw forth; extend; expel”). By surface analysis, proietto + -ile.

senses.note: Also any projectile; pallottola is a more everyday word for a bullet.

etymology: From Medieval Latin, Vulgar Latin promissa (“promise”), from Latin prōmissum (“promise”), from promittō (“to send forth; to promise”).

senses.note: Fare una promessa = to make a promise; mantenere una promessa = to keep a promise.

etymology: From Latin prōmittere.

features.construction: promettere qualcosa a qualcuno; promettere di + infinitive

senses.note: Irregular: promisi, promesso. Promettere a qualcuno di + infinitive.

etymology: From Latin prōmovēre (“to promote”).

fact.text: In Italian schools, essere promosso means passing the year and moving up a class. Failing is essere bocciato.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle promosso, passato remoto promossi.

etymology: Inherited from Latin prōnōmen.

fact.text: From Latin pronomen, made of pro (in place of) and nomen (name, noun). English 'pronoun' comes from the same Latin word: a word standing in for a noun.

senses.note: Masculine despite ending in -e: il pronome, i pronomi.

etymology: From Latin prōmptus.

fact.text: Italians answer the phone with 'Pronto?', literally 'Ready?'. The word comes from Latin promptus, also the source of English prompt.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun: siamo pronti, sono pronta. Pronto? = Hello? on the phone.

etymology: Deverbal from pronunciare (“to pronounce, utter”) + -a.

senses.note: Also spelled pronunzia. Can also mean a person's accent.

etymology: Derived from Latin prōpōnere (“to set forth; to propose; to declare”).

senses.note: Irregular like porre: propongo, proposi, proposto. Proporre di fare = to suggest doing.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōpositum (“plan, intention”, literally “that which is proposed”), neuter form of prōpositum, perfect passive participle of prōpōnō.

fact.text: Doesn't mean 'proposal' (that's la proposta). A New Year's resolution is a buon proposito, a good intention.

senses.note: di proposito = on purpose; a proposito = by the way; a proposito di = about, regarding.

etymology: From Latin prōposita.

senses.note: fare una proposta = to make a proposal. proposta di matrimonio = marriage proposal.

etymology: From Latin proprietārius.

senses.note: Feminine: la proprietaria. Also used for a landlord of a rented home.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prŏprietātem. By surface analysis, proprio + -età.

senses.note: Invariable: le proprietà. proprietà privata = private property. Also means a characteristic (proprietà chimiche).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin proprius.

fact.text: From Latin proprius 'one's own', which also gave English proper and property. That's why the adjective proprio still means 'own'.

senses.note: Ognuno ha le proprie idee. Agrees like an adjective. As an adverb it means 'really, exactly' (proprio così).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin proprius.

fact.text: From Latin proprius 'one's own', which also gave English proper and property. That's why the adjective proprio still means 'own'.

senses.note: Proprio qui = right here; proprio adesso = right now. As an adjective it means 'own'.

etymology: From asciutto (“dry”), with a change of prefix, or perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *perexsūctus, from Latin per + exsūctus. Compare Portuguese presunto.

fact.text: In English 'prosciutto' means cured ham, but in Italian it covers any ham, so you say crudo or cotto. It probably comes from asciutto 'dry', meaning 'thoroughly dried'.

senses.note: Prosciutto crudo = cured ham; prosciutto cotto = cooked ham.

etymology: Inherited from Latin proximus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin proximus, 'nearest', the root of English proximity and approximate.

senses.note: La prossima volta = next time. As a noun, il prossimo = one's neighbour (fellow human).

etymology: From Ancient Greek πρωταγωνιστής (prōtagōnistḗs).

fact.text: From Greek protos 'first' + agonistes 'competitor, actor'. In Greek drama it meant the first, or leading, actor.

senses.note: il/la protagonista; plural protagonisti (m) or protagoniste (f).

etymology: From Latin prōtegere, from prō- + tegō.

fact.text: Comes from Latin pro- 'in front' + tegere 'to cover'. Tegere also gave Latin tegula, the source of English 'tile', and de-tegere 'to uncover', the source of 'detect'.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: protetto. Passato remoto: protessi.

etymology: From Late Latin prōtectiōnem.

senses.note: Protezione solare = sunscreen, sun protection.

etymology: Either deverbal from provare (“to try; to test; to prove; to feel”) + -a, or from Late Latin proba, from Latin probō.

fact.text: It comes from Latin probare, 'to test, to prove', the same root as English prove, proof and probe. That's why one Italian word can mean both 'test' and 'proof'.

senses.note: Also means proof/evidence and rehearsal. Mettere alla prova = to put to the test.

etymology: From Latin probāre. Compare French prouver, Portuguese provar.

fact.text: From Latin probare 'to test', which also gave English prove and probe. Italian keeps the testing idea: provare mostly means to try, and 'le prove' are rehearsals.

senses.note: Provare a + infinitive = to attempt. Also: to try on clothes, to feel (provare dolore), to prove.

etymology: From Latin prōvenīre (“to originate, arise”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin provenire, meaning to come forth. English 'provenance', the origin of an object, comes from the same verb through French.

senses.note: Used with da: provenire da. Conjugated like venire: provengo, provieni, proviene.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin prōvincia.

fact.text: Latin provincia first meant the area of duty or command given to a Roman magistrate. Later it came to mean a territory governed by Rome.

senses.note: Plural province (provincie is older). In provincia also means outside the big cities.

etymology: From Latin prūrītus m .

senses.note: Mi viene il prurito = I get itchy.

etymology: From Latin pūblicāre.
From French publicité.

senses.note: Plural doesn't change: le pubblicità. Also means advertising in general; fare pubblicità = to advertise.

etymology: From Latin ratiōnem, whence also razione (a borrowed doublet). The natural outcome would have been razzone [rat'tsone] (which is attested in some archaic works in Roman vernacular); the reason why the modern form shows a g is that Tuscan literates mistook Northern rason as an outcome of non-existent Latin **rasione~**raseone—whose -sj- indeed evolves regularly into tuscan [ʃ]~[ʒ] and non-tuscan [s]<s> (compare fagiolo from Latin phaseolum, and compare the pronunciation of English vision as "vizhun"—indeed, approvvigionare ultimately comes from Latin visionem with the same assimilation of -sj- into a palatal voiced fricative). Compare other terms ending in -gione. Furthermore, the reason why it’s nowadays pronounced with an affricate rather than a fricative (together with all Italian terms having as the corresponding etymological clusters being -tj- or -sj-, or even -cj- through Gallic languages—see crogiolo) is due to hyper-correction of Tuscan gorgia, i.e. the merging of ungeminated fricatives and affricates into the first ones. Indeed, older spellings with sci or sgi tried to reproduce the ungeminated fricative before the gorgia took place (once it happened, it was more convenient, with merged sounds, to merge the spellings, despite being unetymological).

etymology:
c. 1300, as masculine razzo, the feminine razza is from the early 14th century. The etymology of this word is uncertain, with a large number of controversially discussed suggestions.
Among the most widely accepted suggestions is the one embraced by Französisches Etymologisches Wörterbuch (1922), but was proposed earlier, among others by L. Spitzer (Z. rom. Philol. t. 53, pp. 300–301), which derives the word from Latin ratiō (the nominative, as opposed to ragione, from the accusative ratiōnem, which nonetheless was attested with a similar sense to razza in the late Middle Ages; ratio also came to mean “idea” or “conception of something” in Ecclesiastical Latin) likely via a Vulgar Latin variant *ratia, and underwent a change of gender later from an original form *razzo, or else derived ultimately from generātiō through apheresis.
Another likely origin is from the Latin racēmus, meaning a “cluster or bunch of grapes, berries or similar fruits”, from which the French “raisin” is derived.
Other suggestions include, Lombardic *raiza (compare Old High German reiza (“line”)), Latin rādīx (“root”) or Ancient Greek ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”), Arabic رَأْس (raʔs, “head”), or Old French haraz (“culture of horses”).
