etymology: From re- + agire (“act”).

senses.note: Reagire a qualcosa = to react to something. -isc- verb: reagisco.

etymology: From reale + -izzare. The sense “to become aware of” is a semantic loan from English realize.

fact.text: Traditionally means to make real or achieve. Using it for 'become aware' is borrowed from English realize, and purists frown on it, so rendersi conto is the safer choice.

senses.note: realizzare un sogno = to make a dream come true. For 'become aware', rendersi conto is preferred.

etymology:
Semi-learned borrowing from Medieval Latin reālitātem, from Late Latin reālis (“real”), from Classical Latin rēs (“thing”) + -ālis.
Doublet of realità, which is a learned borrowing.

senses.note: Invariable: la realtà / le realtà. In realtà = actually, in fact.

etymology: From Late Latin reātus (“accusation”).

fact.text: It comes from Late Latin reatus, 'the state of being accused', from reus, 'defendant'. Italian still uses reo for the guilty party, as in reo confesso, 'self-confessed culprit'.

senses.note: The general legal word for any criminal offence. Commettere un reato = to commit a crime.

etymology: From Latin reāctiō.

senses.note: Aereo a reazione = jet plane.

etymology: Borrowed or semi-learned term from Latin recentem. The older form ricente may be inherited, however.

senses.note: di recente = recently.

ignored: Wrong lemma: the context has the adjective reciproco, and this verb is rare.

senses.note: Rare. In everyday Italian people say ricambiare.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin recitāre.

fact.text: This verb looks like 'recite', but its everyday meaning is 'to act'. Un attore recita in un film means an actor acts in a film, and una recita is a show or school play.

senses.note: Also 'to recite' (a poem, a prayer). Recitare una parte = to play a part.

etymology: Deverbal from reclamare + -o.

fact.text: This doesn't mean 'reclaim'. It is a formal complaint to a shop, company or office. Also don't mix it up with réclame, an old word for an advertisement.

senses.note: fare/presentare un reclamo = to file a complaint; ufficio reclami = complaints department.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin recuperāre.

senses.note: Also to make up for: recuperare il tempo perso. Variant: ricuperare.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Spanish regalar.

fact.text: Despite how it looks, it is not related to 'regal'. It probably comes from French régaler 'to treat', which is also the source of English 'regale'.

senses.note: regalare qualcosa a qualcuno. Related noun: il regalo (gift).

etymology: From French régal or Spanish regalo .

senses.note: fare un regalo a qualcuno = to give someone a present.

etymology: From Latin regere (“to rule, govern”).

fact.text: From Latin regere 'to rule, guide', the same root as English regent, regime, region and regulate, which is why it can also mean to govern.

senses.note: Irregular: ressi, retto. Non lo reggo = I can't stand him.

etymology: Inherited from Latin rēgīna; cognate with Spanish reina.

fact.text: Regina is Latin for queen too. The Canadian city of Regina was named in honour of Queen Victoria.

senses.note: Also the queen in chess and cards. Ape regina = queen bee.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin regiōnālis.

senses.note: The same form is used for masculine and feminine. Plural: regionali.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin regiōnem, case form of regiō (literally “direction, line”), derived from regō (“to rule, govern”). Compare rione, an inherited doublet.

senses.note: Capitalised Regione for the administrative body, e.g. Regione Lombardia.

fact.text: Watch out: a film director is a regista, not a direttore. Direttore means a manager, a head, or an orchestra conductor.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: il/la regista. Plural registi (m), registe (f). Also used for theatre and TV.

etymology: From registro + -are.

senses.note: Also to record audio or video. Registrarsi = to sign up or check in.

etymology: From registrare + -zione.

senses.note: Also very common for 'recording' (audio/video).

etymology: From Latin rēgnum.

senses.note: Also means 'reign': durante il regno di = during the reign of. Regno Unito = United Kingdom.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin rēgula as a semi-learned term. Compare Spanish regla, Portuguese regra, French règle.

fact.text: From Latin regula 'straight stick, ruler', which also gave English rule and regular.

senses.note: In regola = in order, all set; di regola = as a rule.

etymology: From Latin relātiōnem.

fact.text: It also means a written report. 'Fare una relazione' at school or work means writing or presenting a report, not starting a romance.

senses.note: Can mean a romantic relationship or affair. 'Relazioni internazionali' = international relations.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin religiōnem (“piety”, “superstition”).
Borrowed from Latin religiōsus.

senses.note: As a noun, il religioso / la religiosa means a monk or nun.

etymology: From Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere. The past participle was contaminated by Latin prehensus (of unrelated prehendere), with the past historic altered by analogy to prendere (past historic presi).

fact.text: From Latin reddere 'to give back', reshaped to rendere under the influence of prendere 'to take'. Through French rendre, the same word gave English render and rent.

senses.note: Rendere felice = to make happy. Also 'to give back'. Rendersi conto = to realize.
A section of a shop, office or factory. In a hospital it means a ward.

etymology: From earlier republica, from Latin rēspūblica, rēs pūblica (literally “the public thing”).

fact.text: From Latin res publica, literally 'the public thing', meaning the affairs of state as something belonging to the people. Italy became a republic by referendum on 2 June 1946.

senses.note: la Repubblica Italiana; Festa della Repubblica = 2 June.

etymology: From Latin reputātiōnem.
From Medieval Latin residentia, from Latin residēns (“residing”), from resideō (“to reside”), from re- + sedeō (“to sit”).

senses.note: Also your officially registered address: avere la residenza a Roma.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin resistere, from re- + sistō.

senses.note: Takes a: resistere alla tentazione. Aux avere.

etymology: Latinized form of older rispirare, inherited from Latin respīrāre.

fact.text: From Latin re- + spirare, 'to breathe'. Spirare is also the source of English 'respiration', 'inspire', 'expire' and even 'spirit', which first meant breath.

senses.note: Noun: il respiro = breath. Fai un respiro profondo = take a deep breath.

etymology: Deverbal from respirare + -o.

senses.note: fare un respiro profondo = to take a deep breath.

etymology: Borrowed from French responsable, assimilated to the native suffix -abile. Cognate with Piedmontese responsàbil.

senses.note: Used as a noun: il/la responsabile (del reparto, delle vendite).

etymology: From responsabile + -ità, modeled after similar formation of French responsabilité and English responsibility in the late 18th century.

fact.text: A fairly young word: it was formed in the late 18th century, modelled on French responsabilité and English responsibility.

senses.note: Invariable. assumersi la responsabilità = to take responsibility.

etymology: From Latin restāre, from re- + stō.

fact.text: Does not mean 'to rest' (that is riposare). It comes from Latin re- + stare 'to stand', so it means to stay put. English 'the rest', meaning the remainder, shares this root.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono restato. Also 'to be left': mi restano due euro.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin rēstituere (“to replace, restore”), with change of conjugation.

fact.text: This comes from Latin restituere, 'to restore', which also gave English 'restitution', meaning the act of giving back what was taken.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: restituisco, restituisci. Restituire qcs a qcn = to give something back to someone.

etymology: Deverbal from restare + -o.

senses.note: Tenga il resto = keep the change.

etymology: From Latin rēte (“net”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin rete, 'net'. English retina is usually traced to the same word, perhaps because of its net of blood vessels.

senses.note: Also net, and a goal in football (segnare una rete). La Rete = the Internet.

etymology: Inherited from Latin retrō.

fact.text: Watch the accent. Without it, retro is the back of something. With it, retrò means 'retro' in the English sense, vintage-styled: uno stile retrò.

senses.note: Invariable. Sul retro = on the back / out the back; il retro del negozio = back of the shop.

etymology: From rettangol(o) (“rectangle”) + -are (“-ar”, adjective-forming suffix).

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine. Plural rettangolari.

etymology: Derived from Latin rēctōrem (“guide, tutor”).

senses.note: The head of an Italian university. It can also mean the priest in charge of certain churches. Feminine: rettrice.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin revīsiōnem.

senses.note: Also a car's periodic roadworthiness test (like the UK MOT) or a machine service.

etymology: From ri- + assumere.

senses.note: Past participle riassunto, which also means 'a summary'. It can also mean to rehire.

etymology: From ri- + avere.

senses.note: Conjugated like avere. Riaversi = to recover, come round.

etymology: From ricco + -ezza.

senses.note: Plural le ricchezze = riches.

etymology: From Latin ēricius (“a hedgehog”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰḗr (“to bristle”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin ericius ('hedgehog'), the same root as English 'urchin', which first meant hedgehog. As a noun, riccio still means hedgehog, and riccio di mare is a sea urchin.

senses.note: capelli ricci = curly hair. As a noun, un riccio is a curl or a hedgehog.

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic rīhhi (possibly through a Vulgar Latin or Late Latin *riccus, *ricus), from Proto-Germanic *rīkijaz.

fact.text: A Germanic word, not a Latin one. It came from Lombardic rihhi, from Proto-Germanic *rikijaz, which is also the root of English rich and German reich.

senses.note: Also 'rich in': ricco di vitamine. Plural ricchi/ricche.

etymology: Deverbal from ricercare + -a.

fact.text: Comes from ricercare. English 'research' and 'search' share its source, Late Latin circare, 'to go around', which comes from circus, 'circle'.

senses.note: Also 'search': la ricerca di = the search for. Fare ricerca = to do research.

etymology: From Latin recepta, feminine of receptus (“received”), from perfect passive participle of recipiō (“to receive”). Compare Sicilian rizzetta.

fact.text: Both meanings, recipe and prescription, come from Latin recipere, 'to take'. Doctors began prescriptions with recipe, 'take!', which became English 'recipe' and the Rx symbol.

senses.note: Also a doctor's prescription (ricetta medica).

etymology: From Latin recipere. Possibly borrowed from a Gallo-Italic language, where Latin /-p-/ > /v/ is a regular change, unlike in Italian. Compare the doublet recepire.

fact.text: Comes from the same Latin word, recipere, as English receive. The v where Latin had p suggests it came in through northern Italian dialects, where p between vowels regularly became v.

senses.note: Related: la ricevuta = receipt. Ricevere ospiti = to receive/entertain guests.

etymology: From ricevere (“to receive”).

senses.note: A formal receipt or proof of payment. A shop's till receipt is usually 'lo scontrino'.
il/la richiedente; richiedente asilo = asylum seeker.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *requaerere, from Latin requīrere with dissimilation of /r–r/ to /d–r/, from re- with quaerere, from Proto-Indo-European.

fact.text: Built from chiedere, which goes back to Latin quaerere 'to seek', so it's a cousin of English require, query and quest.

senses.note: Also 'to require': richiede tempo = it takes time. Past participle: richiesto.
su richiesta = on request; also demand: c'è molta richiesta = there's high demand.
Also riciclare denaro = to launder money.

etymology: From ri- + cominciare.

senses.note: Ho ricominciato (a + inf.), but with a thing as subject: la scuola è ricominciata.

etymology: From Latin recognōscere.

senses.note: Also 'to admit or acknowledge': riconosco di aver sbagliato. Passato remoto: riconobbi.

etymology: From Latin recordārī.

fact.text: From Latin recordari: re- (back) + cor, cord- (heart, mind). To remember was to bring something back to the heart. English 'record' shares this root.

senses.note: Also ricordarsi (di): 'Mi ricordo di te' = I remember you.

etymology: Deverbal from ricordare + -o. Compare Sicilian rigordu.

fact.text: Comes from ricordare, from Latin recordari, which is built on cor 'heart'. To remember was to bring something back to the heart. English record shares the root.

senses.note: Also 'souvenir, keepsake': un ricordo di Roma.

etymology: From ri- + costruire.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: io ricostruisco, loro ricostruiscono

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre.

fact.text: The past participle riso also means 'laughter', and it is spelled the same as riso, 'rice'.

senses.note: To laugh at = ridere di qualcuno/qualcosa. Irregular past: ho riso, risi.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin rīdiculus.

senses.note: Rendersi ridicolo = to make a fool of oneself. As a noun, il ridicolo = ridicule.

etymology: From Latin reductus.

senses.note: Past participle of ridurre. mobilità ridotta = reduced mobility; a prezzo ridotto = at a discount.

etymology: Inherited from Latin redūcere (“to reduce”).

senses.note: Irregular, built on the old form riducere: riduco, riducevo, ridussi, ridotto.

etymology: From ri- + entrare (“to enter”).

senses.note: Very common for getting home: rientrare a casa. Rientrare in = to fall within (a category).
senses.prompt: to go back in, to re-enter

etymology: From Latin referre (“to bear or bring back”).

fact.text: Not usually 'to refer': on its own it means to report or pass on (gli ho riferito tutto). For English 'refer to', use the reflexive riferirsi a.

senses.note: Riferire qualcosa a qualcuno = to report something to someone. Riferirsi a = to refer to.

etymology: Inherited from Latin refūtāre (“to oppose, refute”). The -i- was an influence by fiutare (“to sniff”). Doublet of refutare.

fact.text: Comes from Latin refutare, the source of English refute. The extra -i- came in through the influence of fiutare, 'to sniff'.

senses.note: Rifiutarsi di + infinitive = to refuse to do. The noun i rifiuti means rubbish/waste.

etymology: Deverbal from rifiutare (“to refuse”) + -o.

fact.text: English has the same double meaning: refuse is rubbish, and to refuse is to say no. In Italian, rifiutare means to refuse and rifiuto means both a refusal and rubbish.

senses.note: Usually plural: i rifiuti. In the singular it more often means a refusal.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin reflectere. By surface analysis, ri- + flettere.

senses.note: Riflettere su qualcosa. Past participle riflettuto for 'think'; riflesso for mirroring light.

etymology: From Latin refugium.

fact.text: In the Italian Alps and Dolomites, a rifugio is a staffed mountain hut where hikers and climbers can get hot meals and a bed for the night.

senses.note: rifugio alpino = mountain hut

etymology: From ri- + guardare. Compare French regarder.

fact.text: It is formed like French regarder (re- + guard), which gave English 'regard'. 'Riguardo a' corresponds neatly to English 'with regard to'.

senses.note: Per quanto riguarda… = as far as … is concerned. Non ti riguarda = it's none of your business.
Riguardo a = regarding, about; a questo riguardo = in this regard.

etymology: From Latin relaxāre.

senses.note: Transitive: rilassare i muscoli. For 'to relax' oneself, use rilassarsi.
Rilassati! = Relax! Past tense: mi sono rilassato/a.

etymology: From Late Latin relevium, from Latin relevō (“to raise”).

fact.text: Careful: this is relief in the sense of raised terrain or carving, not emotional relief. Emotional relief, as in 'what a relief!', is sollievo: che sollievo!

senses.note: Also relief in sculpture and emphasis: mettere in rilievo = to highlight.

etymology: From Latin remanēre, from re- + maneō.

fact.text: Comes from Latin remanere, which also gave English 'remain' through Old French. The root manere, 'to stay', also gave English 'mansion', 'manor' and 'permanent'.

senses.note: Irregular: rimango, rimasto. Takes essere. 'Mi rimane...' = 'I have ... left'.
Takes a: rimediare a un errore. Informally also 'to get hold of': rimediare un passaggio (to get a lift).
senses.prompt: to remedy, to make up for

senses.note: Mi sono rimesso dall'influenza. Irregular like mettere: rimisi, rimesso.

etymology: From rin- + chiudere.

senses.note: Rinchiudersi (with essere) = to shut yourself away: si è rinchiuso in camera.
senses.prompt: to shut in, to lock up

etymology: From rin- + fresco + -are.

fact.text: In Italy, a 'rinfresco' is a small reception with drinks and snacks, served after events like weddings, baptisms or graduations.

senses.note: rinfrescare la memoria = to refresh one's memory. Without an object (rinfresca), it means it's getting cooler.

etymology: From rin- + grazie + -are.

fact.text: Made from grazie (thanks) with the prefix rin- and the verb ending -are.

senses.note: Ringraziare qualcuno di/per qualcosa. Ti ringrazio = thank you.

etymology: From Latin renovāre.

senses.note: Also 'to renovate': rinnovare la casa; rinnovare il passaporto = renew the passport.
Also 'to reach, get hold of' someone: non riesco a rintracciarlo = I can't get hold of him.

etymology: From Latin renuntiāre (“to reject, retract, revoke”).

senses.note: Takes a: rinunciare a qualcosa / a fare qualcosa. Noun: la rinuncia.

etymology: Inherited from Latin reus. Compare Romanian rău (“bad”), Dalmatian ri (“bad”). Doublet of the borrowed Italian reo.
ignored: The context 'Ri ... r i ...' is a stammered fragment, and this archaic adjective doesn't belong on a learner card.

senses.note: Archaic and poetic. Not related to the noun rio (stream, Venetian canal).

etymology: From ri- + organizzare.

senses.note: Regular -are verb: riorganizzo, ho riorganizzato.

etymology: Inherited from Latin reparāre.

senses.note: Also 'to shelter': ripararsi dalla pioggia = to shelter from the rain.

etymology: From Latin repetere.

senses.note: Ripetere l'anno = to repeat a school year. Ripetiamo! = let's repeat!

etymology: Alteration of rapido (“fast”) influenced by ripa (“shore”).

fact.text: Probably began as a variant of rapido 'fast' and was reshaped by ripa 'riverbank'. Picture a steep riverbank.

etymology: From ri- + pieno.

senses.note: Used for food: peperoni ripieni = stuffed peppers. As a noun, il ripieno = stuffing.

etymology: From ri- + pieno.

senses.note: As an adjective it means stuffed: peperoni ripieni.

etymology: From Latin reportāre.

senses.note: Can also mean 'to report' (news), or 'to suffer' (riportare ferite = to sustain injuries).
senses.prompt: to bring back, to take back

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin repausāre, from Latin pausāre. By surface analysis, ri- + posare.

fact.text: It comes from Late Latin repausare, built on pausa. English repose and pause come from the same source.

senses.note: Often reflexive: riposarsi (mi sono riposato). Riposare takes avere: ho riposato.

etymology: Deverbal from riposare + -o. Compare French repos, Spanish reposo, Portuguese repouso, Romanian repaus.

senses.note: 'Giorno di riposo' = day off. 'Riposo!' is the military order 'At ease!'

etymology: From Latin reprehendere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin reprehendere, and it can still mean 'to scold' someone.

senses.note: riprendere a + infinitive: ha ripreso a piovere. Can also mean to film or to scold.

etymology: From ri- + pristino + -are.

fact.text: Built from ri- + pristino (original, former state), a cousin of English 'pristine'. To ripristinare is to put something back the way it was.

senses.note: Used for bringing back an earlier state: ripristinare il servizio, i dati, l'ordine.

etymology: From riscaldare + -mento.

senses.note: Also a sports warm-up. Riscaldamento globale = global warming.

etymology: From rischio + -are.

fact.text: English 'risk' came from Italian: the old Italian risco or rischio passed into French as risque, and English took it from French in the 1600s. Where the Italian word came from is still debated.

senses.note: Rischiare di + infinitive = to risk / nearly do (ho rischiato di cadere).

From Old Italian risco, from Vulgar Latin *resecum or deverbal from resecare, via risicare and later riscare, rischiare, both from Latin resecō (“to cut off”). Compare Sicilian rìsicu.

fact.text: English 'risk' came from this Italian word via French risque. One theory traces it to Latin resecare 'to cut off', perhaps meaning sharp rocks that threatened ships.

senses.note: Correre un rischio = to run/take a risk; a rischio = at risk.

etymology: From rischio + -oso.

senses.note: Rischioso = risky; pericoloso = dangerous. Verb: rischiare = to risk.
Also reply or confirmation in emails: in attesa di un Suo riscontro = awaiting your reply.

etymology: From Latin rīsus.

fact.text: Two different words share this spelling. Riso meaning 'laughter' comes from Latin risus, while the grain comes from Greek óryza, which is also the source of English 'rice'.

senses.note: Mass noun, usually singular. Don't confuse with riso = laughter (plural le risa).

etymology: From Latin resolvere, possibly a semi-learned borrowing.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle risolto, passato remoto risolsi.

etymology: From ri- + sparmiare, the latter (now archaic) from Late Latin sparmiāre, from a Germanic source, likely Lombardic *sparōn (“to spare, save”) (compare Old High German sparōn, German sparen), from Proto-Germanic *sparōną. The development of the -m- in the Late Latin form (instead of the expected -n- or -r-) is traditionally attributed to the influence of Frankish *waidanjan (“to earn, gain”) (which also yielded guadagnare). Cognate with French épargner, Occitan esparnhar, and English spare. Related to sparagnare.

fact.text: Related to English 'spare': both go back to Germanic *sparon, which reached Italian through a Lombardic word. German sparen means 'to save'.

senses.note: To save in the sense of rescue is salvare. Also means 'to spare' (risparmiami i dettagli).

etymology: From ri- + spedire.

senses.note: Also 'to send again'. Conjugated with -isc-: rispedisco.

etymology: From Latin respectāre.

fact.text: Latin respectare meant to look back at something again and again (re- + specere, to look, as in spectator). To respect someone was originally to give them a second look.

senses.note: Also means to observe or comply with: rispettare le regole, rispettare una scadenza.

etymology: From Latin respectus.

senses.note: Rispetto per qualcuno. Rispetto a = compared with / regarding. I miei rispetti = my respects.

etymology: From Late Latin respondere, from Latin respondēre.

senses.note: Takes a: rispondere a qualcuno / al telefono. Past participle: risposto.

etymology: From rispondere, corrupted by posta, feminine past participle of porre. Compare Asturian and Spanish respuesta; Catalan, Galician, and Portuguese resposta.

senses.note: Also reply or response. dare una risposta = to give an answer.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin rixa. Doublet of ressa, which was inherited.

fact.text: Comes from Latin rixa, 'quarrel'. The same Latin word also gave Italian ressa, 'a crush of people', which developed naturally over time instead of being borrowed.

senses.note: Scoppiare una rissa = a brawl breaks out.

etymology: Noun use of present participle of ristorare (“to restore”)

fact.text: Literally 'restoring', from ristorare, 'to restore'. The French word 'restaurant' first meant a broth to restore your strength, and later the place where it was served.

etymology: Semi-learned borrowing from Latin resultāre, from resiliō.

fact.text: From Latin resultāre, 'to spring back', from resilīre, the same root as English resilient. A result is what bounces back from an action.

senses.note: Mi risulta che… = as far as I know… Risultare + adjective: è risultato utile.
Essere in ritardo = to be late. Il treno ha 10 minuti di ritardo.

etymology: From ri- + tirare.

senses.note: Also 'to collect' (ritirare un pacco). Cash withdrawals use prelevare. Ritirarsi = to retreat, retire.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin rhythmus, from Ancient Greek ῥυθμός (rhuthmós), from ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek rhythmos, from rheo, 'to flow'. A rhythm was originally a measured flow of movement.

senses.note: Also pace: il ritmo di vita = the pace of life.

etymology: From Latin retornāre, corresponding to ri- + tornare.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono ritornato. Means much the same as tornare.
Andata e ritorno = round trip; al ritorno = on the way back.

etymology: From ri- + trovare. Compare French retrouver.

senses.note: Ritrovarsi = to meet up again, or to end up somewhere.
essere in riunione = to be in a meeting. Can also mean a reunion or gathering.

etymology: From ri- + uscire. Compare French réussir, borrowed via riuscita.

fact.text: Literally ri- + uscire, 'to go out again', so to come out well. French réussir 'to succeed' was borrowed from Italian.

senses.note: Non riesco a dormire = I can't sleep. Also 'to succeed': riuscire in qualcosa.

etymology: From riuscire.

senses.note: From riuscire (to succeed). la buona riuscita = the success (of a plan, event).

etymology: Inherited from Latin revidēre. By surface analysis, ri- + vedere.

fact.text: This is the verb inside arrivederci, 'goodbye', which literally means 'until we see each other again' (a rivederci).

senses.note: Irregular past participle: rivisto. Also means 'to see again': ci rivediamo!

fact.text: Literally 'seen again' (from rivedere). It can mean a military review or a stage revue, but a book or film review is una recensione.

senses.note: A periodical. A shop or depot is not a rivista: use negozio or magazzino.

etymology: From Latin revīvō.

senses.note: Irregular like vivere: past participle rivissuto. Intransitive 'to come back to life' takes essere.

etymology:
From Vulgar Latin rauba, of Germanic origin, via Gothic or Frankish *raub, all from Proto-Germanic *raubaz.
Cognate with Sicilian robba, English robe, rob, and reave; and Scots reif (“robbery, stolen goods”).

fact.text: Shares a Germanic root with English rob and robe. The original idea was plunder, often clothing taken as booty. Despite the look, it means 'stuff', not 'robe'.

senses.note: Mass noun, usually singular: tanta roba = lots of stuff. Roba da matti! = That's crazy!

etymology: Borrowed from French robot, borrowed from Czech robot, from robota (“drudgery, servitude”), from Old Czech robota, from Proto-Slavic *orbota, from *orbiti + *-ota.

fact.text: From Czech robota, 'forced labour'. Karel Čapek made it famous in his 1920 play R.U.R., and his brother Josef suggested the word.

senses.note: Invariable: il robot, i robot. Robot da cucina = food processor.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French roche, from Early Medieval Latin rocca, of uncertain origin. Doublet of rocca.

fact.text: Doublet of rocca 'fortress', which is a castle built on a rock. Both go back to Medieval Latin rocca, the same source as English rock.

senses.note: Rock as material or a large mass; a small stone is un sasso or una pietra.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English rock.

fact.text: In Italian, rock only means the music. A rock in the sense of stone is una pietra or una roccia.

senses.note: Only the music style. A rock or stone is una roccia or una pietra.

etymology: Borrowed from English romantic.

senses.note: Plural romantici / romantiche.

etymology:
Borrowed from Old French romanz, which stems from the Latin expression romanice loqui (“to speak in the Roman way”).
Cognate with English romance (noun).

fact.text: Means a novel, not a romance. It shares a root with English 'romance': Old French romanz, a story told in the everyday 'Roman' tongue instead of Latin.

senses.note: romanzo giallo = crime novel. For a love affair, Italian usually uses storia d'amore.

etymology: Inherited from Latin rumpō, rumpere (“to break”).

fact.text: English bankrupt comes from Italian banca rotta, 'broken bench', the bench being a money-changer's table. Rotta/rotto is the past participle of this verb.

senses.note: Past participle: rotto. Rompersi = to get broken. Colloquially rompere (le scatole) = to annoy.

etymology: From Latin rosa.

fact.text: Latin rosa probably comes from Greek rhódon, 'rose'. That Greek word also gives English rhododendron, literally 'rose tree'.

senses.note: Doesn't change form: scarpe rosa. Romanzo rosa = romance novel; cronaca rosa = celebrity gossip.

etymology: From Latin rosa.

fact.text: Latin rosa probably comes from Greek rhódon, 'rose'. That Greek word also gives English rhododendron, literally 'rose tree'.

senses.note: Plural: le rose. As an invariable adjective/noun, rosa also means pink (il rosa, maglie rosa).

etymology: From Latin russus. Cognate with Sicilian russu.

fact.text: Comes from Latin russus, which goes back to the Indo-European root for 'red'. English red, ruddy and rust come from that same ancient root.

senses.note: Also used for red/ginger hair: capelli rossi.
Also called la rotonda in everyday speech.

etymology: From Medieval Latin rotulāre (“to roll, revolve”), from Latin rotula (“a little wheel”), diminutive of rota (“a wheel”). Doublet of rullare.

fact.text: It comes from Medieval Latin rotulare, from rotula, 'little wheel' (rota = wheel). The same word reached English through Old French as roll, so to roll literally means to move like a little wheel.

senses.note: Takes essere when intransitive (è rotolato giù) and avere when transitive (ho rotolato il masso).
Reflexive: mi rotolo, si rotola. Rotolarsi nel fango = to roll around in the mud.

fact.text: English 'rotunda', a round domed building, was borrowed from Italian rotonda. The most famous one is Rome's Pantheon, nicknamed 'la Rotonda'.

senses.note: US English: traffic circle. Don't confuse it with the adjective rotonda (round, feminine of rotondo).

etymology: Inherited from Latin rotundus; otherwise an assimilated or relatinized form of Old Italian ritondo, from Late Latin retundus, variant of the classical term.

fact.text: Latin rotundus also gave English 'rotund' and 'rotunda'. On Italian roads, una rotonda is a roundabout.

senses.note: tavola rotonda = round table. Figuratively it can mean plump.

etymology: Inherited from Latin rupta [via], compare French route.

fact.text: From Latin rupta via, a 'broken road' cut through the land. The same source gives English route, and also rout, a broken army. Italian rotta can mean that too.

senses.note: cambiare rotta = to change course; a rotta di collo = at breakneck speed.

etymology: Borrowed from French roulotte.

senses.note: Invariable French loanword: la/le roulotte. It is pronounced the French way.

etymology: From earlier ruina, from Latin ruīna.

senses.note: Le rovine = ruins (remains). Andare in rovina = to go to ruin.

etymology: From Latin ruīnāre (“to ruin”). By surface analysis, rovina + -are. Compare Spanish ruinar, arruinar, French ruiner, Piedmontese ruiné, ruviné.

fact.text: Like English 'ruin', it goes back to Latin ruere, 'to rush down, collapse'. That is why it can also mean to crash or tumble down.

senses.note: Transitive with avere. Intransitive 'to collapse, crash down' takes essere. rovinarsi = to ruin oneself.
Past participle of rovinare (to ruin). Sono rovinato! = I'm ruined / I'm done for!

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin raubāre, from Proto-West Germanic *raubōn.

fact.text: A Germanic word that came into Italian through Late Latin raubare. It is a cousin of English rob and robber.

senses.note: rubare qualcosa a qualcuno = to steal something from someone.

fact.text: The musical term 'rubato', where a performer speeds up and slows down freely, is this word. It means 'stolen' because time is taken from some notes and given to others.

ignored: In the context this is only the past participle of rubare (to steal), which should be studied on the rubare card.

senses.note: Past participle of rubare (to steal). In music, tempo rubato means flexible tempo.

etymology: Borrowed from French robinet.

fact.text: Borrowed from French robinet, a diminutive of robin, an old name for a sheep. Early taps were often shaped like a sheep's head.

senses.note: Aprire/chiudere il rubinetto = to turn the tap on/off. Acqua del rubinetto = tap water.

etymology: From Latin rūmōrem ("rustle," "murmur").

fact.text: Looks like English rumour but normally means noise. A rumour is una voce or una diceria. Both words come from Latin rumor, 'murmur, hearsay'.

senses.note: Fare rumore = to make noise.

etymology: From rumore + -oso; cognate with Piedmontese rumoros.

fact.text: Built from rumore, meaning 'noise'. Despite the look, rumore is not a rumour: Italian calls that una voce or una diceria.

senses.note: Used for places, people and machines. For a loud voice or sound, forte is common.

fact.text: Came in through French rôle, from Latin rotulus, meaning 'roll'. An actor's part was once written on a roll of paper, so 'role' and 'roll' are really the same word.

senses.note: di ruolo = permanent, tenured (for example insegnante di ruolo, a permanent teacher).

etymology: From Latin rota

fact.text: Comes from Latin rota 'wheel'. English 'rotate', 'rotary' and 'rotation' come from the same word, all about turning like a wheel.

senses.note: ruota di scorta = spare wheel

etymology: From Latin rūgidus, from ruga (“wrinkle”). Cognate with Piedmontese rùvid.

fact.text: It comes from Latin ruga, 'wrinkle', the same root as English corrugated (as in corrugated iron), which is literally 'wrinkled'.

senses.note: Used for texture, e.g. pelle ruvida (rough skin). Not for 'approximate' or 'rough sea'.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin sabbatum. Compare English Sabbath.

fact.text: From Hebrew shabbat via Greek and Latin, the same source as English 'Sabbath'. English Saturday is named after the god Saturn instead.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian. Sabato = this Saturday; il sabato = on Saturdays.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sabla, from a contraction of Latin sabula, plural of sabulum, variant of sabulō. Compare French sable, Occitan sabla.

senses.note: sabbie mobili = quicksand

etymology: Inherited from Latin saccus, from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos, “sack, bag; sackcloth”), from Semitic.

fact.text: Same word as English sack. It came through Latin saccus from Greek sákkos, which was itself borrowed from a Semitic language (compare Hebrew saq).

senses.note: Un sacco di = a lot of (colloquial): un sacco di formaggio = loads of cheese.

etymology: From Latin sacrificus.
ignored: In context this is a conjugated form of the verb sacrificare; the literary adjective is too rare for a card.

senses.note: Rare literary adjective; the usual word is sacrificale.

etymology: From Late Latin exagium, from Latin exigō (“to examine”).

fact.text: In this sense it comes from Late Latin exagium, 'a weighing', which is also the source of English essay. The 'wise' saggio is an unrelated word.

senses.note: Also a recital or show (saggio di danza). Don't confuse it with the adjective saggio, 'wise'.

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic *sala (“hall”), from either Proto-Germanic *saliz or *salą (both meaning "house, hall").

fact.text: A Germanic loanword brought by the Lombards. Its augmentative salone became French salon, which gave English both 'salon' and 'saloon'.

senses.note: Room for a purpose: sala d'attesa (waiting room), sala da pranzo (dining room).

etymology: From sale (“salt”).

fact.text: English 'salami' is actually the Italian plural. One sausage in Italian is un salame. The word comes from sale (salt), because the meat is cured with salt.

senses.note: Singular is salame. Also a colloquial insult: 'Che salame!' = what a fool!
Also means pricey: 'un conto salato' = a steep bill.

etymology: Deverbal from saldare + -o.

fact.text: In the plural, i saldi are Italy's official seasonal sales. Start dates are set by each region, usually in early January and early July.

senses.note: Saldo del conto = account balance. In the plural, i saldi means the seasonal sales.

etymology: Inherited from Latin salem.

fact.text: English salary comes from Latin salarium, derived from sal 'salt', though the popular story that Roman soldiers were paid in salt is uncertain.

etymology:
Inherited from Latin salīre.
Cognate with Spanish salir (“to go out”) and French saillir (“to stick out”).

fact.text: Latin salire meant 'to leap'. It gave English salient (literally 'leaping out'). Careful: Spanish salir, from the same verb, means 'to go out', not 'to go up'.

senses.note: Irregular: salgo, salgono. Essere when used alone (sono salito); avere with an object (ho salito le scale).

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of salire (“to go up”).

senses.note: In salita = uphill. Don't confuse with è salita in the example, which is the verb salire (went up).

etymology: From sala + -otto; cognate with Piedmontese salòt.

fact.text: Milan's grand Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II is nicknamed 'il salotto di Milano', the city's living room, because people go there to meet and be seen.

senses.note: Also a literary or social salon; 'salotto buono' = the best room, kept for guests.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *salsa, noun use of the feminine of Latin salsus (“salted”), from saliō, from sal.

fact.text: From Latin salsus 'salted', from sal 'salt'. The same salty root gave English 'sauce'.

senses.note: Any sauce, not only spicy salsa. Pasta sauce is often called 'sugo'.

etymology: From Late Latin [farta] salsīcia, ultimately from Latin sāl (“salt”). Compare Sicilian sausizza. In Classical Latin, farcimen.

fact.text: Both this word and English 'sausage' come from Late Latin salsicia, from salsus, 'salted'. Salting was how the meat was preserved.

senses.note: Plural salsicce (no i).

etymology: Inherited from Latin saltāre.

fact.text: Latin saltare, its source, meant 'to dance' and comes from salire 'to leap'. Its cooking sense 'to sauté' matches French sauter, which is where English sauté comes from.

features.construction: intransitive or transitive; avere when transitive, avere or essere when intransitive

senses.note: Also 'to skip' (saltare la colazione). Saltare fuori = to pop up, turn up.

etymology: From Latin saltus.

fact.text: From Latin saltus 'a leap'. English somersault comes from the same word via Old French, and literally means 'over-leap' (supra + saltus).

senses.note: Fare un salto da qualcuno = to drop by someone's place. Salto in alto/in lungo = high/long jump.

etymology: From Latin salūtāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin salus, 'health': to greet someone was to wish them good health. English 'salute' and 'salutary' come from the same root.

senses.note: Also 'to say goodbye'. Salutami tua madre = say hi to your mother for me.

etymology: From Latin salūtem, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, completed”).

fact.text: False friend: this word does not mean a military salute (that is il saluto). It means 'health', so raising a glass and saying it is toasting someone's health.

senses.note: Also said to someone who sneezes ('bless you!'). As a noun, la salute means health.

etymology: From Latin salūtem, from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole, completed”).

fact.text: False friend: this word does not mean a military salute (that is il saluto). It means 'health', so raising a glass and saying it is toasting someone's health.

senses.note: 'Salute!' also means 'Cheers!' when toasting and 'Bless you!' after a sneeze.

etymology: From salutare.

senses.note: Plural saluti also means 'regards' at the end of letters: Cari saluti.

etymology: From Late Latin salvāre (“to save”), from Latin salvus. Compare French sauver, Portuguese and Spanish salvar.

fact.text: Comes from Latin salvus (safe, healthy), the same root behind English salvage and salvation, and behind the Italian greeting salve.

senses.note: Saving money is risparmiare. Salvare un file = to save a file.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin salvē.

fact.text: Ancient Romans used this exact word as a greeting. In Latin, salve means 'be well', the imperative of salvere 'to be healthy', from the same root as English 'salvation'.

senses.note: A polite, neutral greeting. Handy when you are unsure whether to use tu or Lei.
Sano e salvo = safe and sound. Also means 'except': salvo imprevisti = barring surprises.

etymology: Ultimately from Sanskrit चन्दन (candana).

fact.text: Three different words share this spelling in Italian: the sandal you wear, sandalwood (from Sanskrit candana), and a flat-bottomed boat or punt.

senses.note: Usually plural: i sandali.

etymology: From Late Latin sanguem, alteration of Classical Latin sanguinem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁sh₂-én-, oblique stem of *h₁ésh₂r̥ (“blood”). Compare French sang, Romanian sânge.

senses.note: a sangue freddo = in cold blood; carne al sangue = rare meat.

fact.text: In Naples and southern Italy there is also a sweet version: a thick chocolate cream for Carnival. It was traditionally made with pig's blood, which modern recipes leave out.

senses.note: Also called black pudding in British English.

etymology: From Latin sānus, from Proto-Indo-European *swā-n- (“healthy; whole; active; vigorous”).

fact.text: Looks like English sane but means healthy. Sane is sano di mente, literally 'healthy of mind'. Both words come from Latin sanus.

senses.note: sano e salvo = safe and sound. Also: cibo sano = healthy food.
Masculine santo. Before names: Santa Lucia, San Marco. Also an adjective meaning 'holy'.

etymology: Derived from Latin sānctus.

fact.text: Before most male saints' names it shortens to San (San Marco). It stays Santo before s + consonant (Santo Stefano) and becomes Sant' before a vowel (Sant'Antonio).

senses.note: Feminine: santa. Also an adjective meaning holy: acqua santa = holy water.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sapēre, from Latin sapĕre (“taste, know”).

fact.text: Latin sapere meant both 'to taste' and 'to be wise', so 'sa di fragola' means 'it tastes of strawberry'. The same root gives English savour and Homo sapiens.

senses.note: Used for facts and skills (so nuotare = I can swim). For people and places, use conoscere.

etymology: From Latin sāpōnem, from Proto-Germanic *saipǭ.

fact.text: The Romans borrowed this word from Germanic *saipǭ, the same word that became English soap. So the Italian and English words are cousins.

senses.note: Soap opera is also una soap (opera) in Italian.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sapōrem (“taste, flavor”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin sapere, 'to taste', which also came to mean 'to be wise'. That is why Italian sapere means 'to know', and why we are Homo sapiens, the 'wise' human.

senses.note: Sapere di = to taste of: sa di fragola (it tastes of strawberry).

etymology: From s- + bagliare (see also abbagliare). See bagliore. Compare Sicilian sbagghiari for more.

senses.note: Can take an object: sbagliare strada = take the wrong road. Sbagliarsi = to be mistaken.

etymology: Deverbal from sbagliare (“to make a mistake”) + -o.

senses.note: Per sbaglio = by mistake. Fare uno sbaglio = to make a mistake.

etymology: The prefix im- (“into, in”) of imbarazzare (formerly meaning "to impede") is replaced with s- (“remove, reverse”), resulting in a meaning “to remove the obstacle”.

fact.text: Formed by swapping the im- of imbarazzare (once 'to obstruct') for s- 'remove', so it literally means 'to remove the obstacle'. English embarrass comes from the same 'obstruct' family.

senses.note: Mostly reflexive: sbarazzarsi di qcs = to get rid of sth (Si sbarazza della palla).

etymology: From s- + battere, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *exbattere, from Latin battuere.

fact.text: The pronominal form sbattersene is very common slang: 'me ne sbatto' means 'I couldn't care less'. It is rude, so avoid it in polite company.

senses.note: Sbattere la porta = to slam the door. Also: sbattere le uova (whisk eggs), sbattere contro (bump into).
Very common in the imperative: Sbrigati! / Sbrigatevi! = Hurry up!

etymology: From s- + buccia + -are.

fact.text: Made from s- + buccia ('peel, skin'), so it literally means 'to un-skin'. That's why sbucciarsi un ginocchio means to skin your knee.

senses.note: Built from buccia (peel, skin). sbucciare una mela = to peel an apple.

etymology: Derivative of scaffa.

senses.note: Usually the whole shelving unit or bookcase; a single shelf is a ripiano or mensola.

etymology: Inherited from Latin scāla (“stair, staircase, ladder”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin scala, meaning 'ladder' or 'stairs'. The same word gives English 'scale a wall' and escalate, and Milan's opera house La Scala is named after a church that once stood on its site.

senses.note: 'The stairs' is often plural: le scale. Also means ladder and scale (musical, map).

etymology: From scalare + -tore.

fact.text: Comes from scalare 'to climb', from scala 'ladder, stairs', which is related to English 'escalate' and to 'scale' in the sense of scaling a wall.

senses.note: Feminine: scalatrice. In cycling it also means a climbing specialist.

senses.note: scambiare X per Y = to mistake X for Y. It also means 'to exchange, swap'.

senses.note: scambio culturale = cultural exchange. Also railway points.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *excappāre, a verb based on Late Latin cappa (“cloak”).

fact.text: It comes from Vulgar Latin *excappare, 'to get out of one's cloak (cappa)', perhaps leaving a pursuer holding only the cloak. English escape comes from the same word.

senses.note: Colloquially 'Scappo!' = I've got to dash. Takes essere: sono scappato.

etymology: From s- + caricare.

fact.text: Literally 'to un-load': s- reverses caricare 'to load', from Late Latin carricare, which also gave English 'charge' and 'cargo'. Downloading is unloading data.

senses.note: Also to unload, or to offload onto someone: scaricare la colpa su altri.

From Gothic *𐍃𐌺𐌰𐍂𐍀𐌰 (*skarpa) or *𐍃𐌺𐌰𐍂𐍀𐍉 (*skarpō), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skarpaz.

senses.note: Usually used in the plural: un paio di scarpe = a pair of shoes.

etymology: Metathesised form of Early Medieval Latin castula (“basket”), diminutive of a term borrowed from a Germanic language, *kasto, whence also Italian castone, German Kasten. Compare Sicilian scàtulu.

fact.text: Italians say 'rompere le scatole' (literally 'to break the boxes') for 'to pester someone'. It is a polite stand-in for a much ruder expression.

senses.note: In scatola = tinned/canned. Cardboard box: scatola di cartone.

etymology: From Latin excavāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin excavare 'to hollow out', which also gave English excavate. Both are built on cavus 'hollow', as in cave and cavity.

senses.note: Uno scavo is a dig or excavation. Gli scavi are archaeological excavations.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *exēligere, from Latin ex (“out of, from”) + ēligere.

fact.text: From Vulgar Latin *exeligere: ex 'out' + eligere 'to pick out'. The same eligere gives English elect, eligible and elite.

senses.note: Irregular: scelgo, scelgono; past participle scelto.

etymology: From scegliere.

senses.note: fare una scelta = to make a choice; di prima scelta = top quality.

etymology: From scemare.

fact.text: It comes from the verb scemare, 'to diminish, decrease', so a scemo is literally someone whose wits have been diminished.

senses.note: Takes lo. Feminine: la scema. Also an adjective: non fare lo scemo = don't act stupid.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin scēna, from Ancient Greek σκηνή (skēnḗ).

fact.text: Greek skēnḗ first meant 'tent, booth'. It was the hut behind the stage where actors changed costumes, and the word slowly came to mean the stage and then what happens on it.

senses.note: Also 'stage': entrare in scena = to come on stage; fare una scena = to make a scene.

etymology: From a reduction of the prefix in discendere, from Latin dēscendere.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin descendere, from de- 'down' + scandere 'to climb'. The same scandere gives English ascend, descend and even scan.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono sceso. Scendere dal treno = to get off the train.

etymology: Borrowed from English sheriff.

senses.note: Takes 'lo' because it starts with sc-: lo sceriffo, gli sceriffi.

etymology: Deverbal from schermire (“to protect”) + -o.

fact.text: Comes from schermire, 'to protect', so a schermo was first a shield. The same Germanic root gives Italian scherma (fencing) and English skirmish.

senses.note: Il grande schermo = the big screen (cinema).

etymology: Borrowed from Lombardic *skerzan (“to jump merrily, enjoy oneself, jest”) from Proto-Germanic *skertaną (“to hop, jump”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerd- (“to dance, jump”). Akin to Middle High German scherzen (“to frolic, jump merrily, hop up and down”) (German scherzen (“to joke”); Scherz (“joke, sport”)), Norwegian skjerta (“to joke”). More at scherzo.

fact.text: Borrowed from Lombardic, a Germanic language, and related to German Scherz 'joke'. The noun scherzo means 'joke'.

senses.note: Stai scherzando? = Are you kidding? Scherzo! = Just kidding!

etymology: Deverbal from scherzare (“to joke, play, jest”) + -o, from Old Italian scherzare, borrowed from Lombardic *skerzan (“to jump merrily, enjoy oneself, jest”) from Proto-Germanic *skertaną (“to hop, jump”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kerǝd- (“to dance, jump”). Akin to Middle High German scherzen (“to frolic, jump merrily, hop up and down”) (German scherzen (“to joke”); Scherz (“joke, sport”)), Norwegian skjerta (“to joke”).

fact.text: It comes from a Lombardic (Germanic) word meaning to jump about merrily.

senses.note: Per scherzo = as a joke; fare uno scherzo a qualcuno = to play a trick on someone.

etymology: Probably onomatopoeic; the figurative sense influenced by French écraser. Compare Galician escachar. Cognate with Sicilian scacciari.

fact.text: Tuscan schiacciata flatbread is named after this verb: it means 'the squashed one', because the dough is pressed flat by hand before baking.

senses.note: Also to press: schiacciare un pulsante (press a button). Lo schiaccianoci = nutcracker.

etymology: From Lombardic skina, related to Old Saxon skina, German Schiene and English shin.

fact.text: A Germanic loan from Lombardic skina. It is related to English shin and German Schiene (rail, splint).

senses.note: Mal di schiena = backache.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan esquiera, from Old French eschiere, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skarō, whence also Old English sċearu, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to part; split; cut off; sever; divide”). Compare German Schar (“troop”), Danish skare (“host", "crowd”).

senses.note: Case a schiera = terraced (row) houses. Also a host or troop of people.

etymology: From Old French eschiu (“shy, timid”) (cf. eschiver), from Frankish *skeuh (“shy, timid, fearful”), from Proto-Germanic *skeuhaz (“shy, frightened”). Cognate with English shy, Sicilian schifiju (“disgust, mess”). More at shy, eschew.

fact.text: Surprisingly, it is related to English 'shy'. Both come from a Germanic word for 'timid, fearful': disgust is what makes you shrink away.

senses.note: Che schifo! = How gross! Fare schifo = to be awful, to suck.

etymology: From schifo + -oso.

senses.note: Strong and informal. Comes from schifo 'disgust': Che schifo! = How gross!

etymology: Borrowed from Norwegian ski.

fact.text: Borrowed from Norwegian ski, from Old Norse skíð, 'stick of wood'. The Italian spelling sci is pronounced 'shee', which matches the Norwegian pronunciation better than English does.

senses.note: Invariable noun. Fare sci = to go skiing. The verb is sciare.

fact.text: Italian spells ski as sci and says it 'shee'. That is closer to how Norwegians say ski, the language the word comes from, than the English pronunciation.

senses.note: Note the double i in tu scii. Andare a sciare = to go skiing.

etymology: Borrowed from French écharpe, from Old French escharpe, from Frankish *skirpa (“bandoleer”), of either Germanic or Latin origin.

fact.text: Borrowed from French écharpe. In Old French, escharpe was a pilgrim's small bag hung from a strap. English 'scarf' probably comes from the same Old French word.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin scientia.

senses.note: le scienze = the sciences (also the school subject).

etymology: From Latin exsolvere (“to unloose, release, free; to unbind, untie, undo”). Compare Sicilian sciògghiri.

fact.text: From Latin exsolvere, to loosen or release, built on solvere, the root of English solve, dissolve and solution. It also means to untie a knot.

etymology: Deverbal from scioperare + -o.

senses.note: Fare sciopero = to go on strike; essere in sciopero = to be on strike.

etymology: From Medieval Latin siruppus, syrupus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from شَرِبَ (šariba, “to drink”).

fact.text: Comes, via Medieval Latin, from Arabic sharab, 'drink', from the root meaning 'to drink'. English sherbet comes from the same Arabic root.

senses.note: Also cough syrup: lo sciroppo per la tosse.

etymology:
The word is probably of onomatopoeic origin.
From Latin exsībilāre. .

etymology: From s- + comodo.

senses.note: Irregular: scompaio, scomparve, scomparso. Also a euphemism for 'to pass away'.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan esconfire, from Latin *excōnficiō, from ex- + cōnficiō.

senses.note: Irregular: sconfissi, sconfitto. Noun: la sconfitta (defeat).

etymology: Deverbal from scongiurare + -o.

fact.text: Italians 'fanno gli scongiuri' to ward off bad luck, for example by touching iron or making the horns gesture. It is roughly the Italian version of knocking on wood.

ignored: Bad parse: in the context this is the verb scongiurare ('ti scongiuro' = I beg you), not the noun.

senses.note: Fare gli scongiuri = to touch wood (ward off bad luck).

etymology: From s- (“un-”) + conosciuto (“known”).

senses.note: For a woman: la sconosciuta (pl. sconosciute). As an adjective it means 'unknown'.

etymology: From Latin discomputus (literally “calculated off”).

fact.text: Shares its Latin root with English 'discount', which came via Old French, and with English 'compute'.

senses.note: fare uno sconto = to give a discount

etymology: From scontrare + -ino.

fact.text: In many Italian bars you pay at the till first, then show the scontrino to the barista to get your coffee.

etymology: From Late Latin scōpāre (“to brush or sweep away”), from Latin scōpae (“broom”).

etymology: From Latin excurrere.

fact.text: This is the past participle of scorrere (to flow, to run by). So l'anno scorso is literally 'the year that has flowed past'.

senses.note: 'La settimana scorsa' = last week. For 'final', use ultimo instead.

etymology: From Latin scortum (“skin, hide”), via scortea (“leather bag or garment”), nominalization of scorteus (“made of skin or leather”). Compare French écorce, Romanian scoarță, Sicilian scorcia.

senses.note: scorza di limone = lemon peel or zest. Also bark (of a tree).

etymology: Inherited from Latin scrīptōrem.

senses.note: Feminine: la scrittrice.

etymology: From scrivano + -ia.

fact.text: Built from scrivano, 'scribe or clerk' (from scrivere, to write), plus -ia. So it was originally the clerk's place. It is also the word for a computer desktop.

senses.note: A writing desk at home or in an office. A school desk is il banco.

etymology: Inherited from Latin scrībere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin scribere, 'to write', which also gave English scribe, script, scripture and describe.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: scritto. scrivere qcs a qcn = to write something to someone.

etymology: From Latin sculptōrem. Cognate with Friulian scultôr, Lombard scultor, Piedmontese scultor.

senses.note: Takes lo (lo scultore). Feminine: la scultrice.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin sculptūra (“act of carving; sculpture”), derived from sculpō (“to carve”) + -tūra (“-ing, -ure”, action noun suffix).
Inherited from Latin schola. First attested in the 14th century. Compare Sicilian scola.

fact.text: Came through Latin schola from Greek skholē, which originally meant 'leisure': free time spent in discussion and learning. English 'school' and 'scholar' share this root.

senses.note: Andare a scuola = to go to school (no article).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *exquatere, *excotere, a remodelling of Latin excutere on simplex quatere. Compare Romanian scoate (“remove”). Cf. also escutere, a borrowed doublet.

senses.note: Irregular: scossi (passato remoto), scosso (past participle). Scuotere la testa = to shake your head.

etymology: From oscuro, from Latin obscūrus.

fact.text: A shortened form of oscuro, from Latin obscurus, which is also where English gets obscure.

senses.note: Also for colours: blu scuro = dark blue. Opposite: chiaro.
chiedere scusa = to apologize; una scusa = a pretext.

etymology: From Latin excūsāre.

senses.note: Scusa (informal), mi scusi (formal), scusate (to a group) = excuse me / sorry.
Scusarsi con qualcuno per qualcosa: mi sono scusato con lei per il ritardo.

etymology: Probably inherited from Vulgar Latin *exdēradiāre.

senses.note: In this sense it is reflexive: sdraiarsi (mi sono sdraiato). Transitive sdraiare = to lay someone down.

etymology: From sdraiare + -si.

fact.text: A deckchair in Italian is una sdraio, short for sedia a sdraio, literally 'a lying-down chair'. On Italian beaches you can rent rows of them along with an umbrella.

senses.note: Mi sdraio, ti sdrai, si sdraia. Sdraiarsi al sole = to lie in the sun.

etymology: From Latin sī (“if”) or from Late Latin se(d), from Latin sī and quid ("what").

senses.note: Also means 'whether'. Don't confuse it with sé (oneself).

etymology: Univerbation of se (“if”) + bene (“well”).

fact.text: Made by joining se 'if' and bene 'well', so roughly 'even if it's well so'. English albeit was built the same way, from 'all be it'.

senses.note: Takes the subjunctive: sebbene sia stanco, esco.

etymology: From Latin siccus, from Proto-Indo-European *seyk-.

fact.text: It comes from Latin siccus 'dry', which also gave English 'desiccate' (to dry out completely) and the 'sec' on champagne labels, via French.

senses.note: Also 'dried' (fichi secchi) and 'dry' of wine (vino secco).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin saeculum.

fact.text: It comes from Latin saeculum (age, generation), which also gave English 'secular'. Something secular originally belonged to the present age or worldly life, as opposed to the eternal.

senses.note: Centuries are often named by their hundreds: il Novecento = the 20th century, il Quattrocento = the 15th.

etymology: From Latin secundus (“he who follows, second”), from sequor (“to follow”). Cognate with Sicilian sicunnu.

fact.text: From Latin secundus, 'the one that follows', from sequi, 'to follow'. That is why it is related to English 'sequence' and 'sequel'.

senses.note: Agrees: seconda volta. As a preposition, secondo me = in my opinion.

etymology: From Latin secundus (“he who follows, second”), from sequor (“to follow”). Cognate with Sicilian sicunnu.

senses.note: Un secondo! = Just a second!

etymology: From Ancient Greek σέλινον (sélinon).

fact.text: English 'celery' comes from French céleri, which was taken from a northern Italian dialect word, seleri. That word goes back to the same Greek selinon that gave Italian sedano.

senses.note: Usually uncountable, like celery. A stick of celery = una costa di sedano.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sēdēs.

fact.text: Comes from Latin sedes 'seat', related to sedere 'to sit'. The Vatican is the Santa Sede, the 'Holy See', where 'see' also goes back to a bishop's seat.

senses.note: sede centrale = head office; sede legale = registered office. Also venue or seat.

etymology: From Latin sedēre, from Proto-Italic *sedēō, from Proto-Indo-European *sed-.

fact.text: English 'sit' and 'seat' come from the same Indo-European root *sed-. Words borrowed from Latin, like 'sedentary', 'sediment' and 'session', come from it too.

senses.note: Irregular: siedo, siedi, siede. 'To sit down' is usually sedersi: ci sediamo qui.
Irregular: mi siedo, ti siedi, si siede. Siediti! = Sit down!

etymology:
From sedere.

fact.text: It comes from sedere, 'to sit', from Latin sedere. English 'sedentary' and 'session' share that Latin root, and 'sit' is a distant Germanic cousin.

senses.note: An armchair is una poltrona; a stool is uno sgabello.

etymology: From Latin sēdecim.
Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of sedere, sedersi (“to sit”).

fact.text: From sedere, 'to sit', so it is literally a 'sitting'. A séance is called a seduta spiritica.

senses.note: Used for a parliament sitting, therapy session or photo shoot. Can also mean the seat of a chair.

etymology: From segnale + -are.

senses.note: Segno zodiacale = star sign; lasciare il segno = to leave a mark.

etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin sēcrētārius, from Latin sēcrētus. By surface analysis, segreto (“secret”) + -ario (“-ary”).

fact.text: From Medieval Latin secretarius, from secretum 'secret'. A secretary was originally a trusted person who kept their employer's secrets (segreto).

senses.note: Feminine: segretaria. Also the leader of a party or union: il segretario del partito.

etymology: From segretario + -eria.

senses.note: Also 'secretariat'. 'Segreteria telefonica' = answering machine/voicemail.

etymology:

From Latin sescentī (“six hundred”).

fact.text: Goes back to Latin silvaticus, 'of the woods' (silva = forest). English 'savage' has the same source.

etymology: Borrowed from French sémaphore.

etymology: Borrowed from Old Occitan semblar, from Late Latin similāre, a verb based on Latin similis (“similar”). More or less a doublet of somigliare.

fact.text: Borrowed from Old Occitan semblar, which comes from Latin similis 'similar'. It belongs to the same family as English resemble and semblance.

senses.note: Mi sembra che + subjunctive = it seems to me that. Sembra stanco = he looks tired.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sēmen, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₁mn̥.

fact.text: It comes from Latin sēmen 'seed'. English seminar and seminary share the root, through Latin seminarium, 'seed plot' or 'nursery'.

etymology: Attested from ca. 1261. A cross of inherited sempice, semprice with Latin simplicem, from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”) + *pleḱ- (“to plait, to weave”). Compare duplice, molteplice. Partial doublet of scempio.

fact.text: From Latin simplex, literally 'one-fold' (sem- 'one' + -plex 'fold'), the opposite of duplex 'two-fold'. Compare Italian duplice, meaning double.

etymology: From semplice + -mente.

senses.note: Non può semplicemente divertirsi? = Can't he just enjoy himself?

etymology: Inherited from Latin semper; compare Catalan and Portuguese sempre, Spanish siempre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin semper, best known from Semper Fidelis ('always faithful'), the motto of the US Marine Corps.

senses.note: Can also mean 'still' (è sempre lì = it's still there). Per sempre = forever.

etymology: From Latin senātus.

etymology: From Latin senātōrem.

fact.text: Latin senator comes from senex, 'old man'. The Roman Senate was literally a council of elders, and the same root appears in senior and senile.

senses.note: Feminine: la senatrice.
Fused form of 'se no' (if not); both spellings are used. Vai, sennò fai tardi!

etymology: From Latin sēnsātiōnem.

fact.text: It also means 'direction': a senso unico sign marks a one-way street, senso vietato means no entry, and senso orario means clockwise.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French sentier, from Early Medieval Latin sēmitārius, derived from Latin sēmita.
From Latin sentimentum.

fact.text: From Latin sentire 'to perceive, feel', which also gave English sense, sentiment and scent. Italian uses one verb for hearing, feeling and even smelling.

etymology: From Latin sine (“without”) conflated with absentia (“without, in the absence of”). Compare French sans.

fact.text: Comes from Latin sine, 'without', blended with absentia, 'absence', so it is related to English absence. It is a cousin of French sans.

senses.note: Add di before pronouns: senza di te. Also used before an infinitive: senza dire niente.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin sēparāre. Doublet of the inherited severare, older form of sceverare; compare also disceverare.

Past participle of seppellire (to bury).

etymology: From Latin sepultūra.

senses.note: Related verb: seppellire (to bury), past participle sepolto.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin sera dies, 'the late day', from serus meaning 'late'. The same Latin word also gave French soir.

senses.note: Invariable: la serie, le serie. Prodotto in serie = mass-produced.

etymology: From Latin sērius (“grave, earnest, serious”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“heavy”).

etymology: From serrare + -tura.

etymology: From Latin servīre.

From sessanta (“sixty”) + sette (“seven”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + tre (“three”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + otto (“eight”).
From sessanta (“sixty”) + uno (“one”).
From Latin sexus.

fact.text: Latin sexus may come from secare, 'to cut', as in humanity divided into halves. The same root gives English section and dissect, though the link is uncertain.

etymology: From Latin sēta, from saeta, from Proto-Italic *saitā, from Proto-Indo-European *séh₂ito-, *sh₂éyto-, from *sh₂ey-, *seh₂i- (“to bind”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese seda.

fact.text: Latin saeta meant a bristle or coarse hair. 'Silk' came later, from the idea of fine, hair-like threads.

senses.note: Di seta = made of silk. Don't confuse the plural sete with la sete (thirst).

etymology: From Latin sitim, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰgʷʰítis (“decay; destruction”), derived from the root *dʰgʷʰey- (“to decline; to perish”).

fact.text: Watch out: sete is also the plural of seta 'silk', so le sete can mean silks. Context tells you whether someone is thirsty or shopping for fabric.

senses.note: Ho sete = I'm thirsty (lit. I have thirst).

etymology: From Latin septuāgintā, from *septmāginta, from Proto-Indo-European *septm̥̄ḱomt, from earlier *septḿ̥-dḱomt (“seven-ten”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + cinque (“five”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + due (“two”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + nove (“nine”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + quattro (“four”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + sei (“six”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + sette (“seven”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + tre (“three”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + otto (“eight”).
From settanta (“seventy”) + uno (“one”).
From Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
ignored: Using the number as a noun is a secondary use; the numeral sette is studied on its own card.

etymology: From Latin septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥.
From sette (“seven”) + cento (“hundred”).
From Latin September, Septembrem.

fact.text: From Latin septem, seven. In the early Roman calendar the year began in March, so September was the seventh month.

senses.note: Months are lowercase in Italian: a settembre (in September).

etymology: From Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from the Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), derived from septimus (“seventh”). Compare Romanian săptămână.

fact.text: Built on Latin septimus, 'seventh': a week is a cycle of seven days. It is related to sette (seven) and English 'September'.

senses.note: Fine settimana = weekend; la settimana prossima = next week.
Also an adjective: settimanale = weekly. Cf. il mensile (monthly), il quotidiano (daily paper).

etymology: From Latin sectōrem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin secare, 'to cut', so a sector is a 'cut-off piece'. English section, dissect and insect (a body 'cut into' segments) share the same root.

senses.note: Also field or area of activity: il settore pubblico = the public sector.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin sectiōnem.

senses.note: At school, a sezione is a class stream, e.g. la sezione B.
Lo sfiato = a vent or flue, as in lo sfiato del camino (the chimney vent).

etymology: From s- + fiore, compare French effleurer.

fact.text: Built from s- + fiore (flower), like French effleurer. The idea is touching only the 'flower' or top surface of something.

senses.note: Also figurative: to come close to (sfiorare la vittoria), or to touch briefly on a topic.
Also figurative: un ricordo sfocato = a hazy memory.

etymology: From s- + fortuna.

fact.text: In Italy the unlucky number is 17, not 13: Friday the 17th is feared, and some buildings and planes skip the number. In Roman numerals, XVII can be rearranged into VIXI, 'I have lived', meaning 'I am dead'.

senses.note: Che sfortuna! = What bad luck! The opposite of fortuna.

etymology: Deverbal from sforzare (“to force”) + -o or sforzarsi (“to strain oneself, to push oneself”) + -o. Compare French effort, Spanish esfuerzo, Catalan esforç, Portuguese esforço.

fact.text: Built from forza 'force' plus intensive s- (from Latin ex-). English effort was formed the same way, via Old French esforz, from ex- + fortis 'strong'.

senses.note: Fare uno sforzo = to make an effort.

etymology: From s- + frutto + -are.

fact.text: Built from s- + frutto ('fruit'). The idea is draining something of all its fruit, like farming land until nothing is left to grow.

senses.note: Also positive: 'to make the most of', as in sfruttare l'occasione (to seize the opportunity).

etymology: From s- + fuggire.

senses.note: Mi è sfuggito = it slipped my mind, or it slipped out. Takes essere in this sense.

etymology: Deverbal from sguardare + -o, variant of guardare (“to watch”).

fact.text: Comes from guardare 'to look', which Italian borrowed from Germanic *wardon 'to watch over'. English ward and guard come from the same root.

senses.note: lanciare uno sguardo = to cast a glance; a colpo d'occhio is 'at a glance'.

etymology: Borrowed from English shampoo, from Hindi चाँपो (cā̃po, “knead!”), from the Sanskrit root चपयति (capayati, “to pound, to knead”).

fact.text: Came into Italian through English from Hindi cā̃po, 'press! knead!'. In 18th-century England it first meant a massage, and only later washing the hair.

senses.note: Invariable: lo shampoo, gli shampoo. It takes lo because it starts with 'sh'. fare lo shampoo = to wash your hair.

ignored: An onomatopoeic sound identical to English, not a vocabulary item worth a card.

senses.note: Sound used to ask for silence; Italian also writes sst!

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English shock.

senses.note: Borrowed from English and invariable: lo shock, gli shock. Takes 'lo' like other s+consonant words.
An English loanword: lo show, gli show (invariable). E.g. uno show televisivo.

etymology: From Latin se (“him-, her-, it-, themselves”, reflexive third-person pronoun). Cognate with Spanish se and Portuguese se and si.

fact.text: The accent changes everything: without it this is the reflexive pronoun, but with an accent (sì) it means 'yes'.

senses.note: Also impersonal 'one/people' (si dice = people say) and passive (si vende = for sale).

fact.text: Also the present subjunctive of essere ('that it be'), which is where the conjunction comes from. Così sia means 'so be it', the Italian 'Amen'.

senses.note: sia… sia / sia… che: sia Marco che Luca = both Marco and Luca. 'Either… or' is usually o… o.

etymology: Univerbation of sì (“as”) + come.

fact.text: Only means 'since' as in 'because', never 'since' as in time. For time, Italian uses da or da quando: da quando sono qui = since I've been here.

senses.note: Usually starts the sentence: Siccome piove, resto a casa.

etymology: From sicuro + -mente.

senses.note: Rarely means 'safely'. For that, use in sicurezza.

etymology: From sicuro + -ezza. Compare Romanian siguranță.

fact.text: Covers both English 'safety' and 'security': cintura di sicurezza is a seat belt, and sicurezza informatica is cybersecurity.

senses.note: Also means 'security'. Sicurezza sul lavoro = safety at work.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sēcūrus. Compare Spanish seguro.

fact.text: Comes from Latin securus, 'free from care' (se- 'without' + cura 'care'). That gives English secure, and also sure, which came through Old French seur.

senses.note: Also means 'safe, secure': un posto sicuro = a safe place. Sei sicuro? = Are you sure?
