fact.text: Borrowed from Spanish cigarro, whose origin is uncertain. It may come from a Mayan word for smoking tobacco, or from cigarra ('cicada').

etymology: From Latin significāre.

senses.note: Cosa significa? = What does it mean? A common synonym is voler dire.
Qual è il significato di questa parola? Related verb: significare (to mean).

etymology: From Medieval Latin seniōra, feminine form of senior (“lord”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin senior ('elder'), which in the Middle Ages also came to mean 'lord'. It shares this root with English 'senior' and 'sir' and with Spanish señora.

senses.note: As a title: la signora Rossi = Mrs Rossi. Plural signore = ladies (as in 'Signore e signori').

etymology: From earlier segnore, from Latin seniōrem, comparative form of senex (“old”), from Proto-Indo-European *sénos. Doublet of sire.

fact.text: Comes from Latin seniorem, 'older', so a signore was literally 'the elder'. English senior and sir, and Spanish señor, come from the same root.

senses.note: The polite word for a man: un signore anziano = an elderly gentleman.

etymology: From signora (“lady”) + -ina.

senses.note: Used for young or unmarried women, e.g. la signorina Rossi. Many now see it as old-fashioned.

etymology: From Latin silentium.

senses.note: Fare silenzio = to be quiet; in silenzio = silently.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin silentiōsus.
Borrowed from Latin syllaba, from Ancient Greek συλλαβή (sullabḗ).

fact.text: From Greek syllabe, from syn 'together' plus lambanein 'to take'. A syllable is literally a set of sounds 'taken together'.

senses.note: Stressed on the first syllable: SIL-la-ba.

etymology: From Latin similis.

senses.note: Same form for both genders: simile / simili. Simile a = similar to. Also 'such': una cosa simile.

etymology: From simpatia (“sympathy”) + -ico (“-ic, -ical”), ultimately from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sŭmpắtheiă, “sympathy”, literally “suffering together”).

fact.text: Not usually 'sympathetic'. It means nice or likeable. 'Mi è simpatico' = I like him. For 'sympathetic' in the English sense, Italians say comprensivo.

senses.note: Describes people, meaning nice or pleasant. Plurals: simpatici, simpatiche.
Also the past participle of simulare (ho simulato = I faked/pretended).

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin sincērus (“pure, genuine”).

fact.text: A popular story derives Latin sincerus from sine cera, 'without wax', meaning flawless sculpture. Linguists consider this a folk etymology; the real origin is uncertain.

senses.note: Also 'honest, frank': essere sincero con qualcuno. Noun: la sincerità.
Iscriversi al sindacato = to join a union. Can also mean syndicate or cartel.

etymology: From Latin syndicus.

fact.text: From Greek syndikos, an advocate who represented a community, by way of Latin syndicus. The same root gave English syndicate.

senses.note: For a woman, la sindaca is now common, as is il sindaco.

etymology: Borrowed from English single.

fact.text: Only used for people who aren't in a relationship. A single room is una camera singola, and a music single is un singolo.

senses.note: il/la single, invariable: i single. Also used as an adjective: sono single.

etymology: Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin singulāris. By surface analysis, singolo + -are. Doublet of cinghiale.

fact.text: Comes from the same Latin word, singularis, as cinghiale ('wild boar'). The boar was the porcus singularis, the 'solitary pig' that lives alone.

senses.note: Also means 'peculiar, remarkable'. As a noun, il singolare is the grammatical singular.

etymology: From Latin singulus.

fact.text: Not the word for 'unmarried'. For that, Italians use the English loanword single, or celibe (man) and nubile (woman). Singolo means individual or one at a time.

senses.note: Means one or individual (camera singola = single room). An unmarried person is 'single', celibe or nubile.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sinister.

fact.text: Latin sinister simply meant 'left'. Because the left side was linked with bad omens, English 'sinister' came to mean threatening or evil.

senses.note: A sinistra = on/to the left. La sinistra also means the political left.

etymology: From Late Latin systēma, from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma).

senses.note: Masculine despite the -a ending (Greek -ma words): il sistema, i sistemi.

etymology: From sistema + -are.

senses.note: Very versatile: tidy up, fix, settle, or find someone a place. Sistemarsi = to settle in.
Also: to settle down (job, marriage), or to tidy oneself up. Takes essere.

etymology: From Latin situs (“position”), from a noun use of the perfect passive participle of sinō (“to put, lay”).

senses.note: Sito web, sito archeologico. A building site is un cantiere, not un sito.

etymology: From situare + -zione.
From s- + mettere.

senses.note: For quitting an activity: smettere di fumare. To stop moving is fermarsi.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *succursum, from Latin succursus. Compare French secours.

fact.text: From Latin succurrere, 'to run up to', meaning to run to someone's aid.

senses.note: Pronto soccorso = first aid / emergency room. I soccorsi = the rescue teams.

etymology: From Latin sociālis (“of or pertaining to companionship; social”), from socius (“associated, allied; partner, associate, companion”).

fact.text: In business Italian it also means 'corporate'. Capitale sociale is share capital, sede sociale is a registered office, and ragione sociale is a company's legal name.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural sociali. I social = social media.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin societātem ("community, society", accusative form), from socius (“partner, ally”). By surface analysis, socio + -età. The senses of "association" and "company" were borrowed later. Doublet of soccida, which was inherited from the Latin nominative societās.

fact.text: It also means 'company'. That is why Italian business names end in S.p.A. (società per azioni, a joint-stock company) or S.r.l. (società a responsabilità limitata, a limited company).

senses.note: Invariable: le società. Also means 'company, firm'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin sociābilis, remodeled based on -evole. By surface analysis, socio (“affiliate, fellow”) + -evole.

Borrowed from Latin socius (“partaking, associated; partner, associate”), from Proto-Indo-European *sokʷyo- (“companion”), derived from the root *sekʷ- (“to follow”). Compare also the inherited soccio.

fact.text: Comes from Latin socius, 'companion', which goes back to a root meaning 'to follow'. That is the same source as English social, society and associate.

senses.note: Also a member of a club or association. Feminine form: socia.

etymology: From earlier satisfatto, from Latin satisfactus, past participle form of satisfaciō (“reparation, amends”).

fact.text: Literally 'having done enough': from Latin satis 'enough' + facere 'to do, make'. English 'satisfied' comes from the same Latin roots.

senses.note: Soddisfatto di = satisfied with. Also the past participle of soddisfare.

etymology:
From Vulgar Latin *suffīctus, perfect passive participle of Latin suffīgō (“to fasten or fix onto”); compare Classical Latin suffīxus.
Cognate with Piedmontese sofit.
From Vulgar Latin *sufferīre, from Latin sufferre.

senses.note: Past participle: sofferto. Soffrire di = to suffer from (e.g. soffrire di insonnia).

etymology: From Latin subiectum.

fact.text: A school subject like maths or history is not 'soggetto' but 'materia'. This word is for the subject of a sentence, a painting or a discussion.

senses.note: Un bel soggetto = quite a character (ironic).

etymology: Deverbal from soggiornare (“to stay, sojourn”) + -o.

fact.text: The original meaning is 'a stay', from soggiornare 'to stay'. That is why a residence permit in Italy is called a permesso di soggiorno.

senses.note: Also means a stay: un soggiorno a Roma.

etymology: From Latin somniāre (“to dream; to daydream”). By surface analysis, sogn(o) (“dream”) + -are (first conjugation verbal suffix).

fact.text: From Latin somniare, from somnus 'sleep'. The same root gives English insomnia, so a dream is something that comes in your sleep.

senses.note: sognare qualcosa / sognare di + infinitive: sogno di viaggiare.

etymology: From Latin somnium (“dream”), derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Italic *swepnos, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.

fact.text: Comes from Latin somnium, from somnus 'sleep', the same root as English insomnia.

senses.note: fare un sogno = to have a dream; sogni d'oro = sweet dreams.

etymology: From Latin sōlāris.

fact.text: Used for people, una persona solare is a sunny, cheerful, outgoing person. It's a very common compliment in Italian.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine (pl. solari). Crema/protezione solare = sunscreen.

Past participle of the archaic verb soldare (“to pay a soldier or military member”), from soldo (“money, military pay”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese soldado, French soldat, Romansh schuldà.

fact.text: Literally 'one who is paid', from soldo 'pay, money', which comes from the Latin gold coin solidus. English 'soldier' has the same origin, and 'soldi' still means money in Italian.
Soldo comes from Latin solidus, a gold coin. Pay in soldi gave Italian soldato and, by way of French, English soldier: someone who fights for pay.

senses.note: Always plural: i soldi. The singular soldo means 'penny'; non ho un soldo = I'm broke.

etymology: Inherited from Latin soldus, syncopic form of (nummus) solidus (“solid (coin)”) (referring to the gold content), from Proto-Indo-European *solh₂- (“whole”). Doublet of solido and sodo, and likely also saldo.

fact.text: From Latin solidus, a solid gold Roman coin. The same coin gave English 'soldier', which originally meant someone who fights for pay.

senses.note: Non avere un soldo = to be penniless.

etymology: From Sole, from Latin sōlem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥. Cognates include Greek ήλιος (ílios), Icelandic sól, Hindi सूर्य (sūrya), and Russian со́лнце (sólnce).

fact.text: Comes from Latin sol, which also gave English 'solar' and 'solstice'. Even English 'sun' goes back to the same ancient Indo-European root.

senses.note: Prendere il sole = to sunbathe. C'è il sole = it's sunny.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin solidus. Doublet of sodo and soldo.

fact.text: Comes from the same Latin solidus as soldo (coin, money; the solidus was a Roman gold coin) and sodo (firm, as in uovo sodo, a hard-boiled egg).

senses.note: Also figurative: sturdy, reliable (un'azienda solida).

etymology: Inherited from Latin solitus, perfect active participle of Latin soleō (“to be accustomed to”), from which derives defective modal verb Italian solere.

senses.note: di solito = usually; come al solito = as usual; essere solito + inf. = to be in the habit of.

etymology: From Latin sōlitūdinem.

senses.note: Covers both lonely feelings and chosen solitude; context decides which one is meant.

etymology: From Latin sollicitus.

fact.text: From Latin sollicitus. As a noun, un sollecito is a reminder, for example about an unpaid bill.

senses.note: Can also mean solicitous or attentive.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sublevāre. By surface analysis, so- + levare.

fact.text: From Latin sublevare, built on levare 'to raise'. That is the same root as English lever and elevate.

senses.note: Also figurative: sollevare una questione = to raise an issue.

etymology: Derived from Latin sōlus.

senses.note: Agrees with its noun: sola, soli, sole. Da solo/sola = by oneself.

etymology: Derived from Latin sōlum.

senses.note: Same as solamente/soltanto. As an adjective, solo means 'alone': sono solo.

etymology: From solo (“only”) + tanto (used meaning "only" as Latin tantum).

senses.note: Means the same as solo, with a little more emphasis: soltanto un po' = just a little.

etymology: From Latin solūtiōnem.

fact.text: In business Italian it can also mean a payment: pagare in un'unica soluzione means paying in a single lump sum, not in instalments.

senses.note: La soluzione al/del problema = the solution to the problem.

etymology: From Latin summa.

fact.text: From Latin summa, 'the highest (part)'. Romans are said to have added numbers from the bottom up and written the total at the top, which is why sum and summit are related.

senses.note: tirare le somme = to sum up, draw conclusions.

etymology: From Latin somnus, from Proto-Italic *swepnos, from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos, from the root *swep- (“to sleep”). Cognate with Dalmatian samno, French somme, Lithuanian sãpnas, Romanian somn, Spanish sueño.

fact.text: From Latin somnus, which also gives English insomnia. Greek hypnos, the source of hypnosis, comes from the same ancient root meaning to sleep.

senses.note: avere sonno = to be sleepy; the verb is dormire.

etymology: From Latin supportāre (“to carry, bring, convey, transport”), from sub- (“under”) + portāre (“to carry”). Doublet of supportare, a borrowing from French.

fact.text: This is a false friend: it doesn't mean 'to support' but 'to tolerate, bear'. To support someone is sostenere, or appoggiare for backing an idea.

senses.note: Non lo sopporto = I can't stand him. To support someone = sostenere.
senses.prompt: to put up with, to stand

fact.text: The name means 'pressed': the stuffed salami is traditionally flattened under weights while it cures, which gives it its typical slightly flat shape.

senses.note: A Southern Italian speciality. In Tuscany the name is used for a kind of head cheese.

etymology: Inherited from Latin suprā. Compare older sovra and Sicilian supra.

fact.text: Related to 'soprano', the highest singing voice. In Italian, soprano means 'upper' and goes back to the same Latin root, supra ('above').

senses.note: Also a preposition: sopra il tavolo (on/above the table). Di sopra = upstairs.

etymology: Inherited from Latin suprā. Compare older sovra and Sicilian supra.

fact.text: Related to 'soprano', the highest singing voice. In Italian, soprano means 'upper' and goes back to the same Latin root, supra ('above').

senses.note: Takes di before pronouns: sopra di me. Also an adverb: di sopra = upstairs.

etymology:
From sopra- + tutto.
Akin to French surtout and Spanish sobre todo.

fact.text: Literally sopra + tutto, 'over everything'. French surtout and Spanish sobre todo are built the same way.

senses.note: Also means 'above all' or 'mainly'. Written with a double t.

etymology: From sopra- + vivere.

fact.text: Built like English survive: sopra 'over' + vivere 'to live'. Survive comes from Old French sourvivre, from Latin supervivere, 'to live beyond'.

senses.note: Takes essere. To survive something = sopravvivere a qualcosa.

etymology: From Latin surdus (“silent”), from Proto-Indo-European *swer- (“ringing, whistling”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin surdus, 'deaf, dull-sounding'. English 'absurd' comes from Latin absurdus, built on the same word and originally meaning 'out of tune'.

senses.note: Also 'muffled' (rumore sordo) or 'dull' (dolore sordo).

etymology: From Latin soror, from a diminutive form or based on the model of fratello. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *swezōr, from Proto-Indo-European *swésōr.

fact.text: Built on Latin soror, which also gave English sorority. Soror and English sister share one Indo-European ancestor, *swésōr.

etymology: First attested in the 13th century. From sor- + prendere, possibly on the calque of Old French sorprendre.

fact.text: Literally 'to over-take': sor- (over) + prendere (to take). English surprise comes from the related Old French verb, which first meant to seize or overtake suddenly.

senses.note: Irregular: past participle sorpreso. Also 'to catch in the act': l'ho sorpreso a rubare.

ignored: Infinitive plus clitic pronoun; study the verb sorprendere instead.

senses.note: sorprendere + ti.

etymology: From the feminine of sorpreso, past participle of the verb sorprendere.

fact.text: In Italy the small gift hidden inside a chocolate Easter egg is called la sorpresa. Finding it is the best part of Easter for many children.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *subrīdĕre, from Latin subrīdēre.

fact.text: Literally 'to laugh underneath': it comes from Latin sub 'under' + ridere 'to laugh', meaning a quiet, held-back laugh. Compare ridere, 'to laugh'.

senses.note: Smile at someone: sorridere a qualcuno. Il sorriso = the smile.

etymology: From Latin subrīsus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin subrisus: sub, 'under', plus ridere, 'to laugh'. A smile is literally an 'under-laugh', a quiet laugh.

senses.note: The verb is sorridere (to smile). Sorriso is also its past participle.

etymology: From a Vulgar Latin *sorta, itself from Latin sortem, possibly through French sorte.

fact.text: In negative sentences, di sorta means 'whatsoever': nessun problema di sorta = no problem whatsoever.

senses.note: Mostly used in una sorta di = a sort of. Plural sorte.

etymology: From Latin sortem, from Proto-Italic *sortis, from the Proto-Indo-European root *ser- (“to sort, lineup”).

fact.text: From Latin sors, the lot drawn to decide things, which is why tirare a sorte means to draw lots. English sort comes from the same Latin word, by way of French.

senses.note: Phrases: ironia della sorte = irony of fate; tirare a sorte = to draw lots.

fact.text: Built from sorvegliare, 'to watch over' (sopra + vegliare). It matches French surveiller (sur + veiller), which gave English the word surveillance.

senses.note: Telecamere di sorveglianza = security cameras; sotto sorveglianza = under watch.

etymology: Borrowed from French surveiller. First attested in the 19th century. By surface analysis, sor- + vegliare.

fact.text: Borrowed from French surveiller, the same verb that gave English 'surveillance'. Both come from Latin super 'over' + vigilare 'to keep watch', as in English 'vigil'.

senses.note: Transitive: sorvegliare qualcuno/qualcosa. Related noun: la sorveglianza (surveillance).

etymology: From Latin suspendere.

senses.note: Irregular past participle and passato remoto: sospeso, sospesi. Also 'to hang' or 'to interrupt'.

fact.text: In Naples a 'caffè sospeso' is a coffee you pay for in advance so that a stranger who can't afford one can have it later for free. The custom has spread around the world.

senses.note: Past participle of sospendere. In sospeso = pending, unresolved.

etymology: From Latin suspectāre.

senses.note: sospettare qualcosa / che + subjunctive; sospettare di qualcuno = to suspect someone

etymology: Borrowed from Latin suspectus (“mistrusted, suspected”, adjective), perfect passive participle of suspiciō (“to mistrust, suspect”).

senses.note: Can also mean a suspect (a person). As an adjective, sospetto means 'suspicious'.

etymology: From Latin (nōmen) substantīvum.

senses.note: Grammar term; Italian grammars also call a noun simply nome.

etymology: From Latin substituō.

fact.text: Watch the preposition. 'Sostituire il vecchio con il nuovo' means replace the old with the new, but 'sostituire il nuovo al vecchio' means put the new in place of the old.

senses.note: -isc- verb: sostituisco. Sostituire A con B = replace A with B.

etymology: From Latin subterraneus, possibly an adaptation to Italian or semi-learned term.

senses.note: As a noun, il sotterraneo means a basement or vault. The Underground (subway) is la metropolitana.

etymology: From Latin subtīlem (“thin, slender”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin subtilis, the same source as English 'subtle'. It is traditionally explained as sub + tela ('web'), so its first sense was something like 'finely woven'.

senses.note: Also 'fine' (hair, thread) and 'subtle' (un'ironia sottile).

etymology: Inherited from Latin subtus, which is derived from Latin sub. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *supo, from Proto-Indo-European *upo. Cognate to French sous.

fact.text: From Latin subtus, built on sub, which gave English the prefix sub- (submarine, subway).

senses.note: Sotto il tavolo = under the table; di sotto = downstairs; qui sotto = down here.

etymology: Inherited from Latin subtus, which is derived from Latin sub. Ultimately from Proto-Italic *supo, from Proto-Indo-European *upo. Cognate to French sous.

fact.text: From Latin subtus, built on sub, which gave English the prefix sub- (submarine, subway).

senses.note: Use di before pronouns: sotto di me. Also an adverb: è di sotto = it's downstairs.

etymology: From sotto- + lineare.

senses.note: Literally sotto (under) + linea (line). Also used figuratively: to stress, to emphasize.

etymology: From sotto- + titolo.

senses.note: Usually plural for films: un film con i sottotitoli. Also used for a book's subtitle.

etymology: From earlier sottraggere, from Latin subtrahere (“to remove, withdraw”). By surface analysis, sott + trarre.

senses.note: Conjugates like trarre: sottraggo, sottrassi, sottratto. Sottrarsi a = to evade or avoid.

etymology: From earlier spata, from Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē), from Proto-Indo-European *sph₂dʰh₁éh₂, derived from *(s)peh₂- (“to draw”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to do; to put”) + *-eh₂ (feminine noun ending). Doublet of spata.

fact.text: The card suit spades gets its name from Italian or Spanish spada, 'sword'. In Italian, spade is simply the plural of sword, not a digging tool.

senses.note: Plural: le spade. In Italian playing cards, spade is the swords suit.

etymology: From spago + -etto (“meliorative suffix”).

fact.text: Built from spago (string, twine) plus a diminutive ending, so spaghetti are literally little strings.

senses.note: Mostly used in the plural: gli spaghetti = spaghetti (the pasta or dish).

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *spatla, from Late Latin spatula, from Classical Latin spatha (“straight sword”). Compare spatola, a borrowed doublet.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin spatula, meaning 'shoulder blade' (literally 'little blade'). It is the same word as English 'spatula', named for the flat blade shape.

senses.note: 'Alle spalle' means behind someone's back.

etymology: The modern sense of shooting derives jocularly from the older culinary sense, which is from Vulgar Latin *exparāre, formed as ex- (intensive prefix) + parō (“to prepare”).

fact.text: Originally a kitchen word meaning to slit open an animal's belly to clean it. According to Wiktionary, the 'shoot' sense grew out of this as a joke.

senses.note: Can be used without an object (Ha sparato) or with one (sparare un colpo). Spararle grosse = to tell whoppers.

etymology: From s- + (ap)parire (“to appear”). Compare Sicilian spariri.

senses.note: Takes -isc- (sparisco, sparisci). Passato remoto: sparii or sparvi. Sono sparito = I disappeared.
Related verb: sparare, 'to shoot'.

etymology: From Latin spasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós).

senses.note: Takes lo because it starts with s + consonant: lo spasmo, gli spasmi.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *expaventāre, derived from the present participle of Classical Latin expaveō. Compare Spanish, Portuguese, Occitan, and Catalan espantar (also Catalan and Occitan espaventar); French épouvanter; Sicilian scantari; also Romanian înspăimânta.

senses.note: Reflexive spaventarsi = to get scared, to take fright.

etymology: From spavento + -oso.

senses.note: Colloquially also 'tremendous, incredible': un traffico spaventoso = horrendous traffic.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin spatium, whence also Old Italian spazzo (“floor”), an inherited doublet.

senses.note: Also 'room': c'è spazio = there's room. Takes lo: lo spazio.

etymology: Inherited from Latin spatiārī (“go for a walk”). Compare the borrowed doublet spaziare.

senses.note: spazzare via = to sweep away; figuratively, to wipe out or crush.

etymology: From spazzare + -tura.

senses.note: From spazzare (to sweep). Also figurative: junk (cibo spazzatura = junk food).

etymology: From spazzola + -ino.

fact.text: Literally means 'little brush': spazzola (brush) plus the diminutive ending -ino. Italian usually leaves out 'teeth' and just calls it the little brush.

senses.note: Full form: spazzolino da denti. Lavarsi i denti = to brush your teeth.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin speclum, syncopated form of Latin speculum, from the verb speciō. Compare specolo, a borrowed doublet.

fact.text: From Latin speculum 'mirror', from specere 'to look'. That root also gave English speculate, spectacle and inspect.

senses.note: Allo specchio = in the mirror. Takes lo because it starts with s + consonant.

etymology: From Latin speciālis (“specific”, “particular”).

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural speciali.
Same singular form for both genders: lo/la specialista. Plurals: gli specialisti, le specialiste.
Invariable: le specialità. Often for local food: una specialità della zona.
Takes 'in': mi sono specializzato in cardiologia.

etymology: From specializzare + -zione.

senses.note: Also a postgraduate specialist course, e.g. a doctor's medical specialty training.

etymology: From special(e) (“special”, “particular”) + -mente (“-ly”, adverbial derivational suffix).

senses.note: Similar to soprattutto and in particolare.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin speciēs. Doublet of spezie.

fact.text: Latin species also gave Italian spezie, 'spices', via a different route. English has the same pair: species and spice both come from it.

senses.note: Una specie di = a sort of. Invariable: le specie. Also biological 'species'; specie (adverb) = especially.

etymology: From Latin expedīre.

fact.text: From Latin expedire, literally 'to free the feet' (ex + pes, foot), so 'to get something moving'. English 'expedite' and 'expedition' come from the same word.

senses.note: An -isc- verb: spedisco, spedisci. Spedire un pacco = to send a parcel.

etymology: Inherited from Latin expingere, from ex- (“out”) + pingo (“paint”), with a semantic change from “remove colour” to “fade, dim”, probably influenced by extingere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin expingere, 'to paint out'. The sense shifted from removing colour to fading, then to putting out, probably influenced by Latin exstinguere.

senses.note: Irregular: spengo, spento. The opposite is accendere. Also 'to put out' a fire.

etymology: From Latin expendere, from ex- + pendō.

fact.text: From Latin expendere, 'to weigh out' (money was once weighed). English took the same word twice: 'expend', and 'spend' via Old English spendan.

senses.note: For spending time (a holiday, a weekend), Italians usually say passare: passare le vacanze.

etymology: From sperare + -anza, or from Vulgar Latin spērantia, from Latin spērāns. Compare French espérance, Spanish esperanza, Portuguese esperança

senses.note: Finché c'è vita c'è speranza = while there's life there's hope.

etymology: Inherited from Latin spērāre.

features.construction: sperare di + infinitive / sperare che + subjunctive

senses.note: Spero di + infinitive; spero che + subjunctive. Lo spero = I hope so.

etymology: From Late Latin expēnsa, from Latin expēnsus, from expendere. Compare Sicilian spisa, Venetan spexa, Romansh spaisa, spesa, Friulian spese, Ladin speisa, spëisa, Piedmontese spèisa, Old French espoise.

fact.text: From Late Latin expensa, the same source as English expense. It still means cost: le spese are expenses, while fare spese means going shopping in general.

senses.note: fare la spesa = to do the grocery shopping. Also means expense; le spese = expenses.

etymology: Inherited from Latin spissus. Compare Spanish espeso, Portuguese espesso, French épais.

fact.text: Comes from Latin spissus, 'thick, dense'. Things that happen 'thickly', packed close together, happen often, and that is how 'thick' came to mean 'often'.

senses.note: As an adverb, spesso means 'often': vengo spesso qui.

etymology: Inherited from Latin spissus. Compare Spanish espeso, Portuguese espesso, French épais.

fact.text: Comes from Latin spissus, 'thick, dense'. Things that happen 'thickly', packed close together, happen often, and that is how 'thick' came to mean 'often'.

senses.note: As an adjective, spesso means 'thick' (un libro spesso). Più spesso = more often.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin spectābĭlis.

fact.text: From Latin spectabilis, 'worth looking at, notable', from spectare 'to watch'. It shares a root with English spectacle and spectator.

senses.note: Used to address firms in letters, often shortened: Spett.le Ditta Rossi = Messrs Rossi.

etymology: From Latin spectāculum.

senses.note: Che spettacolo! = What a sight! / How amazing!

etymology: From Latin spectāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin spectare 'to look at', the root of spectator and spectacle. In Latin it also meant 'to look towards, concern', and that sense became 'to be someone's job or right'.

senses.note: Spetta a te decidere = it's up to you to decide. Also 'to be due': mi spetta un rimborso.

etymology: From s- + pezzo + -are. Compare Sicilian spizzari.

fact.text: Built from pezzo 'piece', so it literally means 'to make into pieces'. Pezzo and English piece go back to the same Medieval Latin word, probably of Gaulish origin.

senses.note: Used for snapping or splitting: spezzare il pane, spezzare il cuore.

etymology: Borrowed from a Germanic language, perhaps Gothic *𐍃𐍀𐌰𐌹𐌷𐌰 (*spaiha) or from a Frankish cognate, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”). Cognates include obsolete French épie (“spy”), Spanish espía (“spy”), English spy and German spähen (“to peek, to spy”).

fact.text: Borrowed from Germanic and related to English spy and German spähen (to peek). All come from Proto-Germanic spehōną, meaning to look.

senses.note: Always feminine, even for a man: lui è una spia. Also a warning light: la spia dell'olio.

features.construction: indirect object of the person: mi spiace (che + subjunctive)

senses.note: Works like piacere: mi spiace = I'm sorry. A variant of dispiacere.

etymology: From s- + piaggia. The initial s- is an intensifying prefix. Cognate with French plage, Portuguese praia, Sicilian praja and Spanish playa.

fact.text: Related to French plage and Spanish playa. It is the older word piaggia, 'slope, shore', with an intensifying s- added in front.

senses.note: Andare in spiaggia = to go to the beach.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *spiclu(m), contracted form of Latin spīculum, diminutive of spīcum, alternative form of spīca (“ear of grain”). Doublet of spigolo.

senses.note: Uno spicchio d'aglio = a clove of garlic.

etymology: Inherited from Latin explicāre. Doublet of esplicare, which was borrowed. Compare Albanian shpjegoj.

fact.text: From Latin explicare, 'to unfold'. The verb still means both things: to explain an idea, or to unfold a map or a sail.

senses.note: spiegare qualcosa a qualcuno. Also 'to unfold, spread out' (spiegare le vele).

etymology:
From spiegare + -zione.
Doublet of esplicazione.

fact.text: The verb spiegare comes from Latin explicare, 'to unfold', and it still means that too (spiegare le vele, to unfurl the sails). Explaining is literally unfolding an idea.

senses.note: Dare una spiegazione = to give an explanation.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *expingere, from Latin ex- + pangere.

fact.text: On Italian doors you will often see SPINGERE (push) and TIRARE (pull), using the infinitive the way English signs use the imperative.

features.construction: spingere qualcuno/qualcosa; spingere qualcuno a + infinitive

senses.note: Irregular: spinsi, spinto. Spingere qualcuno a fare = to drive someone to do.

etymology: From Latin spiritus, from spiro.

fact.text: Latin spiritus comes from spirare 'to breathe', so spirit was originally 'breath'. The same root gives English inspire, respire and expire.

senses.note: Also wit (avere spirito = to be witty) and alcohol for cleaning or cooking.

fact.text: From Latin spoliare 'to strip', originally stripping a fallen enemy of armour. It is the same root as the English 'spoils' of war.

senses.note: Reflexive: mi spoglio. Takes essere: mi sono spogliato/a.

etymology: From Latin spurcāre. Compare Romanian spurca.

senses.note: The reflexive sporcarsi means to get yourself dirty: mi sono sporcato le mani.

etymology: From Latin spurcitia. Internally, from sporco (“dirty”) + -izia.

senses.note: Usually uncountable. From sporco (dirty).

etymology: From Latin spurcus, with vowel shift reinforced by contamination of porco, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sperH-.

senses.note: Also figurative: shady, obscene. Plurals: sporchi, sporche.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English sport. Doublet of diporto.

fact.text: Italian borrowed this from English, but English sport comes from Old French desport, so it is a cousin of Italian diporto, 'leisure'.

senses.note: Invariable: lo sport, gli sport. Fare sport = to do sport.
Also means sports (centro sportivo = sports centre) and casual (abbigliamento sportivo = casual wear).

etymology: From Latin spōnsāre.

fact.text: From Latin sponsare, 'to betroth', which comes from spondere, 'to promise solemnly'. English spouse and espouse come from the same root, and so does sponsor.

senses.note: Sposare qualcuno = to marry someone. Sposarsi (with essere) = to get married.

fact.text: Sposare comes from Latin sponsare, from sponsus 'betrothed, promised'. English 'spouse' comes from the same word through Old French.

senses.note: Sposarsi con qualcuno = to marry someone; also sposare qualcuno. Ci siamo sposati nel 2010.

etymology: From sposare.

fact.text: Sposare comes from Latin sponsare, 'to promise in marriage', from sponsus 'promised'. The same root gave English 'spouse' and also 'sponsor'.

senses.note: Married to someone = sposato con qualcuno. Also the past participle of sposare (to marry).

etymology: Inherited from Latin spōnsus.

fact.text: From Latin sponsus, 'promised', from spondere, 'to pledge'. The same root gives English 'spouse' and 'sponsor'.

senses.note: 'Gli sposi' means the bride and groom, or the newlyweds. The bride is 'la sposa'.

etymology: From s- (“out of”) + posto (“spot”) + -are.

fact.text: Built from s- ('out of') + posto ('place, spot'), so it literally means 'to take out of its place'.

senses.note: Transitive. Spostarsi = to move (oneself). Also used for rescheduling: spostare una riunione.

etymology: Uncertain. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *disperdicāre, from Latin disperdere, or from Vulgar Latin *dispergicāre, iterative of Latin dispergere, or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *exprecāre ("drive into ruin"), from Latin ex- + precāri.

senses.note: Noun: lo spreco (waste). Che spreco! = What a waste!

etymology: Unknown
Deverbal from squadrare + -a. May correspond to a Vulgar Latin *exquadra, from *exquadro, exquadrāre, from Latin ex- + quadrō, from quadrus. Compare French équerre.

fact.text: English squad comes from this word via French escouade. It also means a set square, the drawing tool, and goes back to Latin quadrus, square.

senses.note: Also used for sports teams: la squadra del cuore = your favourite team.
Che squallore! = How dreary / how sordid! Also used for tacky or depressing things.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin stabilis.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine. Un lavoro stabile = a steady job. As a noun, uno stabile = a building.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin stabilīre.

senses.note: Stabilire una data = to set a date. Stabilirsi = to settle (somewhere).

etymology: From Latin stadium, from Ancient Greek στάδιον (stádion).

fact.text: The Greek stadion was a unit of length of about 180 metres. The oldest footrace at Olympia was one stadion long, and the track where it was run took the same name.

senses.note: Also means 'stage, phase': allo stadio iniziale.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from French stage.

fact.text: Not a theatre stage! This word comes from French and means an internship or work placement. A theatre stage is il palcoscenico.

senses.note: Invariable: gli stage. Pronounced the French way (stahzh). A theatre stage is il palcoscenico.

etymology: From earlier *stacione, from Latin statiōnem. Doublet of stazzo, stazzone, stazio, and stazione, the first two of which were also inherited from Latin, while the latter two were borrowed.

fact.text: Comes from Latin statio, 'a standing, a stopping place', the same word that gave stazione (station). A season was a fixed 'stop' in the year's cycle.

senses.note: Also a TV series season: la prima stagione.

etymology: Univerbation of 'sta (contraction of questa (“this”)) + mattina (“morning”).

fact.text: The 'sta' at the front is a shortening of 'questa' (this). The same trick gives stasera (this evening) and stanotte (tonight).

senses.note: Synonym: stamani / stamane.

etymology: Deverbal from stampare (“to press, stamp”).

senses.note: la stampa = the press; conferenza stampa = press conference. Also printing or a print (le stampe).

etymology: From Frankish *stampōn, from Proto-Germanic *stampōną.

fact.text: From Frankish *stampōn, from the same Germanic root as English 'stamp'. Printing was originally a matter of stamping inked type onto paper.

senses.note: la stampa = printing, and also the press (newspapers).

etymology: From the short past participle of stancare (“to tire out”) in Tuscan; compare the Standard Italian participle stancato.

senses.note: Stanco morto = dead tired. Stancarsi = to get tired.

etymology: Univerbation of 'sta (“this”, apheretic form of questa f sg) + notte (“night”).

fact.text: A fusion of 'sta (short for questa, 'this') and notte, 'night'. Stamattina and stasera are built the same way.

senses.note: Can also mean 'last night'; context decides. 'Stasera' = this evening.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *stantia (“standing, stopping-place”), from Latin stantem, from stāre.

fact.text: English borrowed 'stanza' from Italian for a verse of a poem. In Italian it simply means 'room' (from Latin stare, to stand), so a stanza is a 'room' within the poem.

senses.note: Any room in a house. Stanza da letto = bedroom.

etymology: Inherited from Latin stāre. Cognate with Spanish estar and English state.

fact.text: Its past participle stato is shared with essere, so 'sono stato' can mean 'I have been' or 'I have stayed'. It comes from Latin stare 'to stand', the source of English state.

senses.note: Sto a casa = I'm staying at home.

etymology: Literally, “to stay afoot”.

senses.note: Describes being upright. 'To stand up' (the movement) is 'alzarsi'.
senses.prompt: to stand (to be on one's feet)

etymology: From 'sta (“this”, apheretic form of esta f sg) + sera (“evening”). Compare Romanian astă-seară.

fact.text: This is a shortened 'questa sera' (this evening): 'sta + sera. The same trick gives stamattina (this morning), stanotte and stavolta (this time).

senses.note: Also stamattina (this morning), stanotte (tonight/last night), stavolta (this time).
scuola statale = state school; strada statale = main road. As a noun, uno statale = civil servant.

etymology: From statico.
ignored: This is a bad parse: the list uses the feminine of the adjective statico ('static'), and the noun 'statics' is a rare technical term.

senses.note: The branch of mechanics. Not the same as elettricità statica (static electricity), which uses the adjective statico.

etymology: Inherited from Latin statūs (noun).

fact.text: From Latin status ('standing, condition'), from stare 'to stand', the root of English state, status and estate. It is also the past participle of essere: sono stato.

senses.note: Often capitalized: lo Stato. Also means condition: in buono stato = in good condition.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin statiōnem. Doublet of stagione, stazzo, stazzone, and stazio, of which the first three were inherited from Latin, while the last was borrowed.

fact.text: A doublet of stagione (season). Both come from Latin statio 'a standing, a stopping place', from stare 'to stand'.

senses.note: stazione ferroviaria = railway station; also used for radio/TV stations.

etymology: From stecco (“twig”) + -ino (diminutive suffix).

fact.text: Literally 'little twig': stecco (twig, stick) plus the diminutive -ino. Italians call a very thin person 'uno stecchino'.

senses.note: Also stuzzicadenti. 'Magro come uno stecchino' = thin as a rake.

etymology: Inherited from Latin stēlla, from Proto-Italic *stērlā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr. Doublet of étoile.

fact.text: English star goes back to the same Proto-Indo-European word, *h₂stḗr. Latin stella also gave English stellar and constellation.

senses.note: stella marina = starfish; also used for hotel ratings (un albergo a tre stelle)

etymology: From Latin extendere, whence also Italian estendere (a borrowed doublet).

senses.note: Stendersi = to lie down. Past participle: steso.

ignored: The context uses the noun stereotipo (plural stereotipi); the verb is rare, so study stereotipo instead.

senses.note: Rare; the common word is the noun lo stereotipo (stereotype).

etymology: Italianized form of English sterling.

fact.text: An Italianized form of English sterling, which possibly comes from Old English steorling, 'little star', after the small stars stamped on some early Norman pennies.

senses.note: The British currency. Do not confuse it with the weight 'pound', which is libbra.
lo stesso = the same; after a pronoun it means -self: te stesso = yourself.

etymology: Borrowed from French style, itself borrowed from Latin stilus. Doublet of stelo and stilo, which Italian inherited and borrowed from Latin respectively.

fact.text: Comes from Latin stilus, the pointed tool Romans used to write on wax tablets. Your stylus became your way of writing, then style in general. English stylus has the same root.

senses.note: Stile libero = freestyle (swimming). Avere stile = to have class.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin stīpendium (“military pay, stipend”).

fact.text: From Latin stipendium, a soldier's pay, usually explained as stips 'small coin' plus pendere 'to weigh out'. English stipend comes from the same word.

senses.note: Regular monthly pay. Plural: gli stipendi.

etymology: From s- + tirare.

fact.text: Built from tirare (to pull), it also means 'to stretch'. Stirarsi un muscolo means to pull a muscle, and ironing smooths cloth by stretching it out.

senses.note: Stirare una camicia = to iron a shirt. Il ferro da stiro = the iron.
Mostly in compounds: ferro da stiro (iron), asse da stiro (ironing board).

etymology: Cognate with Piedmontese stìtich.

fact.text: Italian dictionaries trace it to Latin stypticus, from Greek styptikos meaning 'astringent'.

senses.note: Colloquially also means stingy, or slow and unproductive (said of an artist).

etymology: Borrowed from Old French estival, of which the etymology is disputed: either from Medieval Latin aestivālis (“summerly”), in place of Classical Latin aestīvus (whence also Italian estivo), from aestās (“summer”), or from tībiālis (“tibial, of the tibia”), from tībia. Cognate with Sicilian stivala.

fact.text: Italians often call their own country lo Stivale, 'the Boot', because of the peninsula's shape on the map.

etymology: From Latin stomachus.

fact.text: Comes via Latin from Greek stómakhos, built on stóma, 'mouth'. The word first meant the throat or gullet, the opening into the body, and only later the stomach itself.

senses.note: Plural stomaci or stomachi; both are correct.

etymology: Borrowed from English stop.

senses.note: Invariable: gli stop. Also means a car's brake lights (gli stop).

etymology: From Old Italian istoria, borrowed from Latin historia, from Ancient Greek ἱστορία (historía, “learning through research”).

fact.text: English 'story' and 'history' both come from Latin historia, from Greek for 'learning through research'. English split it into two words, but Italian kept just one for both meanings.

senses.note: Also 'affair, relationship': ha una storia con lui.

etymology: From Latin historicus.

senses.note: Also historic. Centro storico = old town. As a noun, lo storico = historian.

etymology: From earlier *strata, from Late Latin strāta (“paved road”), from Latin [via] strāta, feminine of strātus, perfect passive participle of sternō.

fact.text: From Latin via strāta, 'paved road'. Old English borrowed the same Latin word early on, and it became English 'street'.

senses.note: Also 'way': sulla strada giusta = on the right track. Per strada = in the street.

etymology: From Latin extrāneus, possibly through an intermediate adjective *extranearius, or more likely based on the model of Old French estrangier.

fact.text: Comes from Latin extraneus, 'from outside', by way of Old French estrangier. English got strange and stranger from the same source, so a straniero really is a stranger.

senses.note: Also a noun: uno straniero = a foreigner. 'Abroad' is all'estero.

etymology:
A variant of the older stranio, from Latin extrāneus (“external, foreign; strange”), whence also estraneo (a borrowed doublet).
Cognate with English extraneous and Spanish extraño.

fact.text: Comes from Latin extraneus 'external, foreign', the same source as English strange (via Old French) and extraneous, and of Italian estraneo 'outsider'.

senses.note: È strano che… takes the subjunctive.

etymology: From Gothic *𐍃𐍄𐍂𐌰𐍀𐍀𐍉𐌽 (*strappōn), from Latin struppus (“strap”), from Ancient Greek στρόφον (stróphon, “rope”).

fact.text: It goes back through Germanic to Latin struppus, a strap. The same Latin word is the source of English 'strop' and 'strap'.

senses.note: Also to snatch or tear out. Uno strappo = a tear, but also a lift in a car (colloquial).

etymology: From Latin strīga, from strix, from Ancient Greek στρίξ (stríx). Compare Portuguese estria and Romanian strigă.

fact.text: This comes from Latin strix, a screech owl. Romans believed this night bird was a demon that preyed on people, especially babies, and over time the bird-demon became the witch.

senses.note: Also an insult for a nasty woman (hag).

etymology: Borrowed from English stress.

senses.note: Invariable. 'Sono stressato/a' = I'm stressed.

fact.text: Borrowed from English, but it only covers stress as pressure: mi stressi means 'you're stressing me out'. To stress a point is sottolineare, and to stress a syllable is accentare.

senses.note: Means to put someone under stress. 'Stress' as in emphasize is sottolineare.

etymology: From Latin strictus, perfect passive participle of stringō.

fact.text: From Latin strictus, 'drawn tight', which also gave English 'strict'. It is the past participle of stringere (to squeeze), and as a noun it means a strait, as in lo Stretto di Messina.

senses.note: una strada stretta = a narrow street. Opposite: largo (wide), a false friend for 'large'.

etymology: From stronzo + -ata.

fact.text: Built from stronzo plus the suffix -ata. Stronzo literally means 'turd' and is also a common insult (jerk, asshole), so a stronzata is quite literally 'a piece of crap'.

senses.note: Dire stronzate = to talk crap. It can also mean a stupid act or a trivial thing.

etymology: Germanic origin, borrowed from the Lombardic *strunz (“dung”), ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *strunt. Cognate with Sicilian strunzu.

fact.text: Borrowed from Lombardic, a Germanic language, where it meant 'dung'. It is related to Dutch 'stront' (crap), and it still literally means 'turd' in Italian.

senses.note: Strong insult; feminine stronza. Literally means 'turd'.

etymology: From earlier istrumento, instrumento, from Latin īnstrūmentum.

senses.note: Covers tools and musical instruments: suonare uno strumento = to play an instrument.

etymology: From Latin strūctūra.

senses.note: Also a facility, e.g. strutture alberghiere (hotel accommodation) or strutture sanitarie (health facilities).

etymology: From Latin studentem.

senses.note: Feminine: la studentessa. Takes 'lo' (lo studente, gli studenti).

etymology: From Latin studeō, or through studio, from Latin studium. By surface analysis, studio + -are. Compare Spanish estudiar.

senses.note: Transitive: studiare l'italiano = to study Italian.

etymology: From Latin studium (“study”).

fact.text: English borrowed 'studio' from Italian, where it still means study as well as a workroom or a professional's office.

senses.note: Plural studi = studies, schooling. Also an office: lo studio del medico.

etymology:
From Latin stupĕndum, from stupēre.
Cognate with Piedmontese stupend.

fact.text: From Latin stupere 'to be stunned', the same root as stupid and stupor. Something stupendous leaves you amazed; stupid first meant dazed.

senses.note: A strong, enthusiastic word: Che giornata stupenda! = What a gorgeous day!

etymology: From Latin stupidus.

fact.text: Latin stupidus first meant 'stunned, dumbstruck', from stupere 'to be amazed'. A related Italian word, stupendo, means 'wonderful', like English stupendous.

etymology: From Latin stupor.

fact.text: Usually means astonishment, not a dazed 'stupor'. It comes from Latin stupere 'to be stunned', the same root as English 'stupid' and 'stupendous'.

senses.note: Related verb: stupire = to amaze. con stupore = in amazement.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sūsum.

fact.text: Comes from Latin susum, a form of sursum meaning 'upward', literally 'turned up from below' (sub + versum). So the Italian word for 'on' started out meaning 'up'.

senses.note: Vado su = I'm going upstairs; su e giù = up and down. As a preposition it means 'on'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sūsum.

fact.text: Comes from Latin susum, a form of sursum meaning 'upward', literally 'turned up from below' (sub + versum). So the Italian word for 'on' started out meaning 'up'.

senses.note: Combines with articles: sul, sullo, sulla, sui, sugli, sulle. Also means 'about' a topic (un libro su Roma).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin subitō.

fact.text: Its Latin root subitus also gave English 'sudden'.

senses.note: Very common: 'Arrivo subito!' = I'll be right there!

etymology: Borrowed from Latin succēdere, from sub + cēdō.

fact.text: Not 'to succeed' at something, which is riuscire. Confusingly, the past participle successo also works as a noun meaning 'success'.

senses.note: Che succede? = What's going on? Past tense: è successo. Irregular: successo, successe.

etymology: From Latin successivus.

senses.note: il giorno successivo = the following day. Also means successive or consecutive.

etymology: From Latin successus.

fact.text: Watch out: È successo qualcosa means 'something happened', not 'something succeeded'. It is the past participle of succedere, 'to happen'.

senses.note: Also a hit: un successo. Note that Cos'è successo? means 'What happened?' (from succedere).

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *sūculare, *succulare, from sūcus (“juice, sap, moisture”), from Proto-Indo-European *suk-. Compare Latin sūgō (“suck”) (< Proto-Indo-European *sug⁽ʰ⁾-), Italian sucare.

fact.text: Shares its root with succo (juice): both go back to Latin sūcus, 'juice, sap'. Don't mix up succhi (juices) with tu succhi (you suck).

senses.note: Transitive: succhiare una caramella = to suck a sweet. Careful: also has a vulgar slang meaning.

etymology: From Late Latin succus, variant of Latin sūcus. Doublet of sugo. Cognate with Sicilian sucu.

fact.text: This word has a twin: both it and sugo come from Latin sucus. Succo is fruit juice, but sugo is pasta sauce or meat juices. Don't ask for sugo d'arancia!

senses.note: Succo di frutta = fruit juice; succo d'arancia = orange juice. Figuratively, the gist of something.

etymology: Borrowed from French sud, from Old English sūþ, from Proto-Germanic *sunþrą.

fact.text: Italian took this word from French, and French took its compass points from Old English sūþ. So the Italian word for south is really an English word that came back through France.

senses.note: Invariable. Il Sud often means Southern Italy. A sud di = south of.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sūdāre, from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.

fact.text: From Latin sudare, which shares an ancient root (*sweyd-) with English sweat. They are distant cousins, just as sudore is to sweat.

senses.note: sudare sette camicie (lit. to sweat seven shirts) = to work extremely hard.

etymology: From Latin sūdōrem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin sudor, which goes back to the same Indo-European root as English 'sweat'.

etymology: Borrowed from New Latin suīcīdium, from suī (“oneself”) and -cīdium (“-cide”). Up until the 19th century, the plural form was spelled suicidî, to distinguish it from the plural of suicida (“a suicidal person”).

senses.note: Commettere suicidio / suicidarsi = to commit suicide. A suicidal person is un/una suicida.
su + il, used before masculine nouns starting with a consonant: sul tavolo.
Agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: sua madre = his or her mother. Capitalised Suo = your (formal).

etymology: From Latin suus, from Proto-Italic *sowos, from Proto-Indo-European *sewos, from *swé.

senses.note: Agrees with the thing owned, not the owner: sua madre = his or her mother. Suo also = formal 'your'.

etymology: From Latin socerus, variant of socer, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱuros.

senses.note: Plural i suoceri also means 'parents-in-law'. Mother-in-law = la suocera.

etymology: Inherited from Latin solum.

senses.note: Also soil. Suolo pubblico = public land. For the floor of a room use 'pavimento'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sonāre, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *swenh₂- (“to sound, resound”). By surface analysis, suono (“sound”) + -are.

fact.text: Italian splits English 'play' three ways: suonare for music, giocare for games and sports, and recitare for acting a role.

senses.note: Suonare il piano/la chitarra. Also 'to ring': il telefono suona.

etymology: Inherited from Latin sonus.

fact.text: Comes from the Indo-European root *swenh2- 'to sound'. The Germanic cognate *swanaz gave English 'swan', probably meaning 'the bird that sings' or 'the noisy bird'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin soror (nominative) via loss of /-r/ and then adjustment of /-o/ to the more typical (for feminine nouns) /-a/.

fact.text: From Latin soror, 'sister', which also gave English sorority, and goes back to the same root as English sister. Nuns are 'sisters', and a biological sister is now sorella.

senses.note: Before a name it shortens to suor, e.g. Suor Maria.

etymology: From super- + -are, or borrowed from Latin superāre. Compare the inherited and obsolete doublet soprare.

senses.note: Also: to exceed, overtake, pass (an exam). Superarsi = to outdo oneself (Ti sei superato!).

ignored: This is just superare with a pronoun attached; study it on the superare card.

senses.note: superare + la (it).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin superior.

senses.note: superiore a = above/greater than; la scuola superiore (le superiori) = high school.

etymology: From super- + mercato.
From Latin suppōnere.

senses.note: Conjugates like porre: suppongo, supposi, supposto. Usually followed by che + subjunctive.

etymology: Borrowed from French support, from the verb supporter, ultimately from Latin supportāre.

senses.note: Also a stand or holder, or a storage medium. For moral support, sostegno is also common.

etymology: From s- + vantaggio; cognate with Piedmontese svantagi.

senses.note: Essere in svantaggio = to be behind (in a game or contest).

etymology: Deverbal from svegliare (“to wake up”) + -a.

senses.note: Also a wake-up call or waking time. Sveglia! = Wake up! puntare la sveglia = to set the alarm.

etymology: Probably from Old Occitan esvelhar, from Vulgar Latin *exvigilāre [whence also Old French esveillier], from Latin ēvigilāre.

fact.text: Goes back to Latin vigilare, 'to stay awake, keep watch', which also gave English 'vigil' and 'vigilant'. La sveglia means alarm clock.

senses.note: Transitive. To wake up yourself is svegliarsi: mi sono svegliato.
Reflexive: mi sveglio, mi sono svegliato/a. svegliare qualcuno = to wake someone up.

etymology: From s- + viluppo (“tangle”) + -are. Compare Piedmontese svilupé.

fact.text: Literally 'to untangle': s- (un-) + viluppo, 'tangle'. English 'develop' has a similar history: it comes from Old French desveloper, 'to unwrap'.

senses.note: Also used for photos: sviluppare un rullino = to develop a film. Svilupparsi = to develop, to grow.

etymology: Deverbal from sviluppare + -o. Cognate with Piedmontese svilup.

fact.text: Literally an 'unwrapping': s- reverses viluppo, 'tangle, bundle'. English develop is built the same way, from French développer, 'to unwrap' (compare envelop).

senses.note: Paesi in via di sviluppo = developing countries.

etymology: From s- + volgere; cognate with Piedmontese svòlge.

fact.text: Literally 'to unroll', like a scroll (s- + volgere 'to turn'). English develop has a similar story: it comes from Old French desveloper, 'to unwrap'.

senses.note: Irregular past participle svolto. Svolgersi = to take place: la scena si svolge a Roma.

etymology: From s- + voltare.

senses.note: Svoltare a destra/sinistra = to turn right/left. Colloquially, also to turn things around.

etymology: From Latin sē. Compare with French soi, Portuguese si, and Spanish sí.

fact.text: The accent matters. Sé means 'oneself', but se without an accent means 'if'. In se stesso the accent is often left out, and both spellings are accepted.

senses.note: Stressed form used after prepositions: parla sempre di sé. Also sé stesso / se stesso.

etymology: From Latin sīc. In the “yes” sense, from sīc (est).

fact.text: Dante called Italy 'il bel paese là dove il sì suona', the fair land where 'sì' is heard. Medieval writers sorted Romance languages by their word for 'yes', from Latin sic 'thus'.

senses.note: Written with an accent; si without one is the reflexive pronoun ('oneself').

etymology: From Latin sīc. In the “yes” sense, from sīc (est).

fact.text: Dante called Italy 'il bel paese là dove il sì suona', the fair land where 'sì' is heard. Medieval writers sorted Romance languages by their word for 'yes', from Latin sic 'thus'.

ignored: Noun use of 'yes' (un sì); the ordinary meaning is studied on the adverb card sì.

senses.note: Invariable noun: un sì, dei sì. Note the accent; si without it is a pronoun.

etymology: From tabacco + -aio.

fact.text: Italian tobacconists, marked by a big T sign, sell much more than cigarettes: bus tickets, stamps, revenue stamps, lottery tickets and phone top-ups.

senses.note: The shop is la tabaccheria, but people also say 'vado dal tabaccaio'.

fact.text: Never use this for the table you eat at: that is il tavolo. Tabella is only a table of data, a chart or a timetable, like the tabella degli orari (schedule).

senses.note: Not the furniture: a dining or restaurant table is tavolo or tavola.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tacēre, from Proto-Italic *takēō, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *tak- or *tHk-.

fact.text: Comes from Latin tacere 'to be silent', the root of English tacit (unspoken) and taciturn (a person of few words).

senses.note: Irregular: taccio, tacqui, taciuto. Taci! = Be quiet!
senses.prompt: to be silent, to keep quiet

etymology: Deverbal from tagliare (“to cut”) + -a. Compare French taille.

senses.note: Che taglia porti? = what size are you? Shoes use numero. Also a bounty: una taglia sulla testa.

ignored: This is just an inflected form (taglia + lo) of tagliare, so study it on the tagliare card.

senses.note: Imperative taglia + lo. 'Cut it out!' is idiomatically 'Piantala!' or 'Smettila!'.

etymology:
From the gerund of tagliare, meaning a small strip of paper to be separated from a main one. Car service sense is from a time where the procedure was annotated on such a strip.
Compare French coupon from couper (“to cut”) for a similar semantic shift.

fact.text: Comes from tagliare 'to cut': a strip of paper cut from a larger sheet. Car services got the name because the work was recorded on such a strip. French coupon (from couper) shifted the same way.

ignored: In the context, tagliando is the gerund of tagliare (to cut), not the noun. That belongs on the tagliare card.

senses.note: Also a car's routine service: fare il tagliando.

etymology: From Late Latin tāliāre, a verb based on Latin tālea (“cutting taken from a plant”).

fact.text: From Late Latin taliare 'to cut', which also gave Old French taillier. That is where English tailor (literally 'cutter') comes from, as well as detail and retail.

senses.note: Tagliarsi = to cut oneself. Farsi tagliare i capelli = to get a haircut.

etymology: Deverbal from tagliare + -o.

fact.text: Rome's famous pizza al taglio is baked in large trays and sold in cut pieces, usually priced by weight.

senses.note: Taglio di capelli means a haircut. Also used for cutbacks, and for the denomination of banknotes.

etymology: From Latin tālis.

fact.text: Has nothing to do with an English tale (a story, which is racconto or storia in Italian). It comes from Latin talis, meaning 'such'.

senses.note: Un tale can also mean 'a certain person, some guy'. Tale e quale = exactly the same.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Old French talent (“desire, wish”), from Classical Latin talentum (“a Grecian weight; a talent of money; (post-Classical) gift from God; (Medieval) skill, ability”), from Ancient Greek τάλαντον (tálanton, “balance; a particular weight, especially of gold; sum of money; a talent”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *tl̥h₂ent-, from the root *telh₂-.

fact.text: A talent was an ancient weight of silver or gold. The meaning 'skill' comes from the Bible's Parable of the Talents, where servants must make good use of the money they are given.

senses.note: Also a talented person: è un talento, 'he/she is a real talent'.
English loanword, often spelled talk show. Plural doesn't change: i talk show.

etymology: From Latin tālus.
ignored: A bad parse: the intended word is tale (such), and talo is an unrelated rare medical term.

etymology: Univerbation of tale + volta.

senses.note: A bit more formal or written than a volte, which means the same.
Agrees with the noun: tanto, tanta, tanti, tante. Tante uova = so many eggs.

etymology: Derived from Latin tantus.

senses.note: Così tanto = so much. As an adjective it agrees: tanta gente, tanti soldi.

etymology: Derived from Latin tantus.

senses.note: Agrees with what it refers to: tanto, tanta, tanti, tante. Example: Ne ho tanti = I have lots.

etymology: From Latin tapēte, from Ancient Greek τάπης (tápēs).

fact.text: It comes from Greek tápēs 'carpet', the same root behind French tapis and English tapestry.

senses.note: Also a mat; tappeto rosso = red carpet.

etymology: From Latin tardē.

fact.text: Comes from Latin tarde, from tardus 'slow', the same root as English tardy.

senses.note: È tardi = it's late. To be late for something is essere in ritardo.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tardus.

fact.text: From Latin tardus 'slow', which also gave English tardy.

senses.note: Used in tardo pomeriggio (late afternoon) and tarda età. The adverb 'late' is tardi: più tardi = later.

etymology: From Arabic تَعْرِفَة (taʕrifa, “tariff, rate”).

fact.text: Came from Arabic ta'rifa, a list or notice of fees, through Mediterranean trade. English got the word tariff from this Italian form.

senses.note: Also rate, tariff: tariffa ridotta = reduced fare

etymology: From Frankish *taskā, from Proto-Germanic *taskǭ. Perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *das-, *des- (“to fray”).

senses.note: Conoscere qualcosa come le proprie tasche = to know something like the back of your hand.

etymology: From Latin taxa.

senses.note: Strictly a fee for a specific service; a general tax is l'imposta, but everyday speech says 'le tasse'.

etymology: Deverbal from tassare.

fact.text: Three unrelated words share this spelling: rate (from tassare, 'to tax'), badger (from Late Latin taxo) and the yew tree (from Latin taxus).

senses.note: tasso di interesse = interest rate; tasso di criminalità = crime rate.

etymology: From Latin tabula. Doublet of tabula and tavolo.

fact.text: 'A tavola!' is the classic shout calling the whole family to sit down and eat. It comes from Latin tabula, 'board, plank', which is also where English 'table' comes from.

senses.note: Tavola is the dining or laid table (a tavola!). Il tavolo is the table as a piece of furniture.

etymology:
From Latin tabula, with a change in gender and inflection.
Doublet of tavola and tabula.

fact.text: From Latin tabula, meaning plank or board, which also gave English table (through French). Tabula also survives in tablet and tabulate.

senses.note: tavola is often used for the dining table: A tavola! = Dinner's ready!
Invariable: i taxi. Also spelled tassì. Prendere un taxi = to take a taxi.

etymology: From Arabic طَاس (ṭās).

fact.text: Comes from Arabic tas, 'bowl', the same source as French tasse. In slang, la tazza also means the toilet bowl.

senses.note: Also 'mug'. Una tazza di tè = a cup of tea. A trophy cup is la coppa.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tē, from tū.

senses.note: Stressed form: con te, per te, di te. The unstressed object form is ti.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English team.

senses.note: Invariable: i team. Common in business and sport; squadra is the native word.

From Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέατρον (théatron, “a place for viewing”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek théatron, 'a place for viewing', from theáomai, 'to watch'. The word was about the audience watching, not about the stage.

senses.note: Both the building and drama as an art: andare a teatro (to go to the theatre).

etymology: Borrowed from Latin technicus.

senses.note: Female: la tecnica. Also an adjective (technical). In football, il tecnico = the coach.

etymology: From tecno- + -logia.

senses.note: The stress falls on the -i-: tecnologìa.
