From Early Medieval Latin theodiscus, from a Germanic language, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz (“of the people, popular, vernacular”), from *þeudō (“people”) + *-iskaz (“-ish, -ic, -al”). The Old English form is þēodisċ, the Old High German one diutisc (attested ca. 1090 in the Annolied). Compare also Friulian todesc, archaic or regional French thiois, Sicilian tudiscu.

fact.text: From Medieval Latin theodiscus, from Germanic *þiudiskaz 'of the people'. The same root gave German Deutsch and English Dutch.

senses.note: Languages are masculine and lowercase: parlo tedesco, il tedesco è difficile.

etymology: From English television camera. By surface analysis, tele- + camera.

fact.text: Watch out: Italian 'camera' on its own means 'room' (camera da letto = bedroom). English 'camera' comes from camera obscura, Latin for 'dark room'.

senses.note: Also a CCTV/security camera. A camera for still photos is 'la macchina fotografica'.

etymology: From tele- + film.

senses.note: Invariable: i telefilm. Serie TV is also very common.

etymology: From telefono + -are.

senses.note: Needs 'a' before the person: telefono a Marco (not telefono Marco).

etymology: From telefonare (“to phone”) + -ata (verbal noun suffix).

senses.note: Fare una telefonata = to make a phone call.

etymology: From tele- + -fono, influenced by English telephone and French téléphone.

fact.text: Many Italians credit Antonio Meucci, not Bell, with inventing the telephone. In 2002 the US House of Representatives passed a resolution honouring his work.

senses.note: Stress falls on the second syllable: telèfono. Al telefono = on the phone.

etymology: From tele- + giornale.

fact.text: Built from tele- + giornale (newspaper), so literally a 'tele-newspaper'. Italians usually just call it il TG, as in TG1, the evening news on the main RAI channel.

senses.note: Often shortened to il TG, pronounced 'tiggì'.

etymology: From tele- + -gramma.

fact.text: Like problema and programma, it comes from a Greek word ending in -ma. So it is masculine and its plural ends in -i: il telegramma, i telegrammi.

senses.note: Masculine despite ending in -a: il telegramma, i telegrammi.

etymology: From tele- + visione.

senses.note: Often shortened to la tv (said 'ti vu') or la tele. guardare la televisione = to watch TV.

etymology: Inherited from Latin timēre. Compare Portuguese and Spanish temer.

fact.text: From Latin timere, to fear, the same root as English timid.

senses.note: More formal than avere paura di. Temo che + subjunctive = I'm afraid that

etymology: From Latin temperātūra.

senses.note: For a fever, Italians usually say avere la febbre rather than 'have a temperature'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tempestās via the nominative form. Doublet of tempestà.

fact.text: Comes from Latin tempestas, which first meant 'season' or 'weather' and comes from tempus, 'time'. A storm was simply bad weather. Shakespeare's The Tempest is La tempesta in Italian.

senses.note: Also figurative: una tempesta di applausi = a storm of applause.

etymology: From Latin tempus (“time”), from Proto-Indo-European *tempos (“stretch”), from the root *temp- (“to stretch, string”).

fact.text: One word covers both time and weather, as French temps does. English borrowed it as musical 'tempo', and grammatical 'tense' also comes from Latin tempus, through Old French.

senses.note: Not for clock time: 'What time is it?' = Che ore sono? Non ho tempo = I don't have time.

etymology: From Latin temporālis.

fact.text: Latin temporalis meant 'of time'. In Italian, tempo means both time and weather, so a temporale is in effect a bout of bad weather.

senses.note: As an adjective, temporale means 'temporal' (relating to time).

etymology: From Early Medieval Latin or Late Latin tenda, from Vulgar Latin *tendita, substantivized feminine of *tenditus, as a variant form of tentus, perfect passive participle of Latin tendō. Compare Portuguese tenda, Spanish tienda, French tente, Friulian tinde, Romanian tindă, English tent.

fact.text: Comes from Latin tendere, 'to stretch', like English 'tent'. Both a tent and a curtain are basically cloth stretched out.

senses.note: Also a blind or awning. tirare le tende = to draw the curtains.

etymology: Clipping of luogotenente.

fact.text: It's short for luogotenente, 'place-holder' (luogo + tenente), the one who stands in for a superior. English lieutenant is built the same way, from French lieu 'place' + tenant 'holding'.

senses.note: Military rank; also used as a form of address: 'Sì, tenente!'

etymology: Inherited from Latin tenēre, from Proto-Italic *tenēō, stative from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin tenere 'to hold', the source of English tenant (one who holds land), tenacious and tenure.

senses.note: Irregular: tengo, tieni, tiene; future terrò. Tieni! = Here, take it!

etymology: Inherited from Latin tenerum, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“to stretch, draw”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin tener 'soft, delicate', which also gave English 'tender' through Old French.

senses.note: Also 'cute, sweet': Che tenero! = How sweet!

etymology: Borrowed from English tennis.

fact.text: Borrowed from English, which got it from Old French tenez, 'hold!' or 'take this!', probably what the server called out before serving.

senses.note: To play tennis = giocare a tennis.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin tēnsiōnem.

senses.note: Also 'voltage' in electricity: alta tensione = high voltage.

etymology: From Latin temptāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin temptare, 'to handle, test, try'. That verb gave English both tempt and attempt, and Italian keeps both meanings in one word.

senses.note: tentare di + infinitive. tentato omicidio = attempted murder. Also means 'to tempt'.

etymology: From Latin tentativus.

fact.text: This does not mean 'tentative'. It is a noun meaning 'attempt', from Latin tentare 'to try'. A tentative plan in Italian is provvisorio, and a tentative smile is esitante.

senses.note: Fare un tentativo = to have a go; al primo tentativo = at the first try.
in teoria = in theory

etymology: Borrowed from New Latin therapīa, from Ancient Greek θεραπεία (therapeía, “service, medical treatment”).

fact.text: Goes back to Ancient Greek therapeía, which first meant 'service' or 'attendance' and later 'medical treatment'. Caring for the sick was seen as a form of service.

senses.note: terapia intensiva = intensive care; andare in terapia = to see a therapist.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin termināre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin terminus, 'boundary stone'. Terminus was also the Roman god who guarded boundaries. English 'terminate' and 'terminal' share the root.

features.construction: transitive; also intransitive (= to end) with essere

senses.note: Takes avere with an object (ho terminato il lavoro) and essere without one (la lezione è terminata).

etymology: Inherited from Latin terminus or the variant termen, termine, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“through”).

fact.text: Latin terminus was a boundary stone, and Terminus was the Roman god who guarded boundaries. English 'terminal' and 'terminate' come from the same word.

senses.note: Also 'end' (al termine di = at the end of) and 'deadline' (termine ultimo).

etymology: From termo- + -metro.
From termo- + sifone.

fact.text: Literally a 'thermosiphon': early central heating moved hot water through the pipes by convection alone, with no pump. The name stuck to the radiator itself.

senses.note: The household heater. A car radiator is 'il radiatore'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin terra, from Proto-Italic *terzā, from Proto-Indo-European *ters-eh₂, from *ters- (“dry”).

fact.text: Comes from an ancient root meaning 'dry', so earth was the dry land as opposed to the sea. The same root gave English 'thirst'.

senses.note: a terra / per terra = on the ground; also land as opposed to sea.

etymology: Borrowed from French terrasse, from Old Occitan terrassa. Related to terrazzo.

senses.note: Il terrazzo (m.) is also common, often for a large balcony or a roof terrace.

etymology: From Latin terrēnum.

senses.note: Also soil, a plot of land, or a sports field. Un terreno pietroso = rocky ground.

etymology: Derived from Latin terribĭlis.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural terribili.

etymology: From terrore + -ismo.
From terrore + -izzare.

senses.note: Can also mean to terrorize (a population).

etymology: From Latin tertius.

fact.text: Goes back through Latin tertius to the same Proto-Indo-European ordinal as English 'third' and Greek trítos, all built on the word for 'three'.

senses.note: Agrees with the noun: terzo piano, terza finestra.

etymology: Inherited from Latin thēsaurus (“treasure”), from Ancient Greek θησαυρός (thēsaurós, “storehouse”, “treasure”). Doublet of Tesauro (“a male given name”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek thēsaurós 'storehouse, treasure', which is also where English gets 'thesaurus', a treasure-house of words. 'Treasure' comes from the same root.

senses.note: Common term of endearment, used for both men and women. Literally means 'treasure'.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English test.

fact.text: Italian borrowed this from English, but English test goes back to Latin testum, 'earthen pot'. Small clay pots were used to assay precious metals, so a test was first a trial of gold.

senses.note: Invariable: i test. Often a quiz or medical/psychological test.

etymology: From Latin testa. The semantic development is earthen pot → skull → head.

fact.text: Latin testa meant an earthenware pot. Slang shifted it from pot to skull to head, pushing out the older caput. English test comes from a related Latin word for a clay pot.

senses.note: Testa o croce? = Heads or tails? Avere la testa dura = to be stubborn.

etymology: Back-formation from testimonî, plural of testimonio (“testimony; witness”), perceived as testimoni.

senses.note: Il/la testimone. Also a best man or bridesmaid at a wedding, and the baton in a relay race.

etymology: From testimonio + -are.

senses.note: testimoniare contro / a favore di qualcuno = to testify against / for someone.

etymology: Learned borrowing from New Latin textus (“text”), from Latin textus (“woven”), perfect passive participle of texō (“weave”).

fact.text: From Latin textus, 'woven', from texere, 'to weave'. A text was imagined as a woven fabric of words, and the same root gives English textile and texture.

senses.note: Il testo di una canzone = song lyrics; libro di testo = textbook.

etymology:
From Late Latin titta, titia, from Frankish *titta, from Proto-Germanic *titt- (“teat; nipple; breast”), from Proto-Indo-European *tata- (“father; parent; nipple”).
Compare also French tette, Spanish and Portuguese teta, Romanian țâță, English teat. The word is found in many European languages and may simply be ultimately an expressive formation based on infantile language.

fact.text: Related to English teat, through a Germanic word (titt-) that probably started as baby talk. Similar words appear across Europe: Spanish teta, French tette.

senses.note: Slang for breast, usually used in the plural: le tette. Avoid it in polite company.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tēctum (“roof”). Compare French toit, Portuguese teto, Spanish techo.

fact.text: From Latin tectum 'roof', from tegere 'to cover'. The same root gives English protect ('cover in front') and detect ('uncover').

senses.note: Also figurative: a cap or upper limit (tetto di spesa = spending cap).

ignored: The English article 'the' from titles in the contexts; as Italian it is only a misspelling of tè (tea).

senses.note: The correct spelling is tè.

etymology: From Latin tepidus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin tepidus, the source of English tepid. Italian changed the Latin e into ie, much as Latin pede became piede ('foot').

senses.note: Also figurative: half-hearted (un'accoglienza tiepida = a lukewarm welcome).

etymology: From New Latin typhus, from Ancient Greek τῦφος (tûphos).

fact.text: Its first meaning is typhus, the feverish disease. Passion for a team was compared to a fever, which is why a sports fan is a tifoso.

senses.note: Fare il tifo per = to root for. The fans themselves are i tifosi.

etymology: From tifo + -oso.

fact.text: It comes from tifo, which means typhus. Fans are pictured as gripped by a feverish passion.

senses.note: Mainly for sports. Feminine: la tifosa. Fare il tifo per = to support (a team).

etymology: From Latin tigris.

senses.note: Always feminine, even for a male tiger: la tigre maschio.

etymology: From Latin timidus.
Inherited from Late Latin tīmōnem, alteration of Classical Latin tēmōnem; alternatively, directly inherited into Italian from the Classical form, with pretonic /e/ > /i/.

fact.text: Latin temo meant the pole of a cart or the beam of a plough. The word later moved to ships, and it still also means a cart shaft and a plough beam.

senses.note: Figurative: essere al timone = to be at the helm (in charge).

etymology: From Latin typicus.

senses.note: Often means 'local, traditional': piatto tipico = local specialty dish.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin typus (“symbol”), from Ancient Greek τύπος (túpos, “mark”, “figure”), derived from τύπτω (túptō, “to beat, strike”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)tewp-.

fact.text: From Greek túpos, a mark made by striking (túptein, to strike). English type comes from the same word, which is why typing literally means making marks by striking.

senses.note: Feminine: tipa. Che tipo! = What a character!

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tīrāre.

fact.text: Doors in Italy often say 'Tirare' (pull) or 'Spingere' (push). It has nothing to do with English 'tire', and it can also mean to throw or to shoot.

senses.note: tirare su = to pull up / cheer up; also 'to throw'; tira vento = it's windy

etymology: From tirare (“to pull”).

senses.note: tiro in porta = shot on goal; giocare un brutto tiro = to play a dirty trick.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tisana, variant of ptisana, from Ancient Greek πτισάνη (ptisánē, “peeled barley, barley gruel”).

fact.text: Comes via Latin from Ancient Greek ptisanē, 'peeled barley, barley gruel'. The first tisanes were barley drinks, not herbal teas.

senses.note: Often drunk in the evening instead of coffee. Una tisana alla camomilla = a chamomile tea.

etymology: Derived from Latin titulus.

senses.note: Also means headline. Titolo di studio = qualification; titoli = securities, shares.

etymology: From Latin Titius: the name Tizio is usually the first placeholder name, which caused it to become a generic word for "a person".

fact.text: From the Roman name Titius, a stock placeholder name in Latin legal examples. 'Tizio, Caio e Sempronio' still means 'Tom, Dick and Harry'.

senses.note: Feminine: tizia. Often slightly dismissive: quel tizio = that guy.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *tuccāre, of Germanic or onomatopoeic origin.

fact.text: English touch comes from the same Vulgar Latin *toccare via Old French.

senses.note: tocca a te = it's your turn / it's up to you.

etymology: From earlier tollere, from Latin tollō (“to lift, remove”), from Proto-Italic *tolnō, from the Proto-Indo-European *telh₂- (“to bear, endure”).

features.construction: transitive: togliere qualcosa (a qualcuno / da qualcosa)

senses.note: Irregular: tolgo, tolgono, tolsi; past participle tolto. togliersi = to take off (clothes).

etymology: From Late Latin tumba, from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos).

senses.note: Muto come una tomba = silent as the grave.

etymology: Deverbal from tombolare.

fact.text: Italian families play it at Christmas. In Naples each number has a nickname from the Smorfia, a traditional dream-interpretation list. For example, 90 is 'la paura' (fear).

senses.note: A traditional family game at Christmas; shout 'Tombola!' when your whole card is complete.
Usually the metric tonne (1,000 kg). Colloquially, una tonnellata di = a ton of, loads of.

etymology:
From Latin talpa (“mole”) with a change in gender. The original [ɫ] appears to have vocalized to [u̯] in pre-literary Tuscan, with the resulting [au̯] regularly yielding [ɔ], as in Latin aurum (“gold”) > Italian òro. Doublet of talpa.
The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.

fact.text: Surprisingly, it comes from Latin talpa, 'mole', not from a word for mouse. The word moved from one small digging animal to another. Talpa itself still means mole in Italian.

senses.note: Also used loosely for a rat (ratto). Mickey Mouse is Topolino.

ignored: This is an infinitive with an attached pronoun (tormentare + lo). Study it on the tormentare card.

senses.note: tormentare + lo (him/it).

Inherited from Latin tornāre (“to turn”).

fact.text: From Latin tornare 'to turn (on a lathe)', from Greek tornos 'lathe'. English 'turn' comes from the same source, so coming back is literally turning around.

senses.note: Takes essere: sono tornato. tornare a + infinitive = to do something again.

ignored: Bad parse: 'Torno' in the context is 'I return', from the verb tornare, not this archaic noun meaning lathe.

senses.note: Archaic variant of tornio.

etymology: From Latin turrem, from Ancient Greek τύρρις (túrrhis), τύρσις (túrsis), likely ultimately a Mediterranean substrate loan.

fact.text: From Latin turris, from Greek tyrrhis. Ancient writers linked it to the Tyrrhenians (Etruscans), supposedly named for their towers. The Tyrrhenian Sea takes its name from them.

senses.note: Also the rook in chess. La Torre di Pisa = the Leaning Tower of Pisa.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin torrentem, accusative form of torrēns (“rushing”, “torrential”) (originally “scorching", then "powerful", "strengthful", "forceful"), present active participle of torreō (“to scorch, burn, parch”), from Proto-Italic *torzeō, causative of the Proto-Indo-European root *ters- (“dry”).

fact.text: Surprisingly, this comes from Latin torrere 'to scorch', the root of torrid and toast. Torrens meant 'burning' at first, and later 'violent, rushing'.

senses.note: Unlike a fiume (river), a torrente is steep and fast, and its flow varies a lot. Many are dry in summer.

etymology: From Latin turta. Thought to derive from Latin tŏrta f (“twisted”), which yielded tòrta in Italian.

senses.note: Also covers pies and tarts. Torta salata = savoury pie; torta di compleanno = birthday cake.

etymology: From tortello + -ino, hypocorism of torta (“cake”).

fact.text: Emilian legend says an innkeeper invented the shape after glimpsing Venus's navel through a keyhole. The name is a double diminutive of torta, 'cake'.

senses.note: Usually plural: tortellini in brodo (in broth), a Bologna classic.

etymology: From Latin tortum (“a wrong or injustice”), substantive use of tortus, perfect passive participle of torqueō. Compare French tort.

fact.text: From Latin tortum, 'something twisted', from torquere 'to twist'. The same root gives English 'torture' and 'distort'.

senses.note: Avere torto = to be wrong (the opposite of avere ragione). Fare un torto a qualcuno = to wrong someone.

etymology: Inherited from Latin turturem.

fact.text: Comes from Latin turtur, imitating the bird's coo. The 'turtle' in English 'turtle dove' comes from the same word and has nothing to do with the reptile.

senses.note: Also an invariable colour word: color tortora = dove grey/taupe.
