From Latin tussem, from Proto-Indo-European *tud-ti-s- (“cough”), from *(s)tewd-, from *(s)tew- (“to push, hit”).

senses.note: avere la tosse = to have a cough

etymology: Verb-object compound, composed of tosta (“to toast”) + pane (“bread”).

fact.text: Built from tosta (toasts) + pane (bread), the same verb-plus-noun pattern as apriscatole (can opener) and cavatappi (corkscrew).

senses.note: Invariable: il tostapane, i tostapane.

fact.text: In an Italian bar, ordering 'un toast' usually gets you a toasted ham and cheese sandwich. Plain toast is pane tostato.

senses.note: Pane tostato = toast; caffè tostato = roasted coffee.

etymology: From Medieval Latin tōtālis.

senses.note: Il totale = the sum or overall amount: in totale = in total, altogether.

etymology: From totale + -mente.

senses.note: Invariable loanword: il tour, i tour.

etymology: Probably from Old Occitan toalha, from Frankish *þwahilu. Cognate with Portuguese toalha (“towel”).

fact.text: Probably from Frankish *thwahilu, a cloth for washing. Through Old French toaille, the same word gave English 'towel'.

senses.note: A napkin is il tovagliolo, from the same word.

etymology: From tovaglia.

fact.text: A diminutive of tovaglia, 'tablecloth', so literally a 'little tablecloth'. Tovaglia comes from a Germanic word that also gave English 'towel', via French.

senses.note: From la tovaglia = tablecloth.

etymology: Uncertain. Compare catalan tros.

fact.text: Lavorare per un tozzo di pane means to work for a crust of bread, which is the Italian way of saying 'to work for peanuts'.

senses.note: Mostly in 'un tozzo di pane' (a crust of bread). As an adjective, tozzo means stocky or squat.

etymology: From Latin intrā, with influence from Latin inter.

fact.text: Tra and fra mean exactly the same thing. Italians pick whichever sounds better, so they avoid tongue-twisters like 'tra tre' or 'fra fratelli'.

senses.note: Same as fra. Also means 'among', and 'in' for time: tra due giorni = in two days.

etymology: Deverbal from tracciare (“to mark out; to sketch”) + -a.

senses.note: Plural: tracce. sulle tracce di = on the trail of. Also an outline (la traccia del tema).

etymology: From Latin trādere.

fact.text: Comes from Latin tradere, 'to hand over', which also gave English both tradition (handing down) and traitor (handing someone over to the enemy).

senses.note: Also: to cheat on (a partner), and to give away or reveal (a feeling).

etymology: From tradizione + -ale; cognate with Piedmontese tradissional/tradissiunal.
From Latin trādūcō. Cognate with Piedmontese tradùe/tradüve.

fact.text: There's a famous Italian pun, 'traduttore, traditore': translator, traitor. It means no translation is perfectly faithful. The verb comes from Latin trādūcere, 'to lead across'.

senses.note: Irregular like condurre: traduco, tradussi, tradotto. Tradurre dall'inglese all'italiano.

etymology: From Latin trāductiō, trāductiōnis (“transferring, translation”, literally “leading across”), from trādūcō (“to lead across”), from trāns (“across”) + dūcō (“to lead”).

fact.text: A famous Italian pun says 'traduttore, traditore', meaning 'translator, traitor'. The idea is that every translation betrays the original a little.

etymology:
Potentially from Vulgar Latin *trānsfrīcō (“to rub across”), from trans- + frico; Klein instead suggests the Italian has ultimate origin in Arabic تَفْرِيق (tafrīq, “distribution, dispersion”), reshaped to match the native prefix tra- (“trans-”).
Cognate with Piedmontese tràfich/tràfic and Sicilian tràficu.

fact.text: English took 'traffic' from this Italian word (via French) in the 1500s, when it meant trade. Its own origin is disputed: perhaps Latin 'to rub across', perhaps Arabic tafrīq.

senses.note: Can also mean illegal trade: traffico di droga = drug trafficking.

etymology: From Latin tragoedia, from Ancient Greek τρᾰγῳδῐ́ᾱ (trăgōidĭ́ā), from τρᾰ́γος (trắgos, “male goat”) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

fact.text: From Ancient Greek tragoidia, literally 'goat song' (tragos goat + oide song). Why goats is debated: perhaps a goat prize or sacrifice at early drama festivals.

senses.note: Colloquially, any drama or fuss: non fare una tragedia!

etymology: From tramontare (“to set, go down; to fade”, literally “to set beyond the mountains”). Compare Sicilian tracoḍḍu.

fact.text: This comes from tramontare, which literally means to go beyond the mountains, describing the sun disappearing behind the peaks at the end of the day.

senses.note: Also used figuratively for a decline, e.g. il tramonto di un impero (the decline of an empire).

etymology: From tra(i) (imperative of trarre) + -ne.

fact.text: Comes from trai, the old imperative of trarre (to pull), plus ne (from it). So it originally meant something like 'take out of it', which is exactly what 'except' does.

senses.note: Tutti tranne lui = everyone except him. Tranne che = except that.

etymology:
Borrowed from Latin tranquillitātem (“calmness, stillness”).
From tranquille + -ità.

senses.note: In tutta tranquillità = calmly, without hurry.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin tranquillus (“quiet, calm, still, tranquil”), from Proto-Italic *trānskʷīlos.

senses.note: Tranquillo! on its own = Don't worry! / Relax!

etymology: From Frankish *trappa (whence French trappe (“trap”)) + -ola.

senses.note: Trappola per topi = mousetrap. Cadere in trappola = to fall into a trap.

etymology: From tras- + correre; cognate with Piedmontese trascore.

fact.text: Made from tras- (across) + correre (to run), so it literally means 'to run across'. You let the time run through. For spending money, Italian uses spendere instead.

senses.note: Only for time: trascorrere le vacanze. For money use spendere. Il tempo trascorre (it passes) takes essere.

etymology: From tras- + corso.

senses.note: Also the past participle of trascorrere (to spend time): ho trascorso = I spent.

etymology: From trasferire + -mento; cognate with Piedmontese trasferiment.

senses.note: Also used for a job relocation or for moving house (from trasferirsi).

etymology: From Latin trānsferō.

senses.note: Reflexive trasferirsi = to move (house or city). Conjugated like finire: trasferisco.
Mi sono trasferito a Roma. = I moved to Rome. Uses essere.

etymology: From Latin trānsfōrmāre.

senses.note: trasformare X in Y = turn X into Y; trasformarsi = to turn into.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English trash.
ignored: An unadapted English loan, used as a name in the context; its rare Italian sense (tacky kitsch) isn't worth a card.

senses.note: English loan for deliberately tacky, vulgar pop culture. Invariable.

etymology: From tras- + locare.

senses.note: Used for changing home or office. Il trasloco = the move. Takes avere: abbiamo traslocato.
Fare un trasloco = to move house. Use trasferimento for a job transfer.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin trānsmissiōnem.

senses.note: Also a TV or radio programme/broadcast: una trasmissione televisiva.

etymology: From Medieval Latin trānspārentem (“transparent”), present participle of trānspareō, from Latin trāns + pareō.

senses.note: Also figurative, as in English: sincere, open (un processo trasparente).

etymology: From Latin trānsportāre.

senses.note: Also 'to carry away' figuratively: farsi trasportare dalle emozioni.

etymology: Deverbal from trasportàre + -o.

senses.note: I trasporti pubblici = public transportation.

fact.text: It literally means 'sweat through' (tras- + sudare, 'to sweat'). English exude is built the same way, from Latin ex- + sudare.

senses.note: Transitive too: trasuda latte = it oozes milk. Also figurative: trasudare gioia.

etymology: Inherited from Latin tractāre (“to drag; to handle; to practise”), from tractus (“dragged”), perfect passive participle of trahō (“to drag; to extract”).

fact.text: From Latin tractare (to drag, to handle), from trahere (to drag). English 'treat', 'treaty', 'tractor' and 'traction' all come from the same dragging root.

senses.note: 'Si tratta di…' = it's about…; 'quando si tratta di' = when it comes to.

etymology: From Latin tractus.

fact.text: From Latin tractus, from trahere 'to drag'. The same root gives English trait, tract, tractor and attract.

senses.note: Often plural: i tratti del viso = facial features. 'A un tratto' = suddenly.

etymology: From Ancient Greek τραῦμα (traûma, “wound, damage”).

fact.text: Comes from Greek traûma 'wound', and Italian often still uses it for physical injury: trauma cranico means head injury, not psychological shock.

senses.note: Masculine even though it ends in -a: il trauma, i traumi.

etymology: Inherited from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Sicilian tri.
ignored: Using the number as a noun is a secondary use; the numeral tre is studied on its own card.

etymology: Inherited from Latin trēs, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Sicilian tri.
From Vulgar Latin trecentum, from Latin trecenti.
From Latin trēdecim.
Borrowed from French train.

fact.text: Borrowed from French train, from the Old French verb for 'to drag' (modern traîner). A train was first something pulled along behind, like the train of a gown.

senses.note: in treno = by train; prendere il treno = to take the train.

etymology: Inherited from Latin trīgintā, from Proto-Indo-European *tri(d)ḱomt (“thirty”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + cinque (“five”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + due (“two”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + nove (“nine”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + quattro (“four”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + sei (“six”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + sette (“seven”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + tre (“three”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + otto (“eight”).
From trenta (“thirty”) + uno (“one”).
From Latin tribūnal.

senses.note: Andare in tribunale = to go to court. A tennis court is campo.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin trīstis. Compare tristo, inherited from Vulgar Latin trīstus, from the same source.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural tristi.

etymology:
From Late Latin troia, troja, of uncertain origin, but possibly:
* from Latin (porcum de) Troia (“(hog of) Troy”), after the Trojan horse,
* or alternatively of Celtic origin, from a Gaulish root *trogja, from a root meaning “to pull” and thence also “fertile," Proto-Celtic *trāglo-, for which see Latin traho.
* or possibly simply of imitative origin, from the sound of a pig's grunt. Compare French truie, Catalan truja.

fact.text: With a capital letter, Troia is the Italian name for Troy. One theory links the pig meaning to the Roman dish porcus Troianus, a pig stuffed like the Trojan horse.

senses.note: A strong insult. The literal meaning, 'sow', is now regional; the normal word for a sow is scrofa.

etymology: From a Germanic source (Frankish *trumba, Old High German trumpa, Old Norse trumba), all imitative.

fact.text: The trumpet shape shows up elsewhere too: 'tromba delle scale' is a stairwell and 'tromba d'aria' is a whirlwind or tornado.

senses.note: Suonare la tromba = to play the trumpet.

fact.text: Traced to Frankish *thorp 'cluster, village', a relative of English troop and the -thorpe in place names. A crowd came to mean 'too much'.

senses.note: As an adjective it agrees: troppa gente, troppi soldi. As an adverb it never changes: costa troppo.

etymology: From Early Medieval Latin troppus, borrowed from Frankish *þorp (“a cluster, agglomeration", also "collection of houses, village”), from Proto-Germanic *þurpą (“village”), from Proto-Indo-European *trab-, *treb- (“dwelling, room”). Cognate with French trop (“too much”), Piedmontese tròp/trop. More at trop, thorp and troop.

fact.text: Traced to Frankish *thorp 'cluster, village', a relative of English troop and the -thorpe in place names. A crowd came to mean 'too much'.

senses.note: As an adverb it never changes: troppo veloce = too fast. As an adjective it agrees: troppe persone.

etymology: From Vulgar Latin *tropāre, a verb probably based on Classical Latin tropus. Compare French trouver.

fact.text: Probably from Latin tropus 'figure of speech'. To 'find' first meant to invent verses, which gives trovatore (troubadour), as in Verdi's opera Il Trovatore.

senses.note: Andare a trovare qualcuno = to go and visit someone.

etymology:
Deverbal from truccare + -o, from French truquer.
Compare Piedmontese truch, French truc.

fact.text: The same word is also the everyday Italian for makeup: truccarsi means to put on makeup, and a truccatore is a makeup artist.

senses.note: Plural trucchi (the h keeps the hard c sound).

etymology: Inherited from Latin tū, from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂.

fact.text: 'Dare del tu' means speaking to someone informally. Asking 'possiamo darci del tu?' is the Italian way of saying 'let's drop the formalities'.

senses.note: Subject pronoun, often left out: (tu) sei. After prepositions use te.

etymology: From English tunnel.

fact.text: Italian took this from English, but English got it from Old French tonel, 'small cask'. In Middle English, a tonnel was a tube-shaped net for catching birds.

senses.note: Invariable: i tunnel. Road and rail tunnels are also often called la galleria.
Forms: tuo/tua/tuoi/tue. Usually takes an article (il tuo libro) but not before one family member (tuo padre).

etymology:
From Latin tuus, from Proto-Italic *towos.
In the singular, Latin tuum underwent *ʊu > *ou > *ɔu dissimilation, cf. Sardinian tou, and also Latin ōvum > Italian òvo, Spanish huevo, ultimately producing [ˈtwɔu], and a plural [ˈtwɔi]. Italian then underwent its regular *wɔV > *uV sound change, cf. *bwɔe > bue, *mjɛu > mio, producing ultimately [ˈtu.o]. This latter sound change is blocked by a following [i], which explains the plural form tuoi, cf. *mjɛi > miei.

senses.note: Agrees with the thing owned: tuo, tua, tuoi, tue. No article with singular family: tuo padre.

etymology:
From Latin tuus, from Proto-Italic *towos.
In the singular, Latin tuum underwent *ʊu > *ou > *ɔu dissimilation, cf. Sardinian tou, and also Latin ōvum > Italian òvo, Spanish huevo, ultimately producing [ˈtwɔu], and a plural [ˈtwɔi]. Italian then underwent its regular *wɔV > *uV sound change, cf. *bwɔe > bue, *mjɛu > mio, producing ultimately [ˈtu.o]. This latter sound change is blocked by a following [i], which explains the plural form tuoi, cf. *mjɛi > miei.

senses.note: Used with the article: il tuo, la tua, i tuoi, le tue. È il tuo? = Is it yours?

etymology: From Latin tonus (“thunderclap; sound, tone”), from Ancient Greek τόνος (tónos). Doublet of tono.

fact.text: Comes from Latin tonus, which meant both 'thunderclap' and 'sound, tone'. The same word gave Italian tono and English 'tone'.

senses.note: Countable in Italian: 'un tuono' = a clap of thunder.

etymology: Borrowed from French tourisme, from English tourism.

fact.text: English supplied this word: tourism passed into Italian through French tourisme. Tour itself goes back to Latin tornus, a turner's lathe, a tool that turns in a circle.

senses.note: Turismo di massa = mass tourism. Un/una turista = a tourist.

etymology: Borrowed from French touriste, from English tourist.

senses.note: Same form for both sexes: il/la turista; plural i turisti, le turiste.

etymology: Borrowed from French tourner.

senses.note: È il tuo turno = it's your turn. Also a work shift: turno di notte = night shift.

etymology:
From Latin tota via (“always”).
Compare Spanish todavía, Portuguese todavia and French toutefois.

fact.text: From Latin tota via, 'the whole way', meaning 'always'. Old Italian used it to mean 'still', and Spanish todavía still means 'still' today.

senses.note: More formal than 'però'.
Takes the article: tutta l'estate = all summer; tutti i giorni = every day.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Latin tōtus.

senses.note: Takes the article and agrees: tutto il giorno, tutta la casa, tutti i giorni.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin tōttus, alteration of Latin tōtus.

senses.note: Tutto = everything; the plural tutti = everyone. Tutto bene? = All good?

etymology: From tutto (“everything”) + fare (“to do”), calque of French (bonne à) tout faire.

fact.text: Literally 'all-do', from tutto (everything) + fare (to do).

senses.note: Invariable: il/la tuttofare, i/le tuttofare.

etymology: Borrowed from French thé, from Dutch thee, from Hokkien 茶 (tê).

fact.text: Came via French and Dutch from Hokkien tê. Languages that got tea by sea through Dutch traders say te or tea, while those that got it overland say chai.

senses.note: Invariable; written with a grave accent, unlike te (you).

etymology: From Latin ū (the name of the letter V).
ignored: A letter name like this is a stray letter, not a vocabulary word.

senses.note: Letter names are feminine and invariable: la u, le u.

fact.text: Ubriaco comes from Latin ebriacus, from ebrius 'drunk'. The same Latin root gives English inebriated.

senses.note: Ubriaco = drunk. Mi sono ubriacato/a = I got drunk.

etymology: From Late Latin ēbriācus, derived from Latin ēbrius, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁egʷʰ- (“to drink”). Cognate with Sicilian mmriacu.

fact.text: Comes from Latin ebrius 'drunk', the same word behind English 'inebriated'. The opposite, sobrius, gave English 'sober'.

senses.note: Also a noun: un ubriaco = a drunk. Ubriaco fradicio = blind drunk.

etymology: From Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”), from Proto-Italic *awis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis. Doublet of augello, which was borrowed from Occitan. Compare Neapolitan auciello, Ligurian öxéllo, Sicilian auceḍḍu.

fact.text: Comes from Late Latin aucellus 'little bird', a diminutive built on avis (bird), so it originally meant 'birdie'. Avis also gave English 'aviation' and 'aviary'.

senses.note: Careful: also vulgar slang for penis.

etymology: From Old Italian occidere, from Latin occīdō (“to kill, slay”). Compare Romanian ucide.

fact.text: It comes from Latin occidere, which was built on caedere 'to cut, to kill'. That is the same root behind English words ending in -cide, like homicide and pesticide.

senses.note: Irregular past participle: ucciso. Passato remoto: uccisi, uccise.

etymology: Imitative or onomatopoeia.

senses.note: A sigh of boredom or impatience, e.g. Uffa, che noia! Often used by children.

etymology: From earlier officio, borrowed from Latin officium (“duty, office”), derived from ops (“wealth, resources”), ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *h₃ep- (“to work”). Doublet of opificio and officina.

fact.text: Comes from Latin officium, a contraction of opificium, roughly 'work-doing'. It is a cousin of English office and related to Italian officina, a workshop.

senses.note: In ufficio = at the office; ufficio postale = post office.

etymology: From earlier equale, from Latin aequālis, derived from aequus (“equal, even”).

senses.note: Same form for both genders (uguale/uguali). Per me è uguale = it's all the same to me.

ignored: Bare interjection sound with no dictionary meaning, so not worth a flashcard.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ulteriōrem.

fact.text: Comes from the same Latin ulterior 'farther' as English ulterior, but it just means further or additional, never hidden. Ulteriori dettagli are simply more details.

senses.note: Usually before the noun: ulteriori informazioni = further information.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ultimus.

fact.text: From Latin ultimus 'farthest, last', the source of English ultimate and ultimatum.

senses.note: 'Last week' is la settimana scorsa. Ultimo means final or most recent: gli ultimi dieci anni.

etymology: Inherited from Latin hūmidus or ūmidus.

fact.text: In cooking, 'in umido' means stewed, as in carne in umido. And as a noun, 'l'umido' is the organic food-waste bin in Italian recycling.

senses.note: Clima umido = humid climate; panni umidi = damp clothes.

etymology: From Latin hūmōrem. Doublet of humour.

fact.text: From Latin humor, 'fluid'. Medieval medicine taught that four bodily fluids decided your temperament, hence 'mood'. For jokes Italians usually say umorismo.

senses.note: essere di buon/cattivo umore = to be in a good/bad mood.

etymology: From uno, from Latin ūnus (“one”).

fact.text: It comes from Latin unus, 'one'. English 'a/an' also grew out of the word 'one', so both languages made their article out of the number one.

senses.note: Used before most masculine nouns: un libro, un amico. Use uno before s+consonant or z (uno zio), una for feminine nouns.

fact.text: Literally 'a big thousand': mille plus the augmentative suffix -one. English million was borrowed from this Italian word, through French.

etymology: From Latin ūndecim.
Derived from Latin unguentum (“ointment, unguent”).
From Latin ūnicus, from ūnus; see also -ico.

fact.text: Its everyday meaning is often 'only' rather than 'unique': figlio unico is an only child, and a senso unico sign means a one-way street.

senses.note: Figlio unico = only child.
Unirsi a + person/group: unisciti a noi = join us. Reflexive: mi unisco, ti unisci…

etymology: From Latin ūnitātem.

senses.note: The plural doesn't change: le unità. Also means unity, as in l'Unità d'Italia (Italian unification).

etymology: Borrowed from Classical Latin ūniversitātem (“the whole” → (Late Latin) “(whole) group; company; corporation” → (Medieval Latin) “university”).

fact.text: Latin universitas meant 'the whole', then any corporation or guild. Medieval universities were guilds of students and teachers. In Italian the word was also once used for trade guilds.

senses.note: Invariable: le università. 'All'università' = at university.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin ūniversus.

fact.text: From Latin universus, 'all together', literally 'turned into one', from unus (one) plus versus (turned).

etymology: Inherited from Latin ūnus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos.
Inherited from Latin homō (nominative). The plural reflects Latin hominēs.

fact.text: The plural is odd because uomo comes from the Latin singular homo, while uomini comes from the Latin plural homines. The same root gives English human and homicide.

senses.note: The plural is irregular: gli uomini. Can also mean 'mankind' (l'uomo).

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin (*)ŏvum, from Latin ōvum n.

fact.text: One egg is masculine (un uovo), but the eggs are feminine (le uova). The odd plural in -a is left over from the Latin neuter plural ova.

senses.note: Irregular plural: l'uovo → le uova (feminine).
Same form for masculine and feminine; the plural is urgenti.

etymology: From urgente + -mente.
From Late Latin urgentia. Cognate with Piedmontese urgensa/ürgensa.

senses.note: D'urgenza = urgent(ly), as an emergency: intervento d'urgenza = emergency operation.

etymology: Dissimilation of inherited Latin ululāre (“to howl”), ultimately from a reduplicated Proto-Indo-European imitative root.

fact.text: Comes from Latin ululare 'to howl', a word that imitates the sound.

senses.note: Also used of animals howling. Noun: l'urlo (pl. le urla for human screams).

etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin ūsāre. Cognate with French user.

senses.note: Si usa = it's customary, it's in fashion. The adjective usato means 'second-hand'.
Also the past participle of usare. 'Auto usata' = used car; 'l'usato' = second-hand goods.

etymology:
From older escire, from Latin exīre, from ex + eō (“to go”). The word may have been phonetically influenced by the etymologically unrelated uscio (“door”).
Compare Sicilian nèsciri, Catalan eixir, Romanian ieși, Old Spanish exir and Old French issir.

fact.text: Comes from Latin exire, 'to go out', the source of English 'exit'. The u- probably came from uscio (door). Stressed forms keep the old e-: esco, esce.

senses.note: Irregular: esco, esci, esce, escono. Uscire da = to leave (a place); uscire con = to date.

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of uscire (“to go out, to exit”). Cognate with Sicilian nisciuta.

senses.note: uscita di sicurezza = emergency exit. The opposite is entrata.

etymology: Inherited from Latin ūsus (“use, employment”), from Proto-Italic *oissos.

senses.note: Also 'custom': usi e costumi = customs and traditions.

etymology: Probably borrowed from Latin ūtilis.

senses.note: Stress on the first syllable: ùtile. As a noun, l'utile means profit.

etymology: From utile + -izzare.

senses.note: A bit more formal than usare and very common in writing: utilizzare un programma.
The tu command of andare, used to cheer or urge someone on: 'Vai, Italia!'

etymology: Borrowed from French vacance, derived from Latin vacantia (“emptiness, leisure”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin vacantia, emptiness or leisure, from vacare, to be empty. It is a cousin of vacant and vacuum: a holiday is time emptied of work.

senses.note: Often plural: le vacanze. andare in vacanza = to go on holiday.

etymology: From vaccinare + -zione.

fact.text: Vaccine comes from Latin vacca, 'cow', because Edward Jenner's first vaccine used cowpox to protect against smallpox.

senses.note: Verb: vaccinare. Vaccine: il vaccino.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin vagārī (“to ramble, wander, stroll about”).

fact.text: From Latin vagari, 'to wander', from vagus 'wandering'. The same root gives English 'vagabond' and 'vague'.

senses.note: Ho vagato per la città = I wandered around the city. Also used of the mind: la mente vaga.

fact.text: Comes from vaglia, the subjunctive of valere 'to be worth', meaning roughly 'let it be worth', a formula once written on the document. That is why it is masculine.

senses.note: Masculine even though it ends in -a, and invariable: il vaglia, i vaglia. Often 'vaglia postale'.

etymology: Borrowed from French wagon, from English wagon, itself from Dutch wagen.

fact.text: Italian borrowed this via French from English wagon, which itself comes from Dutch wagen.

senses.note: Vagone letto = sleeping car; vagone ristorante = dining car.

etymology: Inherited from Latin valēre.

fact.text: Latin valere meant 'to be strong, to be well'. It is the source of value, valid and valiant, and of the Roman goodbye 'vale!', which meant 'be well'.

senses.note: Irregular: valgo, valgono, varrò. Ne vale la pena = it's worth it; past tense ne è valsa la pena.

etymology:
Borrowed from a language of Northern Italy (cf. Venetan valís, Lombard valiza), from Medieval Latin valesia, valixia, from Late Latin valisia, possibly from Gaulish *valisia (“leather bag”), from Proto-Celtic *wal- (“to enclose, surround”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH-. Or, possibly from Arabic وَلِيهَة (walīha, “large bag”).
Related to French valise and Spanish valija, though it is unclear if either term was borrowed from the other.

fact.text: Related to French valise, which English also borrowed for a travel bag.

senses.note: Fare la valigia = to pack. Plural valigie (sometimes valige).

etymology: From Latin vallem, of uncertain origin. Cognate with Sicilian vaḍḍuni.

fact.text: The phrase a valle means 'downstream' or 'downhill', and a monte means 'upstream'. Figuratively, a monte also means 'at the earlier stage' of a process.

etymology: From Late Latin valōrem, from Latin valeō.

fact.text: Comes from Latin valere, 'to be worth, to be strong', the same root as English 'valour'. Italian kept both senses: a 'medaglia al valore' is a medal for bravery.

senses.note: Also means bravery: medaglia al valore = medal for valour. Valori = values (moral) or valuables.

etymology: From valuta + -are.

senses.note: Stress falls on 'va': io vàluto, tu vàluti.

etymology: Borrowed from French vampire, from Serbo-Croatian vàmpīr, from Proto-Slavic *ǫpyrь.

fact.text: Comes from Serbo-Croatian vampir. The word spread across Western Europe in the 1720s and 1730s, after sensational reports of 'vampire' cases in Serbia.

senses.note: Also the vampire bat.

etymology: Borrowed from French avantage, with rebracketing.

fact.text: Borrowed from French avantage (from avant, 'before'). Its first a- was lost, probably because speakers heard it as part of the article. English 'advantage' has the same origin.

senses.note: essere in vantaggio = to be ahead (e.g. in a match).

etymology: Borrowed from Late Latin variābilis.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural variabili. Often used of weather: tempo variabile.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin varius (“diverse, various”), whence also Italian vaio, an inherited doublet.

senses.note: Before a plural noun it means 'several': vari libri = several books

etymology: Probably from a Latin clipping of vāsculum (“small vessel”). Compare with Friulian vascje.

fact.text: Italians say 'fare le vasche' (doing lengths) for strolling up and down the main street to see and be seen, as if swimming laps in a pool.

senses.note: Also a basin, tank or pond, and a length of a swimming pool: fare dieci vasche (swim ten lengths).

etymology: From Latin vāsum.

fact.text: Latin vās, 'vessel', gave English both 'vase' and 'vascular'. That is why blood vessels are vasi sanguigni in Italian.

senses.note: Also a flower pot or jar. Vaso sanguigno = blood vessel.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus.

fact.text: From Latin vetulus, a diminutive of vetus, 'old'. Vetus is also the root of English 'veteran'.

senses.note: Opposite of nuovo and giovane. For people, anziano is more polite.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vidēre, from Proto-Italic *widēō, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European root *weyd-.

fact.text: Comes from Latin videre, which gave English 'video', 'vision' and 'evident'. Its ancient root *weyd- is also behind English 'wit' and 'wise'.

senses.note: Reflexive vedersi = to see each other or meet up: Ci vediamo! = See you! Past participle: visto.

features.construction: reciprocal: ci vediamo, vi vedete, si vedono

senses.note: Often means to meet up: Ci vediamo domani! = See you tomorrow!

etymology: Inherited from Latin vidua, possibly through a Vulgar Latin *viduva.

fact.text: A true cousin of English 'widow': both come from the same Proto-Indo-European word, which also gave Sanskrit vidhava.

senses.note: Masculine: vedovo (widower). Vedova nera = black widow spider.

etymology: From Latin viduus, through a Vulgar Latin *viduvus.

fact.text: From Latin viduus, 'bereaved'. It shares an ancient Indo-European root with English 'widow', so the two words are distant relatives.

senses.note: Also a noun: il vedovo = widower, la vedova = widow.
Vegan is vegano.

etymology: Inherited from Latin venēnum. The first /n/ was dissimilated to /l/; a more straightforward descendant would have been *veneno.

fact.text: From Latin venenum, the same source as English 'venom'. Over time the first n changed to an l, so venenum became veleno.

senses.note: Also used for venom (snake venom = veleno di serpente) and, figuratively, for spite.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin vēlōcem.

fact.text: From Latin velox, 'swift', the same root as English velocity.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; the plural is veloci. The adverb is velocemente.

etymology: From veloce + -mente.
Borrowed from Latin vēlōcitātem.

senses.note: Invariable: le velocità. Also used for gears: cambio a cinque velocità (five-speed gearbox).

etymology: Inherited from Latin vēndere (“to sell”).

fact.text: From Latin vendere, a contraction of venum dare 'to give for sale'. It is the source of English vendor and vending machine.

senses.note: Vendesi = for sale (on signs). Opposite: comprare.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vindicta (“vengeance”), from vindico (“to claim, to vindicate”), from vindex (“defender”).

fact.text: English borrowed it to mean a long blood feud, but in Italian it is simply the ordinary word for revenge. It comes from Latin vindicta, related to English 'vindicate'.

senses.note: Everyday word for revenge or vengeance, not just blood feuds. Plural: vendette.
in vendita = for sale; vendita all'asta = auction

etymology: From Latin Veneris diēs, variant of diēs Veneris (“day of Venus”).

fact.text: From Latin Veneris dies, 'day of Venus'. English Friday is the same idea: the day of Frigg, the Germanic goddess people matched with Venus.

senses.note: Invariable. il venerdì = on Fridays; venerdì = this Friday. Not capitalised.

etymology: From Venezia + -ano.

senses.note: Lowercase in Italian: sono veneziano. Feminine: veneziana.

etymology: Inherited from Latin venīre.

fact.text: Latin venire is behind many English words: venue, event, advent, convene, convention, and adventure (from ad-venire, 'what comes to you').

senses.note: Irregular: vengo, vieni, viene, vengono; past participle venuto (sono venuto).

etymology: From Late Latin vĭnti, from Latin vīgintī, from Proto-Italic *wīgentī, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wih₁ḱm̥ti, *dwi(h₁)dḱm̥ti.
From venti (“twenty”) + cinque (“five”).
From venti (“twenty”) + due (“two”).
ignored: Secondary noun use of the numeral; studied on the numeral card ventidue.

senses.note: As a noun it can also mean a .22 calibre gun.

etymology: From venti (“twenty”) + due (“two”).
From ventilare + -tore. Cf. English ventilator, Latin ventilator, Piedmontese ventilatur.

fact.text: A hospital ventilator is usually a respiratore in Italian. An everyday ventilatore is just the ordinary electric fan that keeps you cool in summer.

senses.note: An electric fan. A sports fan is un tifoso; a hand fan is un ventaglio.

etymology: From venti (“twenty”) + nove (“nine”).
From venti (“twenty”) + quattro (“four”).
From venti (“twenty”) + sei (“six”).
From venti (“twenty”) + sette (“seven”).
From venti (“twenty”) + tre (“three”).
Inherited from Latin ventus (“wind”), from Proto-Italic *wentos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥ts, from *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin ventus, from an Indo-European root meaning 'to blow'. English 'wind' comes from the same root, and 'ventilate' comes from ventus directly.

senses.note: Fa vento = it's windy. Al vento = in the wind.

etymology: From venti (“twenty”) + otto (“eight”).

ignored: Secondary noun use of the numeral; studied on the numeral card ventuno.

senses.note: As a noun it also names the card game (blackjack).

etymology: From vera (“true”, feminine singular) + -mente (“-ly”). Compare among others French vraiment.

fact.text: The -mente ending comes from Latin mente, 'with a mind', so veramente once meant 'with a true mind'. French -ment and Spanish -mente come from the same source.

senses.note: Veramente? = Really? It can also introduce a correction: Veramente... = Actually...

etymology: From Latin verbum (“word, verb”), from Proto-Italic *werðom (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”), from root *werh₁- (“to speak, to say”) + extension *-dʰ-.

fact.text: Latin verbum simply meant 'word', and it is a distant cognate of English 'word' itself. The grammatical sense 'verb' was modelled on Greek rhema.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Classical Latin viridis, from vireō. Cognate with English verdure, French vert, and various Romance homonyms.

fact.text: Comes from Latin viridis, which also gave English verdant and French vert.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine. Essere al verde means to be broke.

etymology: From verde (“green”) + -ura (“noun-forming suffix”), or from Vulgar Latin *virdūra.

fact.text: Built on verde (green), much as English calls leafy vegetables greens.

senses.note: Usually a singular collective noun: mangio la verdura = I eat vegetables. One vegetable = un ortaggio.

etymology: From Latin virginem.

fact.text: Extra virgin olive oil is olio extravergine d'oliva, and the star sign Virgo is la Vergine.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural vergini. As a noun: la Vergine (the Virgin Mary, Virgo).

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *verecunnia, from Latin verēcundia, possibly influenced by cunnus (“vagina”). Doublet of verecondia, which was borrowed. Compare Galician vergoña ~ vergonza, but Portuguese and Occitan vergonha, Sicilian virigogna ~ vrigogna, Spanish vergüenza.

fact.text: It comes from Latin verecundia, 'modesty, shame', from vereri, 'to respect, fear'. The same verb is behind English 'revere' and 'reverence'.

senses.note: Also embarrassment or shyness. Che vergogna! = how shameful! Vergognarsi = to be ashamed/embarrassed.

etymology: From vergogna + -are.

senses.note: Today almost always reflexive: vergognarsi = to be ashamed (Mi vergogno).

fact.text: The imperative Vergognati! is the everyday Italian way to say 'Shame on you!'

senses.note: vergognarsi di = to be ashamed of. It can also mean 'to feel shy or embarrassed'.

etymology: From vergogna + -oso.

senses.note: When it describes a person it can mean shy or bashful instead.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vēritātem, in this form probably a semi-learned term which was altered based on the Latin etymology. The older, now obsolete forms vertà, vertade, and vertate were inherited.

fact.text: Rome's Bocca della Verità, the 'Mouth of Truth', is an ancient stone mask. Legend says it bites off the hand of anyone who lies, a scene made famous by the film Roman Holiday.

senses.note: Invariable: la verità, le verità. Dire la verità = to tell the truth.

etymology: From Latin vermem, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis.

fact.text: Latin vermis and English worm come from the same Indo-European root. The pasta name vermicelli literally means little worms.

etymology: From Medieval Latin vernix, from Latin veronix, from Byzantine Greek βερενίκη, βερονίκη (bereníkē, beroníkē, “resin amber”), from Ancient Greek βερενίκιον, βερονίκιον (bereníkion, beroníkion, “soda”), from Βερενίκη (Bereníkē). Cognate with Piedmontese vernis/vërnis.

fact.text: English varnish shares its source: Greek beroníkē 'resin', which comes from the name Berenice.

senses.note: Also means varnish. 'Vernice fresca!' = 'Wet paint!'

etymology: Inherited from Latin vērus (“true”), from Proto-Italic *wēros, from a Proto-Indo-European *weh₁-ros, from *weh₁- (“true”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin verus, 'true', the root of English verify and very. Verdict also belongs here: it literally means 'truly said'.

senses.note: Added to the end of a sentence, ..., vero? means 'right?' or 'isn't it?'. È vero = it's true.

etymology: From Latin versāre (“to turn, to twist”).

senses.note: Also means to spill, to shed (tears), or to pay in or deposit money: versare soldi sul conto.

etymology: From Medieval Latin versiōnem.

fact.text: For Italian liceo students, 'la versione' brings to mind the dreaded Latin or Greek translation test. It is also a set exercise in the classical-school final exam.

senses.note: At school it also means a translation exercise from Latin or Greek.

etymology: From Latin versus (past participle of vertere). Cognate to French vers (“towards”).

fact.text: From Latin versus, 'turned', the same word that gives English versus and verse. As a noun, Italian verso can also mean a line of poetry.

senses.note: Also 'around' with times: verso le 11:30. Before a pronoun: verso di me.

etymology: From Late Latin verticālis.

senses.note: Same form for masculine and feminine; plural verticali.

etymology: From Latin vestīre.

fact.text: From Latin vestīre, 'to clothe', which is also the source of English vest, vestment and invest (originally 'to clothe in' an office or robe).

senses.note: To get dressed yourself is vestirsi (essere): mi vesto. Vestito = dress or suit.

fact.text: Comes from Latin vestis 'clothing', the same root as English 'vest', 'vestment' and 'invest' (originally 'to clothe' someone in office).

senses.note: Reflexive: mi vesto, ti vesti… Past: mi sono vestito/a.

etymology: From Latin vestītus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin vestitus, 'clothed', which is related to English 'vest', 'vestment' and 'invest', a word that first meant to dress someone in the robes of an office.

senses.note: Vestito da sera = evening dress. Abito is a more formal synonym.

etymology: From vetro + -ina.

senses.note: guardare le vetrine = to go window-shopping.

etymology: From Latin vitrum, from Proto-Italic *wedrom, from Proto-Indo-European *wedro- (“water-like”), derived from the root *wed- (“water”). Cognate with French verre, Portuguese vidro, Spanish vidrio.

fact.text: Never order 'un vetro' to drink from: a drinking glass is un bicchiere.

senses.note: The material; i vetri are often windowpanes. A drinking glass is un bicchiere.

etymology: See voi.

senses.note: Vi vedo domani = I'll see you (all) tomorrow. Also means 'yourselves'; in formal writing it can mean 'there'.

etymology: From Latin via.

fact.text: English 'via' (as in 'via London') is the same Latin word, meaning 'by way of'. In Italian, Via! on its own also means 'Go!' or 'Away!'.

senses.note: Used in addresses: abito in via Roma. Also 'way, route'.

etymology: Borrowed from Old French voyagier. By surface analysis, viaggio + -are.

fact.text: Shares its origin with English 'voyage'. Both go back to Latin viaticum, the provisions taken for a journey (from via, 'way').

senses.note: Takes avere: ho viaggiato molto = I've travelled a lot.

etymology:
Borrowed from Old Occitan viatge and Old French viage, veiage, from Latin viāticum, from the adjective viāticus, from via (“road, path”) + -āticus (“pertaining to”). By surface analysis, via + -aggio.
Doublet of viatico and cognate to Catalan viatge, French and English voyage, Spanish viaje, Portuguese viagem, Norman viage, Sicilian viaggiu, Maltese vjaġġ, Romanian voiaj.

fact.text: Shares its origin with English 'voyage': both come from Latin viaticum, 'supplies for a journey', from via, 'road'.

senses.note: Buon viaggio! = Have a good trip! Fare un viaggio = to take a trip.

etymology: From Latin vicem.

fact.text: Watch out: this never means 'vice' in the sense of a bad habit. In Italian that is vizio. Here it comes from Latin vice, 'in place of', the same root as English 'vicar'.

senses.note: Invariable: il/la vice, i/le vice. Mostly used as a prefix: vicepresidente, vicedirettore.

etymology: Ultimately from Latin vicis (“change, turn”).

fact.text: Comes from Latin vicis, 'turn, change', the root of English vicissitude and vice- in vice-president. That is why 'a vicenda' means 'in turn' or 'each other'.

senses.note: Often used for news stories or personal affairs: la vicenda giudiziaria. 'A vicenda' = in turn, each other.
In this sense usually plural: nelle vicinanze = nearby. Singular la vicinanza = closeness.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin vicinus 'neighbour', from vicus 'village, neighbourhood'. English vicinity comes from the same root, and il vicino also means 'the neighbour'.

senses.note: Usually followed by a: vicino alla stazione = near the station. Agrees: vicina, vicini, vicine.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin vicinus 'neighbour', from vicus 'village, neighbourhood'. English vicinity comes from the same root, and il vicino also means 'the neighbour'.

senses.note: Vicino a + noun = near (to). Also an adjective (near) and a noun (neighbour).

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus.

fact.text: Comes from Latin vicinus 'neighbour', from vicus 'village, neighbourhood'. English vicinity comes from the same root, and il vicino also means 'the neighbour'.

senses.note: Feminine: la vicina. As an adjective/adverb, vicino means near or close.

etymology: Borrowed from English video.

fact.text: In Latin, video means 'I see'. English built the word on the model of audio ('I hear'), and Italian then borrowed it back, even though in Italian 'I see' is vedo.

senses.note: Invariable: il video, i video.

etymology: From Latin vetāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin vetare, 'to forbid'. English veto is the same verb: in Latin it literally means 'I forbid'.

features.construction: vietare qualcosa a qualcuno; vietare di + infinitive

senses.note: Vietare a qualcuno di fare qualcosa. Common on signs: Vietato fumare (no smoking).

etymology: Inherited from Latin vigilem.

fact.text: From Latin vigil, 'awake, watchful', the source of English vigil and vigilant. In ancient Rome the vigiles were the city's night watchmen and firefighters.

senses.note: Municipal police officer. Female: la vigile or vigilessa. I vigili del fuoco = firefighters.

etymology: From Latin vīlla (“country house”).

fact.text: Latin villa, 'country estate', gave English 'village' and also 'villain'. A villain was originally just a farmhand (Late Latin villanus) who worked on a villa.

senses.note: Ranges from a modest suburban house to a grand estate. It can also mean a public park (Villa Borghese).

etymology: From Old French village. Cognate with Piedmontese vilagi.

fact.text: Italian took this from Old French village, the same source as English 'village'. It goes back to Latin villa, a country house or estate, so 'villa' and 'village' are relatives.

senses.note: Also 'villaggio turistico' = holiday village/resort.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vincere, from Proto-Italic *winkō, from Proto-Indo-European *wi-n-k-, from *weyk- (“to overcome”) with a nasal infix.

fact.text: From Latin vincere 'to conquer', the source of English victory, invincible, vanquish and even convince (literally 'to conquer completely').

features.construction: vincere (qualcosa): vincere una partita, un premio

senses.note: Irregular: vinsi (past historic), vinto (past participle). Ho vinto = I won.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vīnum, from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wéyh₁nom, derived from *wéyh₁ō (“vine, wine”). Cognates include Albanian verë, Armenian գինի (gini) and Greek οίνος (oínos).

fact.text: Latin vinum was borrowed very early into the Germanic languages, which is where English wine comes from. Greek oinos goes back to the same ancient root.

senses.note: vino rosso / bianco = red / white wine

etymology: Borrowed from Latin viola.

fact.text: In Italian theatre, purple is traditionally considered bad luck, so actors avoid wearing it on stage.

senses.note: Invariable: una maglia viola, dei fiori viola.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin violentus.
Borrowed from Latin violentia.

senses.note: The plural violenze means acts of violence.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin virgula. Doublet of vergola, which was inherited.

fact.text: From Latin virgula, 'little twig', because the mark looks like a tiny stick. Italians also use it as the decimal separator.

senses.note: Also the decimal point: 3,5 is read 'tre virgola cinque'.

fact.text: A diminutive of virgola, 'comma', so it literally means 'little comma', much like the British 'inverted comma'. Virgola itself comes from Latin virgula, 'little rod'.

senses.note: Usually plural: tra virgolette = in quotes, also used like the English 'so-called'.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin vīrus.

fact.text: In Latin, virus meant 'poison', 'venom' or 'slimy liquid'. The modern biological sense only appeared in the late 19th century.

senses.note: Invariable: il virus, i virus.

etymology: From Latin vīsiōnem.

senses.note: Prendere visione di = to examine (formal). Film in prima visione = newly released film.

etymology: Deverbal from visitare (“to visit”) + -a.

fact.text: It also means a medical check-up. 'Visita medica' is a doctor's examination.

senses.note: 'In visita a' means 'visiting'. 'Fare visita a qualcuno' means 'to pay someone a visit'.

etymology: From Latin vīsitāre (“to see, to visit”), frequentative of visō.

senses.note: Also used for a doctor examining a patient: il medico mi ha visitato.

etymology: Inherited from Latin vīsus.

fact.text: From Latin visus (sight, appearance), from the same root as 'vision'. English 'visage' comes from the same word by way of French.

senses.note: Synonyms: faccia (everyday), volto (literary).

etymology: Deverbal formed with the feminine past participle of vedere (“to see”).

fact.text: English 'vista' (a fine view) was borrowed from this Italian word. It is the feminine past participle of vedere, 'to see', so it literally means 'seen'.

senses.note: Also 'sight, eyesight': fuori dalla mia vista = out of my sight; a prima vista = at first sight.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vīsitus, from Latin vīsus, or from a form *vīditus.

fact.text: Literally 'seen', the past participle of vedere. A visa is a document an official has 'seen' and approved. English visa comes from Latin charta visa, 'paper that has been seen'.

senses.note: Also the past participle of vedere (seen).

etymology: From Latin vīta, from Proto-Italic *gʷītā, possibly a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wo-teh₂, from the root *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”).

fact.text: It comes straight from Latin vita, which also gave English vital, vitality and vitamin. A CV is a curriculum vitae, Latin for 'course of life'.

senses.note: Also means 'waist' (e.g. 'vita alta' = high-waisted). Plural 'vite' also matches 'la vite' (vine, screw).

etymology: From Latin vitellus. Compare Romanian vițel, French veau, Catalan vedella .

fact.text: English veal comes from the same Latin vitellus, by way of Old French veel. One ancient theory even derives the name Italia from an Oscan word meaning 'land of calves'.

senses.note: A young cow. Plural vitelli.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin victima.

fact.text: The grammatical gender is always feminine, even for a man: 'Marco è la vittima'. Latin victima first meant an animal offered as a sacrifice.

senses.note: Always feminine, even for a man: lui è la vittima.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin victōria, from vincere.
From Latin vīvere, from Proto-Italic *gʷīwō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷíh₃weti (“to live, be alive”).

fact.text: From Latin vivere 'to live', the root behind English vivid, revive, survive and vivacious. The shout 'Viva!' means 'long live!'.

senses.note: Intransitive takes avere or essere (ha/è vissuto a Roma). Transitive takes avere only.

etymology: From Latin vīvus (“alive”, “living”), from Proto-Italic *gʷīwos, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”).

fact.text: Dal vivo means 'live', as in a live concert. Farsi vivo means to get in touch, so 'Fatti vivo!' is a friendly 'Keep in touch!'

senses.note: Opposite of morto. Endings: vivo, viva, vivi, vive.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vōcālis (“speaking, sounding”). By surface analysis, voc(e) (“voice”) + -ale (“-al”, adjective-forming derivational suffix).

fact.text: English vowel and vocal come from the same Latin word, vocalis, meaning 'sounding' or 'having a voice' (from vox, voice). A vowel is literally a 'voiced' letter.

senses.note: Corde vocali = vocal cords. Messaggio vocale = voice message. As a noun, la vocale = vowel.

etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin vōcālis (“vowel”).

fact.text: English vowel and vocal come from the same Latin word, vocalis, meaning 'sounding' or 'having a voice' (from vox, voice). A vowel is literally a 'voiced' letter.

senses.note: Feminine: la vocale. The masculine il vocale is a voice message (short for messaggio vocale).

etymology: Inherited from Latin vōx, vōcem.

fact.text: From Latin vox, vocis, which also gave English voice, vocal and vowel. It goes back to an ancient Indo-European root meaning 'to speak'.

senses.note: Ad alta voce = aloud; a bassa voce = quietly; abbassa la voce = lower your voice.

etymology: From Latin volō through a Vulgar Latin root *volia, or from voglio. Cf. also Romanian voie from root *volia

fact.text: Also means 'birthmark'. An old folk belief held that a pregnant woman's unsatisfied cravings would leave a mark on her baby.

senses.note: Avere voglia di + infinitive = to feel like. Non ne ho voglia = I don't feel like it.

etymology:
From Latin vōs, from Old Latin vōs, from Proto-Italic *wōs, ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *yúHs.
Cognates with the same usage are the French vous and the Russian вы (vy).

senses.note: Plural 'you' (y'all). In parts of the South, Voi is also a polite form for one person.

ignored: An unadapted French interjection that is the same in English; ecco is the Italian word to learn.

senses.note: A French borrowing; the everyday Italian equivalent is ecco.

etymology: Inherited from Latin volāre, from Proto-Italic *gʷelāō.

fact.text: 'Volare' is the famous refrain of Domenico Modugno's 'Nel blu, dipinto di blu', which won Sanremo in 1958 and became a worldwide hit.

senses.note: Takes avere for the activity (ho volato) and essere with a destination or 'via' (è volato via). Also: time flies.

etymology: From Old French volentiers, from Latin voluntāriē, from the adjective voluntārius.

fact.text: Italian borrowed this from Old French volentiers, which is why it ends in -ieri instead of an Italian adverb ending. Modern French still says volontiers. It goes back to Latin voluntarius (willing).

senses.note: On its own, Volentieri! is a warm way to accept an offer: I'd love to! / With pleasure!

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin volēre, regularized from Latin velle.

fact.text: Classical Latin had the irregular velle. Everyday speakers made it regular as volēre, which became Italian volere.

senses.note: Vorrei (= I would like) is the polite way to ask for things. As a modal it often takes the auxiliary of the next verb.

etymology: Borrowed from Latin vulgārem.

fact.text: Latin vulgus meant 'the common people'. Dante's treatise De vulgari eloquentia defended writing in the volgare, the everyday language, rather than in Latin.

senses.note: Also 'vernacular': il volgare = the early Italian vernacular, as opposed to Latin.

etymology: From volare (“to fly”).

fact.text: 'Capire al volo', literally 'to understand in flight', means to catch on instantly. 'Prendere al volo' means to grab something on the fly, like a chance.

senses.note: Both a bird's flight and a plane trip: 'un volo per Roma'.

etymology: Inherited from Latin voluntātem.

fact.text: From Latin voluntas 'will', which also gave English voluntary and volunteer. A volunteer is someone acting of their own will.

senses.note: Invariable plural. Forza di volontà = willpower. Ultime volontà = last wishes. The legal document is il testamento.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volta, from *volŭta (perhaps via *volvita (“a turn”)), from Latin volūta, feminine of volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō. Also possibly from the past participle of volgere (volto), or from the verb voltare. Compare Spanish vuelta; cf. also Spanish bóveda, French voûte. Cognate with Sicilian vota.

fact.text: Traces back to Latin volvere 'to roll, turn', the root of English revolve. A 'time' is literally a turn. The same word also means a vault, like the Sistine Chapel ceiling.

senses.note: una volta = once; due volte = twice; a volte = sometimes; c'era una volta = once upon a time

etymology: From Latin vultus (“expression, face”). Compare Portuguese vulto (“aspect”).

senses.note: More formal or literary than 'faccia'. Don't confuse it with 'volto', the past participle of volgere.

etymology: From Latin vomitāre.

fact.text: Comes from Latin vomitare, from vomere 'to spew out'. The vomitoria of Roman amphitheatres were exits that 'spewed out' the crowds, not rooms for being sick.

senses.note: Figuratively 'to spew' insults. Ho vomitato = I threw up.
Agrees with what is owned: vostro/vostra/vostri/vostre. Usually takes an article: il vostro.

etymology: Derived from Latin vōtum, from voveō. Compare Spanish and Portuguese votar, French vouer.

fact.text: English 'vote' and 'vow' both come from Latin votum, a solemn promise to the gods. Italian votare still keeps both meanings, 'to vote' and 'to vow'.

senses.note: Votare per / contro qualcuno = to vote for / against someone. Il voto also means a school grade.

etymology: From Latin vōtum.

fact.text: English vote and vow both come from Latin votum, 'a solemn promise' (vow arrived via Old French). Italian kept both meanings in a single word.

senses.note: Also very common for a school mark/grade (prendere un bel voto) and for a vow.

etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vocitum.

fact.text: English void comes from the same Vulgar Latin source, *vocitus, by way of Old French vuide. So something vuoto is literally void.

senses.note: Forms: vuoto/vuota/vuoti/vuote. As a noun, il vuoto = the void, empty space.

etymology: Borrowed from French water, and this a pseudo-anglicism, derived from an ellipsis of French water-closet.

fact.text: False friend: il water is the toilet, not water! It is short for 'water closet', and Italians often say it as 'vater'. To ask for water, say acqua.

senses.note: Invariable: il water, i water. Often pronounced 'vater'. Water to drink is acqua.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English weekend.

senses.note: Invariable: i weekend. The native Italian equivalent is il fine settimana.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from English west.

senses.note: Usually capitalised, as in il selvaggio West (the Wild West). Far West is also common.

ignored: An English interjection borrowed unchanged, so there is nothing to translate.

senses.note: English interjection used unchanged in Italian.

etymology: Unadapted borrowing from Ottoman Turkish یوغورت (yoğurt).

fact.text: Comes from Turkish yoğurt. The word is usually linked to yoğurmak, 'to knead', or yoğun, 'thick, dense'.

senses.note: Takes lo (lo yogurt) and doesn't change in the plural: due yogurt.

etymology: Possibly from Latin sabaia (“Illyrian barley beer”, from an Illyrian word probably from Proto-Indo-European *sab- (“taste”)) + -one (augmentative suffix).

fact.text: The origin is uncertain. One theory traces it to Latin sabaia, a barley beer drunk by the Illyrians, plus the augmentative ending -one.

senses.note: Made by whisking egg yolks, sugar and Marsala wine. English calls it zabaglione.

etymology: From Lombardic zeina (“basket”). Doublet of zana (“basket”).

fact.text: A gift from the Lombards, a Germanic people who ruled much of Italy in the early Middle Ages. In their language it meant 'basket'.

senses.note: Takes lo because it starts with z: lo zaino, gli zaini.

etymology: Borrowed from Arabic سِكَّة (sikka, “die for coining, coin”).

fact.text: From Arabic sikka 'coin die'. Venice's gold coin minted there, the zecchino, gave English 'sequin', first meaning the coin and later a small shiny disc.

senses.note: nuovo di zecca = brand new. Also means 'tick' (the parasite).
Mostly used in the fixed phrase pieno zeppo (packed full). Zeppo di = crammed with.

etymology: Derived from New Latin zerum, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “nothing”, “cipher”). Doublet of cifra.

fact.text: From Arabic ṣifr, 'nothing', via Medieval Latin zephirum. The same Arabic word also gave Italian cifra (digit) and English 'cipher'.

senses.note: Takes 'lo': lo zero, gli zeri. In football scores: due a zero = two-nil.

etymology: Derived from New Latin zerum, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr, “nothing”, “cipher”). Doublet of cifra.

fact.text: From Arabic ṣifr, 'nothing', via Medieval Latin zephirum. The same Arabic word also gave Italian cifra (digit) and English 'cipher'.

etymology: From Late Latin thia, from Ancient Greek θεία (theía).

fact.text: Came into Italian from Greek, not native Latin: Greek theia, aunt, became Late Latin thia. Spanish tía has the same origin.

senses.note: Masculine: zio (uncle). Gli zii can mean aunt and uncle together.
Plural of zio. Gli zii can mean uncles only, or a mixed group: i miei zii = my aunt and uncle.

etymology: Inherited from Late Latin thius, from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos). Compare Spanish tío, Portuguese tio, Sicilian ziu, Sardinian tiu or tziu, Venetan sio.

fact.text: Borrowed through Late Latin from Greek theios, 'uncle', like Spanish tío. English 'uncle' instead comes from Latin avunculus, through French oncle.

senses.note: Takes lo: lo zio, mio zio. The feminine is zia (aunt). In slang it can also mean 'dude'.

etymology: Onomatopoeic. Compare Sicilian zittu and zittìrisi.

fact.text: Måneskin won Sanremo and then Eurovision in 2021 with 'Zitti e buoni', roughly 'Shut up and behave', a phrase Italian parents say to noisy children.

senses.note: Sta' zitto! / Zitto! = Shut up! Agrees with the person: zitta, zitti, zitte.

etymology: From Latin zōna.

fact.text: Comes via Latin from Greek zōnē, meaning 'belt' or 'girdle'. The Earth's climate zones were pictured as belts wrapped around the globe.

senses.note: Very common for a local area: nella mia zona = around where I live.

etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *ḱorkeh₂
Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćárkaraH
Proto-Indo-Aryan *śárkaraH
Sanskrit शर्क॑रा (śárkarā)
Gandhari 𐨭𐨐𐨪 (śakara)bor.
Middle Persian 𐭱𐭪𐭥 (šakar)bor.
Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar)bor.
Italian zucchero
Borrowed from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), borrowed from Middle Persian 𐭱𐭪𐭥 (šakar), borrowed from Gandhari 𐨭𐨐𐨪 (śakara), from Sanskrit शर्क॑रा (śárkarā), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *śárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorkeh₂ (“gravel”).

fact.text: It came via Arabic sukkar and Persian from Sanskrit śárkarā, meaning 'gravel' or 'grit'. English 'sugar' and 'saccharin' share this root.

senses.note: Uses 'lo' because it starts with z: lo zucchero.

etymology: From Late Latin suppa, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *supô, *suppa (“slice of soaked bread; soup”) (whence English soup).

fact.text: It comes from a Germanic word for bread soaked in broth, which is also the source of English soup and sop. That is why zuppa inglese is a dessert of soaked sponge cake.

senses.note: Usually a thick soup, often served over bread. Compare minestra (lighter soup).
